person/jeffrey-kushin.text:
Jeffrey Kushin is a consultant and market analyst at CPM Group, the New York-based commodities research and consulting firm founded by Jeffrey Christian that has made precious metals its specialty. He works across the firm's research, consulting, and commentary on gold, silver, platinum, and palladium, and fronts CPM's video outlooks, where he translates the firm's supply-demand modeling into price forecasts ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)). Coverage here is thin — a single appearance in this corpus — so the portrait rests almost entirely on one outing.

That outing, a June 16, 2026 market update, shows a analyst who argues in ranges and time windows rather than slogans. On gold, he called for a "volatile sideways consolidation between now and September" with roughly $4,000 on the low end ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)), and said CPM expected the $4,100 level to be tested again over the following two and a half months, adding that "it may well hold" with further support at $3,800 and below ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)). Silver got the same structure but a more constructive ending: a "very wide range" of $60 to $90 for the next two and a half to three months, "and then higher prices in the final four months of this year" ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)).

The interesting part of the video is the split within precious metals. Platinum he treated bearishly, expecting a $1,600 to $2,000 trade over the next couple of months with a downside skew "because there's greater bearishness" in that market ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)), and palladium likewise as trading sideways "with a downward bend" as bullishness that emerged the prior June continued to bleed out ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)). Underneath the near-term chop, though, his framework is unabashedly fundamentalist: he leaned on CPM's long record, noting that when gold fell to $1,211 in 2014, "we said buy. We were a few years early," with the price having risen since on the firm's supply-demand analysis ([Gold And Silver Market Update: How Low Before Buyers Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)). The candor about being early is telling — this is a shop that would rather be directionally right on fundamentals than tactically punctual.

Because everything on record comes from this one appearance, there is no observable evolution in Kushin's views — the bullish and bearish tags reflect different metals within a single outlook, not a shift over time. Whether he bends more hawkish or dovish on gold as the September window he flagged approaches is, for now, unanswered.

person/jim-zelter.text:
Jim Zelter is one of the most powerful figures in American credit markets, and his résumé explains why. He cut his teeth at Citigroup in high-yield sales and trading and proprietary trading before joining Apollo Global Management in 2006, where he built the firm's capital markets business and helped turn Apollo into a credit powerhouse. He was elevated to Co-President in 2018 alongside Scott Kleinman, and in early 2025 he became sole President of Apollo and joined its board — a move widely read as positioning him as a potential successor to CEO Marc Rowan. He holds an undergraduate degree from Duke and an MBA from Wharton. In short, when Zelter talks about credit, he is speaking about a market he has spent two decades shaping from the inside.

For all that standing, his footprint in this corpus is thin: a single guest appearance on Eurodollar University, and no bullish or bearish calls on record — only one neutral stance. On the topic of credit, private credit and BDCs, his logged comment came on June 23, 2026, when he struck a measured tone on private credit default rates, allowing for "maybe even a little bit of an increase" ([Private Credit Default Rates Just Hit The Point Of No Return](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SibAV9HRe1I)) — a notably muted take on a debate that often skews apocalyptic. With one appearance and one data point, there is no observable arc in his views yet; this page should be revisited if he surfaces again.

person/joseph.text:
Joseph Wang — known across the macro world as "Fed Guy" — is one of the few commentators on the Federal Reserve beat who has actually operated the machinery he now dissects. A former senior trader on the Markets Desk at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, he helped execute Treasury and QE operations before distilling that experience into *Central Banking 101* (2021) and the Fed Guy blog and newsletter, where he writes on Fed policy, reserves, liquidity, and money markets. He appears regularly as a guest on macro-finance podcasts and hosts his own recurring commentary, including a "Markets Weekly" format.

The record in this corpus is small but strikingly lopsided: of eighteen coded stances, eleven are bearish, three bullish, and four neutral — and they all cluster inside a single week in June 2026. That week deserves to be taken at face value, because it catches him at his most emphatic. On the [June 2026 FOMC Debrief](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Njd_JuRuEcI) he argued the evidence points to "a sustained and meaningful decline in risk assets." Three days later, on [Markets Weekly June 20, 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fI3fVnAqi80), he supplied the mechanism: spot Brent had "absolutely plummeted" after the Iran ceasefire, and he read that collapse as a "large disinflationary wave" washing over markets — bearish oil, and by extension bearish the risk complex that had been riding it.

What stands out is that his bearishness runs deeper than an oil trade. On the same June 20 episode he framed the tariff-fragmentation story end to end: Euroland weighing its own tariff wall, German export decline already weighing on growth, and China "moving up the value chain and threatening a wider range of industries in the West" while managing a currency that, by some estimates, is kept structurally undervalued ([Markets Weekly June 20, 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fI3fVnAqi80)). Notably, he coded the Chinese industrial ascent as bullish in its own right — the threat to the West is the flip side of the same observation, and he didn't blur the two.

The nuance matters, though, because he was not uniformly gloomy. He judged the Iran ceasefire "probably going to hold," and on rates he was neutral, flagging exactly the kind of market-versus-narrative gap his desk background primes him to spot: markets were "still pricing in an ongoing mini rate hiking cycle" even as oil slumped ([Markets Weekly June 20, 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fI3fVnAqi80)). The honest caveat is that the coverage here amounts to one interview appearance and one solo Markets Weekly, both in mid-June 2026 — a snapshot, not an arc. It shows a clearly bearish posture with a coherent structural argument behind it; whether that posture is durable or week-specific is something this record cannot yet answer.

person/joseph-wang.text:
Joseph Wang is a financial markets commentator better known by his handle "Fed Guy," the pen behind FedGuy.com, a newsletter and research platform devoted to Federal Reserve policy, market liquidity, and the plumbing of the financial system. His authority on that plumbing is autobiographical: he served as a senior trader on the Open Markets Desk at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, executing Treasuries, agency MBS, and repo to implement monetary policy, and he codified that experience in the 2021 book *Central Banking 101*. Since leaving the desk he has worked as chief investment officer at Monetary Macro, a macro-focused investment firm, and become a fixture on macro podcasts covering Fed operations, quantitative easing, money markets, and dollar liquidity.

The record in this corpus compresses into a single consequential week in June 2026, but it shows a trader's reflexes rather than a pundit's hedging. On the June 2026 FOMC debrief, Wang laid out a rates view with unusual directness: "my base case is that we just hold rates throughout this year," no hikes in 2026. He argued the Fed had already accomplished tightening without moving — "he didn't have to actually hike... tighten financial conditions and raise rates just by his communication" — and that falling energy prices would hand policymakers a disinflationary tailwind. The same day he delivered his sharpest call: the pieces, in his reading, pointed to "a sustained and meaningful decline in risk assets."

Three days later on his Markets Weekly of June 20, 2026, he doubled down on the energy half of that thesis — spot Brent had "absolutely plummeted," a large disinflationary wave — while flagging that markets were still pricing a mini rate hiking cycle, a gap between tape and his base case he was candid about. His geopolitical read was more layered than the headline bearishness suggests: he judged "this is a ceasefire that is probably going to hold" after the Iran war, and even found a constructive thread in China "moving up the value chain and threatening a wider range of industries in the West." The broader trade-war picture, though, stayed grim on his telling — Euroland weighing its own tariff wall, German exports in decline, and a structurally undervalued Chinese currency distorting the landscape.

The stance tally across the digest runs 13 bearish against 3 bullish and 6 neutral, and the lean is real: Wang spent this week arguing that disinflation from collapsing oil, a Fed on hold, and fragmenting global trade point down for risk assets even as he saw the Middle East ceasefire holding. One honest caveat for readers: with coverage spanning only June 17–20, 2026, there is no long arc to chart — no evidence here of a flip from prior conviction, just a coherent and decidedly defensive snapshot from an ex-desk trader who treats Fed communication itself as a policy instrument.

person/maggie-lake.text:
Maggie Lake is a financial journalist and media entrepreneur rather than a market caller, and that distinction shapes everything about how she shows up in this corpus. She spent roughly two decades at CNN as a business anchor and correspondent in New York, covering global markets, the economy, and corporate news, and hosting programs including "Marketplace Africa." She left CNN in 2022 and moved into independent financial media, launching the "Maggie Lake: Talking Markets" newsletter and podcast, where she interviews investors, economists, and market practitioners about macroeconomics and investing. She has also been associated with Real Vision as a host and interviewer, and her signature is accessible, jargon-free breakdowns of macro and market themes aimed at a general audience rather than at specialists.

On the record collected here, she appears exactly once, as an interview guest, and carries no classified market stances at all — zero bullish, zero bearish, zero neutral — with no dated calls or position shifts to trace. That is not a hedge or an evasion on her part; it reflects her actual role in the debate. Lake is a translator and convener, the person who gets practitioners to explain their views clearly, not someone staking her own directional claims on gold, equities, or rates. Readers looking for her strongest calls with dates will not find them in this corpus, and the honest portrait is that her contribution runs through the quality of the conversations she hosts rather than through positions she has taken. The timeline section, in short, is thin by nature of the subject, not by neglect.

person/max-sweaty.text:
Max Sweaty is a figure of thin record in this corpus: he appears exactly once, as an interview guest on The Monetary Matters Network, and that single appearance is the full extent of his documented footprint here. No transcript excerpts, quotes, or named positions were extracted from the conversation, so what he argued for on that show — if he argued for anything at all — is not preserved in the source material underpinning this page.

The classification record is likewise empty: no bullish, bearish, or neutral stances were assigned to him across any topic, and there is no topic timeline to speak of. As a result, this page cannot chart any evolution in his views, name any signature calls, or place him within a broader debate. Readers should treat the absence of detail here as a statement about coverage, not a statement about the person; building out a substantive portrait of Max Sweaty would require either a fuller transcript of his Monetary Matters appearance or additional appearances not currently captured in the corpus.

person/max-wiethe.text:
Max Wiethe is a financial media host, producer, and markets commentator best known for his run at Real Vision, where he hosted and produced programs including The Daily Briefing and various trade-focused segments. His craft is the interview: he regularly sits down with traders, investors, and strategists, and has built his reputation on making markets and investment ideas legible to a retail audience. More recently he has appeared under The Monetary Matters Network banner, continuing the same format-driven approach.

As for his own views, the record in this corpus is thin — two logged appearances, both coded neutral, with no bullish or bearish calls on file. But the substance of his one dated appearance is more interesting than the neutral tag suggests. On June 24, 2026, in an episode framed around how Substack and FinTwit's top researchers actually invest ([The Secret to Investing Like Substack & FinTwit's Top Resea…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IHFVBrwt54s)), Wiethe's sharpest on-record observation was about index mechanics rather than direction: the S&P 500, in his words, is a "slow-moving beast" — it isn't over-weighting Nvidia at the beginning of the run, it's over-weighting Nvidia "once it's already" happened ([The Secret to Investing Like Substack & FinTwit's Top Resea…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IHFVBrwt54s)). It's a tidy distillation of how cap-weighted passive exposure works: the index only concentrates in winners after they've already won, which is precisely the tension anyone trying to beat or supplement the index has to reckon with.

That framing tells you something about Wiethe's role in the debate. He is closer to an analyst-broadcaster than a tipster — the person surfacing how other people's theses work, in this case the independent research crowd, rather than planting his own flag on AI, semiconductors, or the broad market. If his views have migrated over time, the corpus doesn't show it: everything on file sits on a single date, and both stances land on neutral. Treat him, for now, as a well-sourced curator of other investors' ideas whose own directional calls remain an open question.

person/mike-alfred.text:
Mike Alfred is an American fintech entrepreneur who has spent his career turning financial data into businesses, and who has since recast himself as a professional Bitcoin investor and mining-sector commentator. With his brother Ryan he co-founded BrightScope, the retirement-plan ratings company acquired in 2016, and later co-founded Digital Assets Data, a crypto market-intelligence firm whose platform was bought by Coinbase — after which Alfred took a market intelligence role inside the exchange. Today he is best known in markets circles as a relentless presence on X covering Bitcoin and the publicly traded miners, and as a board member of Bitcoin miner Iris Energy (IREN), the company at the heart of his public investing identity. He is a self-described long-term Bitcoin holder, and nearly everything in this record comes from a single June 2026 appearance on Real Vision, an episode pointedly titled "The Hidden AI Trade: Land, Power, & Compute" ([The Hidden AI Trade: Land, Power, & Compute | With Mike Alf…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-p3DhlY2TEk)).

The thesis he laid out there is coherent and blunt. AI has been the only game in town — "the only thing that that has benefited over the last 3 years in mass is AI," with the S&P 500 carried by its largest, most-exposed companies — and the binding constraint on the trade is not chips but electricity: whether you "can spin up heavy-duty infrastructure… that you can keep online and you can run it at low price" ([The Hidden AI Trade: Land, Power, & Compute | With Mike Alf…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-p3DhlY2TEk)). That is the "hidden" leg of his argument: land, power and compute, with Bitcoin miners that already control cheap power positioned to pivot into AI workloads. His conviction is explicitly long-horizon — "over 5, 10, 15 years, I think there's still quite a bit of opportunity here because the market largely still doesn't understand these economic mo[ats]" — and he thinks it would be "a mistake in my opinion" to get too cautious about the theme "unless you really have to manage for like very short-term drawdowns and short-term performance" ([The Hidden AI Trade: Land, Power, & Compute | With Mike Alf…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-p3DhlY2TEk)).

On his own positioning, Alfred is unusually tidy. Bitcoin is "really the only position that I've sort of publicly espoused over that period," he says, describing it as a straight long holding ([The Hidden AI Trade: Land, Power, & Compute | With Mike Alf…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-p3DhlY2TEk)). On IREN the record is formally tagged "neutral," but that label does a lot of diplomatic work: as a director he says "I'm on the board, so I can't… give you advice to buy it," while volunteering that he's "never sold a share of Iron, even though it's gone from 28 to 1 to 75 to 28 to to 60," that "it's unlikely I'd be selling anything," and that his personal bet is "if Iron could pull this off at scale, it'll be very hard to compete with them" — the transcript's "Iron" being IREN itself ([The Hidden AI Trade: Land, Power, & Compute | With Mike Alf…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-p3DhlY2TEk)). The neutrality, in other words, is a governance constraint, not a hesitation.

A caveat about the record itself: this corpus contains one appearance, on one day — twelve bullish stances, two neutral, zero bearish, all from the same interview. There is no timeline to trace, no pivot from skeptic to believer or back; what we can say is that as of June 2026 Alfred arrived with a fully formed power-and-compute thesis and a documented habit of holding IREN through a violent round trip. His consistency is asserted rather than observed here, and anyone citing his track record from this material is really citing one confident hour of television.

person/patrick-boyle.text:
Patrick Boyle is an Irish-born finance professional who has worn most of the hats the industry has to offer: derivatives trader at London investment banks, founder and manager of a volatility-focused hedge fund (the Palomar Fund), and lecturer in finance at King's College London and Queen Mary University of London. He has also written several books on quantitative finance, including *Trading and Pricing Financial Derivatives* and *Financial Derivatives: A Quantitative Finance View*. But his public profile rests mainly on his eponymous YouTube channel, where he delivers dry, frequently sardonic commentary on markets, economics, and business news — the persona of a practitioner who has seen the machinery up close and is unimpressed by the sales pitch.

The stance record captured here is unusually thin, and it should be read with that caveat: every position tagged to Boyle — four bearish, one bullish — comes from a single video, "How to Lose a Global AI Monopoly in One Afternoon," published June 20, 2026. That said, the argument in it is a coherent and pointed one. Boyle's core bearish case is that American AI leadership is being squandered by its own export-control regime. "If AI is not a natural monopoly, and foreign competitors are offering models that are good enough, immune to US kill switches, and 60 times cheaper," the US edge evaporates ([How to Lose a Global AI Monopoly in One Afternoon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0RxMj0L0-fY)). His sharpest line lands on the market implications: "When your target market shrinks from the entire global economy to people who have passed a background check in Washington, your near trillion-dollar…" — the truncation is the digest's, but the direction is unmistakable ([How to Lose a Global AI Monopoly in One Afternoon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0RxMj0L0-fY)).

The flip side of that trade is his one bullish stance, on Chinese AI. Because models from Chinese firms like Jipu and DeepSeek are open-source and self-hostable — "companies can run on their own servers" — he sees them as the natural beneficiaries of foreign buyers who want capability without Washington's leverage ([How to Lose a Global AI Monopoly in One Afternoon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0RxMj0L0-fY)). Worth flagging for the reader: the bearish tags on broad market indices and on rates, bonds, and the dollar all trace back to the same Washington quote, so this is really one integrated argument about US AI dominance rather than four independent calls. There is no earlier positioning in the record to chart — no observable evolution from bull to bear or the reverse — so any claim about how Boyle's views have "moved over time" would be invention. What the record does show is a commentator whose instinct, at least on this occasion, runs against the consensus that AI is a durable American franchise.

person/patrick-ceresna.text:
Patrick Ceresna is a Canadian market strategist and technical analyst who co-founded MacroVoices Media and serves as its Chief Market Strategist — best known as the voice of the weekly "MacroVoices Market Snapshot," where he walks through charts across equities, rates, currencies and commodities, then translates the read into an options structure (a bull call spread, typically) for traders who want the thesis in tradable form. He holds CMT, CIM and DMS designations and has roughly two decades in capital markets. The tally of his catalogued stances — 16 bullish, 7 bearish, 84 neutral — is the most honest description of his method: he's a levels analyst, not a permabull or a doomsayer, someone who spends most weeks marking time and reserves conviction for confirmed inflections.

The mid-2026 record shows that discipline in motion. When the Iranian peace deal triggered a violent repricing around June 18, 2026, he read the crude collapse — from $90 to the $73 handle, close to a 20% drop — as the notable move and leaned bearish on the breakdown ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There’s No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)). Yet in the same week's Trade of the Week he made his cleanest directional call of the summer: oil would settle back above $80 and "maybe even as high as 90" ([Trade of The Week - MacroVoices #537](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqHNNzR9WNc)). By August 13 that call was working — he argued that with the $80 level beaten, crude had every reason to hold the 80-plus area ([Trading Desk - August 13th 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c06eQWQljXo)) — and he went further, flatly rejecting the consensus that oil was too high: "so many people argue with great conviction that oil prices are probably even now too high... I just don't buy it" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)). He had also flagged the second-order trade early, pointing to knock-on opportunities in fertilizers, chemicals and crop inputs disrupted during the crisis ([Trade of The Week - MacroVoices #537](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqHNNzR9WNc)).

On equities he was constructive but precise about the margin of safety. He noted the S&P 500 rallying over 2% to 7,420 on the June 18 de-escalation ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There’s No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)), and by mid-August framed the upside mechanically: a break of the one-week range could take the index to 8,000 within a week, the bulls could easily absorb a 200-point pullback as a dip-buying opportunity ([Trading Desk - August 13th 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c06eQWQljXo)), and it would take roughly 400 S&P points of decline to do real technical damage ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)). But he kept pointing at the crack in the tape — the conspicuous lack of semiconductor participation in the August rally ([Trading Desk - August 13th 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c06eQWQljXo)) — and a week later said the laggards now "hinge on what Nvidia has to say" ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IRHWmEc1QAE)).

Gold is where his patience is most visible — and where his view actually moved. On June 18, even as gold pushed up 4.5% to 4,321 on the risk-off unwind, he refused the bull case: no bullish pivot in the trend yet, another gold bull market coming but lining up differently ([Trade of The Week - MacroVoices #537](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqHNNzR9WNc); [MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There’s No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s7IDIRbZa2o)). A week later, with gold down roughly another 900 basis points toward 4,000, he marked that handle as the line between stabilization and the next major leg down ([MacroVoices #538 Lyn Alden: Is The War Really Over and What…](https://www.macrovoices.com/1537-macrovoices-538-lyn-alden-is-the-war-really-over-and-what-s-next-for-markets)). By August 13, weighing Michael Howell's liquidity thesis, he had turned outright bullish — gold in dollar terms "just simply has to go up" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)) — with the same day's Trading Desk noting the correction may be approaching an inflection ([Trading Desk - August 13th 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c06eQWQljXo)). On rates and the dollar, he called yields near 4.70% a probable key high while cautioning it wasn't an immediate shorting opportunity, and marked the 160 level as "rock solid" overhead resistance where interventions had repeatedly occurred ([MacroVoices #537 Brent Johnson: There’s No Turning Back](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mX2NJ3nxQ)), even as he saw clear dollar strength and flows chasing US equity returns ([Trade of The Week - MacroVoices #537](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqHNNzR9WNc)). The through-line: a technician who names, out loud, the exact number that would change his mind — which is why the neutral column dwarfs everything else.

person/raoul-pal.text:
Raoul Pal is a British macro investor turned financial media entrepreneur, and one of the more prominent voices arguing that the coming decades belong to exponential technologies rather than the traditional economic playbook. His path runs through Goldman Sachs, where he co-managed the European hedge fund sales business in equities and equity derivatives, and GLG Partners, where he ran a global macro portfolio before stepping away from fund management in his early thirties. In 2005 he founded Global Macro Investor, an institutional macro research publication, and in 2014 he co-founded Real Vision, the subscription media company built around long-form investor interviews, where he served as CEO. His own show, *Raoul Pal The Journey Man*, is where his signature "Exponential Age" thesis — essentially a case for Bitcoin, crypto and AI as the dominant macro forces of the era — gets its fullest airing.

His strongest articulation of that thesis came on June 18, 2026, in an episode on AI, Bitcoin and self-sovereignty, where he argued that adoption by the financial system itself was "the thing that was required" for Bitcoin to become "the base of money for the whole system" ([AI, Bitcoin & Self-Sovereignty | Raoul Pal The Journey Man](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nCpeLLNxl-g)). He paired that with a deflationary scenario in which "super abundance" driven by AI makes Bitcoin "actually very important in a massively deflationary world," and made a notably bold structural claim about the AI buildout itself: an "inability for a lot of this infrastructure to go bust, which is a really interesting thing that we've not seen before" ([AI, Bitcoin & Self-Sovereignty | Raoul Pal The Journey Man](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nCpeLLNxl-g)). It is maximalist framing — the tech stack and the money of the next era, converging.

What's more interesting is how quickly the tone shifted. By August 13, 2026, Pal was noticeably more measured on crypto. Discussing the rise of stablecoins and the "small but growing" RWA bucket, he framed the next phase as infrastructure adoption rather than price euphoria ([Why The Next Phase of Crypto Is Bigger Than You Think](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q2TAHZIBpdE)) — and, candidly, conceded that the market "has taken... for getting overexcited earlier," adding that "it'd be nice to get a bit of liquidity back in crypto" ([Why The Next Phase of Crypto Is Bigger Than You Think](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q2TAHZIBpdE)). His macro ledger matched that caution: excess liquidity — liquidity growth above GDP growth — "hasn't been very strong," which in his framework explains why fresh liquidity hasn't flowed through to risk assets ([Why The Next Phase of Crypto Is Bigger Than You Think](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q2TAHZIBpdE)).

The through-line, then, isn't a conversion — nothing in the record shows Pal turning bearish on crypto, and his structural conviction in the Exponential Age is intact. It's a refinement: from Bitcoin-as-money in June to stablecoins, tokenized assets and plumbing in August, with an explicit admission of prior froth and a liquidity-sensitive, near-term neutral stance on markets. Readers should note the corpus here is thin — a handful of dated quotes across two 2026 episodes — so this portrait captures the arc of a single summer rather than the full history of a two-decade public career.

person/raoul-pal-palvatar-ai-avatar.text:
Raoul Pal is a British former hedge fund manager turned macro commentator, and in the past decade one of the most recognizable faces in financial media. He cut his teeth at Goldman Sachs, co-managing the hedge fund sales business in European equities and equity derivatives, then co-managed the GLG Global Macro Fund before retiring from fund management in his mid-30s. Rather than disappearing, he built a second act as a publisher: he founded Global Macro Investor (GMI), a subscription macro research service, and in 2014 co-founded Real Vision, the financial media and education company where he serves as CEO. He hosts the podcast "The Journeyman," is widely known on social media as @RaoulGMI, works largely out of the Cayman Islands, and has spoken openly about his multiple sclerosis diagnosis.

Intellectually, Pal is best understood as a big-picture pessimist about the existing system who converted that pessimism into an aggressive bull case for crypto. His core material is debt cycles, demographics, and what he calls the "Exponential Age" and the "Everything Code" — theses he has popularized arguing that technology-driven compounding is reshaping economies faster than legacy institutions can adapt. That framework made him one of the loudest institutional-finance voices championing Bitcoin, Ethereum, and the broader crypto asset class, a position that defines much of his public profile. "Palvatar," for the record, is an AI-generated avatar of Pal used in Real Vision and related content — a fitting accessory for a man whose brand is built on the exponential thesis.

On the evidentiary record in this corpus, however, Pal's footprint is thin: he appears as a guest on his own show ("Raoul Pal The Journeyman") with a single documented appearance, no tagged bullish, bearish, or neutral stances, and no dated topic timelines. That means the digest offers nothing yet on how his calls may have shifted over time, and no specific market positions can be cited with confidence from this material. Readers should treat the portrait above as biographical context; the dated, citation-backed calls — the substance of a market track record — remain to be captured.

person/shawn-hackett.text:
Shawn Hackett is an agricultural commodities strategist — president of Hackett Financial Advisors and a weather-cycle specialist of the look-at-the-dust-clouds-before-the-balance-sheet school — and in this corpus he appears exactly once, on Real Vision on June 14, 2026, in an episode pointedly titled "Why This El Niño Could Be Different." His pitch that day was that the looming El Niño carries "the implications for many so critical food supply items globally" and, beyond prices, "what it even might mean for governments and geopolitics" — food inflation framed as a macro and geopolitical force rather than a farm-gate curiosity ([Why This El Niño Could Be Different with Shawn Hackett & As…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gsteK2Vl5PA)).

His strongest call is a historical analog: in a comparable prior episode, he argued, "the average price for rice and wheat" rose "600% during that period of time" — a number deployed to suggest the move in grains and softs could be violent rather than gradual ([Why This El Niño Could Be Different with Shawn Hackett & As…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gsteK2Vl5PA)). Layered on top is a more idiosyncratic signal: "some of the highest concentrations of Arabian Peninsula sand in the atmosphere that we've seen since 2002," a dust-load reading his framework treats as a tell for what comes next. The record tags that dust observation as the lone bearish item in an otherwise bullish package — three bullish calls to one bearish, all from the same sitting, which says more about how he stacks evidence than about any hedging of the thesis ([Why This El Niño Could Be Different with Shawn Hackett & As…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gsteK2Vl5PA)).

The honest caveat is that this page currently rests on a single June 2026 conversation, so there is no timeline to trace — no earlier bearish turn or later capitulation, just one concentrated blast of El Niño-for-food-supply urgency. A "bullish China & Hong Kong equities" tag also shows up in the record, but it hangs off the same food-supply-and-geopolitics quote rather than any direct equity call, so treat it as thin until he shows up again ([Why This El Niño Could Be Different with Shawn Hackett & As…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gsteK2Vl5PA)). Whether rice and wheat did anything resembling a 600% run after his appearance, the digest doesn't say — and neither will we.

person/steve.text:
Steve Van Metre is a U.S.-based investment adviser and bond-market commentator whose YouTube channel picks apart the Treasury market, the dollar system, and Federal Reserve policy. He sits firmly in the "eurodollar" school built around Jeff Snider — the argument that global dollar liquidity conditions, not the Fed's policy lever alone, are what actually move markets — and he is a recurring guest on Eurodollar University and on podcasts hosted by Snider and Emil Kalinowski, with yield curves, Treasury issuance, money markets, and the macro cycle as his standing beats.

His signature position is a long-running bullish Treasury thesis, expressed most concretely in the widely followed "TLT trade": long call options on the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF, premised on long-term yields falling hard as recession and dollar-shortage dynamics play out. That trade is his worldview in a single position — a bond rally he expects not because policy succeeds, but because the system is breaking.

The interview record here is compressed into one month — three Eurodollar University appearances on June 14, 21, and 27, 2026 — so there is no documented drift in his views to chart over time; what it shows instead is a coherent, and heavily bearish, through-line: nine bearish and ten neutral marks against just two bullish. On June 14, in [Now That Iran Is Done, The Real Oil Crisis Begins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DTh7cPI8z3E), he ran a deliberately two-sided oil view: a supply shortfall he called "the big shoe to drop over the next couple of months" — the same episode carrying both of his bullish tags, on oil tightness and a China/Hong Kong equities mark — alongside a warning that India could be "without sufficient diesel for several weeks if not months further on." But the bearish half of the same conversation won: he doubted inflation would "just come right down" in the short term, and put the destination for crude at $50 a barrel — not from a supply flood, but "demand destruction, the coming rec[ession]."

A week later, on [Swiss Bond Market Just Gave A Dire Warning to the World](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c2LzapdRuT4), he pushed back directly on surface-level calm: "the shock is growing, it's real," against people who look around, see "spending's up, market's up," and conclude it can't be happening. Asked whether rates keep dropping and go negative, his answer was unqualified — "Absolutely. Will central bankers panic? Absolutely. Is it going to work? I don't think it's going to." Note how neatly that fits the TLT trade: falling yields as confirmation of a liquidity shock, not a policy victory.

By June 27, on [Bitcoin And BlackRock Just Did Something VERY Strange](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=biyCX7UYAfQ), he was mapping the mechanics of the bust: in a recession "they need dollars... they'll take them from anywhere they can get them"; when credit dries up "there's no money for payroll"; private credit has a "déjà vu" feel, with Q3 redemption projections "even higher than they are now" at the BlackRock/Blackstone/Blue Owl/Apollo end of the complex. Bitcoin's slide he reads as a liquidity tell — "nobody's going to gate you if you want to sell it," even if a MicroStrategy-scale seller would plunge the price, because no one closes the door. One honest caveat: a portrait built on a single month of tape can't establish trajectory. Within that month, though, man and trade align completely — the economy is what he's bearish on; the long bond is how he expresses it.

person/steve-van-metre.text:
Steve Van Metre is a Bakersfield, California-based financial advisor and portfolio manager who runs Van Metre & Co., a wealth-management and registered investment advisory firm, alongside a popular YouTube channel and podcast presence devoted to global macroeconomics. His signature framework is the structural dollar-shortage thesis, drawn from Eurodollar-system analysis: the world chronically lacks enough U.S. dollars, and that shortage eventually forces a deflationary bust in risk assets and credit. The practical advice that follows from it is unambiguous — hold dollars and short-duration Treasuries ahead of a liquidity-driven crisis. It makes him one of the more consistent deflationist voices on the macro-podcast circuit, where he appears frequently, including on Eurodollar University.

The dated record here is a single snapshot: his June 27, 2026 commentary on a video titled [Bitcoin And BlackRock Just Did Something VERY Strange](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=biyCX7UYAfQ). Even in that one appearance, the through-lines of his broader thesis are visible. He frames the moment in liquidity terms first: "it's a sign of a slowing economy, a lack of liquidity that is really kind of, you know, at the forefront of my mind right now" ([Bitcoin And BlackRock Just Did Something VERY Strange](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=biyCX7UYAfQ)). That is the deflationist's lens — reading market action as a symptom of tightening dollar access rather than as a rally to chase.

What makes the June 2026 material interesting is that he applied that lens to crypto and institutional flows. On the Bitcoin/BlackRock development, he saw textbook late-cycle behavior: "a market doing exactly what it typically does at this stage before we get to the end point is everybody piles into the last…" — the crowding pattern he treats as a pre-bust tell ([Bitcoin And BlackRock Just Did Something VERY Strange](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=biyCX7UYAfQ)). And he read the underlying driver as his dollar shortage in motion, pointing to "the progression" of funds perceiving that dollars are getting scarce ([Bitcoin And BlackRock Just Did Something VERY Strange](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=biyCX7UYAfQ)). In other words, even the strange institutional-crypto headlines of mid-2026 got slotted into the same Eurodollar frame he has argued for years.

One caveat worth flagging about the shape of this coverage: for a commentator described as strongly dollar-bullish and deflationist, every logged stance in this corpus — three of three — is neutral, and all come from that single June 2026 source. His directional calls (the deflationary bust, the flight to dollars) are standing thesis positions rather than dated calls captured here, so the timeline doesn't show his views *moving* so much as it shows one moment in which he was diagnosing rather than thundering. The portrait that emerges is a man whose argument hasn't shifted — liquidity shortage, late-stage crowding, slowing economy — but who, at least in this snapshot, was content to watch the evidence accumulate before calling the endpoint.

person/tony.text:
Tony's presence in this corpus rests on a single appearance: a guest spot on The Macro Dirt Podcast on June 23, 2026, in an episode headlined around George Noble's takes on stocks, gold, oil and AI ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)). On that show he made one clear, dated call — he was buying crude oil at prevailing levels: "I'm a buyer down here of oil as well" ([George Noble On Stocks, Gold, Oil, and AI @nobull-markettal…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4)). The stance registers on both the crude futures (CL=F) timeline and the broader Oil & Energy theme, though it is the same quote doing double duty rather than two separate calls.

The "as well" in his phrasing suggests he was piling onto a bullish oil case already on the table that day, not carving out a contrarian position. Beyond that, the record is thin and should be read as such: one appearance, one direction, no bearish or neutral stances logged, and no follow-up interviews that would show whether he held, added to, or ditched the oil buy. There is no arc to trace yet. As of late June 2026, Tony's profile is a snapshot — an oil dip-buyer, full stop — and any portrait of how his views move over time will have to wait on further appearances.

person/tony-greer.text:
Tony Greer is a financial markets analyst and newsletter author best known for The Morning Navigator, a daily macro commentary that tracks momentum, liquidity, and price action across equities, currencies, commodities, and crypto. His pedigree is sell-side trading rather than academia: he spent roughly a decade at Goldman Sachs in the firm's currency and commodities businesses before striking out as an independent researcher. That background shows in how he talks about markets — less narrative, more tape. Greer's approach is fundamentally flows- and momentum-driven; he cares about where liquidity is going and what price action confirms, and he has built his public profile largely through financial media and podcast appearances on CNBC, Real Vision, and a circuit of macro-focused shows.

What Greer argues for, at his core, is discipline over conviction: follow the momentum, respect the liquidity backdrop, and let price action arbitrate between bullish and bearish stories. It is a trader's framework rather than a permabull or permabear ideology, which is part of why he circulates widely across media with very different audiences — his lens travels well because it is not anchored to a single asset-class allegiance.

The record captured here, however, is thin on specifics. Greer appears twice as a guest on The Macro Dirt Podcast, but the digest contains no extracted stances, dated calls, or topic timelines — no documented bullish or bearish positions, and therefore no visible evolution in his views over time. For a wiki page intending to track his strongest calls with dates and citations, the sourcing simply is not there yet; anyone relying on this corpus alone would have his framework and biography, but not his market record.

person/tony-greer-and-jared-dillian.text:
Tony Greer and Jared Dillian are a pairing of two trading-desk veterans turned macro commentators — Greer of the TG Macro morning note, with a background as a gold trader at Goldman Sachs, and Dillian of The Daily Dirtnap, formerly head of ETF trading at Lehman Brothers. In this corpus, though, their joint footprint rests on a single appearance: the June 17, 2026 discussion "[Nobody Owns Bonds](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-mvJ6poUk4)," which sweeps across rates, currencies, energy, metals and even private-space assets in one sitting.

The through-line of that conversation is a coherent disinflationary, liquidity-friendly macro view. The headline call is that "bonds may be the world's most underowned asset" ([Nobody Owns Bonds](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-mvJ6poUk4)), paired explicitly with "dollar weakness" and a bearish read on energy amid "collapsing oil prices" ([Nobody Owns Bonds](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-mvJ6poUk4)). That long-bonds, short-dollar, weak-oil configuration is classic disinflation trading — and it makes their hesitation on gold the notable exception. Rather than riding the metals rally, they sit neutral, weighing "what gold's recent correction signals for the precious metals sector" ([Nobody Owns Bonds](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-mvJ6poUk4)). Meanwhile the speculative appetite they decline to spend on gold shows up elsewhere: they ask "whether SpaceX is becoming the ultimate momentum trade as capital rotates across global markets" ([Nobody Owns Bonds](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-mvJ6poUk4)), a tell that they see froth rotating into private-side stories even as they position for lower rates.

The honest caveat: this is a one-day snapshot. Every stance on record dates to June 17, 2026 and a single source, so there is no timeline yet to show whether the bond-bullishness is a fresh turn or a long-held conviction, or how they've handled the gold correction before or since. Treat this as a snapshot of where the two stood on one afternoon, not a track record.

person/val-zlatev.text:
Val Zlatev is a portfolio manager at Diamond Hill Capital Management, the Columbus, Ohio-based asset manager, where he joined as a research analyst in the early 2010s and now co-manages the firm's large-cap equity strategies. His beat is technology and semiconductors — he has discussed memory-chip makers Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix in financial media and on investing podcasts — and his style of argument is bottoms-up and specific: head counts, supply chains, and deal math rather than narrative.

His strongest documented call comes from a single appearance on June 20, 2026, on The Monetary Matters Network, sharing an episode pointedly titled "Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits" with veteran short-seller Jim Chanos. Against the bear case that AI profits are an accounting mirage, Zlatev offered a labor-based rebuttal: "look at head counts over the last three or four years compared to the operating profits of these companies," where the divergence between flat staffing and surging profits is, in his telling, evidence of real productivity rather than financial engineering ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). His structural bull case concentrated in memory, arguing that high-demand memory names trade at "cheap forward multiples" because the physical supply chain constrains how quickly capacity can arrive ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). The framing is unambiguous about where value sits in the AI stack: "Technology is the ultimate differentiator in that game... the value add is in the chips and the wrappers of the chips" ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)).

What makes the appearance worth studying is that the bullishness is selectively applied rather than wholesale. He conceded that where AI infrastructure deals actually disclose their economics, they are "penciling out at 7%, 6%, 5%, 8%" — thin returns that cut against the buildout's math — and he flagged outright "shorting opportunities on a bunch of component makers" selling into PCs and smartphones, the devices being displaced by the data-center boom ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). On the three big memory producers — "one of which is American, two of which are Korean" — he acknowledged the stocks "have gone up so much" even while pressing the structural case ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). He kept two hedges in view: that demand can be tracked in real time through open-routed token counts and GPU rental prices, and that a genuinely new, non-transformer model architecture could scramble the chip stack ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)). His meta-take on the debate itself is notably balanced — "there's probably just as many bears as bulls on the AI argument, which I think is extremely healthy" ([Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val Zlat…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)).

The honest caveat: this is a one-interview record. All thirteen logged stances — six bullish, three bearish, four neutral — carry the same June 2026 timestamp, so there is no arc to trace, no earlier positioning to compare against, no reversals to chronicle. The archive also tags him bearish on precious metals, but the supporting quote is the same 5–8% AI-deal-return passage, not anything about gold or silver; that tag looks like a filing artifact and should not be read as a metals call. What the snapshot does establish is a coherent identity: a memory-and-silicon bull who thinks the bears perform a useful function, checks the hype against token counts and deal math, and is willing to short the casualties inside his own theme.

person/aminvest.text:
aminvest is the sole author and voice behind *AM Invest*, a self-titled, Traditional Chinese newsletter with a distinctly Hong Kong flavour, published on Patreon as a running series of short US-market briefs (美股市況短評). The coverage skews to the names retail crowds actually trade — SpaceX-linked SPCX, semiconductors like Micron, and large-cap financials such as Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley — and the tone is analytical but pointedly contrarian: the recurring move is to ask whether a dip in a heavily hyped stock is truly a bargain, while tracking how mega-cap swings (Micron's, notably) can drag the broader market. The recorded stance mix — 8 bullish, 6 bearish, 6 neutral — reads like a market-timer who calls direction daily rather than a permabull or permabear.

Their most characterful call is on SPCX. On 24 June 2026 they dismissed dip-buyers outright: if you think SPCX breaking below $150 already makes it cheap, "I'd say that idea is a bit naive" ([美股市況短評 (20260624)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161958989)). The same post drifted into provocation — at what price would Elon Musk lose his spot as the world's richest man? "AI's answer to me is $17.61" ([美股市況短評 (20260624)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161958989)). Whether tongue-in-cheek or not, the topic now sits marked bearish.

The June 2026 timeline shows a fast pivot. Mid-month they were constructive: on 15 June they were watching investment banks whose trends were strengthening beyond tech ([美股市況短評 (20260615)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161146651)), and by 18 June they argued that strong-cash-flow large-cap tech, if it pulled back and stabilized, could be a buying opportunity ([美股市況短評 (20260618)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161407746)). Then the turn: 22 June put the index at a "key resistance — attack or defend?" ([美股市況短評 (20260622)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161763918)); 23 June flagged the corporate credit market as already deteriorating and warned Hong Kong stocks may have entered the second phase of a bear market ([美股市況短評 (20260623)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161861803)); and by 25 June the rates-and-credit view had fully flipped, with corporate debt default ratios "already beginning to deteriorate" ([美股市況短評 (20260625)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-162048909)).

That 25 June post is also where their AI view gets genuinely two-sided: many large tech stocks "should rise again," yet many AI-related *and* unrelated companies worldwide will collapse ([美股市況短評 (20260625)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-162048909)) — a barbell of mega-cap survivors versus an AI periphery they expect to die, which is why the topic is now net bearish despite the bullish line on the giants. Elsewhere they stayed noncommittal: Goldman Sachs is "decent, but the price is high, hard to get in" ([美股市況短評 (20260617)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161328901)). Fair caveat: the entire record here spans roughly two weeks of June 2026, so the flip is compressed and the credit-call verdict is still open.

person/person-001.text:
何啟聰是香港衍生產品市場的老手，長期任職於瑞銀，曾官至該行香港區董事總經理兼ETF及場外衍生產品銷售部主管。憑這份履历，他以ETF及上市衍生產品專家身份活躍於本地財經媒體，是香港槓桿及反向產品、窩輪牛熊證市場的知名評論人，談的多是散戶交投、ETF資金流向這類「水底下」的結構問題。在本庫中，他四次以獨立作者／主持身份出現，全部集中在2026年6月的《信報》評論。

他6月19日的文章主線是AI硬件漲價的連鎖反應：宏觀面上，他引述聯儲局主席沃什在首次主持的議息會議上的說法，指美國通脹率遠高於2%目標、能源價格上升只是其中一個升溫原因，立場偏淡 ([AI硬件漲價逼聯儲局入死角](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4435475/AI%E7%A1%AC%E4%BB%B6%E6%BC%B2%E5%83%B9%E9%80%BC%E8%81%AF%E5%84%B2%E5%B1%80%E5%85%A5%E6%AD%BB%E8%A7%92))；個股層面，他將阿里巴巴（09988）與騰訊（00700）的跌勢歸因於AI硬件持續加價推高雲企資本開支，並點出京東（09618）在騰訊及阿里加價後即宣布減價的價格戰格局 ([AI硬件漲價逼聯儲局入死角](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4435475/AI%E7%A1%AC%E4%BB%B6%E6%BC%B2%E5%83%B9%E9%80%BC%E8%81%AF%E5%84%B2%E5%B1%80%E5%85%A5%E6%AD%BB%E8%A7%92))。三天後的6月22日，他以SpaceX「未有盈利仍獲追捧」與港股「有盈利仍被拋售」的強烈對比，襯托對港股定價的懷疑，並翻出中芯H股（00981）2020年A股上市當日大跌、持貨五年才返家鄉的舊帳，提醒投資者兩地溢價遊戲不易玩 ([SpaceX溢價僅馬斯克獨有](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4436065/SpaceX%E6%BA%A2%E5%83%B9%E5%83%85%E9%A6%AC%E6%96%AF%E5%85%8B%E7%8D%A8%E6%9C%89))。

他最重手的一擊是6月26日對海力士槓桿ETF的系統性風險警示：SK海力士槓桿ETF市值不斷暴增，香港投資者已開始買入其兩倍槓桿產品（07709），資產淨值高達1300億元、超過盈富基金（02800）；他點出早前海力士股價因加稅討論急跌、KOSPI 200指數一度跌了一成，正是槓桿產品引致的波幅，並警告一旦海力士股價急挫、槓桿ETF市值再膨脹，或對南韓金融市場構成系統性風險，更預期南韓監管當局未來數星期可能出手 ([海力士槓桿ETF威脅韓股](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4440216/%E6%B5%B7%E5%8A%9B%E5%A3%AB%E6%A7%93ETF%E5%A8%81%E8%84%85%E9%9F%93%E8%82%A1))。值得注意的是，他對海力士正股本身只持中立——他擔心的是衍生結構而非晶片基本面，這正是一個做過衍生產品銷售主管的人才會有的警惕角度 ([海力士槓桿ETF威脅韓股](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4440216/%E6%B5%B7%E5%8A%9B%E5%A3%AB%E6%A7%93ETF%E5%A8%81%E8%84%85%E9%9F%93%E8%82%A1))。

至於觀點遷移，本庫可見的時間線只覆蓋6月19日至26日約一星期，談不上長期軌跡；但短期走向清晰：對中港股市的判斷由6月19日的中性觀察，到6月26日明確升級為看淡 ([海力士槓桿ETF威脅韓股](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4440216/%E6%B5%B7%E5%8A%9B%E5%A3%AB%E6%A7%93ETF%E5%A8%81%E8%84%85%E9%9F%93%E8%82%A1))。整體立場配比是十二個看淡、六個中立、僅一個看好——而那唯一的好倉在可見時間線裡並無蹤影。換言之，他的淡不是喊沽大市式的淡，而是盯住槓桿規模、資金流和資本開支這些「管道」風險的淡；這份樣本裡沒有給出任何具體的看好操作，這本身就構成了一種立場。

person/paul-krugman.text:
Paul Krugman is the rare economist whose scholarly and popular reputations are both first-tier. He won the 2008 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his work on trade patterns and economic geography — New Trade Theory and New Economic Geography — and taught along the way at MIT, Princeton, and the CUNY Graduate Center. But his wider fame rests on the opinion page: more than two decades as a New York Times op-ed columnist (2000–2024), where his Keynesian-leaning commentary on macroeconomics, trade, and politics made him one of the most-read and most-argued-with economic voices in the business. He has since moved to his own newsletter/platform and remains a frequent media commentator on bubbles, markets, and economic policy.

Within this corpus, though, Krugman's record is narrow and deliberately undramatic: two logged stances, both neutral, no bullish or bearish calls on either side of the ledger. Both entries fall on the same date — June 16, 2026 — and the same subject, SpaceX, drawn from a Master Insight piece whose headline frames him as a Nobel laureate savaging the company's valuation ([SpaceX市值一飛沖天 諾獎得主狠批龐氏騙局](https://www.master-insight.com/article/48758)).

The substance is more measured than the headline implies. Krugman's warning was that SpaceX's share price shouldn't be over-rated in the years ahead, and that the stock would take the brunt of the damage if the AI bubble bursts ([SpaceX市值一飛沖天 諾獎得主狠批龐氏騙局](https://www.master-insight.com/article/48758)). Yet he paired that caution with an explicit long-term endorsement — in the long run, he said, he is bullish ([SpaceX市值一飛沖天 諾獎得主狠批龐氏騙局](https://www.master-insight.com/article/48758)). The analytical core of his argument is the IPO-cycle point: hot, first-day "pop" listings historically deliver weak risk-adjusted returns over three years, as profit-taking, lockup-expiry selling, and mean reversion set in, so investors should treat SpaceX as a high-volatility growth exposure whose fate depends on Starlink profitability and Starship execution rather than debut-day froth ([SpaceX市值一飛沖天 諾獎得主狠批龐氏騙局](https://www.master-insight.com/article/48758)).

What the timeline can't yet establish is whether that valuation-skepticism is a pattern or a one-off — two neutral entries on one date are too thin to brand him a habitual bubble-basher here, even though bubble commentary is squarely his beat. What the record does show is his shape as a market commentator: when he is most critical of a hyped listing, he stops well short of a short thesis, layering near-term danger over long-term constructive, and hedging the whole thing on execution. A skeptic with a portfolio view, not a permabear — at least on the evidence so far.

person/person-002.text:
Liu Qiangdong is the founder and chairman of JD.com, and his biography is the classic Chinese e-commerce origin story told in its most compressed form: a poor rural family in Suqian, Jiangsu; a Renmin University degree in 1996; a failed restaurant venture; then a small electronics stall in Beijing's Zhongguancun district in 1998 that grew into Jingdong. The decisive pivot came after the 2003 SARS epidemic, when he moved the business online and built JD.com around a bet his rivals wouldn't make — self-built warehousing and delivery, to guarantee authentic goods and fast service. That logistics obsession scaled into one of the largest Chinese tech listings of its era on the NASDAQ in May 2014, a Hong Kong secondary listing in 2020, and an ecosystem spanning JD Logistics, JD Health, and JD Technology (formerly JD Digits).

He stepped down as CEO in April 2022 but kept the chairmanship and, with it, controlling influence over the company — a status that matters for anyone reading his public statements as signals. His personal reputation carries baggage the corpus should not smooth over: a 2018 sexual-assault allegation in Minnesota that produced no charges and ended in a settled civil suit, alongside the more flattering notes — marriage to Zhang Zetian, hometown philanthropy, and a famously paternalistic management style toward JD's couriers. That last trait is what makes his one recorded market-relevant call so pointed.

On 23 June 2026, per a Hong Kong Economic Journal report, Liu made the declaration that anchors this wiki's classification of him as bearish on China and Hong Kong equities: 「將來都是機械人送貨了，根本不需要快遞員。」— in the future, robots will do the deliveries and couriers won't be needed at all ([京東不要快遞員 三項鐵人再培訓](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4436952/%E4%BA%AC%E6%9D%B1%E4%B8%8D%E8%A6%81%E5%BF%AB%E9%81%9E%E5%93%A1+%E4%B8%89%E9%A0%85%E9%90%B5%E4%BA%BA%E5%86%8D%E5%9F%B9%E8%A8%93)). The irony is hard to miss: the man who built JD's entire brand on its courier network — and his own image on caring for those couriers — is now on record predicting their obsolescence. Whether that constitutes a genuine macro call on Chinese equities or a company-specific automation thesis is not resolved by the source; the corpus labels it bearish, and readers should know that label rests on this single quote.

That caveat deserves stating plainly: beyond the June 2026 entry, this corpus holds no dated calls, no prior stances, and no documented shifts in Liu's views. There is no timeline to chart a movement from bullish to bearish — only one data point, late in the record. Treating Liu as a market commentator would overstate the evidence; he is better read as a controlling founder whose operational pronouncements occasionally carry market weight, and whose one captured stance happens to sit in tension with everything he built.

person/person-003.text:
吳明德 — cited locally as Dr. 吳明德 — is a Hong Kong-based economist and veteran banker whose institutional pedigree runs through a long tenure as a Citibank executive. That banking background shapes his public persona: he is less a market tipster than a monetary-system man, writing in depth on the linked exchange rate system and the property market, the two structural pillars of Hong Kong finance. His regular outlets are local radio and YouTube finance programs, where he is a frequent presence rather than an occasional guest.

What distinguishes his commentary, per the record here, is the insistence on historical framing. When assessing current market conditions he reaches for precedent — most notably reminding audiences that Hong Kong property prices fell roughly 60% between 1998 and 2003, a benchmark he deploys to anchor present-day property discussion. This is a useful editorial habit in a market prone to forgetting its own cycles, though it also means his contribution is context-setting rather than directional calls.

That last point matters for anyone reading this page expecting a track record: the corpus currently contains no dated calls for 吳明德 — zero bullish, zero bearish, zero neutral positions logged, and empty topic timelines across the board. So while he is plainly an established voice on the peg and on property, no documented shift in his views over time can be traced from this digest, and no signature call can be ranked as his strongest. The portrait is of a commentator whose positions on record remain, for now, unwritten.

person/person-004.text:
施永青 is one of those rare figures who sits on both sides of the property ledger — he sells it, writes about it, and opines on it. Born in Shanghai in 1949, he co-founded Centaline Property Agency (中原地產) in 1978 and built it into one of the largest real-estate agencies in Hong Kong and mainland China; in 2005 he added a second platform, founding the free Chinese-language newspaper am730, where his widely read columns range across property, economics and current affairs. Known for free-market views laced with Daoist philosophy, he is among Hong Kong's most quoted voices on housing, and his single recorded appearance in this corpus is as an interview guest opposite 高天佑.

The dated record here is thin — effectively one day — but it captures his position well. In a 17 June 2026 HKEJ piece titled [北水炒風勁 嚇親施永青](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4432968/%E5%8C%97%E6%B0%B4%E7%82%92%E9%A2%A8%E5%8B%81+%E5%9A%87%E8%A6%AA%E6%96%BD%E6%B0%B8%E9%9D%92), he is described as having gone against the crowd, "揚言升幅可達15%" — standing alone in calling for gains of up to 15%. Yet the same article has him alarmed by northbound (mainland) speculative money, warning that "炒家會把樓價推至一個用家負擔不起的水平，繼而妨礙民生" — speculators will push prices to a level end-users cannot afford, thereby harming livelihoods. His stated ideal is prices rising "穩定地緩緩地隨經濟增長一起同步上升", steadily and slowly in step with economic growth. All three threads — the bullish price call, the affordability warning, the equilibrium scenario — come from that [single article](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4432968/%E5%8C%97%E6%B0%B4%E7%82%92%E9%A2%A8%E5%8B%81+%E5%9A%87%E8%A6%AA%E6%96%BD%E6%B0%B8%E9%9D%92), and the corpus accordingly tags him as bearish on both China & Hong Kong equities and China property as of that date.

The apparent contradiction in the stance mix is really a two-layer argument, and it is worth reading it that way rather than as hedging: he is bullish on near-term prices because northbound flows are doing the lifting, and bearish on what those same flows do to the market's social function. That tension — price forecast versus livelihood concern — is the recurring shape of his housing commentary. That said, with only one dated datapoint in this corpus, no genuine movement in his views over time can be traced; the "how his views have shifted" question simply isn't answerable from this record, and readers should treat the June 2026 snapshot as a portrait of a moment, not a track record.

person/person-005.text:
李聲揚 is a Hong Kong–based finance writer and commentator who has made a career of translating value-investing orthodoxy for a Chinese-speaking audience. He writes columns for Hong Kong financial media, has authored Chinese-language books on stock-picking and value investing built on Benjamin Graham– and Warren Buffett–style principles applied to Hong Kong and Chinese markets, and appears regularly as a speaker and podcast commentator on Hong Kong equities and personal investing. In other words, he sits squarely in the Graham-Buffett lineage — the camp that believes the market exists to serve patient buyers of businesses, not to be out-guessed.

The one dated stance in the corpus shows that lineage in its purest form. In a 26 June 2026 piece for HKEJ on macro trading — headlined to the effect that even AI loses money when put to work on it — he went further than the usual "macro is hard" hedging, arguing that "即使能未卜先知，了解局勢走向，對投資近乎是零幫助，甚至是催命符" — that even perfect foreknowledge of where events are heading would be of nearly zero use to an investor, and could even be a death warrant ([宏觀交易過五關 AI落場都輸錢](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4440220/%E5%AE%8F%E8%A7%80%E4%BA%A4%E6%98%93%E9%81%8E%E4%BA%94%E9%97%9C+AI%E8%90%BD%E5%A0%B4%E9%83%BD%E8%BC%B8%E9%8C%A2)). That is a deliberately provocative version of the value-camp position: not merely that macro forecasting is unreliable, but that being *right* about it is worthless or worse. It is a stance logged as neutral rather than bullish or bearish — consistent with a writer whose brand rests on method rather than market calls.

On the question of how his views have moved over time, the honest answer is that the record here is too thin to show a trajectory. The corpus contains a single dated entry, and no logged bullish or bearish calls against which to measure drift or conviction. What the 2026 piece does suggest is continuity rather than conversion: a commentator whose published position on markets is the classic value-investor's refusal to trade on macro narratives at all. Until more dated calls enter the record, that consistency — and the relative absence of directional bets — is the most telling thing the timeline can say about him.

person/person-006.text:
梁天卓 is a Hong Kong economist who writes economics for a living and, unusually for the breed, writes it readably. He holds a doctorate in economics, has worked in the city's financial sector, and is best known as one of the three co-authors of the「經濟3.0」column in the Hong Kong Economic Journal (信報), alongside 徐家健 and 曾國平 — a long-running beat covering applied economics, public policy, law and economics, and Hong Kong current affairs. He also writes solo pieces and appears as a commentator and presenter in Cantonese economics media and podcasts, which gives him a wider local audience than most academics ever get.

What the record actually shows him arguing for is characteristic of the law-and-economics instinct the column is built on. In a 25 June 2026 piece on legalising autonomous driving (自駕), he came out for what he called "較合理的是中間路線" — a limited pilot scheme rather than either a blanket ban or an open door: only systems that pass vetting get approved, trials run in designated districts or on designated routes, and operators must submit data on mileage, takeovers, accidents, near-misses and complaints, with the trial zone expanded or narrowed periodically on the evidence ([自駕合法化 有限度先導計劃可取](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4439041/%E8%87%AA%E9%A7%95%E5%90%88%E6%B3%95%E5%8C%96+%E6%9C%89%E9%99%90%E5%BA%A6%E5%85%88%E5%B0%8E%E8%A8%88%E5%8A%83%E5%8F%AF%E5%8F%96)). It's a market-friendly position, but a disciplined one — he is splitting the difference between the tech boosters who want autonomy unleashed and the safety hardliners who want it banned, and insisting the argument be settled by data rather than rhetoric. That is very much the 經濟3.0 house style: pro-market, empirically fussy, allergic to absolutism.

On how his views have moved over time: the tracked timeline is thin, and it's worth saying so plainly. The corpus holds only one dated entry — that same June 2026 autonomy piece — which is tagged bullish on both China & Hong Kong equities and Robotics, Automation & Autonomy, though the bullishness is really policy optimism rather than a stock call; the argument is about how Hong Kong should regulate self-driving, not which tickers to buy ([自駕合法化 有限度先導計劃可取](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4439041/%E8%87%AA%E9%A7%95%E5%90%88%E6%B3%95%E5%8C%96+%E6%9C%89%E9%99%90%E5%BA%A6%E5%85%88%E5%B0%8E%E8%A8%88%E5%8A%83%E5%8F%AF%E5%8F%96)). With no bearish or neutral records and nothing earlier to compare against, there is no documented drift in his stance — no turn from bull to bear or vice versa that the data can show. A columnist with his output volume almost certainly has more positions on file elsewhere; until they're captured, this page should be read as a portrait drawn from a single, fairly representative frame.

person/person-007.text:

The program covers stock markets and general investing topics for a primarily Chinese-speaking audience. Beyond that, there is very little to go on — no real name, no career history, no firm affiliation. That anonymity is itself worth noting: unlike most figures covered in this corpus, whose personas are anchored to institutional credentials, 狂徒's authority rests entirely on the show and its track record, with the pseudonym functioning as the brand.

The honest state of this record, though, is thin. As of this digest there are no dated calls to point to, the stance ledger is empty (zero logged bullish, bearish, or neutral positions), and the topic timeline — usually the place where a commentator's evolution becomes visible — is blank. So the question of how his views have moved over time simply can't be answered from what's on file; there is no documented shift because there is no documented starting point. That is a coverage gap, not a verdict on the work, and it should be read as an instruction: the show's archives are the obvious next source to mine for dated calls. Until then, any portrait of 狂徒 has to stop at the biography above, because the substance of his market views hasn't been captured.

person/person-008.text:
葉教授 — the honorific translates roughly to "Professor Yip" — is a Cantonese-language commentator on Hong Kong property and the broader economic outlook, writing and speaking under that pen name rather than a confirmed personal identity. Beyond the persona itself, the public record here is thin: no verified biography, no professional affiliation, no confirmed real name. That anonymity is not unusual in Hong Kong's online financial-commentary scene, where market watchers often build followings under adopted titles, but it does mean any portrait has to rest on the commentary rather than credentials — and in this case, even the commentary trail is sparse.

ticker/AAPL.text:
The honest answer about the Apple "debate" in this record is that there barely is one: of thirteen tracked comments, twelve are neutral, one is bullish, and zero are bearish. What passes for discussion here is not a bull-versus-bear fight over fundamentals but a technician's conversation about implied moves and pullback timing. The lone explicit bullish call came on August 6, 2026, from an unnamed contributor who reasoned that "if we get some rotations, maybe Apple wants to start making a pop" after the stock had already taken its drop from earnings — a rotation-chasing, bounce-into-strength thesis rather than a conviction view on the business.

The timeline starts on firmer ground. On June 19, [何啟聰](../People/person-001.md) flagged that Apple had just announced price increases to reflect rising chip and memory costs — the only fundamental thread in the record, tagged "up," and double-edged in the usual way: pricing power on one side, input-cost pass-through on the other. A month later, on July 17, guest Gareth Soloway sounded the closest thing to a bear note in the digest — coded neutral, but directionally cautious — saying that "as we bounce, we should see Apple, for instance, come back in a little bit," i.e., expecting the stock to fade on rallies. Nobody was scored outright bearish, but that is the most skeptical read on offer.

The contradiction worth noting belongs to the August 6 bull. Within days of floating the pop thesis, the same voice was narrating the opposite: on August 11 it observed that "Apple did tag its lower implied move" with weakness there, while Chinese-language commentary that same day noted the stock had rallied for over a month before pulling back again. By August 13 the same speaker had retreated into a coin flip — "wouldn't be shocked to see it come back to the upper weekly or the lower weekly implied move" — which is hedging dressed as analysis. So the pattern is clear and should be stated plainly: no one in this digest actually changed direction, the sole bull went quiet into description within a week, and with a 1/0/12 split the coverage here is simply too thin to claim any real debate exists.

ticker/AMZN.text:
For an asset carrying zero scored bulls and zero scored bears — nine neutral/watch calls — Amazon's commentary tape in August 2026 is oddly lively. The busiest voice is an unidentified technical trader who, on August 8, framed the setup as a breakout watch: "maybe we can break out and get some sort of continuation and try to target up to that big round number up there around 300" (unnamed commentator, Aug 8, 2026). Three days later they had the stock "holding strong... almost towards its upper weekly implied move" (unnamed commentator, Aug 11, 2026). So the technical case is constructive but conditional — momentum toward $300, not conviction.

The wobble came on August 13: "I wouldn't be shocked to see it come down into that area" (unnamed commentator, Aug 13, 2026). That reads as a pullback hedge, not a bearish turn — and indeed the same voice zoomed out to the strongest bull argument in the corpus on August 24, invoking Amazon's own history: the company was crushed in the dot-com bust, the commentator argued (in Cantonese), before using the internet to send the price up roughly forty-fold from its pre-burst high (unnamed commentator, Aug 24, 2026). The implication for today's AI-bubble anxieties is deliberate — drawdowns in a structural winner are entries, not endings. It's the classic survivor-analogue bull case, and it's telling that it comes from the same person who was mapping downside scenarios a week and a half earlier.

The institutional layer belongs to Goldman Sachs, cited secondhand through an author and tagged bullish on the capex supercycle (Goldman Sachs via citing author, Aug 27, 2026). Per that citation, Amazon and four other giants are expected to spend about $75.5 billion on AI capex in 2026, up roughly 80% year over year, inside Goldman's projected ~$5.3 trillion of cumulative big-tech capex from 2025 through 2030. For the bull reading, that reframes Amazon's spending as demand-driven capacity rather than empire-building — the spend itself is the thesis.

What's conspicuously absent is an actual bear. Nobody in the corpus plants a sell flag on Amazon; the closest thing is the August 13 pullback hedge and the implicit question of whether $300 gets reached at all. The real debate, then, is about degree and path rather than direction: a conditional technical grind toward a round number versus a five-year capex supercycle with a dot-com survival story for ballast. The neutral consensus label arguably undersells how constructive the chatter leans — though with one anonymous trader carrying most of the tape-level commentary and the Goldman figure arriving secondhand, the neutrality may say as much about the thinness of coverage as about anyone's conviction on the stock.
