News-driven additions include the ETF-holdings piece on 11 September 2020 ([CPM Group - Changing Dynamics In ETF Holdings - Jeffrey Christian](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X7l3Jq4O5uw)), the post-election treatment on 6 November, the 1933 political parallel on 4 December, an unusual rhodium pitch on 20 January 2021 ([CPM - Who Should Be Investing In Rhodium?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sK-K96qJLh8)), and the January 2021 Reddit-silver moment. Per the deep-read, the only new content inside the flagged recurring items is a business update (increased consulting demand, 12 June 2020), an account of a meeting with Wall Street Silver (9 August 2022), and a rebuttal to a comment-section critic who claimed a silver promoter knows more than CPM Group (5 August 2025). The pattern is telling: novelty arrives on the consulting-revenue and feud side of the ledger, while the market argument itself keeps circling the same myth-busting core — an introduction video from 18 August 2020 suggests the shop was simultaneously recruiting a new audience for old material ([Introduction To CPM Group](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g7zSiFjuYuM)).

The explicit "something has changed" moments are rare and quotable, and both come from outside the market commentary proper. On 12 June 2020 the change was commercial: "we found ourselves providing increased volumes of consulting." On 9 August 2022 it was interpersonal: "I met with Jim Lewis of Wall Street Silver" — the author engaging directly with a critic rather than rebutting him in the abstract. The 5 August 2025 entry is flagged as new but carries no quoted change declaration in the evidence, so whether the author framed it as a turning point is unverifiable here. On cadence: within 2020 the reuse cycle is roughly fortnightly; around the yearbook months it is annual; and the recurring flag persists at roughly yearly intervals out to 2025 even as archive density collapses — the visible timeline runs only to 12 March 2021, the archive holds 54 items of which just 31 are dated here, and the post-2021 deep-read items come without links, so the late-period picture is thin and should be read as provisional.

study/cpm-group/topic/silver-supply-and-.text:
CPM Group's silver coverage is, by its own architecture, a rerun. The load-bearing claim — that refined supply comfortably covers fabrication demand, and that deficit and shortage talk is narrative rather than arithmetic — predates the video archive itself. A deep-read from August 2015 already has Jeffrey Christian citing the "advent of LED lighting for example" and "demand reduction due to the higher prices" as the real story, while conceding only that "people expect that the supply increases to continue." A decade on, in November 2025, the sentence is nearly unchanged: "Newly refined silver production from mine production and from secondary recovery from scrap continues to outstrip fabrication dem[and]." The delivery vehicle runs on an annual spring cadence — the [2019 Silver Yearbook Launch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-jGHFUKTio) in April 2019, the [Annual Silver Update](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bo8jT0XPcbM) in May 2021 (re-delivered wholesale for a different audience as the [2021 Silver Update for Chinese Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hklab62wIy0) two months later), the [2024 Silver Market Outlook](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AutbJDWZfr0), and [Silver Facts And Fantasies 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W5ReHm2dbLk) in March 2025. Even a July 2021 title shrugs at the loop: [Gold and Silver: It Is Still All About Demand](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o0Vb7ZwJfzs).

Title reuse is the clearest fingerprint of the recycling. "How Much Silver Is Really Available" ran on [September 15, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IPMS5mYzvXE) and again, verbatim, on [January 16, 2024](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xD7w6o21Ujk) — four months apart. [The Truth About Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hCZKS5WVbsw) (May 2023) became [The Truth About Silver Demand and Price](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7ypNBIi2LAE) (February 2024). The "Facts and Fantasies" brand stamps three videos in twelve months: [March 5, 2024](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4XYHRtWy3GQ), [March 15, 2024](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jh0Mv34sa6w), and [March 18, 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W5ReHm2dbLk). Around these flagships sits an event-driven rebuttal cycle that fires whenever prices spike or shortage chatter trends: [Silver, Gamestop, and WallStreet Bets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N54_h29SeUY) in January 2021; the 2022 inventory double-tap of [The Relationship Between The Silver Price, Inventories, and Comex Positions](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HFQ9NuYCmDY) and [Low Silver Inventories Do Not Cause High Silver Prices](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=71QcOEr8EaE); [Silver Deficits Don't Exist And Other Silver Myths](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k7muhimpCms) in August 2023; [The Silver Shortage Chimera](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9SpxKkghmu4) in April 2024; and, in February 2025, [Silver Déjà Vu: Why Prices Spiked Higher And What Comes Next](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6V-f8U28HGM) — a title that openly concedes the rerun. Quiet stretches (mid-2021 through early 2022) coincide with quiet prices; 2023–2025 run at roughly one silver video a month.

Genuinely new material is scarce, and only one deep-read is flagged as non-recurring: the February 2022 comparison of Berkshire Hathaway's 1998 silver purchase to modern "drain the swamp" theories — an actual new argument. The rest of the novelty is empirical. May 2021 brought the LBMA clerical error, aired days after the yearbook launch: "london inventories are 116 million ounces less than somebody mistakenly said they were at the end of march," promptly defused with "the mistake as egregious as it was... is actually not important to the real silver market." April 2022 added a named-price rebuttal of a specific promoter. April 2023 added supply-response data ("Chinese production in 2022 seems to have been static," "only one small project started production in Indonesia"). March 2024 contributed coin-market color on Maple Leafs versus Eagles; April 2024 a margin comparison ("the profit margin on primary silver producers last year was about 29%"). March 2025 pulled in macro plumbing — "we have 40 million ounces of record gold uh inventories" (the transcript says gold mid-silver-talk, which tells you how interchangeable the inventory template is) and "we've seen some central banks starting to move gold into the New York Fed." November 2025 added a fresh estimate: "This year we're looking at about 135 million ounces of investment demand on a net basis."

The moments the author says something *has* changed are telling, because the changes are almost always on the other side of the debate. In 2015 the changes were structural — LED lighting, price-driven demand destruction. By June 2021 the change was merely terminological: "some people now call that a primary deficit." In April 2022 it was promoter behavior: "now he's touting thousand ounce bars," "charging like 31 or 32 or 33 dollars an ounce," while "our clients were buying silver thousand ounce bars... at 29 not at 31 or 32 or 33." In September 2025 it was price: "They got up to $45.90 some odd cents earlier this morning" — followed instantly by the insistence that nothing else had: "we're not particularly seeing tight supplies... the supply is really not that tight." By November 2025 a real change finally registered on the demand side — "The silver market for the smaller investment products has been gutted by sales" — though the supply conclusion stayed put. Four deep-reads are flagged flatly as new="nothing" (August 2015, April 2024, September 2025, and one of two November 2025 passes). The cadence, in short: an annual flagship, spike-triggered rebuttals, and perhaps two genuinely new facts a year — a framework with fixed supply meeting an argument environment that, from CPM's chair, never really changes either.

study/cpm-group/topic/macroeconomic-outl.text:
The macroeconomic-outlook file is less an argument than a franchise with a refresh schedule. The archive runs from a lone 2015 oil-market video ([What You Need To Know About The Oil Market](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6FepdXXoaNs)) through near-silence until December 2020 ([CPM Group - Gold's Place In An Overly Optimistic 2021](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I7AYzgLgTC8)), then settles into a roughly monthly cadence from 2022 onward, with bursts of twice-monthly output in late May/early June 2023 ([CPM Market Outlook](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=klUnij1aNw0), [Market Update: The Truth About the Economy](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GG2yfKiZPzc)) and January 2025 ([Gold and Silver Price Insurance](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BUltNqTHmm0), [Disaster Recovery, Recessions, and Metals](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kd-9enetTGY)). The deep-read makes the recycling explicit: of fifteen closely-dated entries, fourteen are flagged recurring, one (June 30, 2023) is bluntly logged as containing "nothing" new, and the only non-recurring item in the whole set is the January 4, 2021 vaccination clock — "it's going to take at least six months for a significant enough portion of the population... to be vaccinated" — which is a pandemic timeline, not a macro thesis.

The recycled spine is recession timing, and it is a treadmill. By August 2021 the framing was already apocalyptic in title if not in substance ([The Imminent Economic Collapse](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sRqbuPl9c_k)). In May 2022 came the one genuinely new argument of that stretch — a 1987-crash analogy used to argue equity volatility didn't mean imminent recession — wrapped around the recurring call that "recession is obviously coming, but it could be two years away," which echoed through that summer's videos ([How Inflation, Interest Rates and Recession May Affect Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=10zL22_Y39s), [How Long The Recession Will Last](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zp8K-lh1Bu4)). By November 2022 the date had slipped — "it is most likely uh that it would be 2024 2025," with the author noting "we've seen various banks mark down their probabilities of a recession starting in 2023." October 2023 repeated the same 2024–2025 expectation ([Preparing For The Next Recession](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuUnsDXzh9k)), now garnished with "Global growth slowing" and "industrial production has slowed." In December 2023 the herd itself became the story: consensus had swung from "we're about to fall into a recession" to "there's not going to be a recession," and "now we're starting to see Market consensus shift back to well there could be a recession in 2024." The forecast only hardened in 2025 — February's "the potential for a recession in the next 12 to 24 months... has increased" and pressures "indicative of potential recession sooner rather than later" grown "more prominent over the last nine months" ([What Really Happens To Gold During A Recession](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IkdJaAIn7II)), then May's sharpest self-revision in the corpus, "We have increased the depths of the recession that we are projecting" ([U.S. GDP Shrinks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jJ-9wWwfojQ)), then September's stretch of duration: "we do see problems continuing and we see them continuing for a longer period of time than we had been have been projecting."

Genuinely new material almost always arrives as a data release dropped into the reused frame. January 6, 2023 was the December jobs report — "they showed a strong economy 223 new thousand new jobs created," with the wrinkle that "markets didn't necessarily take it that way they said oh this is kind of weak" ([Gold and Silver Prices Jump On Jobs Report](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YopGzQ_iFds)). May 31, 2023 was the data-dense outlier: M2's percent change going negative ("it's never been negative before but now it is"), month-to-month CPI back in its pre-2021 range, and unemployment "the lowest that it's been since like the 1960s." June 2023 added Fed stress tests — 23 systemically important banks absorbing a $540 billion loss — even as the same date is elsewhere logged as containing nothing new, a contradiction worth holding onto. October 2023 contributed record Treasury demand: "interest rates have risen bond prices have fallen," yet "demand for the US Treasury Securities bonds and notes and t- bills has not declined it's actually risen," feeding the long-running debt thread ([The Debt To Fear](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gPw0A4N34P8), [What The US Debt Means](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-PCuBTkczDs)). The dollar thread repeats the same way — "Dollars not crashing yet sorry for those who were impatient for it" in January 2023, versus a rising-dollar video a year earlier ([What The Rising Dollar Means For Gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TBXzM5GSB_w)) — until September 2024 quantified it: up "1.7% last Friday from where it had been in January" and "2.9% from... September 20th of 2023." The mid- and late-2024 entries survive only in Chinese-language transcripts (a Reuters survey in June, with 18% of central-bank reserve managers planning to add dollar holdings; November's foreign Treasury holdings of $8.67 trillion, up $170 billion in September alone ([The Future of Gold and Silver Prices](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=21tRkw9MKkI))). March 2025 brought the one stagflationary print — "It showed uh weaker economic activity and higher inflation" — with gold at $3,124, and May 2025 added tariff front-loading: "demand was brought forward into the first quarter and into March by investors buying automobiles and other goods in advance of" anticipated tariffs.

The shape of the debate is a forecast that never resolves, only re-dates: from May 2022 through late 2023 the recession sits perpetually one-to-two years out, and the real inflection doesn't come until 2025, when the language flips from timing to severity and duration — at which point the "new" content is still mostly fresh numbers in an old argument. The author's posture is consistent throughout and mildly contrarian: skeptical of collapse-mongers (the May 2023 "Charlatans" title, the snark at dollar-crash "impatience") while maintaining a slow-rolling recession call. Two corpus caveats: the deep-read runs to September 2025 while the archive stops in mid-June 2025 ([Middle East Tensions](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kC0W0g9WhL0)), so recent months are thinly covered, and with fourteen of fifteen sampled entries flagged recurring, the reuse count likely understates rather than overstates the pattern.

study/cpm-group/topic/geopolitics-and-po.text:
Jeffrey Christian's geopolitics coverage runs on an event clock, not a calendar. The archive holds a single 2021 entry ([Worldwide Risks, Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MMzgPml9Kho), September 10) before Russia's invasion of Ukraine trips the series into a weekly rhythm: seven videos in five weeks from March 8 to April 12, 2022 — the initial rally call as [Russia Looks For Buyers](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=20QsWnUrRD0), the [long-term commodity outlooks after Russia](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JutgSZHugvQ), two March war-market updates, then the April run on [Russian gold and the ruble](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7q88UbXPoC0) and ["Often Amazed, But Never Surprised"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7QRS6YAiqto). Across the entire deep-read record, exactly one video is flagged as genuinely new rather than recurring — the March 18, 2022 installment ([The Wartime Market: Why Gold and Silver Prices Are Not Reacting The W…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=77RCqH8YI64)), and even its title concedes the war-risk template wasn't working. That is where Christian declares a regime change three times over: "we are in a wartime market," that Putin "has destroyed russia's stature on the world plate stage," and that the war "demonstrated that there are numerous problems with their much vaulted uh military restructuring."

The Russian-gold thread is the most heavily recycled material in the file. It launches with the April 2022 ruble pieces, resurfaces through the [European natural gas scare](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OrJeb7JfHxY) of October 2022 and the [Wagner-era unrest](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jOMCS0SJHW4) of June 2023, and by an August 9, 2024 deep-read (recurring, but with new documentation — the archive itself skips from July to October that year) Christian is reporting that "俄罗斯一直在用黄金为其政府、国家和战争提供资金" — Russia has been funding its state and the war with gold since 2022 — while its central bank avoids dollars and euros ("俄罗斯央行尽可能避免使用美元和欧元作为资金"). Two months later the theme gets its question-mark reprise in [Will Russian Gold Flood The Market - Should Investors Be Worried?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VR5YhXKP6XU). The other substantive update lands November 11, 2022, when he revises the war's trajectory: "Russia's marching toward losing the war," with "signs of internal dissent" inside Russia and a Chinese "hard line has become even harder" — a genuinely shifted assessment, though still flagged recurring because the frame (what does Russia mean for metals) never changed.

The domestic-politics thread repeats on a four-year election clock with filler between. ["How High Can Gold Go After the US Election?"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nlSXt8Fkww0) (November 6, 2020) recurs as ["Gold and Silver After 2024 Elections"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i5VkhPikqoo) (November 15, 2024), with [The Cost of Political Dysfunction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7W3jEZqWWGQ), [Political Turmoil And What Comes Next](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HGZgA8ooH2Q) and [The Politics Of Gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OSSy8tfVqEE) as intermediate installments. Between elections he reaches for historical analogy — [Politics and Gold, The Lessons of 1933](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PVznAwB10mQ) — which matches the deep-read finding that his 2015 oil-market material (predating this archive) was already recycling "the first big increase in oil prices came in 1973" and the arrival of "institutional hot money," in a video whose new-information field reads, flatly, "nothing." The same 2015 reads had OPEC having "lost some of its market power over the last 10 years" and "Saudi Arabia has said to OPEC we will keep our production hi" — material that resurfaces neatly in the June 2024 [Saudi Oil Impact](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6JvZ4Uhb6Es) update. Around the 2024 vote, a deep-read dated November 19 flags one change only: "我们消除了一个不确定因素——总统人选确定" — the single uncertainty of the presidency has been removed. The follow-through on January 10, 2025 bolts fresh numbers onto the deficits-drive-gold frame: employment data that "came in very good," Elon Musk's doubts about budget cuts, and "interest rates have been rising over the last week or so."

The Middle East and tariff thread shows the recycling at its most mechanical — and where it visibly strains. [How War Between Israel And Iran Could Impact Gold And Silver Prices](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H3KpZZ9_pnI) (October 2024) and [Will Tariffs Extend The Bull Market?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KYxf_7fcHgs) (April 2025) re-run the war-risk template; the June 13, 2025 surge video ([Gold And Silver Prices Surge: Economic Concerns As Middle East Tensio…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kC0W0g9WhL0)) carries the sharpest genuinely new claim in the late record — that the London meeting produced only an "agreement was that they would continue to talk," contradicting "the US government saying that the tariff trade war" had been resolved. By March 2026 the frame breaks in public: prices ["Jump As War Risk Grows"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U_W0iRucHyg) on March 10, then ["Are Falling Despite Iran Conflict Escalati…"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jl8g4HfCWzA) one week later — same conflict, opposite arrows, which is the clearest evidence that this is a format rather than a forecast. The spring 2026 cluster then rotates the standing cast of state actors — [India warning citizens off gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hk3kpcMhsEY), [China mattering "more than ever"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H8jB9O1y_nk), a [CIA-gold silver update](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2UJgqCeQ_fU) — before settling back into the evergreen warning mode of ["New Risks Are Building Fast!"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O-RRUlGQb6o).

The net cadence: one geopolitical video in quiet years (2021) versus seven or eight in shock years (2022, 2024), compressing to weekly only during acute episodes like the March–April 2022 invasion cluster and the May–June 2026 run; mid-cycle years are bridged by war-plus-rates hybrids like [War, Interest Rates, and Alerts](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0jhdk5xt6JI), the [China-and-Japan commentary](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KD0RCTD9zDI) and ["Silver Plated Missiles"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rniBAo17ZhI). Of the eight deep-reads, only March 18, 2022 is wholly new; the rest are recurring frames with dated updates bolted on. One caveat worth stating plainly: the deep-read evidence samples eight videos against a 31-item archive, two of them from 2015 before the archive even begins, so the novelty judgments here rest on a thin slice of the series.

study/cpm-group/topic/monetary-policy-an.text:
Across 29 videos from January 2021 to June 2026, CPM Group's monetary-policy commentary is less a chain of arguments than a small stock of theses restated on a schedule. The rates-versus-gold explainer is the workhorse: it surfaces as [CPM Group - Interest Rates: Gold's Most Complicated and Important Rel…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y39eAhDCdI4) in January 2021, [Why Interest Rates Won't Hurt Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RiRYdTEmEpw) in August 2021, [How Interest Rates May Affect Gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=im271XZWR18) in May 2022, [What Future Lower Interest Rates Mean For Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ju03xyxarVk) in December 2023, and [Gold And Silver Market Update: Why Interest Rate Changes May Mislead …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-6Zt6_Rj4EQ) in June 2026 — roughly an annual rerun with only the sign of the rate move flipped. The gold-versus-inflation explainer runs on the same clock: [The Real Relationship Between Gold and Inflation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5o9BHtiXJ_M) (October 2021), [What Makes Gold An Excellent Hedge Against Inflation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kYkxdMHkAG0) (August 2022), [What Inflation Means For Gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4nHl7qMQnKk) (September 2022), and [Gold And Inflation: It's Not So Simple](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aiGDIKClJT8) (February 2023). A third template — the inflation-recession-outlook combo — recurs in [How Inflation, Interest Rates and Recession May Affect Gold and Silve…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=10zL22_Y39s) (June 2022), [2024 Gold And Silver Forecast: Inflation, Recession, and Profiting Fr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3BGoTQ7i_vg) (May 2024), and [Gold And Silver Market Update: Inflation, Recession, and Precious Met…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XmWL2vGkk-o) (April 2025). Even the punchline is recycled: [Why Lower Inflation Will Lead To Higher Gold and Silver Prices](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lzZ7Thf5OVE) (December 2022) and [Gold and Silver Soar As Inflation Falls Flat: This Is Why](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fo9SbQlJbdc) (November 2023) are the same disinflation-is-bullish argument twelve months apart.

The cadence tracks the inflation cycle, not the ideas. The titled archive is dormant after January 2021 until late August, then runs hot — eight videos in the final twenty weeks of 2021 and ten across 2022, close to biweekly — before thinning to five in 2023, two each in 2024 and 2025, and one in 2026. The deep reads confirm the recycling: of ten segments examined, only the May 14, 2021 treatment of the April CPI/PPI release is flagged as non-recurring, and it contains the archive's last genuinely new analytical points — the base-effect argument ("you're measuring it against april 2020 which was the beginning of the lockdown") and the observation that "the core inflation figures were actually higher than the headline figures which is unusual." After that, "new" means whatever print just landed. An August 13, 2021 segment is marked new = nothing, its only changes a record in Fed reverse-repo volumes and a Gary Gensler regulatory aside; September 24, 2021's novelty is one CPI report ("the only component of the cpi that was up more than two percent was petroleum-based energy"; used autos "actually was down about one and a half percent") plus the dot plot; March 18, 2022 and January 6, 2023 are both new = nothing outright. The lone lane-change is a late-2021 detour into [Nostalgia For A Gold Standard That Never Was](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gTCGEdqDwWk) and [What the Constitution REALLY says about Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NDU7yndPMC0), after which it is back to CPI-and-Fed material. The one new exogenous variable is war, which enters the frame in April 2022 ([Gold and Silver Prices Rise as Inflation and War Take Its Toll, This …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jWAqgYvBuV0)); the closest things to new arguments are title-level tweaks — [The Rise Of Gold: More Than Just Inflation (Part 1)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jk5ZPSXui3Y) in February 2022 and the "Not So Simple" walk-back of the simple hedge framing in February 2023.

The "something has changed" moments cluster on data days, and the author flags each one. September 24, 2021: the Fed "basically agreed with that" transitory framing, projecting rates "up to about two percent by 2023" — a shift the channel then headlines as [Gold and Silver Are Adjusting To A New Monetary Policy Regime](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0obgfA3eB0Q). December 14, 2021, in [Gold and Silver Show Weakness As Concerns Over Inflation Rise, What W…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L_igFqCmfZI): "the producer price index data came out for the united states and it was very high," so "gold and silver fell and they fell significantly" and "silver broke below 22," with money-supply growth cited "around 65 percent." March 18, 2022: "the feds said hey we're going to be even more aggressive fighting inflation than everybody thought," with "six… interest rate hikes" expected. May 20, 2022 brings the first real turn — "inflation data has started to peak and turn down," and Ukraine "may develop in a way that further reduces the war premium." November 11, 2022: the market's "most probable expectation… is another 50 basis point increase" in December followed by 25s, on "signs of peaking inflation," feeding directly into December's lower-inflation-is-bullish thesis. January 6, 2023: the Fed "doesn't see the inflation going away anytime soon" and would be "lucky if they get down to about five percent."

The loudest change-flags come at the end of the covered evidence. On December 1, 2023 the author declares the regime over: "The FED has stopped raising interest rates," "interest rates do look like they're Peak they peaked," and "what's happened interest rates have fallen" — "now they're down to about 4.2%" on the ten-year, with long rates having "come down much more sharply" than short rates and cuts expected "sometime in the march to May period of time." That is the last deep-read in the digest; what follows — [Precious Metals Update: How Inflation and Fed Policies Affect Gold an…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZHxPejxwviU) (August 2024), the April 2025 outlook, and [Gold, Silver, and the Fed's Warning of What's Coming Next](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hgp1yn1I-Y8) (October 2025) — looks from titles alone like the old templates relabeled, but there is no transcript evidence after December 2023, so whether anything new entered post-pause cannot be established here. What the record does show is a fixed framework (rates don't mechanically hurt metals; the inflation link is complicated) re-run against each fresh print, while the framing itself whipsaws: [Critical Time For Silver as Inflation Wanes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AbmjEzDxiGY) in November 2021 gives way within weeks to rising-inflation worry and then [Prepare For Higher Interest Rates and Lower Gold and Silver prices - …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3iijoftbjEk) in January 2022 — a tension with August 2021's rates-won't-hurt thesis the archive never explicitly resolves.

study/cpm-group/topic/central-bank-gold-.text:
Central bank gold is a workhorse topic in this archive — thirteen pieces between April 2021 and February 2026, arriving in bursts rather than on a steady drumbeat. Three landed in 2021 alone: the Hungarian purchase story in April ([The Impact of Hungarian Central Bank purchases and record London inve…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tn8tkU67WHE)), a practices overview in June ([Central Bank Gold Practices; US Debt and Gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fimg7ZB8wGA)), and a "central banks seen waiting to buy" piece in October ([Central Banks Seen Waiting To Buy More Gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FFUYu5z2xm8)). The topic then thinned out — the Russia question of June 2022 ([Has Russia Just Sold Its Gold?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4LQa4a0hNgM)), a China-reserves dig in January 2023 ([Uncovering the Truth Behind China's Gold Reserves & Silver Mine Reser…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BNUrHI4gHNY)), and a back-to-basics explainer in September 2023 ([Central Bank Gold Buying Explained](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NLGWwaA8hYU)) — before 2024 became the densest year, with five pieces from January through November. The recycled spine never moves: who is buying, who is holding back, and why central banks want the metal at all, restated most nakedly in August 2024's "Why Central Banks Own Gold And Investors Should Too" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ETnOdXK0jLM)).

The deep-read flags confirm the recycling pattern: nearly every dated entry is marked recurring, and the "new" material inside them is mostly data refreshes and rebuttals rather than new frameworks. On 2023-02-22 the contribution was rebutting claims about central banks "dumping" the dollar, with the author complaining "there's a tremendous amount of misinformation about Central Bank activity both with the dollar and with gold." By January 2024 ([Gold Market Update: Central Bank Buyers and Sellers](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=soQnqRYSKeU)) he was correcting his own numbers — "2022 did not see 20 million ounces that was a mistake... our view was it was about 10.2 million ounces" — while tallying the fresh 2023 data ("China has reported December and they bought another 290,000... so they their purchases uh are about 7.2 7.3 million ounces"), naming the sellers (Turkey, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan), and clarifying that no central bank is plotting a return to the gold standard. March 2024's addition was similarly evergreen: silver stays out of reserves because its market is too small.

Genuinely new arguments are scarcer. The only deep-read entry flagged non-recurring is 2024-08-09 ([Which Central Banks Are Not Buying Gold And Why It Matters To You](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UGckn7Inkww)): Ghana enters the story — "加纳... 找到柴油进口商，表示如果进口商愿意，可以用黄金而不是美元支付柴油货款" (Ghana approached diesel importers offering payment in gold rather than dollars) — a stress case of gold as payment for essentials, paired with the blunt pushback "不，实际上，大多数中央银行的黄金储备都非常低" against tales of heavy African accumulation. The same episode flagged a behavioral turn — "过去一年，尤其是自四月以来几个月的高金价，改变了央行的黄金买卖活动" — plus a cautionary tale about a bank that decided to buy in 2010 and "至今仍未开始购买黄金," which undercuts survey-based predictions. The other real pivot is 2025-03-28: "That's a 40% decline in the volume of gold being purchased," with the baton passing outright — "It's been investment demand, strong investment demand that has driven the gold price" — a reweighting that September 2024's both-drivers framing ([Central Bank and Investor Demand Are Driving Gold Prices Higher](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DJbciTJrSms)) hadn't anticipated.

The explicit "this has changed" moments, in order: the narrative turning misinformation-heavy (Feb 2023); China's 7.3-million-ounce total, the 2022 correction, and the transparency claim — "there's been a great increase in uh transparency on the part of central banks over the last 20 or 30 years" — plus "China... made an announcement of changing their attitudes toward gold" (Jan 2024); price-driven behavior change (Aug 2024); and the 40% decline with investment demand taking over (Mar 2025). Note the transparency argument itself gets recycled: announced in January 2024, it resurfaces as the thesis of February 2026's [Central Bank Gold: Secrecy To Transparency](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZeV-xWUOjy8), with the secrecy angle already teased in November 2025's [A Secret Plan To Buy Gold? What Central Banks Are Really Doing](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4B0f0LUn-0) — the same point arriving in new clothes two years later. One caveat: the 2021–22 items, the late-2024 cluster ([The Countries Still Boosting Gold Reserves, And What They Have In Com…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FpyNS_gfSX4)), and the 2025–26 pieces are titles only in this digest, so fine-grained reuse inside them can't be verified here.

person/adrian-day.text:
Adrian Day appears in this corpus exactly once — as an interview guest on David Lin's show — and that single appearance is essentially all the recorded evidence we have. There are no documented bullish, bearish, or neutral stances in the digest, and the topic timelines are empty. That means no dated calls, no quotable positions, and no way to trace how his views have moved over time. For an analyst whose public career has been built on taking positions in precious metals and resource equities, the silence here is the story: whatever he argued in that conversation wasn't captured in a form this corpus can cite.

Widely known context fills in the outline, if not the substance. Day is the chairman and CEO of Adrian Day Asset Management, a long-standing fixture in the gold-investing world, and the author of books on global and resource investing — a profile that makes him a natural fit for the kind of macro-and-metals programming David Lin hosts. But none of that translates into citable claims here. We can't say what he was bullish or bearish on, when he said it, or whether it marked a shift from prior thinking.

The honest verdict: this page is a stub, and deliberately so. Rather than pad it with generic biography dressed up as analysis, we've kept it to what the record shows — one guest appearance, zero stances logged, no timeline. If Day returns to the show or other coverage enters the corpus, the portrait can be rebuilt around dated calls and a real stance history. Until then, readers should treat his inclusion as an index entry rather than a track record.

person/andrew-kang.text:
Andrew Kang is a cryptocurrency investor and venture capitalist, best known as the founder and partner at Mechanism Capital, a crypto-focused investment firm. In this corpus he appears through a single long-form conversation — "The Next Breakout Investing Opportunity?" on Raoul Pal's *The Journey Man*, dated August 20, 2026 ([The Next Breakout Investing Opportunity? w/ Andrew Kang | R…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2qsUh1sMDfs)) — and what's striking about it is how far beyond crypto the discussion ranges for someone whose career was built there.

His headline claim from that appearance: the total AI market cap is going to be "at least 10, 20, 30x times larger than Bitcoin," a statement he makes while explicitly volunteering that he still likes Bitcoin ([The Next Breakout Investing Opportunity? w/ Andrew Kang | R…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2qsUh1sMDfs)). He grounds the scale argument in private markets rather than public tape, pointing to how OpenAI and Anthropic "in the span of three years just speedrun to a trillion dollars" in private valuations ([The Next Breakout Investing Opportunity? w/ Andrew Kang | R…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2qsUh1sMDfs)).

The most concrete agenda item is robotics. Kang states plainly that "the goal is to be one of the largest robotics investors in the world," with reinvestment aimed at increasing robotics equity exposure ([The Next Breakout Investing Opportunity? w/ Andrew Kang | R…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2qsUh1sMDfs)). He frames it using an explicitly borrowed template: "Micro Strategy, their TAM was Bitcoin. At their peak, they reached around a hundred billion dollars in market cap. Our TAM is the… market cap" ([The Next Breakout Investing Opportunity? w/ Andrew Kang | R…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2qsUh1sMDfs)). He also reaches outside crypto for a compounding model, citing companies like Constellation Software and TransDigm "where their whole business model is based on acquisitions" ([The Next Breakout Investing Opportunity? w/ Andrew Kang | R…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2qsUh1sMDfs)) — the vocabulary of a traditional equity operator applied to a robotics thesis.

A note on how much weight this can bear: all eleven stances logged from this appearance classify as neutral — no bullish or bearish calls on Bitcoin, MSTR, or anything else — so what the record captures is a thesis statement, not a set of tradeable positions. And because it is a single snapshot from one date, there is no timeline of view movement to chart here. What the coverage does show, thin as it is, is the shape of an interesting argument: a crypto-native investor conceding his home market's ceiling while mapping the MicroStrategy playbook onto a different, larger TAM.

person/andrew-kang-robo-strategies-robo-.text:
Andrew Kang writes and publishes under the Robo Strategies / Robo Global Strategies banner, and within this corpus he appears as a guest on Raoul Pal's *The Journey Man* — a circuit where macro and digital-asset themes dominate the conversation. That placement alone says something about where he sits in the debate: alongside the Pal orbit of macro-to-crypto commentators rather than in traditional equity research.

Beyond the byline and the appearance, though, the record here is thin, and it is worth saying so plainly. The digest contains no dated calls, no recorded quotes, and no directional stances — zero bullish, zero bearish, zero neutral — and the topic timeline is empty from oldest to newest. There is exactly one instance of him in a solo author/host role in this collection. In other words, there is nothing in the current corpus to anchor a "strongest call" or to trace a shift in his views over time.

So the honest portrait, for now, is a stub with a clear shape: a commentator positioned in the Pal-adjacent macro/crypto conversation, whose actual positions — on bitcoin, on liquidity, on anything — have not yet been captured in dated form. person/andy-unanue.text:

person/ben-cowen.text:
Ben Cowen occupies a distinctive corner of crypto commentary: less the permabull market evangelist, more the engineer-turned-analyst who frames Bitcoin's cycle behavior in terms of quantitative benchmarks — realized price, log regression bands, dominance cycles — and then refuses to promise which way the next move breaks. That measured, conditional style is exactly what shows up in the snapshot this corpus has of him. On August 25, 2026, discussing whether Bitcoin's rally had legs, he laid out the downside scenario first: if the price was "rejected here at around like 80 81k," he saw "still a chance that we go lower" and "search out the realized price" — his go-to on-chain level for where a bear case would naturally bottom ([Why Is Bitcoin Suddenly Exploding? Will The Rally Continue?…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gTn7-oSb_ic)).

Yet the same commentary carried the bullish contingency. In the same breath as that warning, Cowen told viewers to "just prepare yourself ideally for a bull run" ([Why Is Bitcoin Suddenly Exploding? Will The Rally Continue?…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gTn7-oSb_ic)). That pairing — a hard level that would confirm weakness, and an instruction not to sleep on the upside — is the signature move. He rarely plants a flag on direction; he plants flags on the levels that would *force* a directional call.

It's worth being plain about the limits of the record here: the digest contains only these two entries, both from the same day, both coded neutral, with no earlier or later timelines showing movement in his views. So this page can't yet chart an evolution in his stance the way it can for louder analysts — and that absence is arguably in character. Cowen's value proposition, as this single snapshot suggests, is not the dramatic reversal but the disciplined both-sides framing: name the rejection level, respect the realized price below it, and stay positioned for the bull case anyway.

Her headline argument from that conversation is about where crypto's marginal buyer went: "I think that for your marginal crypto buyer that AI sucked a lot of air out of the room" — the same risk-hungry retail dollar that would otherwise chase tokens is currently feeding the AI trade ([Why The Next Phase of Crypto Is Bigger Than You Think w/ Bl…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q2TAHZIBpdE)). She extended the diagnosis to crypto's narrative engine itself, arguing it became "impossible to sustain that type of constant transformational news flow" — the sector had conditioned itself to need perpetual revolution, and that pace ran out of road ([Why The Next Phase of Crypto Is Bigger Than You Think w/ Bl…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q2TAHZIBpdE)). It's a more structural explanation than the usual "AI took the liquidity" line: the crowding-out is real, but crypto's exhaustion was partly self-inflicted.

The constructive half of her thesis is about plumbing, not price. Different blockchains are suited to different things, she argued, which makes interoperability "absolutely key" — the endgame is a fully interoperable landscape rather than a single winning chain ([Why The Next Phase of Crypto Is Bigger Than You Think w/ Bl…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q2TAHZIBpdE)). Within that, she named the prize: the winner will be whoever can "abstract away the back end and bridging" — all the friction that crypto natives tolerate and everyone else won't ([Why The Next Phase of Crypto Is Bigger Than You Think w/ Bl…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q2TAHZIBpdE)). person/ceo-cotec.text:
Julian Treger is the Chief Executive Officer of CoTec Holdings Corp., a Toronto Venture Exchange-listed investment company that hunts for disruptive technologies and scales them to improve productivity, safety and sustainability in the natural resources sector. He is very much a resources man running a technology vehicle: before CoTec, he co-founded and served as managing partner of London-based Audley Capital Advisors, a private equity firm focused on extractive industries — a background that explains the way he pitches the company, less like a venture capitalist and more like a portfolio investor marking up assets.

The clearest snapshot of what he argues for comes from a single long-form appearance, on "Pitch Rick Ep #2," dated 2026-08-19. There he laid out what is essentially a sum-of-the-parts case. His Mag Iron stake — CoTec owns 17% — was just marked at a $550 million valuation in an internal rights-issue raise ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)). Next, he said CoTec was about to take Hypermag to market to raise money hub by hub, with the first hub valued in the several hundreds of millions ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)). The endgame, as he described it, is an IPO to raise ideally around $200 million of equity, after which the vast bulk of CoTec's stake would be spun off to CoTec shareholders ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)). On the debt side, he said the company is engaged with two commercial banks as well as XM to fund roughly $100–120 million of project finance ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)).

He was notably direct about the timeline and the balance sheet. Revenues, he said, are expected to start "at the end of next year or the beginning of '28" — an 18-month window from the interview — meaning CoTec is candidly pre-revenue for the foreseeable future ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)). And the cash position is thin: around $10 million, bolstered somewhat by warrant exercises in the second quarter ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)). That is the crux of the debate around Treger's pitch: large internal valuation marks against a small cash buffer and an 18-month runway to first revenue. He doesn't paper over that gap — he simply argues the capital plan (debt, hub-level raises, then an IPO and spin-out) closes it.

As for how his views have moved over time: the record here can't say. Everything dated in this corpus comes from that one August 2026 appearance, and all of it codes neutral — there are no earlier bullish or bearish calls to measure a shift against. Coverage of Treger is thin, and what exists is a valuation-and-financing story rather than a documented evolution of conviction. person/chris-vermeulen.text:
Chris Vermeulen is the founder and chief market strategist of The Technical Traders, an independent research service built around technical analysis — market commentary and trade alerts aimed at ETF swing traders working equities, indices, and precious metals. His public profile runs through financial media, most notably repeated appearances on David Lin's show, where he frames the conversation around trend identification, market timing, and risk management rather than macro prophecy. That framing matters for reading his record: he tends to describe what price is doing and what conditions would change his mind, not to plant flags.

The two appearances on file show that method at work. On June 25, 2026, in an interview pointedly titled around a "24% Collapse Incoming" red flag ([24% Collapse Incoming: Trader Reveals Shocking Market Red Flag…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0f1pMEpQ61U)), Vermeulen's actual commentary was more measured than the thumbnail. He argued falling oil "definitely helps the economy" and should help control inflation to some degree, noting that energy runs about 10% of the average investor's after-tax spending, with food the bigger household expense ([24% Collapse Incoming: Trader Reveals Shocking Market Red Flag…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0f1pMEpQ61U)). On the AI trade he refused to pick a side, calling it "a very convoluted bubble" — one where enormous real earnings sit underneath a debate about whether it's a bubble at all ([24% Collapse Incoming: Trader Reveals Shocking Market Red Flag…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0f1pMEpQ61U)).

By his next appearance on August 20, 2026, the tone had shifted from caution to a rare outright directional call. He described the S&P 500 chopping sideways for months with the Nasdaq pulling back ([Interest Rates Explode: 'Everything Blows Up' Once This Leverage…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=81UzjvXn2no)), laid out his level-based framework — the index "should run 3% or 5%" under those conditions — and then delivered his clearest stance in the record: "it ended up holding and now we've got this next leg higher started" ([Interest Rates Explodes: 'Everything Blows Up' Once This Leverage…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=81UzjvXn2no)). That bullish read on the S&P 500 is the strongest call in his file. Precious metals, by contrast, got no such commitment: he acknowledged the frenzy — "everybody's going haywire… to the moon… they're going higher" — but stopped short of calling a top or chasing ([Interest Rates Explode: 'Everything Blows Up' Once This Leverage…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=81UzjvXn2no)).

It's worth being honest about the shape of this record: it's thin — two dated appearances — and it skews heavily neutral (one bullish stance against eight neutral ones), which is less indecision than a technician's habit of speaking in conditionals. But the trajectory is visible all the same: from red-flag caution in late June to constructive on the index by late August, without ever joining the gold euphoria. Whether that discipline ages well is exactly what the next set of appearances should settle.

person/danielle-dimartino-booth.text:
Danielle DiMartino Booth occupies a specific niche in macro commentary: she is one of the few prominent Fed critics who actually sat inside the building. After roughly a decade at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, where she served as an advisor to Bank President Richard Fisher, she left to argue her case from the outside — founding the research firm Quill Intelligence, publishing the Daily Feather, and writing *Fed Up*, a book-length case against Fed policymaking culture. Within this corpus, however, her documented footprint is a single interview appearance opposite David Lin, and nothing else.

Her public reputation rests on a consistent thesis: headline statistics flatter the economy, and both markets and the Fed get burned by believing them. She has built that brand on granular skepticism of labor-market data, close attention to credit stress beneath a calm surface, and a view that the central bank systematically misreads the economy it is steering. Those are the broad strokes of who she is and what she argues for — but it bears repeating that they come from her well-known public persona, not from anything recorded here.

As for how her views have moved: this record cannot say. The ledger shows zero logged bullish, bearish, or neutral positions and an empty topic timeline, so there is no dated sequence of calls to chart — no "turned cautious in March" moments, no reversals, nothing to anchor an evolution. That absence reflects thin coverage rather than a lack of conviction; Booth's public commentary is rarely shy of positions. Until more of her appearances are logged with dates and stances, this portrait will have to stand on biography alone.

person/darius-dale.text:
Darius Dale is a macro investor and risk-management strategist best known as the founder of 42 Macro, an investment-research firm selling systematic asset-allocation and risk-on/risk-off signals to institutional investors and RIAs since roughly 2021. Before that he spent about a decade at Keith McCullough's Hedgeye Risk Management, rising to portfolio manager. His method is regime-based investing driven by growth, inflation, and policy — packaged in frameworks cited as "D.A.M.E." (debt, assets, markets, economics) and a "T.I.P.S."-style trend-following risk-management process — and he works the macro-podcast circuit regularly, including Forward Guidance and MacroVoices.

The record in this corpus is narrow — two appearances, eight days apart in August 2026 — but it forms one coherent picture. On Forward Guidance's ["The Growth Strategy Trapping The Fed"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vvMTOKRR0SE) (August 12, 2026), Dale called it "a great short to medium-term outlook for stocks, gold, bitcoin, and commodities, not so much for the dollar... and bonds," while flagging "bubble-like conditions in the equity market" and bond-market trouble from all the extra nominal GDP growth, with r-star now priced above the real effective funds rate — in his telling, a signal beamed straight back to the bond market.

Eight days later on [MacroVoices #546](https://www.macrovoices.com/1546-macrovoices-546-darius-dale-darius-dale-for-potus-2028) — episode title, I kid you not, "Darius Dale for POTUS 2028" — he scaled the same view into a "Fourth Turnings" framework: "buckle up, expect some volatility, but twenty twenty-six is gonna be a... great year for risk assets, stocks in particular," with S&P 500 returns and earnings growth historically strong in such eras, just with wider max-min ranges. The structural engine underneath is a geopolitically driven supply-demand imbalance in the Treasury market that widens over time, forcing policy responses and an erosion of Fed independence, with money-supply growth accelerating sharply through financial repression and dollar debasement ([MacroVoices #546](https://www.macrovoices.com/1546-macrovoices-546-darius-dale-darius-dale-for-potus-2028)).

His most concrete calls came on that August 20 appearance: Bitcoin is "going to soar past its all-time high last August. It's a matter of when, not if," and gold will go "way back past its... all-time high in January," while "the dollar tends to be debased substantially during Fourth Turnings, particularly against a more base form of money, which is gold" ([MacroVoices #546](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VBIeV5Ix7b0)). On rates he expects policy to turn substantially more dovish over the next 18 months than what's currently priced, with the policy rate ending below even the lowest estimates on the forward curve — yet he simultaneously put fair value around 5.75–5.80% on the 10-year and close to 6.50% on the 30-year, with yields backing up first before real 10-year yields decline substantially and Treasury price declines get curtailed by policy intervention ([MacroVoices #546](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VBIeV5Ix7b0)).

Two caveats on the shape of this file. The stance ledger tags all 36 entries neutral, which undersells how plainly directional the talk is — constructive risk assets, hostile dollar and long bonds. And because coverage clusters in a single month, the timeline shows no evolution of views, just one thesis delivered twice with unusual consistency. The genuinely interesting tension is in the rates section: yields backing up toward his own 5.75% fair value while forecasting a far more dovish Fed is a gap most commentators can't hold open — Dale resolves it through the Fourth Turnings logic (nominal growth up, real yields down, policy forced to follow) rather than the standard dovish-equals-lower-yields playbook. Whether that framework survives contact with the tape is, on this record, still an open question.

person/darius-dale-guest.text:
Darius Dale is the founder and CEO of 42 Macro, and on Forward Guidance he plays the role of the framework-driven macro generalist — someone more comfortable ranking assets against each other than planting a flag on any single one. His episode "The Growth Strategy Trapping The Fed," from August 12, 2026, is the clearest snapshot of that style in this corpus, and it's also one of the appearances logged as a solo hosting/authoring turn rather than a straight interview ([The Growth Strategy Trapping The Fed | Darius Dale](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vvMTOKRR0SE)).

But the more interesting part is the tension he builds into the same appearance: alongside the constructive tape call, he flagged "bubble-like conditions in the equity market" and "issues in the bond market associated with all that extra nominal GDP growth" ([The Growth Strategy Trapping The Fed | Darius Dale](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vvMTOKRR0SE)). Read together, the stance is: ride the liquidity-driven upside near term, but treat it as a bubble you're trading, not a foundation you trust — which is why the coding here lands him neutral across equities, gold, bitcoin, the dollar, and S&P 500 exposure rather than cleanly bullish or bearish.

As for how his views have moved over time: this record can't say. The corpus holds a single dated appearance, all of it from August 2026, with no earlier calls to compare against. That's thin coverage for a strategist whose whole brand is regime-switching, so any claim that Dale "turned" on any asset would outrun the data. What the record does show, on one day at least, is a coherent house view: everything rallies except the dollar and bonds, and the everything-rally itself is the problem the Fed eventually has to deal with.

person/dave-collum.text:
Dave Collum is an organic chemist by trade and a macro pessimist by avocation — a longtime Cornell University professor who built a second career as a finance commentator, best known for his lengthy and irreverent annual "Year in Review" essays, originally published on Peak Prosperity and widely passed around sites like Zero Hedge. His framing is skeptical and Austrian-economics-influenced: bubbles, debt, central bank policy, gold, and the fragility of fiat currency are his recurring beats, and he has been a regular guest on finance podcasts such as MacroVoices to make that case.

The clearest documented snapshot of his current thinking comes from an August 13, 2026 interview, and it is a stacked-bubble argument: "we have an AI bubble on top of a real estate bubble on top of a general equity bubble on top of... private credit," in his telling ([Dave Collum: The AI Bubble Will Break Down VERY Quickly](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ku8l-I6IU1A)). Within that stack, he singles out AI as the likely first domino — "the AI bubble could be the one that you see first" — and argues the boom could unravel quickly, pointing to AI companies raising hundreds of billions of dollars amid pervasive optimism ([Dave Collum: The AI Bubble Will Break Down VERY Quickly](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ku8l-I6IU1A)). That is his strongest recent call: not a general crash forecast, but a specific claim about which layer of the froth gives way first.

His positioning on hard assets runs alongside that call. Gold "continues to play a major role in his portfolio," platinum is described as one of his preferred commodity trades, and his gold price talk is deliberately hyperbolic — asked what gold could be worth in twenty years, he answers "infinity," then hedges into "it could be worth 100,000 but it could be worth 200,000" ([Dave Collum: The AI Bubble Will Break Down VERY Quickly](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ku8l-I6IU1A)). Worth noting the tell in the hedging: despite the infinity rhetoric, he explicitly says a dollar collapse in the next ten years is something he doesn't think will happen ([Dave Collum: The AI Bubble Will Break Down VERY Quickly](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ku8l-I6IU1A)). That's the characteristic Collum move — maximalist-sounding theater on metals, with the actual stated forecast more measured.

One caveat about the record here: the coded timeline is thin, anchored to that single August 2026 interview, and every scored stance in it is neutral — fourteen neutrals, zero bull or bear calls. That's partly an artifact of the source material (descriptive quotes rather than scored positions), but it also reflects how Collum operates: his views live in long-form essays and conversation rather than clean, datable calls. The bubble thesis and the metals conviction are well documented; a track record of specific, dated predictions is not something this digest can establish.

person/doug.text:
"Doug" is about as thin a subject as a profile can have: identified only by first name in the available record, with no surname, firm or professional title to anchor him. What the material does show is a man who appears as an interview guest and stock commentator in the junior mining space, speaking — by his own framing — as a shareholder rather than a promoter. Nearly everything in his file flows from a single appearance, an August 17, 2026 conversation pointedly titled [80 Projects and 17 Royalties, But Can They Really Monetize …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M0eDetccI5M). His central position is a stake in GGL Resources Corp. (GGL.V), the TSX Venture-listed junior explorer he considers substantially undervalued on unrecognized asset value.

His argument, such as it is, is a patience trade built on catalysts. On GGL he is specific about the trigger: he's optimistic the share price "will go up quite well" once the company completes the deal for the Hopper ([80 Projects and 17 Royalties, But Can They Really Monetize …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M0eDetccI5M)). In the strategic-metals discussion he even puts a clock on it — "very optimistic that if we were to do this interview again in a year's time" at least one of the anticipated catalysts will have been realized ([80 Projects and 17 Royalties, But Can They Really Monetize …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M0eDetccI5M)). The same logic extends across his other names: Trifecta has "pretty good assets" that aren't "being fully valued yet at all" and have "room to run up" ([80 Projects and 17 Royalties, But Can They Really Monetize …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M0eDetccI5M)), all against a macro backdrop he cites of continued strength in precious metals and sustained interest in critical metals ([80 Projects and 17 Royalties, But Can They Really Monetize …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M0eDetccI5M)).

What's striking is the gap between the optimism of his language and the neutrality of his record: across eight logged statements there is not one outright bullish or bearish call. He is a holder, not a table-pounder — "I'm quite comfortable holding on to them for the time being," he says of his positions, precisely because they "haven't had the runup yet in this market" ([80 Projects and 17 Royalties, But Can They Really Monetize …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M0eDetccI5M)). His most candid moment comes on SMD.V, where he concedes that over the past ten years a buyer "would have been down," the company having then sat "on the shoulder of a very active exploration program" ([80 Projects and 17 Royalties, But Can They Really Monetize …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M0eDetccI5M)) — and where he warns that value recognition "is going to take one of a number of catalysts" rather than arriving on its own ([80 Projects and 17 Royalties, But Can They Really Monetize …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M0eDetccI5M)).

On the question of how his views have moved over time: they haven't, observably. Every dated item comes from the same day and the same interview, so this is a snapshot, not a trajectory — there is no before-and-after to chart. One curiosity worth flagging for future editors: he is described as a shareholder, yet several quotes drift into insider cadence — "we've been getting our ducks in line… to get some of our projects in play" ([80 Projects and 17 Royalties, But Can They Really Monetize …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M0eDetccI5M)) — an ambiguity the thin record never resolves. Until more appearances surface, Doug's file amounts to one honest interview from a patient junior-mining holder betting that catalysts, not conviction alone, will do the repricing.

person/doug-ceo-strategic-metals.text:
Doug runs Strategic Metals (SMD.V), and the honest way to describe his public posture is that of a portfolio-keeper rather than a promoter. ([80 Projects and 17 Royalties, But Can They Really Monetize …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M0eDetccI5M)). Doug's answer is patient but conditional. Where he does get concrete is on execution and on the past. On the operational side, he points to a couple of years spent "getting our ducks in line" to move projects into play ([80 Projects and 17 Royalties, But Can They Really Monetize …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M0eDetccI5M)). More striking is his candor on the backward-looking question: asked about the ten-year shareholder experience, he acknowledged flatly that "you would have been down," because a decade ago the company was still "on the shoulder of a very active exploration program" that has since receded ([80 Projects and 17 Royalties, But Can They Really Monetize …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M0eDetccI5M)). A note on limits: the record here is thin — a single interview, everything dated 2026-08-17, and all of it classified neutral, with no bullish or bearish calls on the tape. That means no view trajectory can be traced; whether Doug's catalyst talk hardens into a specific monetization event is exactly what future coverage would need to capture.

person/eric-balchunas.text:
Eric Balchunas is a Senior ETF Analyst, and one of the small handful of people whose names function as shorthand for the entire exchange-traded fund beat. His public profile is built at Bloomberg, where his core work is parsing fund launches, flows, fees and the structural quirks of the ETF wrapper, and amplified by an unusually large following for someone in a data-heavy research role — his running commentary on ETF flows has become one of the market's go-to real-time sentiment gauges. The clearest statement of his worldview came in book form with *The Bogle Effect* (2022): his through-line argument is that cheap, transparent, passively managed structures are still mid-conquest of the expensive active fund complex, and that Jack Bogle's fee war is the single most consequential force reshaping asset management. He is, in short, an evangelist for the low-cost index revolution — and a persistent skeptic of anything charging more to deliver what a broad ETF already provides.

That positioning makes him easy to summarize in broad strokes and surprisingly hard to score in a stance-shaped corpus. His daily output is descriptive — who launched what, how much money moved, which fee got cut — rather than the buy/sell verdicts that map cleanly onto bullish/bearish/neutral grids. He is famous for narrating events like the spot bitcoin ETF approval saga, but narrating a story is not the same as putting a rating on it.

Which brings up the honest limitation of this page: the extracted record behind it is thin to the point of empty. There are no dated calls, no captured quotes, no stance placements (zero across all three buckets), and no topic timelines — the digest doesn't even record his employer or full role title. A reader coming here for his strongest documented calls with dates, or for evidence of how his views have shifted over time, will not find it yet. That is a gap in the corpus, not necessarily evidence he hasn't taken positions; it just means this portrait will have to stay a sketch until the record catches up with how much he actually says in public.

On that last point, the record here is thin, and it's worth saying so plainly. person/frank-giustra-relayed-by-jay-mart.text:
Frank Giustra is the kind of figure whose name carries weight in resource-market circles well before any single call attached to it: a Canadian financier who built his fortune financing and growing mining companies, and who in recent years has become one of the more prominent public voices arguing for gold ownership and against unanchored fiat money. In this corpus, however, his views arrive secondhand — relayed through Jay Martin's interviews — and that framing matters, since what we have is Giustra as presented on someone else's stage.

That said, the record here is unusually thin. There are no dated calls, no logged stance mix, and no topic timelines for him at all — nothing marking when he turned bullish or bearish on anything, or whether his convictions shifted as gold's run progressed. For a man whose pronouncements on gold and monetary policy move retail sentiment in this space, the absence of a timestamped track record is itself the notable finding: it tells you more about the gaps in coverage than about any change in his thinking.

So the honest portrait is short. Giustra is a gold advocate and monetary skeptic by broad public reputation, and a recurring guest voice on Jay Martin's platform by this corpus's account. Whether his conviction has strengthened, wavered, or rotated across specific commodities is a question this digest simply cannot answer — and we won't pretend otherwise.

person/gareth-soloway.text:
Gareth Soloway is a veteran technical analyst — the sort of guest who talks in gap fills, trend lines and measured moves rather than macro narratives — and in this corpus he appears exactly once, as an interview guest on David Lin's show dated July 17, 2026 ([75% Tech Crash; Gareth Soloway Reveals Shocking Bottom For …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxFD9ufn8wg)). That single appearance is the entire record, and it should temper any grand portrait: seven logged stances, all neutral, not one outright bullish or bearish call on file. What the session does establish is his signature grammar of conditionals. On the S&P 500 he noted the market is "still above this trend line, which is around 7330 or so," warning that "if it breaks below that, that's where things start to fall apart and markets likely come down much, much harder and faster" ([75% Tech Crash; Gareth Soloway Reveals Shocking Bottom For …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxFD9ufn8wg)). Name the level, sketch both sides of it, commit to nothing until the chart decides — that is the method on display.

His most concrete observations that day were on oil and semiconductors. On crude, he flagged a gap fill "at around 67" that price had already tagged, and framed the pressure on oil as one-directional and political — "he is going to do whatever he has to do to get that oil price down" ([75% Tech Crash; Gareth Soloway Reveals Shocking Bottom For …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxFD9ufn8wg)). On the semiconductor ETF, he contextualized rather than predicted: the sector's nature is "very sharp pullbacks, very sharp recoveries," pointing to February 2025, when it fell 36% before a big rebound ([75% Tech Crash; Gareth Soloway Reveals Shocking Bottom For …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxFD9ufn8wg)). On mega-cap tech he described rotation, not exit — investors asking "where can we rotate that capital into?" and landing on names like Apple, which had made new all-time highs, with Apple due to "come back in a little bit" as the broader market bounced ([75% Tech Crash; Gareth Soloway Reveals Shocking Bottom For …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxFD9ufn8wg)).

There is a real tension worth flagging between the packaging and the substance. The video carries an apocalyptic title — "75% Tech Crash" and a "Shocking Bottom" ([75% Tech Crash; Gareth Soloway Reveals Shocking Bottom For …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxFD9ufn8wg)) — yet every quoted position is studiously two-sided: above 7330 the trend holds, below it things fall apart; semis are violent but historically recover; Apple is a destination for rotating capital. Either Soloway's crash case lives entirely in the un-quoted stretches of that interview, or the thumbnail is doing far more work than the chart. The record here doesn't settle which, and it shouldn't pretend to.

As for how his views have moved over time — the timeline simply can't say. One appearance, one date, all-neutral stances: there is no before and after to compare, no pivot to date. What can be said is that his default register is the conditional technical map rather than a directional verdict, and anyone wanting to know whether he actually turned bearish on tech — as the title implies — will need more appearances than this corpus currently holds.

person/gareth-soloway-guest.text:
Gareth Soloway is a Chief Market Strategist and technical analyst — a chart-first market commentator whose reputation rests on reading price structure rather than macro storytelling. Within this corpus, though, his record is thin: a single appearance dated July 17, 2026, on an episode titled "[75% Tech Crash; Gareth Soloway Reveals Shocking Bottom For …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxFD9ufn8wg)." That's the entire timeline, so any portrait of how his views have moved over time simply can't be drawn from what's on file here — there is one snapshot, not an arc.

What the snapshot shows is more measured than the episode's alarmist packaging. His stance mix on record is three neutral calls and nothing else. On Apple, he framed it tactically rather than directionally: "as we bounce, we should see Apple, for instance, come back in a little bit" ([75% Tech Crash; Gareth Soloway Reveals Shocking Bottom For …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxFD9ufn8wg)). On AI and semiconductors, he described investor behavior — capital actively looking for a rotation destination, "names like Apple, which has made new all-time highs" ([75% Tech Crash; Gareth Soloway Reveals Shocking Bottom For …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxFD9ufn8wg)) — a characterization of flows, not a buy or sell verdict. And on the semiconductor ETF SMH, his contribution was pattern-matching on volatility: "very sharp pullbacks, very sharp recoveries," pointing to the sector's 36% drawdown last February before a big rebound ([75% Tech Crash; Gareth Soloway Reveals Shocking Bottom For …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxFD9ufn8wg)). The through-line is a technician describing ranges and round trips, not a permabull or permabear.

That gap between thumbnail and transcript is itself worth noting: the show sold a "75% tech crash," while the strategist they booked was on the record hedging, contextualizing, and declining to pick a side on every topic extracted. Readers should take this page as a first sketch — one appearance, one link, no documented shifts. If he returns to the corpus, the interesting question will be whether the neutrality of July 2026 was a resting position or a pause before a directional call.
