person/harry.text:
Harry — who shows up here under the "High Yield Harry" banner — is, on the current record, a credit-market commentator captured at exactly one moment: an August 24, 2026 appearance on a show framed around the provocative question of whether private equity is broken ([Is Private Equity Broken? High Yield Harry on Wall Street's…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YOnxRmI6CV8)). That's the entire corpus on him — one source, one date, five stances, all coded neutral. So the honest framing up front: this is a sketch of a single argued position, not a track record, and anyone looking for a documented evolution of views won't find one yet.

His position sits deliberately between the two camps the episode title sets up. On the stress side, he notes that even well-established funds are seeing redemption rates climb quarter over quarter, and he expects the sector's 5% redemption-rate limit to come into play as that pressure builds ([Is Private Equity Broken? High Yield Harry on Wall Street's…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YOnxRmI6CV8)). He roots the strain in the rate regime rather than fraud or collapse — four years of high rates have stressed portfolio companies' free cash flow, with knock-on effects for how these holdings are valued ([Is Private Equity Broken? High Yield Harry on Wall Street's…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YOnxRmI6CV8)). But he resists the "broken" verdict: in his view, private credit is actually more advantageously positioned to "loan to own," restructure, and work through distressed situations rather than be flattened by them ([Is Private Equity Broken? High Yield Harry on Wall Street's…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YOnxRmI6CV8)). He adds an institutional-level point that cuts against treating private credit as an exotic appendage — in his telling, allocators are simply using it to replace credit products they would historically have accessed elsewhere ([Is Private Equity Broken? High Yield Harry on Wall Street's…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YOnxRmI6CV8)).

As for how his views have moved: the timelines show nothing to chart, since everything dates to the same day. What the record does establish is a distinctive shape to his argument — real redemption pressure and rate-squeezed cash flows, yes, but a structural case that private credit's restructuring toolkit leaves it better placed than the doom framing implies ([Is Private Equity Broken? High Yield Harry on Wall Street's…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YOnxRmI6CV8)). Whether he turns that nuanced stance into a directional call — on BDCs, on the redemption cycle, on where rates break something — is the open question this page can't yet answer.

person/harry-dent.text:
Harry Dent is an economic forecaster, financial newsletter author, and investment strategist — a name long associated with loud, cycle-based crash forecasting. Fair warning, though: the record on him here is thin. Everything below comes from a single dated appearance, an August 18, 2026 discussion of the "Everything Bubble," so treat this as a snapshot of his argument rather than a track record you can grade.

The snapshot is nonetheless coherent, because both positions hang off the same hook: a major crash. On equities, Dent's advice is to wait for the bust rather than buy ahead of it — the market is "going to be on sale for the best price," and once it is, "you want to buy things like QQQ, the NASDAQ 100, that captures the raciest side" ([Harry Dent on the Everything Bubble — And the Only Safe Hav…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TInyOyKDOgI)). The bond leg completes the trade: "buy the TLT or the 30-year Treasury bond and get a little higher interest and potential for a doubling or more if there is a major crash" ([Harry Dent on the Everything Bubble — And the Only Safe Hav…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TInyOyKDOgI)). In other words, QQQ is the post-crash entry and TLT is the crash itself paying you.

Note the shape of that, because it's characteristically Dent: neither call is a direction bet on today's tape, which is presumably why both are coded neutral. One is an entry plan gated on a downturn he expects; the other is an explicit crash hedge with leverage-like upside ("a doubling or more") if the downturn is severe. As for how his views have moved over time — the digest can't say. One date, one source, two conditional picks. There's no timeline here, just a single evening's advice from a forecaster whose whole brand is the evening before.

person/ian-harris.text:
Ian Harris enters this corpus the way a lot of commodity commentators do — through an interview chair rather than a published track record. He appears once as a guest, on David Lin's show, and the corpus cannot confidently pin down who he is: several people named Ian Harris work in finance, most prominently a London-based insurance-sector analyst formerly associated with Investec, but none clearly matches the copper-mining commentary captured here. So this portrait has to rest on what he said rather than on an established public profile, and readers should treat the identity as unresolved.

What he said, though, is remarkably consistent. In a June 18, 2026 appearance framed around a supply shock ([The Next Asset To 3x Is Driven By Insane Supply Shock | Ian…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K1EYafiD8BM)), he argued that "copper is no longer just trading like Dr. Copper" but on "a structural deficit that is anticipated and an insatiable demand," and put it more bluntly: "I think metals are the next oil, right? And I think the biggest component… that is copper." He also sketched a sequencing view of the metals trade — that the move "starts in gold and then goes to silver and then goes to copper" — positioning copper as the last leg of a rotation out of precious metals.

By the time he sat down with David Lin on August 13, 2026 ([Ian Harris: The Smart Money Is Rushing To Copper](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5ql9wm7AQs8)), the thesis had grown a geopolitical spine. The world, in his telling, "has woken up to say that this whole globalization thing is falling apart" after having "handed way too much power to China" — while China has already done the work of securing its own position, building smelting capacity and buying into projects early. His sharpest observation of the two interviews is about silence: institutional buyers "know if they say it too loud, the prices go up on everything," so they're "trying to grab a little bit here and there while they still can." That's a description of why the copper story stays under-telegraphed, coming from someone describing it on a podcast — an irony he doesn't seem to register, or doesn't mind.

The timeline shows no reversal, only deepening: June's supply-and-rotation mechanics became August's deglobalization-and-China framing, with the underlying call unchanged. What's odd is the stance ledger — eight positions coded neutral, zero bullish or bearish, despite rhetoric that sounds structurally bullish on copper. The coding is arguably fair: Harris narrates what "the smart money" is doing and where the market is heading rather than stamping his own rating on it. That's the shape of his commentary — descriptive, confident about the forces, deliberately noncommittal about the trade. With only two interviews on record, there's no history of calls to grade him against, and this page should be updated if his identity or track record surfaces.

person/jay-martin-citing-reuters-colombi.text:
Jay Martin is a Vancouver-based figure in the resource-investing world, best known as the CEO of Cambridge House International — the company behind the Vancouver Resource Investment Conference — and as host of The Jay Martin Show, the podcast that grew out of the old Cambridge House podcast brand. His show functions as a meeting point for investors, economists, geologists, and mining executives, and his own commentary orbits macroeconomics, precious metals, energy, and the political geography of mining jurisdictions. That last item is worth emphasizing: Martin's framing tends to treat *where* mines operate as a variable as important as the commodities themselves, which is the natural posture for someone whose business depends on connecting junior resource companies with retail and institutional capital.

The corpus gives one concrete example of how he makes that jurisdictional case. In discussing Colombia, he leaned on a Reuters report relayed through the Colombian Mining Association forecasting roughly $3.6–4 billion of investment flowing into the country's mining sector — a data point he used to ground an argument about where mining capital is headed rather than relying on pure narrative. It's a small window into his method: macro and jurisdictional storytelling, backed where possible by third-party reporting.

What the record here does *not* show is a track record of dated calls. There are no tracked bullish, bearish, or neutral stances and no topic timelines for Martin in this digest, so any claim about how his views have shifted over time would be speculation. That's a genuine gap — Martin is a talker rather than a position-taker in the analyst sense, and his influence runs through curation (who he platforms, what conferences he stages) more than through on-the-record forecasts. This portrait will be worth expanding if and when specific calls with dates enter the record; on current evidence, the strongest documented specifics are his institutional roles and the Colombia investment framing.

person/jeff-christian.text:
Jeff Christian is a Managing Partner at CPM Group, the commodities research consultancy he's long been associated with, and in precious metals circles he occupies a particular niche: less a market cheerleader than a forecaster who will put a specific annual average and year-end range on gold, hedged but numerical. The record in this corpus is a snapshot of that style. Speaking on August 25, 2026, he laid out the firm's working numbers — an average gold forecast for the year of roughly $4,450, which he indicated would likely be revised upward from there ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7bgdCd8hJFw)).

His most concrete call from that appearance is the year-end target: gold in the $4,800 to $5,000 range, possibly "a little higher" ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7bgdCd8hJFw)). He layered tactical caution on top of the structural view, allowing for a pullback in early September while maintaining that the metal would rise from that dip into year-end ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7bgdCd8hJFw)). Read together, the substance is constructive — rising targets, higher revisions — even if his delivery is the measured tone of an analyst defending a model rather than talking a book.

Two caveats worth flagging. First, the corpus codes all three of these stances as neutral, and that's fair to the letter of his language: he rarely says "buy," he says what the price will average and where it will trade, which is a different rhetorical register than the bull/bear shouting match around him. Second, this coverage is thin — every entry comes from a single August 25, 2026 appearance, so there is no timeline here showing how his views have moved over the years. What it does show, clearly, is a forecaster at $4,450-and-rising averages with a $5,000 year-end bullseye, which is itself a position worth tracking against what follows.

person/jim-bianco.text:
Jim Bianco is the founder, president, and CEO of Bianco Research, a Chicago-area macro and fixed income research shop he started in 1998 to serve institutional investors. Over nearly three decades he has built a reputation as one of the more closely watched voices on Federal Reserve policy, inflation, and bond market strategy, with a regular presence in financial media, industry podcasts, and panels. He belongs to the breed of analyst whose value lies less in screaming directional calls and more in framing how the machinery of monetary policy actually behaves.

That framing instinct shows in his recorded commentary. In an appearance on *The Fed Just Changed the Rules for Investors with Jim Bianco* ([August 23, 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lFpQuOEzGzc)), he made his clearest stated preference on record: "I've been a fan of the Fed not doing forward guidance anymore," arguing that the policy keeps "setting the stage" for markets in ways that backfire. The same conversation captured his read on why economic data releases matter less than investors assume — in his telling, the market is "more worried about monetary policy than it is about the stat" ([same appearance](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lFpQuOEzGzc)). His evidence for that hierarchy was the bond market's own behavior: after one day of yields falling on a data print, "they turned around and they went back up even higher than they were before the number" ([same appearance](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lFpQuOEzGzc)). It is a coherent thesis — that Fed communication, not incoming data, is the dominant force moving rates — and it puts him squarely in the camp of Fed skeptics who think the central bank talks too much, even if the substance of his argument is analytic rather than a trade recommendation.

As for how his views have moved over time: the record here can't say. Every logged stance — all three — is neutral in tone and drawn from that single August 2026 appearance, and the corpus contains no bullish or bearish calls on rates, bonds, the dollar, or anything else. That is a fair reflection of what Bianco appears to be in this material: a process-and-framework commentator rather than an out-on-a-limb forecaster. Readers looking for his directional convictions will need to go beyond the sources currently on file; what this page can establish is his standing, his longevity, and his specific argument that forward guidance does more harm than good.

person/jimmy-connor-bloor-street-capital.text:
Jimmy Connor is a Canadian investor and financial commentator who runs Bloor Street Capital, a Toronto-based investment research and commentary firm. His background runs through capital markets and money management, but his most visible platform is the Bloor Street Capital podcast and YouTube channel, where he sits down with fund managers, analysts and resource-sector investors — a format that puts him less in the role of forecaster and more in the role of interviewer and curator of other people's market views. There's also a colorful biographical wrinkle worth noting: before finance, Connor was a nationally ranked junior tennis player in Canada, which he has parlayed into the trading world's favorite crossover narrative — the athlete-turned-investor.

In this corpus he appears only as an interview guest, a single appearance, and the record of his own positioning is strikingly empty: no bullish or bearish calls, no topic timeline of shifting views, nothing dated to hang an argument on. That's not necessarily damning — commentators who build their brand around interviewing sharp money managers often deliberately keep their own book opinions diffuse — but it does mean any portrait of Connor as a caller of markets has to wait for a fuller paper trail. What can be said plainly is that his contribution to the investment conversation, at least as documented here, is access and dialogue rather than a public track record of positions.

The honest summary: Connor is best described as a node in the resource-investing media ecosystem — a Toronto-based host whose value lies in drawing out the theses of others — rather than a commentator whose own stances can be traced through time. Readers looking for his strongest calls won't find them in this record, and the coverage here is simply too thin to claim a view evolution one way or the other.

person/john-miniotis.text:
John Miniotis is the President, Chief Executive Officer and a Director of Abra Silver (ABRA.V), and his public footprint in this corpus is, so far, exactly one appearance: a long-form interview with Jimmy Connor published August 14, 2026, framed around the host's question of whether there's "More To Come" after the stock's 45% year-to-date run ([Abra Silver Up 45% YTD - More To Come?  | John Miniotis and…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9RbfUZb2Z2c)). That single-source record shapes how to read him. All thirteen extracted statements classify as neutral — no surprise for a founder-type executive walking through his own project. He makes no market call here on gold or silver outright, even though both metals underwrite his entire story.

The pitch centers on Diablillos, which he describes as "one of the largest, fully permitted… primary silver projects in the world," with robust economics "in a jurisdiction that's improved dramat[ically]" — Argentina, on the widely known geography ([Abra Silver Up 45% YTD - More To Come?  | John Miniotis and…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9RbfUZb2Z2c)). The economics are built on deliberately conservative assumptions: the study used "$50 for silver long term, $3,650 for gold," which he notes is "of course well below where we're sitting today" ([Abra Silver Up 45% YTD - More To Come?  | John Miniotis and…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9RbfUZb2Z2c)). That's the standard developer argument — bankable at bear-case prices, leveraged to anything better — and his optimism lives in the asset claims and the price-deck gap rather than in any forecast, which is why the transcript reads neutral.

The timeline he laid out in August 2026: a "steady stream of news flow" from the exploration program through year-end and into next year ([Abra Silver Up 45% YTD - More To Come?  | John Miniotis and…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9RbfUZb2Z2c)); construction activities beginning next year, with "April of 2027" the date he gave ([Abra Silver Up 45% YTD - More To Come?  | John Miniotis and…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9RbfUZb2Z2c)); and a roughly two-and-a-half-year build to "Q4 2029 when we hit commercial production" ([Abra Silver Up 45% YTD - More To Come?  | John Miniotis and…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9RbfUZb2Z2c)). On financing — the perennial junior-developer choke point — he reported active conversations across three options and called the project "very, very financeable" ([Abra Silver Up 45% YTD - More To Come?  | John Miniotis and…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9RbfUZb2Z2c)). The re-rating thesis is the kicker: once construction starts, he expects the market to move Abra Silver "into that developer category" ([Abra Silver Up 45% YTD - More To Come?  | John Miniotis and…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9RbfUZb2Z2c)).

The second act is Yellowhead, which he claims would, in year three, be "the largest primary silver mine globally," with silver accounting for more than 50% of revenue ([Abra Silver Up 45% YTD - More To Come?  | John Miniotis and…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9RbfUZb2Z2c)). Take the enthusiasm with the obvious grain of salt — this is a seller of the story, on a show whose own title does some of the hyping. And because the record is one interview on one date, there's no view drift to chart here; the only moving timeline is his construction schedule. Whether April 2027, the financing close-out he hinted at, and Q4 2029 hold is precisely what future coverage should test him on.

person/john-miniotis-ceo-abra-silver-res.text:
John Miniotis is a mining finance lifer — more than 25 years in the resource sector, most of it on the capital-markets side of the table in mining-focused investment banking — who crossed over to the operating side as co-founder and chief executive of Abra Silver Resource Corp. The company's story rests on its flagship asset: the Diablillos silver-gold project in Salta Province, Argentina, which Abra has advanced through a sustained program of resource expansion drilling. That background matters for how you read him. He comes to the microphone as someone who has spent his career structuring and financing mining companies, and his commentary reflects the priorities of that world: drilling results, resource growth, and the investment case for a developing silver asset.

His public-facing role, as this corpus captures it, is the operator-advocate rather than the markets pundit. His one logged interview appearance — on Jimmy Connor's precious metals and mining-focused program — covered silver market dynamics and the company's exploration progress, which is to say the two things a silver exploration CEO is booked to discuss. It is worth being plain about the limits of the record here: no bullish, bearish, or neutral calls are scored against Miniotis, there are no dated topic timelines, and consequently there is no "strongest call" to name and no visible movement in his views over time. His appearance history in this corpus is a single data point, not a curve.

That thinness shapes the portrait more than anything else. What the file supports is straightforward: Miniotis is the face of a Canadian-listed silver developer pushing a flagship project in Salta Province, a jurisdiction whose political and fiscal profile is part of any honest discussion of the asset, and he makes that case on precious-metals programming. Whether his conviction on silver broadly has strengthened or wavered across the years simply is not visible in what's on file. Anyone looking for a dated track record of Miniotis as a market commentator will have to wait for more appearances.

person/julian-cotec-ceo.text:
Julian Treger is the Chief Executive Officer of CoTec Holdings Corp., a TSX Venture Exchange-listed investment company built around a single idea: that the next leg of value in mining comes not from discovering ore bodies but from disruptive technologies in mineral processing and metal production. He comes to that thesis as a career natural resources man — he co-founded Audley Capital Advisors, a London-based firm specializing in resources, and has managed resource-focused funds and sat on mining company boards. At CoTec that background translates into a portfolio of process bets: green iron ore pellet and pig iron production initiatives, magnesium extraction through Magratea Metals, and cyanide-free gold leaching via EnviroLeach.

The clearest window into how he argues comes from his August 19, 2026 appearance on Pitch Rick Ep #2, where the subject was CoTec's pig iron play. His case rests on a wide cost-price spread: domestic pig iron at a production cost of roughly $300 to $350 against a pig iron price of $500 to 550 ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)). To capture it, he laid out a $350 million capital plan — $200 million of debt and $150 million of equity — to reformat the concentrator and bring the plant into production ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)). The development path is equally explicit: environmental studies through the rest of the year, a bankable feasibility study the following year, then permitting ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)).

What stands out in the interview is the financial candor. Nearer term, CoTec needs about $8 million over the next 18 months ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)), and Treger frames the value gap — $2 million today against roughly $100 million in NPV before beneficiation — as the measure of what the team believes it is building ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)). More telling still, he volunteers that CoTec "obviously" will not be raising at the $2.5 billion pre-tax valuation, and that any raise will come at a significant discount to it ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)). A chief executive conceding dilution risk up front, in a market segment not exactly famous for it, is worth more than a dozen bullish soundbites.

One caveat belongs in any honest portrait: the recorded coverage here is thin and one-dimensional. All seven tracked statements date to that single August 19, 2026 interview and are coded neutral — this is an executive walking through a financing and development roadmap, not making directional market calls. There is no documented arc showing his views shifting over time; the timeline is a snapshot, not a track record. Read him, for now, as a resources investor betting on process technology, who at least in this one appearance was unusually straight about what the equity would and would not be worth along the way.

person/justin-huhn.text:
Justin Huhn is a newsletter publisher and uranium market analyst — in the uranium investing world he's best known as the man behind the Uranium Insider newsletter, where he's built a following parsing the fuel-cycle: miners, utilities, term contracting, and the supply-demand math that drives the spot price. That's the niche he occupies, and it's a fairly crowded one, which makes it worth asking what actually distinguishes his calls.

On the evidence in this corpus, the answer isn't yet clear, because the record here is thin — a single dated entry. On August 22, 2026, Huhn laid out a framing that the classifier logged as neutral: "we're entering or just about to enter what is typically a strong seasonal period and this year I think is going to be no exception" ([Justin Huhn: The Uranium Market Is Setting Up for a Major M…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eDPDUFOi6Uw)). person/mark-skousen-oxford-club-skousen-.text:
Mark Skousen occupies a familiar lane in the free-market investment world: economist, author, newsletter editor, and — perhaps most distinctively — founder of a major annual conference. The corpus tracks him under the Oxford Club / Skousen Report umbrella, and he's long been associated with the Austrian-school tradition, having spent decades arguing that sound money, low debt, and savings-driven growth are the preconditions for healthy markets. He is, in other words, exactly the kind of commentator you'd expect to be nervous about a $40 trillion national debt — and the record here shows precisely that.

His one dated appearance in the file, from August 22, 2026, comes from a discussion of whether Treasury can keep yields contained ([The Market's $40T Question: Can Treasury Keep Yields Under …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SWsGPoxqcR0)). There he offers his most quotable line in the digest: "Stock market is never never commit suicide, but it can be murdered" — his way of saying markets rarely collapse on their own momentum, but Washington can kill them, with federal debt "approaching $40 trillion" as the murder weapon ([The Market's $40T Question: Can Treasury Keep Yields Under …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SWsGPoxqcR0)). On where to hide from that risk, he's explicit but hedged: "there's no place to hide except to go to gold or go to the Bitcoin. But probably gold," citing central banks "buying gold hand over fist" ([The Market's $40T Question: Can Treasury Keep Yields Under …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SWsGPoxqcR0)). The relative call — gold over Bitcoin, with official-sector demand as the tiebreaker — is the closest thing to a positioned view in the entire record, even though the classifier tags it neutral.

On how his views have moved: they haven't, at least not visibly here. All four topic entries — crypto, geopolitics, precious metals, and rates/bonds/dollar — come from that single August 22, 2026 source and all carry neutral tags, so there is no before-and-after to narrate. That's worth saying plainly rather than papering over: this is a portrait built from one conversation. What the snapshot does show is a consistent temperament — fiscal alarm paired with hard-asset hedging — and if his long public record of free-market advocacy is any guide, that combination is less a recent turn than his default setting. person/massil-beguenane.text:

That uniformity is itself informative: this is a diagnostician of flows, not a directional caller, at least on the evidence preserved here.

His method shows up clearly in the specifics. On August 13th he walked through the yen after a huge move and noted that "yen positioning is actually still net short," meaning "more short covering is still possible" — fuel left in the tank ([Trading Desk - August 13th 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c06eQWQljXo)). Same session: the 2-year sitting at the 100th percentile of positioning while the 10-year sits at the opposite extreme; SPX speculators at the 96th percentile and the Dow even more extreme at the 99th; gold having rotated to neutral while silver remains under-owned with large specs near the zeroth percentile. A week later on MacroVoices he extended the same lens: 10-year and 30-year positioning at the bottom decile on a multi-year lookback, Nasdaq prices near highs while positioning shows the lowest score in five years, and gold having "fell sharply" without the large funds ever giving up their positions ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.macrovoices.com/1546-macrovoices-546-darius-dale-darius-dale-for-potus-2028)). He also flagged something structural in that appearance — that the US had "proved that they'll be intervening in the markets," first in the yen and then in bonds.

Where does he actually plant a flag? Almost nowhere outright, but the closest thing to a forward argument in the record is his sugar thesis: if Brazil diverts more sugarcane into ethanol or India becomes a net importer, "the market will be forced to price a much higher" level ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.macrovoices.com/1546-macrovoices-546-darius-dale-darius-dale-for-potus-2028)). His other leanings are similarly hedged — room for "further moves against the dollar" if the trend is just beginning, and an oil recovery that happened "without large funds aggressively chasing it," which he says supports a range-bound story more than a breakout. On the timeline question: there is no movement to trace, because the corpus spans barely two weeks in August 2026 and his stance mix never leaves neutral. person/matt-radisson-ceo.text:
Matt Manson is the president and CEO of Radisson Mining Resources, a TSX Venture-listed gold explorer advancing the O'Brien project in Quebec's Abitibi region along the Cadillac-Larder Lake break. He isn't a first-timer: Manson co-founded Stornoway Diamond Corporation and ran it as president and CEO through the Renard kimberlite discovery and the build-out of Quebec's Renard diamond mine. That developer's résumé shapes how he sells Radisson — less as a lottery ticket, more as an ounces-manufacturing process with checkpoints.

His stated playbook is incrementalism. In an August 26, 2026 interview — pegged to Agnico's $57 million investment in the Quebec gold project, with a title that pointedly asks whether it's enough — he laid out resource updates done "on a step-by-step basis," one already completed the previous March and more expected, backed by what he promises will be a dense run of drilling-related news flow ([Agnico Invests $57M in Quebec Gold Project, But Is It Enoug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bY40DOJPvxk)). On funding, the philosophy is selling slices rather than the whole loaf: "We're selling 15% of the business here. I don't think we're ready to sell 100% of the business because this is a growing resource" ([Agnico Invests $57M in Quebec Gold Project, But Is It Enoug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bY40DOJPvxk)). It's a coherent pitch for a junior: dilute in increments, keep the upside of a resource that's still compounding.

The numbers he leans on are the growth curve and drill conversion. By his telling, the project held 900,000 ounces in 2023, a million and a half across all categories the following year, and 2.3 million ounces in the current count, against a target of "3 to 4 million ounces" — with drilling "hitting 80% of the time" ([Agnico Invests $57M in Quebec Gold Project, But Is It Enoug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bY40DOJPvxk)). He doesn't bother with false modesty, either: "there's no better gold mining company out there" is how he frames the sector pecking order ([Agnico Invests $57M in Quebec Gold Project, But Is It Enoug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bY40DOJPvxk)).

It's worth being plain about what the tracking record shows — and doesn't. All seven coded stances are neutral, clustered on a single date, so there is no visible migration in his views: no gold-price calls, no macro turns, just a consistently promotional-but-ordered case for one asset. The honest caveats are that this portrait rests on one August 2026 conversation, and that even within it Manson hedges at the edges ("likely" on the next update, an unfinished "if I was a bet…"). Whether the 80% hit-rate arithmetic and the 3-to-4-million-ounce ambition actually close the gap Agnico's $57 million left open is precisely the "but is it enough" question the interview's own title poses — and nothing in the record so far answers it ([Agnico Invests $57M in Quebec Gold Project, But Is It Enoug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bY40DOJPvxk)).

person/michael-howell.text:
Michael Howell is a liquidity-first macro man — Managing Director of CrossBorder Capital and the analyst behind the "Capital Wars" framing of global finance — and his single appearance in this corpus, MacroVoices #545, "Warsh vs. The Markets" (August 13, 2026), shows the method in full. He reduces the tape to simple anatomy: "there are two moving parts, Eric. One of those is the currency of denomination" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)). Almost everything else in the hour — gold, oil, the yuan, crypto — is downstream of that frame, which is both his appeal and the reason his record reads as framework analysis rather than a wall of directional arrows.

His most committed call in the record is gold, and the mechanism is China: "the story of why gold is going up and going down," he argued, is "all about Chinese devaluation" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)). Beijing, in his telling, can run a regime of "maintaining a stable yuan US dollar externally while trying to devalue the yuan internally" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FsPoAmywH3U)), and that internal devaluation leaks into hard assets, because "as liquidity increases, it fuels precious metals" — an obvious monetary inflation hedge, in his phrase ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)). When it was put to him that "the correction is over" and "the new move higher is on," his answer was "100%" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FsPoAmywH3U)). He then set the level: assume gold is "underpinned at $4,000 an ounce, maybe it's higher, who knows" — and "gold is probably going up, at least on my estimation" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)).

The $4,000 anchor feeds straight into his oil number. Take the long-run average gold/oil ratio — historically "around about 20 times," maybe a stretched 30 — divide it into the gold price, and "we still get an oil price of $135 a barrel so substantially above where we are" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)). He flags the method's softness himself — "that may be way way off the scale... We're just triangulating here" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)) — but the episode treats the conclusion as landed: a "very persuasive argument in favor of higher oil prices and also in favor of higher bond yields," agreed "on both scores" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)). The lone outright bearish tag in his record is the dollar: a scenario he walked through "would be really bad for the dollar in my estimation and it would cause the gold market to shoot up" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)) — though the digest doesn't preserve what trigger he had in mind.

On crypto he stayed neutral but not kind: when the S&P dropped 25%, "Bitcoin dropped 75%," even if "some of that drop in crypto is already in the bag" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FsPoAmywH3U)). The ledger — three bullish, one bearish, sixteen of twenty neutral — is an honest portrait: Howell is a triangulator, not a flag-planter, and even his biggest numbers arrive wrapped in hedges. With just one dated appearance there is no timeline of his views drifting across months to track; the movement the corpus shows happens inside the interview itself, from "maybe it's 30 times" hedging to an unqualified "100%" on gold's next leg higher.

I can't name a strongest call here because none is on record; the corpus simply hasn't captured one. The honest summary is that his contribution in this corpus is his framework and his argument, not a trackable sequence of positions.

What that argument amounts to, in his public body of work, is the claim that passive flows have altered price discovery itself — that money moving into index vehicles mechanically supports large index constituents regardless of fundamentals, with consequences for bubbles, dispersion, and volatility that the market has been slow to price in. Whether that thesis fully holds is contested, and a single guest appearance can't settle it. If later entries add dated calls or a stance history, this portrait should be expanded accordingly; on the current record, there is little more to say without inventing it.

person/mike-strategist.text:

That framing positions Mike as a structuralist rather than a timer, someone whose market view flows from flows rather than forecasts.

Beyond that single entry, though, there is little to chart. There is no documented evolution in his views, no prior calls to score him against, and no role history to anchor his authority — the record is, plainly, thin. The Japanese policy commentary and the passive-flow thesis suggest a strategist engaged with macro plumbing and market mechanics rather than headline-picking, but whether his S&P 500 neutrality has hardened, softened, or ever moved at all is something the available material simply does not show.

person/milton-berg.text:
Milton Berg is a market strategist and technical analyst, and in this corpus his record is essentially a single snapshot: one appearance on August 12, 2026, framed around "The Worst Panic in 4 Years Just Happened" ([The Worst Panic in 4 Years Just Happened. Here's Why Milton…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Idj7jAOtE50)). Everything dated here comes from that one piece, which is worth saying up front — there's no multi-year trail of calls to reconstruct a migration in his views. What the snapshot shows instead is a technician working through an unusually split picture of the market, and saying so out loud.

His one outright bullish stance in the record is on the S&P 500. In that August discussion he laid out a median projection of 8,565.42 within a year of "the signal" — another 10.42% above where the index stood at the time — while anchoring the call to historical analogs in which the median return after this signal was 37% within a year ([The Worst Panic in 4 Years Just Happened. Here's Why Milton…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Idj7jAOtE50)). Notably, he framed the panic itself as something that "didn't really affect the broad market at the S&P," positioning the event as a technical signal rather than a fundamental rupture ([The Worst Panic in 4 Years Just Happened. Here's Why Milton…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Idj7jAOtE50)).

The bullishness comes wrapped in a lot of caution, and the surrounding calls are the more interesting part of the file. He flagged signs of a top in the semiconductor index back in June, which "ultimately proved to be a top in the semiconductor index and the Nasdaq 100 and the Nasdaq" ([The Worst Panic in 4 Years Just Happened. Here's Why Milton…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Idj7jAOtE50)). He described private credit as "really collapsing in a way," observed the 30-year bond trading at its highest levels in what he took to be decades, and argued the Fed chair would be "forced to raise rates" whether he wants to or not ([The Worst Panic in 4 Years Just Happened. Here's Why Milton…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Idj7jAOtE50)).

Read together, the picture is a barbell: double-digit upside on the broad index, but tops called in its tech leadership, a credit niche breaking, yields at generational highs, and a rate hike he considers inevitable. The obvious way to square that — a market broadening out beyond semis even as its former leaders roll over — is consistent with his numbers, but he doesn't spell the mechanism out in this material, so it stays an inference. The stance mix underscores the same caution: one bullish call, zero bearish calls, eight neutral observations. With the entire record resting on a single August 2026 document, any claim about how Berg's views have shifted over time simply isn't supportable here — this wiki can say what he argued and when, but not yet how he's moved.

person/missile-macrovoices-trading-desk.text:
Missile is the pseudonymous handle of an anonymous trader who appears as a panelist on the MacroVoices Trading Desk, the trading-commentary segment attached to Erik Townsend's MacroVoices podcast. Nothing about the person behind the nickname — professional history, employer, background — is publicly disclosed, which is itself part of the appeal: on a desk where the argument is about positioning rather than personality, the handle does the work. The commentary style is short-horizon and flow-oriented, the kind of read that cares less about where a market *should* go and more about who is already positioned there — crowded shorts, forced buying, and what happens when those two meet in index futures, currencies, and metals.

The dated record for this contributor currently runs to a single appearance: the August 20, 2026 desk segment on MacroVoices episode #546 with Darius Dale ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IRHWmEc1QAE)). Even within one segment, the through-line is distinctive. On indices, Missile noted the NASDAQ climbing even as "the big money, the CTAs, the trend following funds are putting on their seat belts" — price strength sitting on top of positioning that wants no part of it ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IRHWmEc1QAE)). On gold, the observation was the opposite of a fresh call: large holders "really never abandoned this trade," a state of affairs Missile framed as the defining story of the past couple of years ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IRHWmEc1QAE)). And on bonds, the argument was political as much as positional — that big money "surely doesn't want to fight the US government," leaving long positions that may need to unwind, with the early evidence already visible across the market ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IRHWmEc1QAE)).

As for how the views have moved over time: the record can't answer that yet. All three logged stances are neutral, and the timeline contains exactly one date, so there is no before-and-after to point to. That neutrality should be read for what it is rather than dismissed as fence-sitting — this is a positioning analyst describing what large players are actually doing, not issuing directional forecasts. The portrait here is honest about its thinness: one episode, three reads, all flow-watching rather than calls. As more desk segments get logged, the interesting question becomes whether Missile's reads on CTA positioning and gold's steadfast large holders translate into directional conviction — or whether the pseudonym stays purely a reader of other people's books.

person/mohamed-cisse-ceo-avanti-gold.text:
Mohamed Cisse is the chief executive of Avanti Gold (AGC.CN), an early-stage gold company sitting on a roughly three-million-ounce deposit in the DR Congo — a position that raises exactly the question the one long-form interview in this corpus poses in its title: is it really economic? [3M Ounces of Gold in DR Congo, But is it Really Economic? |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j_t-RAAdzA8). Beyond that August 12, 2026 conversation, the record here is thin — one source, one date, no price calls and no stated track record — so this is a portrait of a single snapshot rather than a demonstrated evolution of views.

What Cisse argues for is sequencing. His case rests on how little work the deposit has actually seen: in his telling, "this 3.1 meter analysis has been discovered with only 20,000 m of drilling," and all of it was "historical drilling" rather than his own [3M Ounces of Gold in DR Congo, But is it Really Economic? |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j_t-RAAdzA8). Under-drilling, for him, is the opportunity — he sees "a lot of quick wins to increase the resource" and wants to "expand these resources very quickly" [3M Ounces of Gold in DR Congo, But is it Really Economic? |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j_t-RAAdzA8). The plan he lays out is explicit: take the deposit "to a reasonable size from then start the PE process" [3M Ounces of Gold in DR Congo, But is it Really Economic? |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j_t-RAAdzA8). Grow the ounces first; ask the economic question second.

Notably, nothing in the record reads as a market call — all three entries code neutral, which is fair, because Cisse is describing a work program rather than making an investment argument. The one observation worth making about the shape of the debate: the interview frames the story as whether 3 million Congolese ounces are "really economic," and on this record Cisse's answer is to defer the question. By his own account the preliminary economic assessment is something he intends to *start*, meaning the economics remain an open item, not an established fact. Whether the "quick wins" in resource expansion actually land — and whether a PE ever validates them — is precisely where the coverage ends.

person/nomi-prins.text:
Nomi Prins is the rare commentator whose authority comes from having been inside the machine she now critiques — a former Wall Street managing director who reinvented herself as one of the sharpest chroniclers of central bank power, best known publicly for books like *Collusion* and *All the Presidents' Bankers*. In this corpus, though, her record is unusually concentrated: every entry traces to a single interview dated August 23, 2026, titled "Gold To $6,000, Silver Buying Opportunity, Copper To $7" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Hnok1i10K0)). That means what follows is a snapshot, not a track record — and it should be read as one.

The August interview lays out a structural gold thesis rather than a simple price punt. Her core argument is that central banks around the world "are turning to gold to diversify not just against the dollar" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Hnok1i10K0)), and that the buying has room to run — she estimates the typical bank still has "about 5% more gold to buy," effectively doubling its allocation to return to historic reserve levels ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Hnok1i10K0)). Beneath that sits a supply argument: the market remains "very close to a deficit for gold based on current demand," before any demand growth at all ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Hnok1i10K0)), plus a claimed "distortion, a dislocation" between paper and physical pricing in gold and silver ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Hnok1i10K0)). On levels, she sees roughly $6,000 "around the turn of the year" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Hnok1i10K0)) and "probably 8,000 next year," with fresh forecasts promised in January ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Hnok1i10K0)). Her logic for ignoring pullbacks is that central bank buyers simply don't stop — "It didn't stop buying at 5,500. It's not stopping at 4,500. It didn't stop last year at 3,500" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Hnok1i10K0)). The title's "Copper To $7" earns a mention, but the transcript excerpt offers no real support for it beyond the headline ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Hnok1i10K0)) — a thin leg of the thesis.

On rates, she called for the Fed to "hold rates in September" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Hnok1i10K0)), and framed some fiscal or monetary maneuver to strip debt off the system as "the first of many such moves which will grow in magnitude" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Hnok1i10K0)) — the intervention theme that has defined her career-long argument that official liquidity, not fundamentals, sets the tape. Whether her September hold call proved right isn't captured here; the corpus doesn't say.

As for movement over time: there is none visible in this digest. One date, one source, and every stance coded neutral — eleven of eleven ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Hnok1i10K0)). That's worth flagging plainly. The neutral coding arguably undersells the material, since $6,000-then-$8,000 gold is a directional call by any plain reading, but the transcript excerpts themselves are explanatory in tone — she's describing a mechanism, not ringing a bell. A proper portrait of how her views have evolved will need earlier and later appearances; this page currently rests on one long August afternoon.

person/patrick.text:
Patrick Ceresney is the co-host of MacroVoices and, functionally, the show's resident technician — after the headline macro interview wraps, he takes the charts (indices, gold, oil, the dollar) and works through levels, triggers and probabilities rather than handing down verdicts. The record here reflects that temperament precisely: fourteen neutral readings, not one outright bullish or bearish stance. That reads less like fence-sitting than method — his phrasing runs to "on balance of probabilities," gated scenarios and retracement math, and he openly polices his own hedging mid-sentence.

The cleanest window into his process is the S&P 500. On August 13, 2026, in the post-interview segment of episode #545 with Michael Howell, he laid out an upside trigger: a short-term catalyst breaking the market out of its one-week trade range to fresh highs could take it to 8,000 within a week — but only, he stressed, if the MAG7s were participating ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)). A week later on episode #546 with Darius Dale, with the market pulling back, the emphasis flipped from breakout mechanics to retracement tolerance: a pullback to 7,600 was "par for the course," a fifty-percent retrace "very typical," and he saw himself "far from seeing significant technical damage" on the index ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.macrovoices.com/1546-macrovoices-546-darius-dale-darius-dale-for-potus-2028)). Same neutrality, different posture — the shift from "what has to happen for 8,000" to "what pullback is still benign" is the tell of a level-watcher, not a closet bull or bear.

Gold carries his most committed trade thesis in this window. On August 13 he framed it directly: gold continues recovering for the next two months, targeting the April high on GLD ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)). By August 25 the thesis was intact and unchanged — he was watching for "legitimate progress back to those April highs near 4,800 over the next few months" ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028 (U…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UAGEIxhyL8c)). Two episodes, two weeks, one target, no drift — the closest thing to an actual position in the record.

Elsewhere he refuses the directional label even when the setup tempts it. On the dollar (August 20) he conceded the action had "neutralized the prior bull market," then immediately checked himself: "does that make me an outright bear on the dollar? Probably not" ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.macrovoices.com/1546-macrovoices-546-darius-dale-darius-dale-for-potus-2028)). Oil, as of August 25, stays elevated on balance of probabilities with a shot at moving higher; semiconductors as laggards hinge on what Nvidia has to say ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028 (U…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UAGEIxhyL8c); [MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.macrovoices.com/1546-macrovoices-546-darius-dale-darius-dale-for-potus-2028)). And on Bitcoin he took the technician's habitual deference to the macro frame, engaging Dale's fiscal dominance and financial repression argument to set up where scarce assets — Bitcoin included — sit in it ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.macrovoices.com/1546-macrovoices-546-darius-dale-darius-dale-for-potus-2028)).

One honest caveat: everything above comes from a two-week slice, August 13–25, 2026, across just two episodes (#545 and #546), so there is no long arc of conversion or reversal to reconstruct. What the window does show is consistent — an analyst whose "neutral" is not indecision but a discipline of pricing conditionality, and who would rather tell you exactly which level invalidates his read than commit to a direction.

person/patrick-macrovoices-trading-desk.text:
Patrick — the derivatives and market strategist who co-hosts the MacroVoices podcast (widely known as Patrick Ceresna) and fronts its weekly Trading Desk segment — is the chart-side counterweight to the show's macro interview format. Where guests make sweeping directional arguments, his job on the Trading Desk is to convert the week's price action into levels, scenarios and trade structures, and the recorded record reflects exactly that: eleven positions tagged neutral, none outright bullish or bearish, all logged from the August 20, 2026 session alongside guest Darius Dale ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IRHWmEc1QAE)).

His most concrete call from that session was on the S&P 500, and it was a defense of the trend: "far from seeing significant technical damage," with prior highs acting as support and retracement lines, and even another 50 points of downside still consistent with a generally bullish trend. He reserved "serious" trouble for a selloff reaching the 7,400–7,500 area ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IRHWmEc1QAE)). The same conditional style marked his Nvidia preview ahead of earnings: on balance of probabilities a beat with solid guidance, but the real signal would be how traders respond to the print, since the semiconductor laggards now "hinge on what Nvidia has to say" ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IRHWmEc1QAE)).

On rates and currencies he was marginally more willing to declare a regime change. He noted bonds had reversed off 30-year Treasury yields near 5.30% and framed what follows as the open question ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IRHWmEc1QAE)). On the dollar he went further — the prior bull market "has neutralized" — but pointedly refused the bearish extension: "does that make me an outright bear on the dollar? Probably not." He left the dollar index as a range question, asking whether it returns to the 96–100 band that prevailed through 2025 and the first half of 2026, and flagged a resumption of dollar weakness with yen strength as "the thing to watch" ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IRHWmEc1QAE)).

He also builds trades, not just commentary: that week's trade of the week took Darius Dale's thesis that fiscal dominance and financial repression have arrived, and positioned around scarce assets as the beneficiaries ([MacroVoices #546 Darius Dale: Darius Dale for POTUS 2028](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IRHWmEc1QAE)) — a fair picture of his role as the person who stress-tests guest theses into actionable structures.

One caveat belongs on the record: every dated item in the corpus comes from that single August 20, 2026 episode, so there is no timeline here from which to trace a shift in views. The all-neutral tagging is a function of his method — levels and conditionals rather than verdicts — not evasion; he demonstrates the distinction himself by declaring the dollar bull neutralized while stopping short of bearish. Until more Trading Desk sessions are logged, this is a portrait of technique, not of evolution.

person/patrick-addressed-by-name-in-tran.text:
Patrick Ceresna is a derivatives-market specialist and options strategist who, as co-host of the MacroVoices podcast alongside Erik Townsend, delivers the show's weekly market recap — a running technical read across the S&P 500, gold, silver, crude oil, the dollar index, the yen and, increasingly, bitcoin. He is also the founder of Big Picture Trading, an educational platform built around macro-driven trading and options strategies. His signature tool is CFTC Commitments of Traders data: he reads futures positioning the way other commentators read Fed statements, citing, for example, speculators going net short NASDAQ contracts by the tens of thousands as a tell on where the crowd is trapped.

The record here is essentially a single snapshot — MacroVoices #545, the August 13, 2026 conversation with Michael Howell, "Warsh vs. The Markets" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)) — but it captures his method well. His strongest conviction sits in commodities. On gold he argued that "gold prices in US dollar terms are going to skyrocket as well... Going gold just simply has to go up," while carefully declining to chase the move, saying "I wouldn't want to battle new all-time highs by year end, but I think that the trend is in place" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)). On oil he was outright contrarian against the prevailing view that prices are too high and will collapse once the Strait of Hormuz crisis resolves: "so many people argue with great conviction that oil prices are probably even now too high and are going to come down. I just don't buy it" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)). He also weighed the structural argument that commodity trends are being bid up by US–China competition ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)).

Everything else in that episode is deliberately neutral, and the stance mix — 4 bullish, 0 bearish, 12 neutral — reads like a technician cataloging trend states rather than a pundit picking fights. On the S&P 500 he framed risk in precise levels: it would take "a substantial decline in the tune of about 400 SNP points" to start doing the technical damage that would matter ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)). On bitcoin he invoked a comparison in which the S&P dropped 25% while bitcoin dropped 75%, noting that "some of that drop in crypto is already in the bag" ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)). The dollar call stayed conditional — "overall we actually are structurally still in a bull trend," but with a verdict promised within a week or two — and the yen trade was framed the same way: if the dollar weakens, the yen should rally ([MacroVoices #545 Michael Howell: Warsh vs. The Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xn3Mkp6FCss)).

As for how his views have moved over time, the digest can't say: every dated entry comes from that one August 2026 episode, so this is a still frame, not an arc. What the frame does show is a consistent posture — bullish where trend and positioning align, agnostic everywhere else, and unwilling to argue with his own indicators, as when he hedged his gold call rather than fight all-time highs. It's a thin file — one transcript, one date — and it should be read as exactly that.

person/patrick-karim.text:
Patrick Karim — better known online as "badcharts1" — is a proprietary futures trader and technical chartist who reportedly left the private sector around 2011, armed with a computer science background, to trade futures full-time. His method is unapologetically systematic: rules-based breakout and mean-reversion setups judged on weekly and monthly timeframes, anchored to tools like the 36-week moving average and to what he calls expansion phases. The discipline that defines him is a refusal to treat every breakout as actionable — as he puts it, not all breakouts are "mathematically playable" as trades ([Patrick Karim: Gold is Bottoming & Setting Up Its Next Big …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Bim10l6khY)). A chart can tell you price is going higher and still not offer a trade worth taking, and that distinction is the through-line of his public commentary.

His most substantive documented appearance, dated August 8, 2026, is a video framed around gold bottoming and setting up its next major move ([Patrick Karim: Gold is Bottoming & Setting Up Its Next Big …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Bim10l6khY)). His core argument there is deflationary of metals-bug enthusiasm: gold and silver are bouncing but have not yet confirmed the larger breakouts many investors are waiting for, and on the monthly chart, in his words, "there's no breakout" ([Patrick Karim: Gold is Bottoming & Setting Up Its Next Big …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Bim10l6khY)). At the same time he sketches a concrete bullish path: price may go sideways for a while, then "double it up" on the way to 8,300, with the weekly chart entering an expansion phase away from the 36-week moving average ([Patrick Karim: Gold is Bottoming & Setting Up Its Next Big …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Bim10l6khY)). That pairing — a big number on the horizon, but no confirmed signal yet — is the most characteristic call in his record.

The same appearance covers his wider map. On US equities, he directs anyone hunting a possible bear market to zoom in on the daily chart ([Patrick Karim: Gold is Bottoming & Setting Up Its Next Big …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Bim10l6khY)). person/ray-dalio-as-summarized-by-eurodo.text:

There is a telling gap in the framing here — the source headlines it as his most terrifying warning yet, while the corpus classification reads it as a neutral take rather than an outright bearish call. That tension between apocalyptic packaging and measured classification is itself characteristic of how Dalio's debt commentary circulates: he tends to describe slow-motion fiscal mechanics rather than forecast an imminent break, and summaries of him often amplify the alarm beyond the argument.

On movement over time, the file can't say much. With one entry and no earlier positions on record, there is no observable drift — no before-and-after to chart against his better-known public trajectory on US debt sustainability. Readers looking for how his views have shifted will need the primary sources; this wiki page, for now, documents one snapshot of a familiar Dalio theme: that Treasury demand strain is a structural problem officials would rather manage quietly than confront openly.

He described the Pheasant Creek property — "over 200 km" in the transcript's garbled rendering — as ground that "joins the Sunday Creek exploration development project of Southern Cross," ([Gold Project Near Fosterville, But Can They Deliver Economi…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6PT8ub33Klk)) which places the company's tenements in immediate adjacency to one of central Victoria's most closely watched exploration corridors. The Fosterville name is doing a lot of work here: it is the district that made high-grade gold famous in the Victorian goldfields, and proximity to it is the core of the Crossroads pitch.

His second claim from the same appearance sharpens that thesis: "there seems to be a deep-seated structure there that joins up Lockington and Fosterville," with "Tiglets" at the bottom end of the trend ([Gold Project Near Fosterville, But Can They Deliver Economi…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6PT8ub33Klk)). In other words, Rex's case is not just that Crossroads sits near good ground, but that a deep crustal structure connects its project to the Fosterville system itself — the kind of structural-continuity argument junior explorers in Victoria lean on heavily. Notably, both recorded data points from that day are classified as neutral stances, and they are descriptive geology talk, not directional calls on gold or anything else.

That is the honest limit of this record. The corpus shows zero bullish and zero bearish positions from Rex, both entries date to the same day, and one is tagged "China Property & Real Estate" — an obvious misclassification, since "property" in his quotes means a mining tenement, not Chinese real estate. person/rick-rule.text:
Rick Rule is one of the most recognizable names in natural resource investing: he founded Global Resource Investments, served as President & CEO of Sprott U.S. Holdings, and now runs his own shop under Rule Investment Media. Over decades he built his reputation as a contrarian buyer of unloved resource assets — gold, silver, uranium, and the small-cap mining equities most institutions won't touch.

The record in this corpus comes almost entirely from a single late-August 2026 appearance, "[Why Rick Rule Is Buying Gold Now: Monetary Shock Incoming](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lYQw_7Myw2g)," and it captures his thesis in miniature. He frames gold not as a chart trade but as a hedge against monetary debasement, arguing the US government is trying to drive down bond yields while continuing what he bluntly calls a "program of counterfeiting" — a word he pauses mid-sentence to qualify, suggesting he knows exactly how provocative it is ([Why Rick Rule Is Buying Gold Now: Monetary Shock Incoming](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lYQw_7Myw2g)). His Treasury math backs the point: on his working assumptions, a genuinely riskless counterparty should demand roughly 150 basis points over the real yield, a framework for what long rates *ought* to be rather than a prediction of where they're headed ([Why Rick Rule Is Buying Gold Now: Monetary Shock Incoming](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lYQw_7Myw2g)).

The genuinely interesting wrinkle is that despite the buy-now headline, Rule is openly nervous about the tape. "Whenever I see a momentum-driven chart... I get concerned for the very, very near term," he says — and he's beginning to see exactly that in gold ([Why Rick Rule Is Buying Gold Now: Monetary Shock Incoming](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lYQw_7Myw2g)). Read carefully, the position is a two-clock trade: secular conviction in the monetary-shock thesis paired with near-term caution about parabolic price action. The all-neutral stance coding across this digest fits that tension better than any clean bull-or-bear label would.

A plain caveat: that one item, dated 2026-08-26, is essentially the entire record here. Rule's career clearly spans decades of resource-cycle calls, but this corpus contains no earlier entries and no documented shifts — so any claim that he "turned" bullish or bearish at a particular moment would be invention rather than evidence.

person/robin-wigglesworth.text:
Robin Wigglesworth is a financial journalist and the Financial Times' global finance correspondent — the author of *Trillions*, which chronicled the rise of index investing — and he hosts his own show on the Monetary Matters Network. In the corpus he appears as a solo host, and his role shapes everything else about his profile: he is not a stock-picker putting ratings on names, but a finance reporter using historical analogy to frame where the system's stress is building. That shows up in his stance mix, which is 0 bullish, 0 bearish, 6 neutral — though "neutral" undersells how uneasy some of his actual commentary is.

His single captured appearance, the August 17, 2026 episode on the $1.5 trillion of hidden debt fueling the AI boom, lays out his framework. The core argument: "whenever a transformative new technology comes that typically manifests itself in both the stock and the bond market and sometimes the most dangerous" ([The $1.5 Trillion of Hidden Debt Fueling the AI Boom | Robi…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kZXjQZWUHH0)). In other words, the AI story isn't just an equity story — the credit market is where the hidden leverage lives. He scales the moment historically, noting that AI data centers represent "a few trillion dollars" today but arguing the comparison only becomes meaningful when scaled to the size of the US economy against past technological buildouts ([The $1.5 Trillion of Hidden Debt Fueling the AI Boom | Robi…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kZXjQZWUHH0)).

His sharpest language is reserved for credit. On private credit, he steps back from the noise to deliver a structural warning: "I think it's going to be a bad default cycle. It's started already" ([The $1.5 Trillion of Hidden Debt Fueling the AI Boom | Robi…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kZXjQZWUHH0)). And on the debt propping up AI-adjacent companies, he argues investors "have penciled in… I suspect unrealistic recovery rates when a lot of these companies are not going to have any recoveries whatsoever" ([The $1.5 Trillion of Hidden Debt Fueling the AI Boom | Robi…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kZXjQZWUHH0)). Calling that "neutral" is a classification artifact — a bad-default-cycle call with recoveries going to zero is about as cautious as journalism-as-analysis gets without issuing a sell rating.

One honest caveat: the corpus holds only this one episode, so there is no visible evolution of his views over time — no earlier stance to have moved from. What the single data point does establish is his throughline: when a speculative boom arrives, watch the bond market, not just the ticker.

person/ron-butler.text:
Ron Butler is a Canadian mortgage broker who has become one of the country's most visible housing commentators — the co-founder of Toronto-based Butler Mortgage, a regular presence on BNN Bloomberg and CBC, a frequent guest on finance and real-estate podcasts, and '@ronmortgageguy' on social media. His beat sits at the practical end of the housing debate: where mortgage rates are going, what renewal dynamics mean for Canadian borrowers, affordability, and home-price outlooks weighted heavily toward Ontario and British Columbia.

His clearest documented call is a pessimistic one for sellers: he has argued that elevated rates and available inventory would keep Canadian homebuyers in a buyer's market through 2026 and potentially into 2027. The corpus's dated record of his thinking comes from a single July 13, 2026 appearance on a video pointedly titled ["Housing Is Now Crashing: No Rebound For 18 Months Warns Exp…"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ls5lglIDTOA). There his macro read was diagnostic rather than directional: "The Canadian economy is weak. Uh, the United States economy is fine," he said, framing both countries as running a "K-shaped economy" while conceding "you can make some case that there are aspects of the US economy that are slightly overheated" ([Housing Is Now Crashing: No Rebound For 18 Months Warns Exp…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ls5lglIDTOA)).

On the supply side he was blunter, arguing that "decline is the only expected answer" and that there is "not really any rationale for a home builder to want to start new projects" under the conditions he described ([Housing Is Now Crashing: No Rebound For 18 Months Warns Exp…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ls5lglIDTOA)). The same appearance shows how far he'll range beyond renewals when prompted — into oil, no less. He flagged WTI holding above $100 a barrel as a live variable for North American inflation, and argued that "the basic math" of the last closing of the straits should have pushed prices "a lot closer to $150 a barrel" than what markets actually delivered ([Housing Is Now Crashing: No Rebound For 18 Months Warns Exp…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ls5lglIDTOA)). It's a useful reminder that despite the mortgage-broker day job, his commentary treats housing as a macro story — rates, energy, and the broader economy all feed his read on prices.

A caveat on the record itself: this corpus logs seven stances for Butler and all seven are neutral, with the entire timeline collapsing into that one July 2026 appearance. So there is no documented drift in his views here — no earlier bullish phase or later capitulation to chart. What the record does show, consistently, is a commentator whose throughline is extended weakness: a rates-and-inventory-driven buyer's market stretching into 2027, a weak Canadian economy underneath it, and no business case for builders to add supply. Treat the oil and US-economy remarks as texture around that core thesis rather than as standalone calls.

person/scott.text:

person/steve-hanke.text:
Steve Hanke is a professor of applied economics at Johns Hopkins University, and in the wider public debate he is one of the most recognizable voices on monetary disorder — a career spent designing currency boards and chronicling hyperinflations, from his advisory role on Argentina's convertibility regime in the 1990s to his widely circulated estimates of runaway inflation in Zimbabwe and Venezuela. His intellectual brand is sound money and hard constraints: deep skepticism of central bank discretion, hostility to fiat mismanagement in emerging markets, and famously blunt dismissals of bitcoin as money in any functional sense. That is the public figure. What this research corpus actually captures of him is far narrower — and the gap between the two is itself worth noting.

Per the digest's own record, Hanke appears exactly once, as an interview guest on David Lin's show, and that single appearance yields no logged stance in any direction: zero bullish, zero bearish, zero neutral calls, and no topic timelines whatsoever. For a commentator whose public style is built on pointed, dated calls — he typically names the currency, the number and the horizon — the absence of a single recorded position here is striking. It is also, fairly read, a statement about the corpus's coverage rather than about Hanke's convictions.

So the honest verdict on this page: it cannot yet show how his views have moved over time, because the timeline is empty, and it cannot name his strongest calls with dates, because none are logged in the source material. Rather than dress up silence as analysis, the right framing is that Hanke enters this corpus as a portrait without a track record — a significant, opinionated economist caught in a single frame. Readers who want his directional record will have to go to his public commentary directly; any movement in his views is, for now, undocumented here.

person/steve-keen.text:
Steve Keen is an economist best known as one of the loudest institutional critics of neoclassical economics — a self-styled heretic whose work draws more on Hyman Minsky and Irving Fisher's debt-deflation tradition than on the equilibrium models he made his name attacking. His general reputation, built over decades of public writing and books like *Debunking Economics*, rests on the argument that private debt accumulation, not exotic financial products alone, is the engine of financial crises — a position that put him among the heterodox economists widely credited with warning about the 2008 crash before it happened. That is the broad-strokes portrait, and it comes from public knowledge rather than the sourced record here.

Beyond that, the honest answer is that this page is running on fumes. The digest behind it contains no dated calls, no stances on any asset or policy, and no timeline of positions — nothing, in other words, on the questions a reader of an investment research corpus actually cares about: what did he recommend, when did he say it, and did he change his mind? The stance tally reads zero across bullish, bearish and neutral, which is a coverage gap, not a profile of a man famous for taking strident positions.

So treat this as a stub. Keen is clearly a figure worth tracking in a corpus like this — his debt-first framing makes him a recurring contrarian reference point in macro debates — but until the timeline data is filled in, any specific claim about when he turned on this asset or endorsed that policy would be invented, and this page won't do that.
