The other substantive entry is a level framework, not a call. On August 21, an unidentified speaker framed round numbers across the grain complex — "$7 wheat, $5 corn, approaching 13 soybeans, these are levels that if they hold" — a conditional, technical way of saying watch these supports rather than bet on direction. The sentence famously cuts off before telling us what happens if they don't hold. The timeline is also thinner than it looks: a July 16 entry for the same speaker is empty, meaning the real coverage window is barely a week in late August 2026. No one in this record changed their mind, because no one staked out a position long enough to flip from.

ticker/^DJI.text:
The recorded record on the Dow skews distinctly bearish, and it skews analogical. On July 6, an unnamed commentator writing in Cantonese flagged what they see as a bubble of the same magnitude as the early-2000s tech bust and the 2009 Lehman collapse — with the interesting part of the argument being the transmission mechanism rather than the bubble itself: bank stress cascading from the unwind, and a fight over whether the response is aggressive rate cuts or deeper stress in the banking system, either of which whipsaws US markets (July 6, unnamed speaker). Six weeks later, on August 18, a speaker the digest leaves anonymous — though he refers to himself as "Harry," pointing to longtime boom-and-bust forecaster Harry Dent — escalated the bear case to its logical extreme: the Dow would be "lucky" to fall only as much as it did from 1929 to 1932, a decline he puts at 89%. His kicker is the sharpest line in the record: today's Dow, he argues, "is more like the Nasdaq" — meaning the old blue-chip index now carries the concentrated, high-multiple risk profile of the late-90s tech index, so the Depression analogy applies more directly than skeptics assume (August 18, "Harry").

The bull side of this debate is nearly invisible as a live position. The only bullish-flavored entry is the same speaker's own retrospective — people used to tell him "there's no way in the hell the Dow's going to hit 10,000 by 2000" (August 18, "Harry"). That's a credibility claim, not a call, but it's also the clearest evidence of a mind changed over the long arc: whoever this is built his reputation on a boom forecast for the Dow and now anchors the crash case. Whether that track record strengthens or undercuts his 89% call is exactly what the bulls would contest — if any were on the record.

They aren't. The consensus tags three neutral voices, but the digest includes nothing they said, so the middle of this debate — the "overvalued but not 1929" camp — is a blank page. On what's actually documented, the timeline runs one direction: from bubble-and-bank-stress warning in July to full Depression-analogy crash call by August. Take it as a record of the bear argument's escalation, not a verdict on the index.

ticker/^HGX.text:
The recorded debate around ^HGX, the PHLX Housing Sector Index, is less a bull-versus-bear fight than a proxy war over the long end of the Treasury curve. The one commentator our coverage tracked in this window put both sides of the trade on the record the same day, August 22, 2026: bearish if the 10-year can't be brought down, warning that "if they're unable to do so and yields continue to rise" the housing index faces continued pressure; bullish on the flip side, arguing that if "they manage to take the long end down and that's better for housing," the index could shoot meaningfully higher. That's a textbook rates-conditional framing — homebuilders are levered to mortgage costs, so the bull case and the bear case here are literally the same mechanism with the sign flipped on yields. Nobody on record disputes that linkage; the entire question is which way the 10-year breaks.

What's missing is the actual disagreement. The consensus tally reads mixed — one bull, one bear, one neutral — but this digest surfaces only a single, unnamed voice (logged as "?" in the record) holding both conditionals simultaneously. An earlier entry dated August 11, 2026 carries no quote at all, so it's impossible to say whether that was a genuine neutral stance, a hedge, or simply a gap in the transcript. In other words, the bull-versus-bear structure on this page is currently a frame without a fight: the tally implies opposing camps, but the only documented call is one person hedging both directions against the same yield scenario.

Readers should treat this accordingly. The timeline is thin — a blank entry on August 11, then the dual-sided conditional on August 22 — and coverage doesn't yet include anyone willing to stake out an unconditional view on the index itself. The honest summary of the debate, such as it exists: direction of ^HGX equals direction of the long bond, full stop, pending somebody actually picking a side.

ticker/^HSI.text:
The record on Hong Kong equities in this corpus is lopsided enough that "the debate" is almost a misnomer: the aggregate tally reads neutral/watch, but that balance comes from a wall of no-opinion coverage. Among the voices who actually committed to a direction, there are zero bulls. What's on file is a macro bear and a local commentator who talked himself into one.

The macro case comes from [Jeff Snider](../People/jeff-snider.md), who on June 27, 2026 framed Hong Kong as a casualty of dollar-system stress: when the Eurodollar system isn't doing well, he argued, the world turns risk-averse just as the global economy is reversing — and China is "not doing well. In fact, it's accelerating to the downside." That's the entire bull/bear architecture in one sentence: Hong Kong equities as high-beta exposure to a Chinese economy that is deteriorating, not stabilizing.

The more interesting trajectory belongs to an unnamed Cantonese-language commentator who circles the index for two months before landing bearish. On July 23 he was running crash scenarios — the index shedding 5% in a single week, and in a transition shock lasting two to three weeks, drawdowns of as much as 50%. A month later, on August 23, he conceded the strongest bull point anyone in this file offers: valuations are cheap relative to global peers and US equities, a genuine positive. But he immediately smothered it with the sanctions risk hanging over Chinese enterprises. By August 28 the hedging was gone — after a fall of roughly 3,600 points from around 66,200 and an equally quick recovery, his verdict was that any such bounce "can only be treated as a rebound," not a turn in the trend.

So the shape of it: the bull case exists only as a caveat inside a bear argument, the timeline runs from scenario-mongering in July to outright bearishness by late August, and nobody on record flipped the other way. The neutral consensus is really an absence of conviction, not a counterargument.

ticker/^IRX.text:
The file on ^IRX reads less like a debate and more like a monologue. Two calls, one speaker — unnamed in the corpus — one week apart in August 2026, both leaning the same direction: the front end of the bill curve rolling over. On August 15 the speaker noted that "even term sofa rates like bill rates are moving and rolling over having never really bought into the rate hike or imminent rate hike" — the pointed claim being that the short end never priced the tightening in the first place, so there is no hawkish expectation to unwind. By August 22 the same voice had added a mechanical layer to the story: "what's going to happen is that banks and money market funds, particularly banks, are going to have to go out and buy more T-bills," a forced-demand argument in which structural buyers press yields lower regardless of what the Fed says.

Strip away the scoring and the substance here is a coherent lower-yields case built on bill demand — banks and money market funds absorbing supply — layered on top of an expectations story about a front end that never priced the hikes. But the corpus tags both calls neutral, and there is a defensible logic to that: ^IRX is a short-rate index, not a stock, and "yields down" is an observation about the rate complex rather than a directional trade. Still, the neutral/watch consensus (0 bullish, 0 bearish, 2 neutral) should be read for what it is — an absence of coverage, not a settled midpoint between two argued positions. Nobody has taken the other side. There is no bull arguing the rollover is noise, no bear contending that bill supply overwhelms money-market demand, and nobody making the case that the hikes do get priced eventually.

On the question of who changed their mind: no one, visibly. It is the same speaker, consistent in direction across the week, with the August 15 and August 22 entries complementing rather than contradicting each other — expectations first, flows second. The genuine gap is attribution: with the speaker unnamed, there is no track record to weigh and no way to judge conviction. Until a counterparty enters the ledger, this page documents one analyst's short-end thesis, not a debate — and readers should treat the "consensus" label accordingly.

ticker/^KS11.text:
The KOSPI debate is, on paper, barely a debate at all: the corpus tally sits at zero bullish, zero bearish, and five neutral — a "watch" verdict — and nearly every substantive call comes from a single, unnamed cycle-timing analyst (the digest doesn't attach a name to him). What both voices in the record agree on is the backdrop. The guest analyst observed on June 17 that "the KOSPI basically doubled this year," and the cycle analyst recounted on July 5 that Korea had risen two and a half times off its starting point into August — a run that ended when the index "plummeted on July 2nd." What followed is the fact that frames everything since: by August 12 the KOSPI was down nearly 44%, in what the cycle analyst describes as a major crash into a cycle date, panic selling, "margin calls all over the place" — a market that "was liquefied."

The bull case is pure capitulation contrarianism. The cycle analyst's argument is that a crash landing precisely on a cycle date, with forced liquidation everywhere, is itself the signal — exhaustion, not trend — and on that basis he is carrying a long position as of August 12.

The bear case, such as it is, comes from the same mouth on the same day. Despite the long, he expects a retest: the index "gapped into its recovery high date," and in his framework a gap into a recovery high is a warning rather than a launchpad, making him short-term bearish even while positioned for upside. Sharper still is his conditional from that session — drawdowns between 12 and 19% are normal, but anything beyond 19% "suggests something different" and means it's "going to go much lower." Here lies the genuine tension in the record: a 44% collapse clears his own 19% threshold by a wide margin, which by his logic argues the break was structural rather than a routine correction — yet he's bought it anyway. He is long the reversion and braced for the retest, and the digest gives no evidence he has reconciled the two.

As for who changed their mind: nobody cleanly did. The guest analyst's June 17 remark was observation, not a stance, and the July 5 commentary was retrospective framing rather than a call. The only real pivot on record happened inside one analyst's head between early July and August 12 — from narrating a two-and-a-half-times rally to buying the wreckage of it, and even then with a retest caveat bolted on. Notably, no named bear ever put a short on the record; the bearish view exists only as hedging inside a long. The neutral consensus, in that light, looks less like indecision than an honest reflection of a market where the sole analyst with a view is arguing with himself.

ticker/^NDX.text:
The Nasdaq 100 debate in this record is really a story about one technician's whipsaw through August 2026, with a single firm bear — [Milton Berg](../People/milton-berg.md) — planted on the other side. The official tally (1 bullish, 0 bearish, 6 neutral) makes this look like a calm, consensus-bullish tape, but the actual calls tell a jittier story: the most vocal bull spent the month talking himself out of, and then partially back into, the trade.

The unnamed technician (the transcript record doesn't attach a name) started the month constructive. On August 6 he read the index as "overall… still correcting," noting "it's a nine today. Does that stop it? Maybe." — a measured, if cryptic, nod to his count rather than a full-throated buy. By August 12 the tone had turned sharply cautious: "Nasdaq 100, same too. Same situation. You had a panic low, short big rally, a gap, which looks exhausted because it didn't follow through…" That's the pivot in this record — a gap he once might have read as strength he now flagged as exhaustion. Yet two weeks later, on August 25, he flipped back to leaning up, arguing that "if we happen to gap lower it is very possible that we actually get a close above the opening print," while hedging with the expectation of "some explosive volatility in either direction." That last call is the tell: his August 25 stance is less a conviction bull case than a bet on violence in both directions, with a slight upward tilt.

Against that, [Milton Berg](../People/milton-berg.md) delivered the only outright bearish call on the tape, also on August 12 — the same day the unnamed technician turned cautious. Berg's framing was retrospective and confident: the prior action had "proved to be a top in the semiconductor index and the Nasdaq 100 and the Nasdaq." Note that Berg tied the index to the semiconductors, implicitly making the chip complex the swing factor for the whole NDX — a linkage the bull side never directly contests.

What's striking about the shape of this debate is how little actual bull-versus-bear disagreement there is. Nobody in the record argues against Berg's top call; the bulls' strongest August 12 evidence (the exhausted gap) and the bear's evidence (the top) point at the same price action read two ways. And the six neutral stances in the tally essentially decline to fight on either side. The honest summary: one persistent bear, one technician who oscillated from bullish to cautious to conditionally bullish in nineteen days, and a field of abstainers. If the gap-resolve thesis is right, the bulls get the last word; if Berg's top holds, he was early and alone — which is where he usually likes to be.

ticker/^RUT.text:
For a small-cap index that just printed its fastest momentum in half a decade and then gave back more than 12%, the recorded debate around the Russell 2000 is conspicuously hollow: zero analysts on the bull side, zero on the bear side, three sitting at neutral/watch. The only real texture in the file comes from a single, unnamed speaker commenting on August 12, 2026 — and the corpus doesn't even attach a name to the voice, which is worth flagging as an attribution gap rather than papering over.

The story that speaker tells is a two-act technical retrospective. Act one is strength: off the March low, the Russell 2000's 10-day rate of change was "the greatest in 1,260 days, which I think is 5 years," and on the very day the S&P bottomed, the Russell sat above its 5-day moving average — a streak that had run 16 consecutive days. That's the kind of tape bulls would cite as proof of a durable rotation into small caps. Act two undercuts it: a gap-based call that "proved successful" as the index "ultimately declined a total of 12.07%."

So the actual debate isn't bull versus bear — it's the same data set pointing both directions: record five-year momentum against a double-digit drawdown. Nobody in the record changed their mind, nobody planted a flag, and the neutral cluster reads less like conviction than a standoff.

ticker/^SOX.text:
The striking thing about the SOX debate as of the August 12, 2026 commentary is that there isn't one — not in the conventional bull-versus-bear sense. The consensus tally reads zero bullish calls against one bearish and six neutral, which means the actual argument is between outright bears and a large crowd standing on the sidelines. Milton Berg carries the bear flag, pointing to the signs of a top in June that "ultimately proved to be a top in the semiconductor index" — a clean, unambiguous call that treats the June turn as settled fact rather than open question ([Milton Berg](../People/milton-berg.md)).

The only real tension in the record comes from a second, unnamed voice — and it's tension within a single position, not between camps. This speaker is long, but explicitly short-term bearish: they suggest the SOX, alongside Korea's KOSPI, "may rally, may peak right around here, and trade back down to the lows." Their evidence is a historic rally of over 100% in the index, followed by a failure to push meaningfully above prior gap levels and a subsequent 16.64% decline. In other words, a structural bull with a tactical bear case layered on top. It's also worth flagging the hedging in their language — "this is a signal, but... this is not an important signal. We had so many signals" — which reads like someone aware their technical toolkit has been firing so often it's lost discriminating power.

On timeline: everything in the record lands on the same date, so there's no documented mind-changing to narrate — no one flipped, no one doubled down across weeks of calls. The June top is the shared anchor: Berg treats it as confirmation of a completed topping process, while the long-positioned speaker treats it as context for why the index's failure at the old gap highs matters. That's the shape of the debate, such as it is — thin coverage, one hard bear, one conflicted bull, and six neutrals whose silence is arguably the most telling data point in the file.

ticker/^TYX.text:
The entire August 2026 debate over the 30-year Treasury yield revolves around one number: roughly 5.3%. On August 20, [Patrick](../People/patrick.md) flagged that "bonds reversed off of yields that were near around 530 on the 30-year Treasury yield," explicitly framing that level as a ceiling candidate — the open question being whether the reversal holds. It mostly did, though unconvincingly. Unnamed commentary noted on August 25 that even after "what he did" — an apparent intervention in the bond market — the 30-year was "still hanging right up there," before yielding modest ground: by August 28 the same tracking showed the yield had touched 5.3% but pulled back to "closer to 5.2%, 10 basis points lower" after the intervention. Ten basis points is not a trend; it is a truce.

The case for lower yields rests on the view that the intervention itself is disinflationary rather than inflationary. Jeff argued on August 23 that the policy move under discussion was "not going to be inflationary" and "not going to lead to higher interest rates. It's going to lead to the exact opposite." The structural middle ground came on August 24, when unnamed speakers observed that long-term yields are elevated relative to the post-2008 era but have "not broken decisively away from levels first reached in 2023" — and, crucially, made their call conditional: watch term premiums and inflation compensation, because "if any of that changes... long-term yields will break higher relative to the front." That conditionality is the honest center of this debate: nobody claims a clean break in either direction, only a set of tripwires.

The yield-higher camp is smaller but sharper. [Milton Berg](../People/milton-berg.md) was bearish bonds as of August 12, pointing to "the 30-year bond at the highest levels in... decades." [Rick Rule](../People/rick-rule.md) made the most explicitly conditional call of the group on August 26: if free markets set rates, a riskless counterparty would demand roughly 150 basis points over the real yield — the implication being that current yields only look adequate because something other than the market is setting them.

What is striking is how little committed conviction surrounds all of this. The recorded tally runs 2 bullish against 0 bearish with 24 neutral — an overwhelming majority unwilling to pick a side. The debate, in other words, is not bulls versus bears so much as intervention versus term premium: one camp reads the reversal off 5.3% and the 10-basis-point easing as proof the ceiling holds, while Berg's "highest levels in decades" and Rule's free-market arithmetic suggest that if the intervention's grip slips, the long end breaks higher relative to the front — and the coverage here is thin enough that nobody has yet been forced to reconcile the two.

ticker/^VIX.text:
The honest headline for the VIX page right now is that there isn't much of a debate — the tracked commentary splits zero bullish, zero bearish, three neutral, and even the attribution is murky: the digest records the quotes without naming who said them. Coverage is thin enough that one of the three entries, dated July 2, 2026, carries no quote at all. So rather than a bull-versus-bear fight, what you have is a watch-list tension building over three days in mid-July.

That tension comes into focus on July 19, when the commentary notes the market closing "at a believe a new high print on the year" while the VIX was "only trading at 18.77%." This juxtaposition is the crux of every volatility debate: either a sub-19 VIX against record equity highs signals complacency — cheap insurance before a storm — or it's the market correctly pricing an environment where nobody fears the downside. Notably, the speaker doesn't pick a side. They lay the two facts next to each other and let the contradiction sit, which is exactly why the consensus lands on "watch" rather than a call.

Three days later, on July 22, the same commentary drifts toward the cautious reading, arguing that rising implied correlations "typically" come before volatility — a technically fair point, since when correlations climb, diversification fails and hedging demand tends to spike across the board. But even that observation stops short of a directional call. It's a conditional warning about regime risk, not a prediction that the VIX goes up.

The timeline, then, runs from silence (July 2's empty entry) to an open question (July 19's high-prints-plus-low-VIX puzzle) to a correlation red flag (July 22). Nobody changed their mind because nobody staked a position to change. If you're looking for a spark in this corpus, it's the implied-correlation thread — that's the only argument on the page with any forward lean, and even it ends in an ellipsis.

study/cpm-group/topic/gold-silver-price-.text:
The archive runs on two clocks. Annual yearbook launches anchor it — April 2015, then March 2017, March 2019, and March 2020 — and from July 2020 the video feed itself becomes a metronome, publishing commentary nearly every week: July 6, August 4, August 14, August 31, September 4 and 18, October 2, 9, 16, 23, 30, November 6, 13, 30, December 4, 11, 18, straight through into 2021 [([Jul 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zTueacq7_r8), [Oct 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YPfeR2Kml4I), [Dec 18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Hu3yedI5Dbg))]. Several entries — August 14, October 2, October 30, November 30 — are even logged twice, same URL, same date, which is almost too on-the-nose for a recycling audit [([Aug 14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ukhj3jSRAQE), [Oct 30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2KmnouE61Yg))]. The deep reads confirm the recurrence is structural: every sampled item is flagged recurring, and two — May 19, 2020 and one of the three September 29, 2023 entries — record new="nothing" outright; an August 18, 2023 read is likewise "this week's snapshot only."

What repeats is a skeleton: today's gold and silver levels, the range "we've been talking about for a while" (May 31, 2022), fresh client trade recommendations ("cpm group today has issued new trade recommendations for gold and for silver," November 9, 2021; again "yesterday monday the 18th" in April 2022), and imperative titles like "No One Should Be Short On Gold" [([Aug 31, 2020](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fRzghWogdJg))]. Market-state declarations are stock phrases too — "the gold price dropped 27 today" (September 24, 2021), "gold is now broken above 1800 it's actually broken above 1820 today uh it's gotten up to about 1832" (November 9, 2021). The most literal act of recycling comes May 31, 2024, when the video re-shows the 10-year silver projection chart from the 2021 Silver Yearbook, with Mike Hollings objecting they were "giving away uh what we charge a lot for" — and in the same breath the old forecast is walked back: "actually higher projections than we have now we've lowered the projections," a long way from 2021's call for annual average silver to "exceed $40."

Genuinely new material enters in two registers. Mostly it is level-setting — the week's digits ladder upward across the archive: $1,600–$1,800 gold and $22–$27 silver ranges (April 9, 2021), downside targets of 1,780 and possibly 1,680 (July 30, 2021), five-quarter consolidation bands of 1,740–1,900/1,740–2,000 (September 24, 2021), the record $1,798.97 annual average (December 21, 2021), then $2,538 intraday (August 2024), $2,700 (October 2024), roughly $3,000 (March 2025), $3,500 after "a $500 surge in about 10-12 days" (April 22, 2025), nearly $3,900 (September 30, 2025), over $4,200 (November 14, 2025), $4,500 (January 6, 2026), above $4,600 with silver near $71.38 (August 28, 2026). The other register is exogenous shocks: Ukraine's "major battle is starting today as we speak" (April 19, 2022), the post-CPI spike to $1,975 (November 14, 2023), the July 7, 2025 tariff-deadline whipsaw, and January 2026's shutdown-delayed data that "may be economically hostile" and "could add to the fuel." The earliest new-material flag is franchise-building rather than markets — August 21, 2020, when silver-focused commentaries spin off from the gold feed. Occasionally the loop pauses to keep score: the July 15, 2021 trade call largely materializing at $1,837, and platinum printing 904 against the projected 905 bottom (September 29, 2023).

The moments the author says something has changed are, tellingly, mostly confessions about timing. July 30, 2021: "we had thought that the prices would be a little bit stronger uh but they haven't been." May 31, 2022: "we thought that the prices would show a little bit more strength than they have." February 22, 2023: "prices have been weaker than some people expected they've been weaker than CPM group expected actually." November 14, 2023: "we have moderated some of our expectations for how high prices will go over the last several years." Meanwhile the core call never moves — April 9, 2021's "we do still expect higher gold and silver prices later at toward the last four months of this year and into 2022 and beyond" is the same deferral restated for years — until it finally cashes on May 31, 2024: "we thought we'd enter a period of sharply higher prices 2024 2025 and we are." The bookend arrives August 28, 2026, in the same grammar: "Instead, investor buying began earlier" than the expected timeline. Wrong on the clock, right on the compass, repeatedly.

Only once does the argument itself change rather than the numbers. On April 22, 2025, amid the $3,500 breakout, CPM flags that the safe-haven reflex has decoupled: "This time around, we're not seeing a surge into the dollar, and we're not seeing a surge into treasuries" — investors turning to gold alone, unlike the 1978–1980 and 2002–2011 spikes, as "the dollar has fallen and treasury bonds have fallen and gold prices have risen sharply." Everything else is the same machine with updated digits, right down to Jackson Hole serving twice as a calendar landmark — two-sided scenarios around it in August 2025, then a year later the note that "the gold price took off last year after the Kansas City Fed uh Jackson Hole conference." The cadence of reuse, in short, is metronomic — weekly-to-monthly updates inside annual yearbook re-anchors — the directional call barely moves for five years, and "change" is declared most often as an apology for being early.

study/cpm-group/topic/debunking-myths-an.text:
This archive is a debunking franchise, and its most striking feature is how little the raw material changes over two years. The core myth set is fixed by late 2020 and early 2021: that gold and silver are manipulated, that physical shortage is imminent, that the dollar relationship dooms gold, and that collapse is around the corner. The "myth vs reality" framing is on the table by July 2020 ([Gold: Myth vs Reality](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtuyP7NiPsg), July 17, 2020), and the conspiracy/manipulation thread runs from February 2021 ([Conspiracy Theories, Manipulation…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9rVxB_tvGuM), February 5, 2021) through ([Who's Been Fooling Whom In Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nnX-4J3WOlk), August 17, 2021). The clearest evidence that this is recycled stock material, not fresh analysis: the May 5, 2021 upload is explicitly a re-run — [Conspiracy Theories Are A Distraction (2008)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lM-Wl8tCaJg) — meaning the argument predates this entire archive by over a decade.

The recycling loop is easy to map because each standing myth gets re-debunked on a several-month cycle. Shortage claims: addressed in June 2021 ([The US Mint "Global Silver Shortage" Explained](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gVEVhwK4UOc)) and again almost a year later ([Ample Supplies If You Know How To Look](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jDwWMa22XcQ), May 24, 2022). Collapse-and-hyperbole claims: August 2021 ([The Imminent Economic Collapse…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sRqbuPl9c_k)), December 2021 ([Overcome Misinformation and Fear…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dwkmQyCIdyQ)), May 2022 ([Fatal Market Hyperbole](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sOZzfktO8ko)). Foundational nostalgia gets the same treatment ([Nostalgia For A Gold Standard That Never Was](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gTCGEdqDwWk), August 27, 2021), as do the dollar-inversion and rates myths ([Gold and the Dollar Can Rise Together](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EdlOqZEF_xA), November 13, 2020; [Why Interest Rates Won't Hurt Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RiRYdTEmEpw), August 20, 2021).

Genuinely new information enters only when the outside world forces it in, and it arrives in tight clusters. The February–March 2021 silver squeeze produced five items in under three months, including the event-specific [Silver Futures Contract Default Not Likely](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C1EYmE719jY) (February 23, 2021), a credibility defense of CPM's own record ([CPM Group's Record On Silver…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bxcPKsYf25o), March 3, 2021), and a direct open letter to the silver community ([The Company You Keep](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7K3yzsxzlaI), April 27, 2021). The war in Ukraine triggered the second genuine infusion: [The Wartime Market](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=77RCqH8YI64) (March 18, 2022) and [The Truth About Russian Gold and The Ruble](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7q88UbXPoC0) (April 4, 2022). Everything else — the inflation relationship, the constitutional arguments, the "real factors" explainer ([The Real Factors Driving Gold and Silver Prices](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E5KqE4MVKbo), December 23, 2021) — is elaboration of the standing framework, not new material.

On the specific question of moments where the author says something HAS changed: the digest here is title-level only, with no transcripts, so I cannot quote spoken claims and won't invent them. The only verbatim language available is the titles themselves, and notably their rhetoric runs the other way — they insist nothing fundamental has changed, that the same debunked narratives keep returning. The closest title-level change-assertions are denials of others' change claims: [No Smash Down In Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJ6GSblMPwU) (August 13, 2021) rejects the claim that a smash-down occurred, and the dollar piece asserts a relationship (both rising together) that the standard narrative denies. The cadence tells the real story: 2020 runs at roughly monthly pace, 2021 accelerates to near-biweekly during the squeeze and again in a five-video August burst, and 2022 settles into event-paced monthly output. The template re-fires every two to six weeks under market stress, but the underlying argument — the myths are old, the fundamentals are knowable, nothing has really changed — never updates.

study/cpm-group/topic/investment-strateg.text:
The spine of this archive is a single evergreen thesis — you should own some gold and silver — recycled across formats, while the genuinely dated material is the thin tactical overlay on top. The clearest verbatim reuse is the "how much should you own" explainer, which runs on February 4, 2022 as ["How Much Gold and Silver You Should Own in 2022"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GFrA3KxXYIw) and resurfaces on October 11, 2022 with the year simply stripped out, ["How Much Gold and Silver You Should Own"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0lLi8EEVgkE) — the same content with an expired freshness stamp removed. The same argument also gets retitled rather than updated: "Gold and Silver: The Reasons to Invest" (October 12, 2021) becomes ["Why Gold and Silver Are Important Investments"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cUkLJcNj2E8) the following July, and the safe-haven framing of March 2021, ["What Makes Gold And Silver Safe Havens?"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tIAu3Z9qgtQ), is rebadged for the 2022 inflation environment as ["What Makes Gold An Excellent Hedge Against Inflation"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kYkxdMHkAG0). The allocation pitch is a permanent fixture; only the justification label rotates with the macro cycle.

The tactical layer is where new material actually enters, and it clusters hard in mid-2020. The recommendation series runs nearly identical titles four days apart — June 8 ([CPM Gold Trade Signal and Recommendation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KzmKuzuz2DQ)) and June 12 ([CPM Gold Trade Signal and Recommendation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jbWsOJYnrtg)) — then pivots to argument on July 14 with a specific piece of new content, the case against ["$10,000 gold"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qjkFnDZ2YME), a direct engagement with the hyper-bullish retail targets of that moment. April 2021 brings a second burst of new material: a week-apart silver-buying pair, ["Affordable Silver Premia"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O7xMB0DEw6k) and ["Buying Silver Smartly"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iARhszarP_A), plus an outlier format — ["The Company You Keep – An Open Letter to Silver Investors"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7K3yzsxzlaI) — the only "open letter" in the visible archive, landing squarely in the post-squeeze silver milieu. The genuinely new operational content, and the thing this topic is named for, arrives only in early 2022: a hedging curriculum running from ["How To Hedge Long Gold and Silver Investments"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iHl_riZ_jhM) on January 14 through ["Effective Hedging For Producers"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NeBvwPjQbC4) on March 4, which extends the retail hedging argument to a producer audience for the first time.

A caveat on the "quote them when something changed" requirement: this archive is title-level only, so no verbatim on-camera statements are available, and I won't invent any. But the change-language lives in the titles themselves, and it marks a coherent sequence. "Why It Is Time To [Stand Aside](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=efUpv9lqFe8)" (July 27, 2020) is the first explicit de-risking signal; "Backfield In Motion" ([October 30, 2020](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2KmnouE61Yg)) implies re-engagement; ["short term SELL recommendation"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JFZi4kXULCI) (January 22, 2021) is the bluntest directional break; and ["STAND ASIDE recommendation for Gold; BUY for Silver"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q8N1yQ5R8c0) (March 16, 2021) splits the book by metal for the first time. The 2021 close reframes the whole year as changed conditions — ["Hard Gold and Silver Market Lessons Learned in 2021"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c3pZ-qhhw0Y) — and the 2022 regime change is summed up in four words: ["Stay Long and Hedge"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DEMbMttQ8tI). That last one is the sharpest pivot in the file: after two years of alternating buy/stand-aside signals, the settled position becomes permanent ownership wrapped in a hedging discipline.

On cadence: 2020 is genuinely tactical, with recommendation updates roughly every three to six weeks (June 8, June 12, July 14, July 27, [September 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E5JhBGif3Q8), [November 20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1CANPjTFnH8)). 2021 degrades into a monthly evergreen drip — portfolio diversification (May 14), ["Best Times To Buy... Heading Into Summer"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m__yw5BAV3Q), a volatility warning (["July 2"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e-9_12Som2A)), a GDP-and-buy-signals piece (["October 22"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_Qta2pUGmTc)), and a misinformation argument (["December 7"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dwkmQyCIdyQ)) — high reuse, low new information. 2022 fragments into clusters (Jan–Mar hedging, then an explainer run) with a roughly ten-week silence between ["How To Lose Your Money"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6LQH-_o6ko4) on April 26 and the July 8 "Why Important" piece. Two honesty notes: the timeline header claims 69 items but shows 30, so these cadence reads likely undercount; and the underlying shape of the debate never actually changes — the allocation thesis is constant, and what recycles is the packaging around it.

study/cpm-group/topic/metals-supply-and-.text:
The spine of this archive is a calendar, not an argument. CPM Group's reuse cadence is annual and almost mechanical: a gold yearbook every spring (March 26, 2019; March 24, 2020; March 23, 2021; April 6, 2022), a silver yearbook or outlook every April–May (April 23, 2019; May 11, 2021; May 10, 2022; May 16, 2023), and PGM coverage stacked in mid-year (June 30, 2020; July 13, 2021), supplemented by an off-cycle [market alert on the energy transition and PGMs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sZb5sH7W1sw) on October 21, 2022. Between those fixed deliverables, the same fundamentals framework gets re-applied to whatever the news hands over. The densest stretch is June–July 2021, with six items in nine weeks — including two separate PGM pieces eight days apart ([July 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o0Vb7ZwJfzs) and [July 13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ehnP-WKg6N4)) — which suggests volume driven by client demand rather than by anything new in the metal balances.

What actually repeats, beyond the publishing schedule, is the core claim: supply is ample; demand is the whole story. That argument is restated with near-identical wording across at least four titles in eighteen months — ["The Fundamentals Still A…"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cmYTa9fDLY8) (June 25, 2021), ["It Is Still All About Demand"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o0Vb7ZwJfzs) (July 9, 2021), jewelry-demand commentary with Jeffrey Christian (December 3, 2021), ["Ample Supplies If You Know How To Look"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jDwWMa22XcQ) (May 24, 2022), and ["Plenty Of Available Metal!"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CdXwDvPhsaI) (December 6, 2022). The repeated "still" and "ample" framing is the tell: continuity *is* the brand here, and the supply-scare narrative is the recurring foil it pushes against — whether that foil is the [US Mint "global silver shortage" of June 2021](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gVEVhwK4UOc) or the [2.4 billion ounces of above-ground gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C_arxbNhm1o) invoked in February 2022.

Genuinely new information enters only when the macro environment forces it. January 8, 2021 brings the Capitol events as a gold-market catalyst; February 17, 2021 introduces the commodities super-cycle debate, which the title ["Economics 101 vs Commodities Super Cycle"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bp4IOm8hPks) frames as an external claim to be rebutted rather than a house thesis. Russia's invasion produces a [March 8, 2022 piece on gold rallying as Russia looks for buyers](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=20QsWnUrRD0). The one truly new recurring thread is the energy transition: it first appears in the [October 2022 PGM alert](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sZb5sH7W1sw), gets a dedicated supply question on [March 17, 2023 — can solar demand deplete silver reserves?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F673kCAYyZo) — and then pivots by [May 26, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AOiIWRI6FJ4) to "The Energy Transition Will Be Delayed," a shift from metal-balance arithmetic to macro-skepticism. China's opaque reserves ([January 27, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BNUrHI4gHNY)) and shifting institutional money in mining ([April 18, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0XRMaFy1j5o)) round out the newer material, though both read as one-offs rather than threads.

On the specific question of moments where the author says something *has changed*: the honest answer is that this digest carries titles and dates only, so I cannot quote any verbatim declaration of change without fabricating one, and I won't. The title-level evidence actually cuts the other way — explicit change-language appears just once ("Changing Institutional Investment Trends In Mining," April 18, 2023), while the markers that recur are all continuity claims ("Still All About Demand," "Fundamentals Still A…," "Ample Supplies"). Two caveats on completeness: this excerpt shows 31 of the 64 archived items and cuts off at May 26, 2023, so anything said later is unknowable from here. But within the record shown, the pattern is a house view that treats fundamentals as essentially unchanging and locates all the drama in the news cycle — which is either consistency or staleness, depending on how much you think the 2021–2023 energy-transition and super-cycle debates actually moved the goalposts.

study/cpm-group/topic/economic-outlook-a.text:
The archive's shape tells you most of what you need to know. It opens with a one-off dollar-strength piece in June 2016 ([How Strong is the US Dollar 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QSBDIUoKWV0)), then goes silent for four years before relaunching in August 2020 with Jeffrey Christian and CPM Group under a title that is essentially the entire thesis: "All Roads Lead To Gold" ([CPM Group - All Roads Lead To Gold - Jeffrey Christian](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNkMV4Je9Fk)). From there, every macro subject — debt, inflation, recession, politics — is resolved into the same gold-and-silver conclusion. One honest caveat before the timeline: this digest consists of titles and dates only, with no transcript text, so the "change" moments below are quoted from exact title wording rather than spoken remarks.

The single most recycled asset in this corpus is the recession itself. It debuts as "The Imminent Economic Collapse" on August 31, 2021 ([The Imminent Economic Collapse and What It Means For Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sRqbuPl9c_k)), re-enters through the inflation-and-rates lens in June 2022 ([How Inflation, Interest Rates and Recession May Affect Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=10zL22_Y39s)), gets a duration estimate a month later ([How Long The Recession Will Last And How It Will Affect Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zp8K-lh1Bu4)), is declared flatly in October 2022 ([A Recession Is Coming - This Is Why](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dvWvJK5b8Kw)), reappears as a question in March 2023 ([Gold and Silver Market Update: The Next Recession?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QyOCdpZkhtU)), becomes preparation material by October 2023 ([Preparing For The Next Recession With Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuUnsDXzh9k)), and is still headlining the 2024 forecast in May 2024 ([2024 Gold And Silver Forecast: Inflation, Recession, and Profiting](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3BGoTQ7i_vg)). Notably, no item in the timeline is titled as the recession having actually arrived — the call stays permanently prospective for nearly three years. Two other threads recycle alongside it: US debt, which runs from the October 2021 debt-ceiling piece ([The Debt Ceiling and Silver Trading Patterns](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cWcWZxI5WEY)) through "The Debt To Fear" ([Gold Market Update: The Debt To Fear And How To Prepare](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gPw0A4N34P8)) to "What The US Debt Means" in April 2024 ([What The US Debt Means For The Economy, Gold, and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-PCuBTkczDs)); and the imperative to prepare, which appears in three consecutive titles from October through December 2023.

The declared regime changes are worth quoting as they stand. On October 5, 2021 the title announces a "New Monetary Policy Regime" ([Gold and Silver Are Adjusting To A New Monetary Policy Regime](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0obgfA3eB0Q)); seven weeks later, "New Economic Realities Set In" ([Gold and Silver Plunge As New Economic Realities Set In](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WmMk8JglQo8)) — two structural breaks announced within two months of each other. The 2023 versions get more hedged: "Complex Transitions In The Economy" in February ([Complex Transitions In The Economy, Gold, and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SdIoiDRgDNI)) names change without direction, and March's "The Beginning of The End (of What?)" ([Gold and Silver Market Update: The Beginning of The End (of What?)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ikmXhMagKSQ)) declares an inflection point with its own question mark attached. Whether stronger language was used inside the videos cannot be verified from this digest.

Genuinely new arguments enter only a handful of times. February 2021 brings the super-cycle-versus-Economics-101 framing ([Economics 101 vs Commodities Super Cycle](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bp4IOm8hPks)); June 2021 adds the institutional layer of central bank gold practices ([Central Bank Gold Practices; US Debt and Gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fimg7ZB8wGA)); October 2023 introduces political dysfunction as a cost driver ([The Cost of Political Dysfunction and Its Impact On Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7W3jEZqWWGQ)); and July 2024 offers the first real divergence call — gold resilient, silver struggling, "economic surprises" in play ([Gold Is Resilient But Silver Struggles](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-3hVHJt95Jk)). The pattern in each case is the same: a new driver gets welded to an unchanged conclusion. The recommendation never rotates even as the justification cycles from debt ceiling to rates to dysfunction and back to debt.

The cadence is itself evidence of reuse. After the 2020 relaunch there is a burst of six items between August and November 2021, near-monthly output from June 2022 through January 2023, a double in March 2023, another cluster October–December 2023, then a slowdown to roughly quarterly in 2024. Output intensity peaks exactly when recession language peaks in 2022 and thins as the timeline moves into 2024 without any "it happened" item — the publishing rhythm tracks the fear cycle, not the arrival of new information.

study/cpm-group/topic/geopolitics-and-po.text:
The geopolitics thread in this CPM Group corpus begins where you'd expect: the November 2020 US election. Jeffrey Christian laid out the gold-and-silver landscape heading into the vote on October 9, 2020 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=375ocZPpiqI)), followed it with an "Election and its Aftermath" piece on October 23 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yCcUJABE6F8)), and by December 4 was folding the result into history — "Politics and Gold, The Lessons of 1933" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PVznAwB10mQ)), reaching back to the Depression-era gold recall for a framework. The template is set immediately: an external political shock, then the question of what it means for gold and silver. It fired once more on January 8, 2021 — "Gold Fell As DC Burned," two days after the Capitol riot ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gN-aOb4Iqag)) — and then the topic goes silent for eight months.

Geopolitics returns on September 10, 2021, genericized to "Worldwide Risks" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MMzgPml9Kho)), and here genuinely new arguments enter: a September 17 piece on what the Constitution "REALLY" says about gold and silver ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NDU7yndPMC0)) — a legal-textual angle absent from the 2020 material — and an October 1 tie between the debt-ceiling standoff and silver trading patterns ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cWcWZxI5WEY)). Then the war. "The Finance of War: Russia, Gold, and Silver" lands February 18, 2022, six days before Russia invaded Ukraine ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZdP2OsZ8eIo)), and triggers the densest stretch in the archive: eight more titles in seven weeks, March 7 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pHw0NWad6U0)), March 8 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=20QsWnUrRD0)), March 18 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=77RCqH8YI64)), March 22 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nZrR3D_TfDc)), March 25 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ki_Z9JP0lZs)), April 4 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7q88UbXPoC0)), April 8 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7QRS6YAiqto)) and April 12 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jWAqgYvBuV0)). The cluster recycles itself as it runs — "Russia looks for buyers" (March 8) becomes "The Truth About Russian Gold and The Ruble" (April 4), then Russian gold again on April 8. The one real analytic shift inside the burst is March 18, when the title itself flags that prices are "Not Reacting" the way the war script predicted ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=77RCqH8YI64)); the April 8 subtitle, "Often Amazed, But Never S…," meanwhile signals continuity of view, not conversion.

Then silence again: nothing between April 12 and December 9, 2022, when the topic reappears at its maximal register — "What It Will Take For The United States To Survive; Buy Gold and Silver" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oVwkOBsOpn8)). A January 3, 2023 reset follows ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j-nVH8El7SQ)), and on February 24 the corpus adds a genuinely new argument: digital currencies "Are Coming," as the title has it, and what that means for the metals ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FNE_KONKfW4)) — the clearest "something is about to change" claim in the whole run. After that, 2023 is single-shot reactions reusing the 2022 template on smaller shocks: "Gold and Silver As Russia Faces Unrest" on June 27 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jOMCS0SJHW4)), then "Vladimir Putin's Golden Pipedream" on July 11 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m2gPR0OSap8)) — the Russian-gold thread resurfacing sixteen months after April 2022. October 3's "The Cost of Political Dysfunction" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7W3jEZqWWGQ)) is the 2021 debt-ceiling frame recycled two years on, and the year closes with new actors and props: China and Japan on November 28 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KD0RCTD9zDI)) and "Silver Plated Missiles" on December 8 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rniBAo17ZhI)).

2024 supplies the corpus's most explicit verdict, and it is a denial of change: on May 14 the title declares "De-Dollarization Is A Myth, A Joke, Nonsense - Oh Yes, And Gold" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RvpspvE0Sas)) — as close as this archive gets to the author saying the feared regime shift isn't happening, and arguably a rebuttal to the de-dollarization excitement his own 2022 Russian-gold coverage fed. A caveat worth stating plainly: this digest is title-level only, so every "changed" statement quotable here comes from a title, not a transcript. The 2020 template then reruns for the 2024 election — "Political Turmoil And What Comes Next" on June 28 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HGZgA8ooH2Q)) and "The Politics Of Gold" on July 2 ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OSSy8tfVqEE)), a near-echo of the December 2020 piece — flanked by new single entries on silver manipulation "Facts and Fantasies" (March 19, [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wQ6JyzDdmbs)) and Saudi oil (June 11, [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6JvZ4Uhb6Es)). On October 4 the war template fires once more for Israel and Iran ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H3KpZZ9_pnI)) — and the record stops there, days before the election the summer cluster was aimed at.

The cadence, in short, is event-reactive rather than continuous: weekly bursts around the 2021 debt ceiling, the spring-2022 invasion and the 2024 election run-up, separated by two eight-month silences (January–September 2021; April–December 2022). What recycles is the prism — shock, then gold and silver — plus specific threads on long leashes: Russian gold from March 2022 to July 2023, Washington dysfunction from October 2021 to October 2023, politics-and-gold from December 2020 to July 2024. What's genuinely new each cycle is a discrete argument: 1933 history, constitutional text, digital currencies, China/Japan, Saudi oil. And what is conspicuously absent is retraction — at title level there is no "I was wrong" anywhere, only the March 2022 admission that prices weren't cooperating and the May 2024 dismissal of de-dollarization. One last note: the archive is labeled 49 items, but the supplied timeline ends October 4, 2024, so anything after that date simply isn't visible here.

study/cpm-group/topic/fed-policy-inflati.text:
This corpus runs on a single engine: the relationship between Fed policy, inflation, and gold, first formalized in January 2021 with ["Interest Rates: Gold's Most Complicated and Important Rel…"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y39eAhDCdI4) and its March sequel [on rates, money supply, inflation and gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HMoJhcwhp-g), after a stray 2016 dollar video and two 2020 CPM Group appearances ([August](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNkMV4Je9Fk), [November](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EdlOqZEF_xA)). The cadence tells its own story: monthly through mid-2021, then compressing hard as the inflation trade heated up — two titles in October 2021, four between November 2 and December 14 (two of those four days apart), all re-asking why gold ignores rising prices ([Oct 15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5o9BHtiXJ_M), [Nov 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AbmjEzDxiGY), [Dec 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LqwpX2Qgck4), [Dec 14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L_igFqCmfZI)). Peak density lands January–June 2022, with eleven videos including three in June alone ([Jun 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tbpqSM5puYU), [Jun 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L-R8CIE_qME), [Jun 24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=10zL22_Y39s)). The deep-read record shows the reuse formula plainly: one relationship model, refit to each new data print, with entries clustering on CPI, PCE, and FOMC days.

The recycled blocks are identifiable by date. The "rates won't hurt gold" thesis launches August 20, 2021 (["Why Interest Rates Won't Hurt Gold and Silver"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RiRYdTEmEpw)), is restated March 7, 2022 with the framing that "[n]ow it's from zero percent to two percent" — unlike past cycles starting from 4–7% — and again on July 29, 2022, when fed funds at 2.5% is still "at levels lower than what you" saw before 2006 (the [nearest archive entry](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yMBt_3OUVDQ) picks up the macro thread weeks later). The inflation-gold explainer recurs October 2021, [August 2022](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kYkxdMHkAG0), and [February 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aiGDIKClJT8) ("It's Not So Simple"). The "highest inflation since 1981" comparison enters via an April 2022 chart update and becomes a [June 10, 2022 title](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L-R8CIE_qME). Peaking-inflation signs flagged in late September 2022 ([nearest video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TBXzM5GSB_w)) are repeated nearly verbatim on November 11. And the Fed-versus-market disconnect runs from the November 2022 CME FedWatch path, through the explicit May 16, 2023 segment on diverging Fed guidance and market perception, to the August 2024 warning about cut-cut certainty and the August 29, 2025 note that strong data complicated a September cut. Data-day clustering is heavy: April 12, 2022 alone spawns three segments off one CPI print (the 1.2%/8.5% numbers, a rebuttal of viewers asking why CPI excludes rent and mortgages, and the 1981 chart), and July 29, 2022 two off the PCE release.

The moments the author says something has changed are the spine of the timeline. December 7, 2021: "the fed has announced that given stronger and more persistent inflation than perhaps some of them thought unexpected" — the pivot itself, compounded by the observation that 10-year yields "have actually come down" since taper talk began. April 12, 2022: "yes we're at the highest inflation since 1981 now," immediately qualified as "a short-term one-year two-year spike in inflation," not a 1970s regime. July 29, 2022 is the most honest change-call: "we've probably seen the bulk of the increases in interest rates now already," alongside the admission that the 75bp hike "did not have the… effect that a lot of people including cpm group expected" on commodities and stocks. By November 11, 2022: "there are signs of peaking inflation there are signs that we are potentially moving toward peaking interest rates." Then January 5, 2024 flips direction — "the decline will be slower than it has been over the last 18 months" — and August 13, 2024 notes markets had swung to assuming a September cut. The final and only genuinely non-recurring entry, November 4, 2025, records the biggest change of all: "the Fed signaled that it was growing increasingly concerned about economic weakness," after which gold "came off very sharply two weeks ago and it's been treading water this week, waiting for a direction."

What's actually new in five years of tape is surprisingly little: the short-term-spike-not-1970s framing (April 2022), the hike-commodity decoupling concession (July 2022), inflation affecting metal *availability* rather than just price (May 2023), the FedNow-versus-gold-standard detour ([August 4, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y6LEB_R7gA0)), and the January 2024 warning that new US, UK, and EU regulations were reducing market efficiency. Nearly everything else is new data poured into the old mold — CPI prints, FedWatch paths, PPI, the 56.6% tariff front-running in autos, Jackson Hole. The framing also whipsaws: the November 2, 2021 title has inflation "wanes" while the November 19 through December 14 titles treat it as rising pressure, a contradiction the model absorbs without comment. Note the thin spots too: there are no archive items around the November 2022 or May 2023 deep reads, and the linked record ends [September 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9u03GgrWg1A), so the later cadence — quarterly in 2024, irregular through 2025 — rests on transcripts alone, spacing out exactly as the inflation story faded until the Fed's own dovish turn reset the question.

study/cpm-group/topic/market-structure-a.text:
This digest is titles, not transcripts, so an honest caveat first: I cannot quote any spoken "this has changed" moment, because none are recorded here — the closest evidence is the title language itself, which turns out to be unusually candid about the recycling pattern. The corpus opens with a stray — "What You Need To Know About The Oil Market" on August 13, 2015 ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6FepdXXoaNs)) — then goes silent for over five years before reopening on January 29, 2021 with silver, GameStop and WallStreetBets ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N54_h29SeUY)). That Reddit squeeze, not any shift in metal fundamentals, is the founding trigger of this entire timeline.

The 2021 run — roughly one video every three weeks — establishes the recycle loop within months. February brings "Conspiracy Theories, Manipul…" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9rVxB_tvGuM)) and "Silver Futures Contract Default Not Likely" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C1EYmE719jY)); March 4 launches the franchise with "Silver Fact and Fantasy" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OrzpZKm-oGc)). New information enters only at the edges: Hungarian central bank buying and "record London inve…" in April ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tn8tkU67WHE)), the US Mint's "Global Silver Shortage" in June ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gVEVhwK4UOc)), Basel III that same month ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cmYTa9fDLY8)), energy markets in November ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mh-Nt8iNTac)), and inflation paired with Comex inventories on November 19 ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ScFb681FrjA)). The year's one title-level change-claim in the author's own words sits on November 9: "Investment Demand is up as Gold and Silver Inventories are close to r…" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7FnCTOBpyhA)) — a rare moment of marking something as moving rather than debunking a claim that it is.

2022–2023 is where the standing thesis gets named and then defended on schedule. "Gold and Silver – Ample Supplies If You Know How To Look" (May 24, 2022) is the position stated in eight words ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jDwWMa22XcQ)), backed by the long-running 2.4-billion-ounce gold stock figure from February ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C_arxbNhm1o)); "Silver Facts and Fantasies II" that June numbers the franchise ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w00fMT8MVHg)). Genuinely new material is scarce and event-driven: the JP Morgan verdict and spoofing record of August 12, 2022 ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QbvxQQNH-j0)) changes the legal landscape the manipulation debate runs on, and the China price premium of September 26, 2023 ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G_nmXQPblq4)) is the other real addition. In between, ownership ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wEfAOXG0gcY)) and open interest ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Cf-qpQ-gXxg)) re-litigate the same inventory question.

By 2024 the recycling is overt. "How Much Silver Is Really Available," first run September 15, 2023 ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IPMS5mYzvXE)), reruns verbatim on January 16, 2024 ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xD7w6o21Ujk)) — identical title, four months apart. March alone carries two franchise editions: "Silver Facts and Fantasies 2024" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7RFr43p2RJQ)) and, eighteen days later, "Manipulation And Silver In A Dangerous World," where "A Dangerous World" is the only new argument — geopolitics grafted onto the old frame ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wQ6JyzDdmbs)). "The Silver Shortage Chimera" in April restates the shortage-debunk that dates to mid-2021 ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9SpxKkghmu4)). Then the cadence compresses into an update format: July 9 and July 12 three days apart ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2QvIGvGL0NM), [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T_5awixMpcM)), December's medallion-pricing and China item ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q_bZEnVCYK4)), and February 21, 2025's "Is Fort Knox Empty?" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qxQPTPfGqJA)) — a new trigger that structurally rhymes with the conspiracy-theory video that opened the run in 2021.

The verdict on cadence: triggers rotate — WallStreetBets, the JP Morgan verdict, China's premium, Fort Knox — but the core argument barely moves. Inventories-are-ample, physical-versus-paper, and manipulation-is-overstated get restated on an annual rhythm under the "Facts and Fantasies" brand, with "How Much Silver Is Really Available" as the literal re-run. What genuinely changed over four years is cadence, not content: from squeeze-driven triage in early 2021 to a scheduled market-update format by late 2024.

study/cpm-group/topic/cpm-group-research.text:
The spine of this archive is CPM Group's yearbook calendar, and it recycles with near-liturgical precision. A gold survey lands in late March almost every year: the [CPM Gold Yearbook 2019](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QgF10YLHwM0) on March 26, 2019, the [2020 Gold Update and Yearbook](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OWNX0_Q6H80) on March 24, the [2021 Annual Gold Update and Yearbook Launch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IeKmZxnun2Q) on March 23, then the [2022 Gold Market Update](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lWLKVeBmVWk) on April 6, the [2023 Gold Market Outlook](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RKKvN5BthpQ) on March 28, the [2024 Gold Market Outlook](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcjARQIttqU) on March 26, and the [2026 Gold Market Outlook](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UUHFqhtDezM) on March 24. Silver follows roughly a month behind — the [2019 Silver Yearbook Launch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-jGHFUKTio) in April 2019, the [2021 Silver Update](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bo8jT0XPcbM) on May 11, the [2022 Silver Market Forecast](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YbpwAZcr6Pw) on May 10 — and platinum group metals hold down the summer slot: [2020](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dYlXqaZ6hds) on June 30, [2021](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ehnP-WKg6N4) on July 13, [2022](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AkmHW6aHP8E) on July 27, and the [2023 Virtual Seminar](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7JX7KY-HM4) on July 25. The one broken link in the chain is 2025, where no March gold outlook appears; the closest item is the [May 30, 2025 update](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=96tv-e29gpc), whose title cuts off at "CPM Group's 39…" — given the firm's mid-1980s origins, almost certainly a marker of its 39th year, but the truncation leaves that to inference.

The genuinely new material arrives in one dense burst: early 2021. On January 22, CPM issues a [short-term SELL recommendation for gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JFZi4kXULCI) — a live trading stance, not a yearbook. Eight days later comes [Silver, Gamestop, and WallStreet Bets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N54_h29SeUY), pure exogenous news from the Reddit squeeze moment, and the archive's only real-time crisis response. That triggers a defensive stretch: [CPM Group's Record On Silver, Process, Research, and Manipulation Theories](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bxcPKsYf25o) on March 3, the [Silver Fact and Fantasy webinar](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OrzpZKm-oGc) on March 4, and an [Open Forum On Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O1-rPAF-usQ) on May 26. The most consequential moment, though, is March 16, when the title itself announces the shift: [CPM issues STAND ASIDE recommendation for Gold; BUY for Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q8N1yQ5R8c0). Within eight weeks gold moved from SELL to stand aside while silver flipped to a buy — the clearest "this has changed" beat in the record. July 2021 then adds a one-off regional repackaging, twin [silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hklab62wIy0) and [gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qrk3pbwMasI) updates for Chinese markets that never recur in this archive.

A second recycling lane is the evergreen self-explainer: [Introduction To CPM Group](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g7zSiFjuYuM) in August 2020, [How CPM Group Approaches Investing In Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cRmrgRsFcf4) in March 2022 — roughly one methodology video every year and a half. Genuinely new arguments are rarer: copper enters the frame only via the [July 12, 2022 Q&A](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d3O1uEv63pk), and [The Cost Of Free Gold And Silver Research](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gC934toho44) in February 2023 is the one video aimed at the research business itself rather than the metals. The manipulation-debate franchise also shows a long reuse gap — the March 2021 fact-and-fantasy material doesn't resurface until [Silver Facts And Fantasies 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W5ReHm2dbLk) on March 18, 2025, four years later under nearly the same name.

On the question of quoted changes: this archive consists of titles, not transcripts, so there are no verbatim "things have changed" quotes to pull, and I won't manufacture any. The changes survive only as the calls and formats themselves — the January-to-March 2021 stance shift, and the year-end wrap format, which appears on [December 18, 2020 as "2020 Review and 2021 Outlook"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Hu3yedI5Dbg) and doesn't return until [December 19, 2025 as "2025 Review and 2026 Outlook"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bHSDEaQOTg8). One softer change worth flagging: the 2026 outlook's title pivots to self-description — "The Definitive Source for Gold Data and Ins…" — a branding posture with no precedent in the earlier, plainer titles.

As for cadence: 2021 alone carries eleven of the thirty-one items, nearly all clustered around the squeeze and its aftermath. Then the record thins hard — nothing between July 28, 2021 and March 29, 2022, nothing after the July 2023 PGM seminar until the single [2024 gold outlook](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcjARQIttqU), then a near-twelve-month silence until March 2025. Whether that reflects slower output or incomplete archiving, the digest doesn't say. What it does show is a firm running on fixed annual slots, inserting new content only when the market forces it, and periodically reissuing its own origin story between the yearbooks.

study/cpm-group/topic/investment-demand-.text:
The spine of this archive is a single argument, restated for nearly six years: metals prices are a demand story. It gets its cleanest early statement on July 9, 2021 — ["PGMs: The Hidden Gems; Gold and Silver: It Is Still All About Demand"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o0Vb7ZwJfzs) — and then cycles forward almost mechanically: investment demand rising as inventories draw down ([November 9, 2021](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7FnCTOBpyhA)), the same logic flipped into a price forecast (["The Real Reason To Expect Higher Gold and Silver Prices"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eIWsZmI7yJk), November 3, 2023), and again with central banks bolted onto the investor bid (["Central Bank and Investor Demand Are Driving Gold Prices Higher"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DJbciTJrSms), September 10, 2024). One caveat up front: this digest is titles only, so where spoken claims of change are asked for, the verifiable record is title language. I quote those titles verbatim and flag that no transcript quotes exist in this record.

The template recycling is unusually visible. ["Gold and Silver: The Reasons to Invest"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sHLqHDmqvW0) (October 12, 2021) returns as ["Why Investors Are Rushing to Gold and Silver"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QjgAi6ZEbls) (April 2, 2024) and again as ["The Real Reason To Invest In Silver NOW!"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jK0e9_KuWxI) (October 22, 2024). The "what's really driving" frame runs twice in three weeks: ["Gold Price Hits New Highs: What's Really Driving the Market"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3QJAUiShVvw) (March 28, 2025) and ["Gold And Silver Prices Surge Higher, What's Really Driving Markets?"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ruN0LUahwk8) (April 18, 2025). The "new highs" format itself is a reusable shell, deployed April 5, 2024 ([record-breaking gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CZN3yx2csco)), March 2025, and December 12, 2025 (["Silver Price Hits New High As Gold Surges"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rVQ8iCxePbM)). The explanation rarely changes; only the price chart it is draped over does.

The cadence tracks price action, not new information. Coverage clusters at market highs — three items in ten days in April 2024 ([April 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QjgAi6ZEbls), [April 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CZN3yx2csco), [April 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qp6t8zi9WJw)), five between late March and June 2025, and a December 2025 pair — and goes quiet when nothing is happening: nothing at all between November 9, 2021 and December 16, 2022, and only four items across all of 2022–2023. Genuine new arguments arrive roughly once or twice a year: the Gamestop/WallStreetBets retail squeeze ([January 29, 2021](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N54_h29SeUY)), PGMs entering the frame ([July 9, 2021](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o0Vb7ZwJfzs)), crypto as a source of new metals buyers ([December 16, 2022](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8OUBvfJRPvU)), who actually owns the silver ([January 17, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wEfAOXG0gcY)), institutional flows into mining ([April 18, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0XRMaFy1j5o)), the behavioral critique that [silver investors buy high and sell low](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S4f-LjNClZI) (January 19, 2024), gold's divergence from a lagging silver ([August 13, 2024](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5xr1ufuLY_U)), and the dollar-exit question ([June 24, 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VTWAdZpeBMI)). Notably, the topic's namesake — ETF flows — appears exactly once, in the inaugural ["Changing Dynamics In ETF Holdings"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X7l3Jq4O5uw) (September 11, 2020), then vanishes from the record entirely; "investment demand" carries the franchise alone.

The explicit change-claims, to the extent they can be quoted from titles, come at moments already noted: "Changing Dynamics" (September 2020), "Changing Institutional Investment Trends" (April 2023), "Record-Breaking" prices and "the 2024 Surge" (April 2024), and ["The Gold and Silver Renaissance"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lDJxdLaOxcQ) (December 29, 2025). But the one unambiguous regime break is the final entry: ["How Low Before Buyers Return"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8) (June 16, 2026) is the first title in the entire archive framed around a decline rather than a rally — after years of recycling the same bullish demand thesis, the frame has to explain the buyer's absence instead of his arrival. The tensions along the way are worth keeping in view: retail investors are panic-buyers in January 2024 and pro-grade operators five weeks later (["How Educated Gold And Silver Retail Investors Can Invest Like The Pros"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SqLC5biSWUY), February 23, 2024), and silver "struggles to keep up" in August 2024 only to become a "NOW!" buy by October. The honest read: this is an evergreen argument machine, fired on a market-event trigger, with new ideas entering at a trickle while the demand thesis does the heavy lifting in every regime.

person/andrew-cheung.text:
Andrew Cheung shows up in this corpus with almost no biography attached — no role, no affiliation on record — and a single dated appearance: July 8, 2026, on a YouTube discussion pointedly titled "All Crypto To $0? Bitcoin's Biggest Risk Is Arriving Faster…" ([All Crypto To $0? Bitcoin's Biggest Risk Is Arriving Faster…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWOFw-CUrQA)). What distinguishes him in that appearance is not a directional call but technical triage. The quantum-threat debate around Bitcoin tends to collapse into either doom or dismissal; Cheung's contribution sits in the middle, splitting the question into what actually breaks and what doesn't.

On the cryptography, he is blunt that the scarier framing overreaches: "quantum computer cannot break into the PQC signature and they also cannot break into the quantum safe encryption" — a direct rebuttal to the AI-assisted-hacking narrative the episode's title gestures at ([All Crypto To $0? Bitcoin's Biggest Risk Is Arriving Faster…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWOFw-CUrQA)). The genuine vulnerability he flags is narrower: if a private key is compromised "by reverse engineering from the the public key, then that means you lose your your token. You lose your asset" ([All Crypto To $0? Bitcoin's Biggest Risk Is Arriving Faster…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWOFw-CUrQA)). On timing, he defers to the vendor roadmap rather than the hype cycle — "you need to to wait until 2030 or something," pointing to IBM's own prediction of delivering the first fully fault-tolerant quantum computer ([All Crypto To $0? Bitcoin's Biggest Risk Is Arriving Faster…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWOFw-CUrQA)). That is the closest thing to a dated call in his record, and it is a "not yet," not a crash call.

He ventures one step into the AI debate as well, arguing that "if there's any one single factor that is preventing AI from doing the maximum, you know what? It's privacy" ([All Crypto To $0? Bitcoin's Biggest Risk Is Arriving Faster…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWOFw-CUrQA)) — a natural bridge given the episode's subject matter. Beyond that, the record is thin and should be said so plainly: four stances, all neutral, all from one source on one date. There is no demonstrated movement in his views over time, and no bullish or bearish call to anchor a verdict — just a single, technically grounded frame on quantum risk that this corpus has captured.

person/jeff-dorman.text:
Jeff Dorman is a chief investment officer, best known in digital-asset circles as the CIO of crypto-focused asset manager Arca. That said, the record assembled here is unusually thin: a single dated entry, one neutral stance, no documented bullish or bearish calls. What follows is a portrait of one analytical moment, not a track record.

That moment is instructive, though. In a late-June 2026 interview on investor sentiment in crypto and macro, Dorman pushed back on the prevailing narrative that geopolitics was driving markets, flatly calling the move "a earnings-fueled rally" and adding, "the war was a distraction." He grounded the claim in history: in his telling, there's no precedent across the past fifty years of a Middle East war producing any long-lasting market impact ([Why Investors Say Sentiment Looks Wrong in Crypto & Macro M…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3LVb6esEFOk)). Filed as neutral on geopolitics and defense, the stance is really a bet against narrative-driven framing — an argument that fundamentals, not headlines, set the tape.

It's a contrarian posture in a news cycle that rewards war-talk, and it says something about how Dorman frames debates: earnings first, noise second. But the timeline here shows no movement to chart — no earlier positions, no evolution, no contradictions. Whether that earnings-first lens holds up as a durable worldview can't be judged from one entry; the corpus simply doesn't yet give us the before and after.

person/liaquat-ahamed.text:
Liaquat Ahamed occupies an unusual seat in financial media: he is neither a strategist running a book of calls nor a permabear hunting clicks, but a career fixed-income investor who turned the 1930s into his analytical toolkit. Born in Kenya to a South Asian family and educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and Columbia, he started at the World Bank before spending roughly two decades managing fixed-income assets in New York and London, including as a partner at Fischer Francis Trees & Watts, and later served on PIMCO's Global Advisory Board while writing on economics for the Financial Times and The New York Times.
