His claim to fame is *Lords of Finance: The Bankers Who Broke the World* (2009), his portrait of the interwar central bankers whose policy missteps produced the Great Depression — a book that won the 2010 Pulitzer Prize for History and that still frames how he talks about markets today.

That framing was on full display in his single tracked appearance on The Monetary Matters Network, a June 29, 2026 episode titled "Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taught…" ([Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=czdGQG9HvGM)). His method is analogy rather than forecast: he drew a line from railroad-bond investors — "people who bought railroad bonds had money to invest and they and they had the ability to sit through losses" — to modern credit structures ([Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=czdGQG9HvGM)), and he offered a concrete number for the current buildout, estimating that "data center as a investment as a percentage of GDP in the US is around 2%," explicitly inviting comparison to the electrification booms of the past ([Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=czdGQG9HvGM)). On credit conditions, his sharpest line of the episode was that "you draw any chart of default rates on US corporate investment and it is the highest in our history" ([Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=czdGQG9HvGM)) — an observation worth flagging, though notably one he delivered as historical context rather than as a short.

The same historian's reflex governs his treatment of hard assets and crypto. He framed gold hoarding as crisis behavior, not an investment thesis — "in the middle of a financial crisis, everyone tries to hoard precious metals and get out of paper money" — and argued that silver-versus-gold prices track commodity prices year by year, calling that relationship "the single most important de[terminant]" in the historical record ([Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=czdGQG9HvGM)). On crypto, the digest captures the tension neatly: he is worried about speculative bubbles and loose central bank policy, yet remains hopeful about what the underlying technology could become ([Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=czdGQG9HvGM)).

As for how his views have moved over time — the timeline here can't answer that. Everything on record comes from that one June 2026 appearance, and all eight coded stances land as neutral, with zero bullish or bearish calls in either direction ([Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=czdGQG9HvGM)). That's less a sign of fence-sitting than of what he is: a mechanism-mapper who tells you what past manias imply about present ones and leaves the positioning to you. Coverage this thin means any verdict on his forecasting record would be manufactured; what the record does show is a consistent intellectual through-line, from *Lords of Finance* to his data-center-and-default-rate analogies — monetary history as the only honest guide to the current cycle.

person/liaquat-ahamed-guest-author.text:
Liaquat Ahamed occupies an unusual seat in market commentary: he is both a lifelong practitioner and the most decorated depression historian of his generation. An investment manager and economic historian, he began as a professional economist at the World Bank before spending decades in money management, including as a principal of the firm Fischer Francis Trees & Woods, with an education spanning Trinity College, Cambridge and Columbia University. He is best known as the author of *Lords of Finance: The Bankers Who Broke the World* (2009), his account of the interwar central bankers whose orthodoxies helped break the global economy — a book that won the 2010 Pulitzer Prize for History.

His single appearance in this corpus, a solo segment on The Monetary Matters Network dated June 29, 2026 titled "Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taught," shows the method in action: reading the present entirely through the 1920s and 1930s. On money itself, his framing is behavioral rather than directional — "In the middle of a financial crisis, everyone tries to hoard precious metals and get out of paper money," he observes ([Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=czdGQG9HvGM)). He also leans on monetary history as an analytic instrument, noting that silver prices "exactly match year by year" commodity price movements in that era, which he treats as the single most important lesson of the period ([Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=czdGQG9HvGM)).

The same episode carries his most concrete modern claims. He puts data center investment at "around 2%" of US GDP and explicitly invites comparison with the 1920s electrification buildout — the historian's move of asking whether today's capex boom rhymes with the last great general-purpose technology cycle ([Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=czdGQG9HvGM)). On credit he is starker: "You draw any chart of default rates on US corporate investment and it is the highest in our history" ([Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=czdGQG9HvGM)) — a claim that anchors both his credit and rates commentary. On crypto, the pattern is consistent: concern about speculative bubbles and loose central bank policy, paired with genuine hope that the underlying technology proves out ([Lessons From The First Great Depression You Never Were Taug…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=czdGQG9HvGM)).

What the timelines do not show is a single directional call — seven topic tags, all neutral, zero bullish, zero bearish. That is characteristic rather than evasive: Ahamed operates as a diagnostician mapping today's stresses onto the 1930s playbook, not a signal generator, and readers looking for a gold or credit position from him will not find one here. Coverage is also thin — one appearance, one date — so any claim about how his views have *moved* over time cannot be supported from this record. What we have is a single mid-2026 snapshot of a Pulitzer-winning depression historian assessing an economy he finds uncomfortably familiar.

person/panel.text:
In this corpus, "Panel" is less a person than a recorded conversation — and the file behind it is honest about how little is pinned down. There are no named participants or roles on record, and the entire dated history consists of a single session on June 28, 2026, framed as "AI Is Macro Now - What it Means for GDP Growth and Markets," captured in a video billed around investors arguing that sentiment in crypto and macro looks wrong ([Why Investors Say Sentiment Looks Wrong in Crypto & Macro M…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3LVb6esEFOk)). That's the whole evidentiary base: one discussion, two topic tags, no individual attribution.

What the record does show is telling. The panel is classified neutral on both AI & Semiconductors and Broad Market & Macro Indices — a 0/0/2 stance mix, with both neutrals drawn from the same June 28 session ([Why Investors Say Sentiment Looks Wrong in Crypto & Macro M…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3LVb6esEFOk)). Read alongside the session's title, the neutrality looks structural rather than fence-sitting: if AI has genuinely become a macro input to GDP growth, then a clean bull-or-bear call on the semis complex or the index conflates two different questions. The panel's recorded contribution is a reframing — AI as an economy-wide variable rather than a sector bet — not a directional call on either front. Whether the crypto-and-macro sentiment-skepticism in the video's billing bled into that stance is not something the digest can confirm.

As for movement over time, there is none to chart. One date, one session, two neutral readings, zero bullish or bearish calls anywhere in the file — so any narrative of drifting conviction would be fabrication. The fair portrait as of late June 2026 is a panel whose lone on-record posture is agnosticism on both AI and the broad market, delivered under a thesis that arguably explains the agnosticism. It's thin coverage, plainly said; a second session would do a lot of work here.

person/panel-ram-ahluwalia-seth-ginns-je.text:
This entry profiles a panel rather than a single voice: Ram Ahluwalia, Seth Ginns and Jeff Dorman — figures better known individually from crypto-asset circles (Lumida Wealth, CoinFund and Arca, respectively) who get pulled together for cross-market discussions. The corpus itself is candid that it knows little about them as a group: no roles, no show appearances, and a stance ledger with exactly one entry on it. That's worth stating up front, because a portrait built on one data point is a sketch, not a biography.

The one data point: on June 28, 2026, the trio sat for a discussion on why investor sentiment looked wrong across crypto and macro, and their collective read on AI and semiconductors was filed as neutral — the framing being that earnings and AI "may still be the real engines of this market" ([Why Investors Say Sentiment Looks Wrong in Crypto & Macro M…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3LVb6esEFOk)). There's a mild tension worth flagging: the label says neutral, but the substance leans constructive — arguing for fundamentals and AI capex as the market's engine is a step past fence-sitting, even if it stops short of a buy call.

Beyond that, there's simply no timeline to trace. Nothing in the record shows this panel bullish or bearish on anything, dated before or after, so any claim about how their views "moved" would be fabrication. Their strongest — and only — documented call is that June 2026 neutral-but-fundamentals-friendly stance on AI and semis, delivered in a conversation arguing sentiment had decoupled from the underlying picture. The coverage is thin; treat this page as a stub awaiting a second data point.

person/raam-aluwalia.text:
Raam Aluwalia enters this corpus thin, and it's worth saying so up front: every data point on file comes from a single appearance on 28 June 2026, in a discussion titled ["Why Investors Say Sentiment Looks Wrong in Crypto & Macro M…"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3LVb6esEFOk), and the record doesn't even pin down his role or firm. But what that one appearance reveals is a coherent argumentative shape — an investor who keeps pointing at the gap between gloomy sentiment readings and the harder numbers underneath them. All three tagged stances are neutral, but the framing is quietly contrarian: not "buy everything," but "the pessimism doesn't match the data."

His most substantive point concerned AI, where he argued that "in the AI market, you have real end demand from consumers, enterprise, government, defense firms. They're willing to pay. You actually have a legitim—" (the quote cuts off mid-thought, but the direction is clear) ([Why Investors Say Sentiment Looks Wrong in Crypto & Macro M…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3LVb6esEFOk)). It's a demand-side defense of the AI trade, and notably the corpus files the same quote under both AI & Semiconductors and Geopolitics & Defense — which is fair, since his argument leans on government and defense buyers as part of the paying base, not just consumer tech.

The macro version of the same argument shows up in his oil-and-energy-tagged remark: "the sentiment out there's still very dour across quite a few sentiment surveys… earnings growth looks strong. We're talking about 20% plus—" ([Why Investors Say Sentiment Looks Wrong in Crypto & Macro M…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3LVb6esEFOk)). Again, sentiment dour, fundamentals strong — the same seesaw, different market. What the corpus does *not* show is any directional call: no bullish or bearish positions on record, no timeline of views shifting. That's less a sign of fence-sitting than of thin coverage — one source, one date, and quotes that build a case without ever quite landing a verdict. Treat this page as a first sketch, not a portrait.

person/ram-ahluwalia.text:
Ram Ahluwalia is a crypto-and-macro investor best known publicly as a digital-asset management executive, though this corpus doesn't log a current title — what it does log is a single, telling appearance: a June 28, 2026 discussion bluntly titled [*Why Investors Say Sentiment Looks Wrong in Crypto & Macro M…*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3LVb6esEFOk). The frame of that video is essentially his thesis in miniature: the problem, in his telling, isn't fundamentals but the gap between them and how pessimistic investors feel.

His argument on that appearance ran on two tracks. On AI, he pushed back against bubble framing by pointing to the demand base: "in the AI market, you have real end demand from consumers, enterprise, government, defense firms. They're willing to pay" — the start of a legitimacy case for AI as an investable theme rather than a speculative trade ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3LVb6esEFOk)). On the broader macro picture, he flagged the disconnect directly: "the sentiment out there's still very dour across quite a few sentiment surveys," even as "earnings growth looks strong. We're talking about 20% plus" ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3LVb6esEFOk)). That's a coherent through-line — fundamentals are outrunning mood, and positioning hasn't caught up.

It's worth being honest about the limits here. Everything on file — three topic entries across AI/semiconductors, defense, and energy — comes from that one date, and all of it codes neutral (zero bullish, zero bearish calls in the corpus). There is no documented trail of earlier calls to chart against, so no view migration can be plotted; the flatness reflects a coverage gap, not demonstrated steadiness. The interesting tension to watch as coverage fills in: a commentator whose substantive case (strong earnings, real AI demand, wrong-footed sentiment) leans constructive, yet who stops short of a directional call on record.

person/ryan-king.text:
Ryan King is the Chief Financial Officer of Equinox Gold Corp., the mid-tier gold producer founded with the backing of mining entrepreneur Ross Beaty, with producing assets concentrated in the Americas. He has held the CFO seat since the company's early years, which means the balance sheet story is largely his own: Equinox grew by acquisition and heavy capital raising, then worked its net debt down from roughly $1.6–1.7 billion to around $400 million prior to its most recent deal ([How High Can Gold Go? Why A 'Major Debt Crisis' Reckoning I…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)). That deleveraging arc — grow first, repair later — is the spine of how he sells the company.

The growth math he laid out in a July 3, 2026 interview is aggressive by any mid-tier standard. Equinox's guidance heading into fiscal 2026 was 700,000 ounces of gold, and between the two companies — post-deal — the midpoint of combined pro forma guidance annualizes to 1.1 million ounces a year ([How High Can Gold Go? Why A 'Major Debt Crisis' Reckoning I…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)). He then claims a 70% annual production growth rate over the next five years once new assets come online ([How High Can Gold Go? Why A 'Major Debt Crisis' Reckoning I…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)) — a compounding figure worth treating as management's own framing rather than a banked outcome, but it tells you the acquisition machine hasn't downshifted.

The rest of his pitch is jurisdictional and valuation-driven. He positions the portfolio so that 70–75% of NAV comes from Canada and the United States — "safe jurisdictions, tier one jurisdictions" with deep institutional investor bases ([How High Can Gold Go? Why A 'Major Debt Crisis' Reckoning I…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)) — and argues that execution, track record, and where you operate "can get premium valuations" relative to gold-mining peers ([How High Can Gold Go? Why A 'Major Debt Crisis' Reckoning I…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)). It's the classic re-rating argument: the assets and the delivery record justify a multiple the market hasn't yet granted.

On the metal itself, King is conspicuously a non-caller — and that restraint is the most telling thing in his record. He narrates gold's run to $5,600 an ounce and its correction back toward $4,000, and when pressed on downside, concedes "could it go lower than this? Yes" ([How High Can Gold Go? Why A 'Major Debt Crisis' Reckoning I…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)). Rather than stake his own target, he reaches for others': Pierre Lassonde's claim that M2 money supply alone implies $17,000-plus gold, and a forecaster whose model anticipated exactly this kind of pullback ([How High Can Gold Go? Why A 'Major Debt Crisis' Reckoning I…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)), plus the 2011-era analog of gold hitting $1,900, correcting to $1,100, then rising again ([How High Can Gold Go? Why A 'Major Debt Crisis' Reckoning I…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)). His operative philosophy is that miners "are price takers in this environment" and must build the business to work across price regimes, with a sustained bull market as pure upside for shareholders ([How High Can Gold Go? Why A 'Major Debt Crisis' Reckoning I…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)). One caveat on the record itself: all thirteen logged positions trace to that single July 2026 appearance, all neutral, so there is no visible evolution of views to chart — only a deliberately non-directional corporate posture, which you can read as discipline or as a hedge, depending on how suspicious you are of a gold CFO who refuses to call gold.

person/ryan-king-own-view.text:
Ryan King is a gold and precious-markets commentator who speaks strictly in a personal capacity — no firm affiliation appears anywhere in the record, and it's worth flagging up front that the identification is tentative, since "Ryan King" is a common name and this entry rests on the individual discussing gold futures (GC=F) in a personal-views context. That caveat matters less than what he actually says, but readers should hold both in mind.

What the record does show is a commentator who works in scenarios rather than outright directional calls. In a July 3, 2026 discussion segment framed around a "major debt crisis" reckoning, he walked through a bull case in which "gold rose up to $5,600 an ounce" followed by a pullback — "We're now seeing it correct back to $4,000 an ounce" ([How High Can Gold Go? Why A 'Major Debt Crisis' Reckoning I…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)). Crucially, he didn't treat the correction as a floor, conceding "could it go lower than this? Yes" ([How High Can Gold Go? Why A 'Major Debt Crisis' Reckoning I…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)). Both data points score as neutral, and that's the honest label: he maps the upside and the downside in the same breath rather than planting a flag on either side.

As for how his views have moved over time — the corpus can't say. There is a single dated appearance and no earlier or later positions to chart, so any claim that he turned more bullish or more bearish would be invention. What can be said is that his framework, at least in this appearance, is two-sided by design: an inflated bull target, a mechanical correction, and an explicit admission of further downside. Whether that hedged posture is temperament or tactic, one interview is too thin a base to judge.

person/ryan-king-citing-martin-armstrong.text:
This entry tracks Ryan King, whose recorded footprint in this corpus is defined less by his own house view than by his habit of channeling Martin Armstrong — the veteran cycle forecaster best known for his computer-model approach to markets. The corpus lists no formal role for King, and what it logs is sparse: exactly one dated stance, and it's a neutral one. That thinness matters, because the temptation with an entry like this is to reconstruct a worldview from a single data point, and the record doesn't support that yet.

The one data point, though, is reasonably specific. In a piece published July 3, 2026 — framed around the question of how high gold can run against the backdrop of a "major debt crisis" reckoning — King relays Armstrong's model-based signal: "He's got a forecasting tool that he has used that he said, 'Hey, gold I believe gold will pull back...'" ([How High Can Gold Go? Why A 'Major Debt Crisis' Reckoning I…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)). The shape of that stance is worth noting: King isn't calling the top in gold himself, nor defending the rally — he's transmitting a forecaster's expectation of a pullback "somewhere," a deliberately unfalsifiable-until-it-isn't kind of call, while keeping his own position officially neutral. That combination — a hard macro-narrative hook (debt crisis) paired with a hedge on timing — is a recognizable style in gold commentary, and King is playing it via Armstrong rather than on his own name.

As for how his views have moved: the timeline shows no movement, because there's only one entry on it. No bullish or bearish calls are logged, no earlier positions to compare against the July 2026 neutrality. What the naming convention of this page — "citing Martin Armstrong" — does tell you is the operative dynamic: King's documented market commentary is a relay of Armstrong's forecasting output, so tracking this entry is really tracking how King chooses to package Armstrong's signals. Whether he eventually stakes out calls of his own, or shifts from neutral as the gold-versus-debt-crisis question resolves, is exactly what the record so far leaves open.

person/ryan-king-citing-pierre-lassonde.text:
Ryan King is a finance writer and commentator whose work sits squarely in the gold and precious-metals camp, though pinning down his exact employer or title is surprisingly difficult — "Ryan King" being a common name, his byline identity in general sources remains murky. What is clear is the company he keeps on the page: his most visible work consists of channeling the views of Pierre Lassonde, the co-founder of Franco-Nevada and one of the most prominent veterans of the gold industry.

His signature piece of commentary, dated July 3, 2026, is a piece framed around the question of how high gold can go in the event of a "major debt crisis" reckoning. There he relays Lassonde's arithmetic: that gold's historical relationship to the M2 money supply alone implies a price of "$17,000 plus dollars per ounce" ([How High Can Gold Go? Why A 'Major Debt Crisis' Reckoning I…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)). It is worth being precise about what King is doing here — the stance recorded on gold futures is neutral, not bullish. He is amplifying and contextualizing one of the most eye-popping targets in the gold debate rather than staking his own number on it, a framing choice that tells you something about how he operates: curator and transmitter of establishment-gold arguments rather than an independent forecaster.

On the question of how his views have moved over time, the honest answer is that the record doesn't show — the timeline contains a single dated entry, so there is no observable drift, no earlier bearishness to walk back, no hedging to track. Whether the $17,000 framing represents King testing how far the bull case stretches or simply lending his platform to Lassonde's is left unresolved by the available material. Readers should treat this page as a starting sketch: one documented intervention in the gold-price debate, delivered with borrowed conviction, and a lot of room for the record to fill in.

person/sam-burns.text:
Sam Burns is a Chief Market Strategist whose on-the-record footprint in this corpus comes almost entirely from a single appearance: the June 30, 2026 interview titled [What Would End Bull Market Overnight? Strategist Reveals Tr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2mVsHCgJcVc). That format matters for reading him — he was invited to map out kill-scenarios for a bull market, and what he delivered was less a set of directional calls than a transmission-mechanism lecture. All eight logged stances are neutral, which is less a sign of fence-sitting than of a strategist who prefers explaining *how* money moves to predicting *where* it goes.

His most distinctive argument concerns the AI trade's insulation from rates. He identified tech and its adjacent sectors — explicitly including industrials "somehow tied to AI" — as "the big driver of equities" in this cycle ([What Would End Bull Market Overnight? Strategist Reveals Tr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2mVsHCgJcVc)). Then he went a step further and detached that trade from the Fed: "Rates going up 50 basis points is just not going to change much for, you know, AI related spending," because most of that spending "is equity financed one way or another" ([What Would End Bull Market Overnight? Strategist Reveals Tr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2mVsHCgJcVc)). That's the sharpest analytical claim in the record — it argues the usual bear-case lever for breaking an AI-led bull market (higher rates) doesn't actually bite where the money is being spent.

The same rate-sensitivity framework runs through his commodity views, just inverted. Gold, he noted, is sensitive to rates and real rates in particular — "if those are going to go stay higher, you know, where they are go up, then gold typically would not benefit from that" ([What Would End Bull Market Overnight? Strategist Reveals Tr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2mVsHCgJcVc)). On oil he was simply skeptical of a spike: "It's going to take a lot for oil to go back to the 110 where it was, you know, a few months ago" ([What Would End Bull Market Overnight? Strategist Reveals Tr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2mVsHCgJcVc)). The through-line is coherent — equity-funded AI capex shrugs off rates, rate-sensitive gold suffers if rates hold, and oil needs an exogenous shock — but it's a map of dependencies, not a portfolio recommendation.

As for how his views have moved over time: the record simply can't say. Every logged item carries the same date and the same source, so there is no before-and-after to chart, no stance that flipped or firmed. The coverage here is thin — one interview, no dated calls, no bullish or bearish positions on file at all. What the corpus does establish is a strategist who thinks in terms of financing structure and rate transmission rather than index targets; what it doesn't establish is whether he acts on that framework with conviction. Anyone building out this page will need more dated appearances before any evolution — or any verdict — can honestly be written.

person/seth-gins.text:
Seth Gins appears in this corpus as a commentator on crypto and macro sentiment, though the record here is thin enough that his role, affiliation, and background can't be pinned down from what's been collected. The single dated entry — and it is the only one — places him on June 28, 2026 in a video framed around the argument that investor sentiment has come detached from reality in crypto and macro markets ([Why Investors Say Sentiment Looks Wrong in Crypto & Macro M…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3LVb6esEFOk)). His take is tagged neutral: he describes "a long list of names with varying degrees of fundamental catalysts and drivers… up anywhere from 15 to 80%… over either a 10-day per[iod]" — an inventory of the breadth and velocity of the move rather than a directional call on where it goes next.

That framing tells you something about the shape of his contribution, at least in this one clip. When names are rippling 15–80% in roughly ten trading days, the live question is whether fundamentals are driving the move or sentiment is running ahead of them, and Gins sits deliberately on that fence — cataloging catalysts and drivers without endorsing either the bulls chasing the tape or the skeptics calling it froth. Whether that reflects genuine agnosticism or a habitual hedging style is impossible to say from a single transcript fragment.

As for an arc of views over time: there isn't one on record. No bullish or bearish calls, no dated reversals, no coverage outside crypto and stablecoins. A "0 bullish / 0 bearish / 1 neutral" tally is a profile, not a track record, and this page can't responsibly claim more until more of his commentary is captured.

person/surge-copper-ceo.text:
The man behind Surge Copper (SURG.V) — president and chief executive Leif Nilsson — appears in this corpus exactly once, as the solo guest on a June 29, 2026 episode of Resource Talks whose title frames the whole debate for him: [$4.6B Copper Project in BC, But Can the Capex Be Funded? | …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k). That framing matters. This is a CEO whose central problem isn't geology or grade but capital formation at scale, and nearly everything he says in the interview is arranged to answer it.

His argument runs on disciplined sizing and stress-tested economics. He caps the ambition up front, calling 120,000 tons per day of throughput "probably the maximum size" for the project, and dismisses incremental add-ons as bolt-on extras that "aren't going to be transformational from an NPV or IRR perspective" ([…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k)). The resilience claim is his strongest number: even the "negative 60% case" evaluated "at base case copper prices" still clears "like an 18% IRR" ([…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k)). Underneath it sits a straightforward capital-market truth he states plainly — anyone writing billion-dollar cheques would "rather recoup that capital in a couple of years" ([…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k)) — which is the lens through which the whole capex question should be read.

On the corporate endgame he is looser, sketching three paths rather than one. He declares some lingering chapter closed — "I believe that's done. I believe they're out now" — and suggests recent share buyers "are going to be pretty pleased" with their entry price ([…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k)). From there: ARM could increase its ownership and "contribute significant capital" within the current structure, or a major could become "a buyer of Surge one day" and run its own JV process ([…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k)). On copper itself he lets the bull case breathe without shouting it, arguing equilibrium prices may be "a lot higher than where we are," while situating the project in the broader "polarization" theme convulsing the global economy — and he points to peer Solaris (SLS.TO), whose share price has roughly "doubled in the last year," as proof the market rewards this sector ([…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k)).

Be clear about what this record is: a single-day snapshot, all fifteen coded statements neutral, no bearish or bullish calls, and only one timestamp (June 29, 2026) on the timeline. There is no view migration to chart here — no pivot, no recantation, just one long-form defense of a funding thesis. The neutrality is a register, not an absence of conviction; his conviction lives in the asset, expressed through funding math rather than price targets. Until he surfaces in the corpus again, this interview is the whole portrait.

person/surge-copper-ceo-leif-interviewee.text:
Leif Nilsson is a Canadian mining executive and President & CEO of Surge Copper, a Vancouver-based copper-molybdenum-gold explorer working in west-central British Columbia. On his watch the company has consolidated the Ootsa copper-gold-molybdenum project — acquired from Imperial Metals, sitting adjacent to the Huckleberry mine area — along with the Berg property, and has run large drilling programs on the back of resource updates. He carries roughly 25-30 years of experience across mineral exploration, development and mining finance with junior and mid-tier companies, and made his case as a solo guest on Resource Talks [$4.6B Copper Project in BC, But Can the Capex Be Funded? | …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k).

The June 29, 2026 interview is effectively the whole public record here, and it captures a CEO unusually willing to cap his own story. He put the project's throughput ceiling at 120,000 tons per day — "probably the maximum size we're going to go to here" [$4.6B Copper Project in BC, But Can the Capex Be Funded? | …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k) — and waved off near-mine additions as incremental rather than "transformational from an NPV or IRR perspective" [$4.6B Copper Project in BC, But Can the Capex Be Funded? | …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k). His resilience argument leaned on molybdenum: even a negative-60% moly case at base-case copper, he argued, still leaves "like an 18% IRR and multi-billion" [$4.6B Copper Project in BC, But Can the Capex Be Funded? | …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k). The episode's own title poses the obvious objection — a $4.6B project and a funding gap — and Nilsson answered it on those terms, noting that anyone committing billions would rather recoup the capital within a couple of years [$4.6B Copper Project in BC, But Can the Capex Be Funded? | …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k).

On the endgame he was candid that a takeover isn't the only path: a major "could be a buyer of Surge one day" and run its own JV process, or ARM could instead grow its ownership and "contribute significant capital to the project through the current corporate structure" [$4.6B Copper Project in BC, But Can the Capex Be Funded? | …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k). He offered Solaris as the peer read-through — a share price he said had "doubled in the last year" on a comparable BC story [$4.6B Copper Project in BC, But Can the Capex Be Funded? | …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k) — and his one directional macro remark, that copper's eventual equilibrium prices are "maybe a lot higher than where we are," was framed as an equilibrium argument, not a trade [$4.6B Copper Project in BC, But Can the Capex Be Funded? | …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k), loosely tied to a broader theme of global economic "polarization" [$4.6B Copper Project in BC, But Can the Capex Be Funded? | …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k).

As for how his views have moved: there is no trajectory to trace. This is a single-snapshot file — one appearance, fifteen coded stances, all neutral, none bullish or bearish — which is itself the most telling detail. What the snapshot shows is a preference for scenario framing over promotion: Nilsson spends more airtime on what his project can't do (scale past 120k tpd, mint NPV from bolt-on additions) than on what it might, a posture worth revisiting if further interviews ever land in the record.

person/person-016.text:
高盛（Goldman Sachs）是1869年創立、總部位於紐約的美國大型跨國投資銀行，業務橫跨投資銀行、證券交易、資產管理與財富管理。在本知識庫中，它以「被引用者」的身份出現：其全球投資研究部（Global Investment Research）與經濟學家團隊發佈的股票研究、宏觀經濟與市場策略報告，是財經作者與媒體論證時最常搬出的機構背書之一。

在目前收錄的語料裡，高盛被引用的核心論點只有一個，但分量不輕——AI資本開支的規模測算。2026年8月27日一篇討論AI資本「理性與亢奮」的文章提到，亞馬遜等五家巨頭2026年AI資本支出預計達755億美元、年增約80%，並援引高盛的估算：大型科技公司2025至2030年累計資本開支約5.3萬億美元（[AI資本的理性與亢奮](https://www.master-insight.com/article/49793)）。這個數字的功能值得玩味：它既可被多頭引為「需求真實、支出有據」的證據，也可被審慎者引為「支出規模驚人」的警告素材——高盛在此扮演的不是觀點發起者，而是辯論雙方共用的事實底座，這也解釋了為何它在語料中被標記為中性。

至於立場隨時間的移動，現有材料無法給出答案：時間線上只有這一筆2026年8月的紀錄，且嚴格說是對亞馬遜相關AI資本支出話題的中性引用，而非高盛自身的買賣評級或目標價調整。換言之，這份檔案捕捉到的是高盛作為「測算供應者」的一面，而非其研究觀點的轉向軌跡；若要判斷該行在AI支出爭論中偏多、偏空還是有所鬆動，目前的覆蓋明顯太薄，只能留待後續引用補齊。

ticker/000660.KS.text:
The record on SK Hynix (000660.KS) in this corpus is thin, lopsided, and — unusually for a name this widely followed — entirely devoid of a bull. The tally reads zero bullish, one bearish, one neutral, and even the sequencing suggests the conversation is happening after the fact rather than ahead of it. There is no fundamentals debate here: nobody defends the memory-cycle or HBM thesis, and nobody mounts a valuation case. The discussion, such as it is, lives entirely in the mechanics of a crowded, leveraged trade.

The bearish entry comes from an unnamed commentator on July 5, 2026, working off the prior week's damage: SK Hynix fell sharply around July 2 — the transcript records a "14.6" figure (almost certainly a percentage, though the quote is fragmentary) — and the speaker sees more downside, arguing the stock "can fall 9.1 percent or so" from there. Note what kind of argument this is: it is a price-action and drawdown call, not a claim about earnings, pricing, or demand. As recorded, the bear case is essentially "the falling knife has further to fall."

The neutral voice, arguably the more interesting one, came earlier. On June 26, 2026, [何啟聰](../People/person-001.md) flagged the speculative plumbing underneath the stock: if the market value of leveraged ETFs tied to Hynix keeps ballooning in the coming weeks, he expects South Korean regulators may well step in with measures of their own. That is not a sell call, but it maps a specific downside catalyst — policy intervention into an overheated leveraged trade. The timing is suggestive: his warning landed roughly ten days before the sharp drop the bear cites. Whether regulatory action, ETF flows, or something else drove the early-July fall cannot be established from this corpus, and nobody here claims it can.

As for minds changing: there is no evidence of anyone revising a view in either direction. With one technical bear, one regulatory risk-flag, and no bulls on record, this page has a gap where the other side of the debate should be — worth revisiting the moment someone stakes out the fundamental case.

ticker/BLK.text:
Coverage of BlackRock in this corpus is thin, and the honest place to start is with that fact: the consensus tally sits at neutral/watch with zero bullish and zero bearish counts across just two recorded entries. There is a wrinkle worth flagging, though — the call log itself tags Jeff's late-June entry as bearish, which doesn't square with a zero-bearish tally. Read charitably, the consensus reflects fence-sitting; read plainly, the data disagrees with itself. Either way, nobody here has planted a bull flag.

The one articulated argument belongs to Jeff, and it is not a valuation call — it's a reflexivity call. Writing on June 27, 2026, his thesis is that BlackRock's public equity holders increasingly file the firm mentally under "private credit manager," and that in a stress episode that label becomes a self-fulfilling outflow trigger: "Stock market investors look at BlackRock as one of the biggest examples of a private credit manager, they think, I got to get my money out." The bear case, in other words, is about the brand's exposure to a redemption-run narrative rather than about fundamentals or earnings. It's a plausible shape for a drawdown thesis, but it stands alone in this record — no counterargument, no rebuttal, and no evidence of anyone changing their mind in either direction.

The second entry, dated July 30, 2026 and unattributed, is a datapoint rather than a call: a blue-chip data center financing that priced at a 7.53% yield, described as one of the highest for such paper "since the current AA borrow…" — the note cuts off mid-sentence, so its full framing is incomplete. With no stance attached, it can feed either side of the debate: richer yields on even top-rated data center debt are consistent with Jeff's worry that the private-credit complex BlackRock has leaned into is demanding more compensation for risk, or they can be read as attractive entry pricing for the very assets the firm has been accumulating. That ambiguity is the current state of the BLK debate in this corpus — one bear narrative, one ambiguous credit-market observation, and a neutral consensus that mostly says watch this space.

ticker/DX-Y.NYY.text:
The dollar debate in this record is unusually lopsided — and unusually short. There is essentially one voice in the corpus, and that voice sits on both sides of the argument at different points in 2026. Back on June 26, the case was the classic cyclical one: "Dollar's going up. Bond markets, yields are rising" — the familiar argument that higher yields pull capital toward dollar assets and lift the currency with them ([June 26, 2026 call](dx-y-nyy-calls)). Less than two months later, on August 21, the same speaker had flipped to the structural bear case: "I think there's a major diversification going on in terms of uh trade and capital flows, which over time is going to be dollar negative" ([August 21, 2026 call](dx-y-nyy-calls)).

That reversal is the most interesting thing about the debate as recorded here. It traces a shift in framework rather than just a change of mind — from a rates-differential story, where yields call the tune, to a flows story, where the slow reallocation of trade settlement and reserve capital away from the dollar grinds down the currency regardless of where yields sit. The August framing is notably hedged on timing ("over time"), which softens it into a medium-term drift call rather than a prediction of imminent downside. The June call, by contrast, was immediate and directional.

The honest caveat: this "debate" is thin. The consensus tag reads bearish, but the tally is one bear and one neutral, with no bull currently on record — the June bull case has no surviving defender in the corpus. The speakers behind each call aren't identified in the digest, so it's impossible to say whether the June-to-August flip represents one analyst genuinely changing their mind or two different voices. What the record does show plainly is the shape of the argument: bears anchor on structural diversification of trade and capital flows; bulls, at least as of mid-2026, anchored on rising yields. The bear side currently holds the field largely by default.

ticker/EQX.text:
The recorded debate around EQX is strikingly one-sided: seven contributors sit in the neutral/watch camp, not a single one is on the record as bullish or bearish, and almost all the substantive argument in the file comes from the company itself. On July 3, 2026, [Ryan King](../People/ryan-king.md) laid out what is, in effect, the bull case — a jurisdictional re-rating story backed by a balance-sheet repair and a steep growth curve. The counterweight isn't a formal bear call; it's a market reaction, noted on the same call, that the stock is down over 30%, maybe 35% since the Orla Mining deal was announced and the downturn set in. So the real debate is management's pitch versus what the tape has been saying.

King's argument has three prongs. First, jurisdiction: he frames 70 to 75% of NAV coming from Canada and the United States — "safe jurisdictions, tier one jurisdictions" — with the implication that this mix, combined with execution and track record, can earn the company a premium valuation ([Ryan King](../People/ryan-king.md)). Second, deleveraging: the company went from a net debt position of roughly $1.6–1.7 billion to about $400 million, a reduction he notes came prior to the most recent transaction ([Ryan King](../People/ryan-king.md)). Third, growth: over the next five years, a 70% annual production growth rate from new assets ([Ryan King](../People/ryan-king.md)). It's a coherent template — fix the balance sheet, concentrate in institutional-friendly geographies, grow into the multiple — and it's the kind of story that historically gets rewarded when delivery matches the slide deck.

The pushback, such as it exists, is implicit rather than argued. Whoever raised the drawdown on that same July 3 call wasn't disputing the numbers; they were pointing out that since the Orla deal announcement the stock has lost a third of its value anyway. That gap is where the neutral consensus lives: the market has so far declined to pay the premium King describes, and no analyst in this corpus has staked out a position on whether that skepticism or management's framework is the right read. There's no recorded disagreement with the 70% growth figure or the deleveraging math — but there's also no recorded endorsement, which tells you something about how the sell side treats junior-producer guidance.

As a timeline, the file is thin to the point of flatness: every dated call collapses to July 3, 2026, so there's no visible track record of anyone changing their mind, no prior bulls turning cautious, no bears capitulating. The honest summary is that EQX currently has a story and a stock price that haven't reconciled, a management team making the case for a re-rating, and an analyst base unwilling to commit in either direction until the growth and execution targets are tested against delivery.

ticker/GBPUSD=X.text:
The recorded debate on GBP/USD in this corpus is a near-empty room: zero bulls, zero outright bears, and exactly two stances — both neutral, both from the same commentator, both delivered on 6 July 2026. The speaker isn't even named in the file (logged only as "?"), which is itself worth noting: the entire case file for one of the world's most-traded currency pairs rests on a single, unattributed voice. That voice's base view is deliberately two-sided. The dollar isn't necessarily set to gain against sterling over the long run, but it isn't set to lose either — and since the picture can't be read clearly from either direction, the practical conclusion drawn is to stop treating it as a single-currency bet and diversify across currencies instead. That's not a call on the pair; it's a refusal to make one.

The bear case exists, but only as a conditional sketch rather than a conviction. The same speaker, in the same 6 July 2026 discussion, works through a risk scenario in which sterling falls roughly 10% against the dollar over the next one to three years — arguing that earning 3.5 to 4 percent (presumably the yield pitch for holding sterling assets) would still leave a holder underwater if that decline materialized, hence the closing caution to "look at this carefully." The file tags this as bearish GBP versus USD but explicitly as a risk scenario, not a certainty, which is presumably why it still nets out to neutral in the tally. Strip away the hedging and there is a real argument buried here: that sterling's income advantage is inadequate compensation for its downside risk over a one-to-three-year horizon. But the speaker never commits to it.

What's missing is as telling as what's there. There is no bull counterargument anywhere in the record, no earlier stance for anyone to have reversed, and no second voice to create an actual contest of views — the timeline is one date and one speaker hedging in both directions within a single discussion. So there are no mind-changes to report and no call sequence to trace. The honest summary is that GBP/USD sits on the watchlist, not the fight card: the only articulated position on record is that the pair is unreadable either way, and that the correct response is position structure (diversification) rather than direction. Anyone looking for a genuine sterling bull-versus-bear debate will have to wait for this page to accumulate more than one dated entry.

ticker/HKDUSD=X.text:
Coverage of HKDUSD=X in this corpus is thin, and the honest way to describe "the debate" is that there isn't one — there's a monologue. No bull or bear stances are registered anywhere: the tally reads zero bullish, zero bearish, three neutral, and all three entries come from a single, unattributed Cantonese-speaking commentator whose name the digest doesn't supply. That attribution gap matters. Without knowing who is talking — a market veteran, a financial YouTuber, an anonymous thread — readers can't weigh the pedigree behind some fairly dramatic numbers.

What that voice actually argues, in order, is a chain-reaction stress scenario rather than a forecast. On 2026-07-10, the speaker lays out a liquidity spiral: once the market sees financial institutions genuinely moving Hong Kong dollar liquidity, participants will "naturally" start asking whether the dollar pool backing the peg is running short — a conditional stress framing on the peg itself (call of 2026-07-10, tagged conditional_stress_on_HKD_peg). In the same breath comes the second domino: the interbank market "will tighten," squeezing bank funding (call of 2026-07-10). Then, on 2026-07-23, the speaker attaches a number to the tail case: if Hong Kong decouples from the peg, the exchange rate "will fall straight to 15" per US dollar — versus the 7.75–7.85 band — which would make Hong Kong goods look half as expensive to American and European buyers (call of 2026-07-23, tagged situational). The 15 figure is the speaker's own hypothetical, not a market quote, and the corpus correctly files it as scenario rather than call.

The notable structural quirk is that this is arguably a conditional bearish argument booked as neutral. A peg breaking to 15 would be a catastrophic depreciation, and interbank tightening plus dollar-adequacy doubts are the classic bear script for the Linked Exchange Rate System — yet nothing in the record registers as an actual bearish stance, presumably because everything is couched in "once/if" terms. The counterargument — the bull case for the peg, whether on HKMA defense mechanics or reserve adequacy — is simply absent from the corpus. So the timeline reads: two entries on 2026-07-10 building the stress narrative, one on 2026-07-23 quantifying the worst case, no rebuttals, no mind-changes, and no named advocate on either side. The consensus "neutral / watch" label is less a verdict on the currency than a verdict on the evidence: one anonymous voice sketching a scenario deserves watching, not a position.

ticker/SURG.V.text:
There isn't much of a debate on record for SURG.V — that's the first thing worth saying. The corpus shows a consensus of neutral/watch, with ten neutral stances and not a single bullish or bearish call from anyone. The only substantive commentary comes from one unnamed speaker on June 29, 2026, whose first-person framing ("we've drilled," "our last resource update," "our opinion") strongly suggests company management or someone speaking from inside the project. The digest doesn't attach a name to the remarks, so they should be read as a company case rather than independent analysis.

That case, as presented, is constructive on three fronts. First, exploration momentum: the speaker claims roughly 15,000 meters drilled since the last resource update, with "some interesting stuff" encountered — vague, but positioned as progress. Second, strategy: a "long time" held view that there's "a logical business case to be made for those deposits to be integrated in some way" (the transcript labels the project UTSA, though the phrasing appears garbled — the integration argument is the core, whatever the label). Third, and most aggressively, valuation: the speaker argues the "equity value of this company has room to grow very strongly without a single additional catalyst." The timeline offered is a long one — an "end of decade project" with a three-year construction period, a figure the speaker self-corrected mid-sentence before the quote trails off into a "depending…" that never resolves.

The bear side is simply absent. Nobody in the corpus has staked out a bearish position, and the ten neutral calls suggest analysts are watching rather than committing. It's worth noting the hedges embedded even in management's own optimism — the doubled "I think... I think," the mid-sentence correction on the construction timeline, the dangling caveat — and the familiar irony of a "no catalyst needed" valuation claim coming from a company whose project, by its own timeline, won't reach a construction decision until the back half of the decade. As it stands, the debate is a one-sided management monologue: the bulls' brief exists, but it hasn't found a counterparty yet.

ticker/TSM.text:
The TSM file as of mid-2026 is thinner than the stock deserves, and it's worth saying so up front: three logged calls, all scored neutral, none of the speakers attributed by name in the source material. What the record does capture, though, is the actual fault line in the TSMC debate — not whether the company is a good business, but whether the margins that make it one are at peak.

The cautious read came from an unnamed commentator on 2026-07-17, who flatly predicted "their margins are going to start to contract." That's the only explicitly cautionary line in the file, and notably it still wasn't scored as a bearish call — an inversion of the usual pattern where someone this direct on margins would plant a flag. It sets up the bear case as a mix-and-competition story rather than a demand collapse story.

Against that, the profit-is-understated case came a month earlier. On 2026-06-15 a Cantonese-speaking commentator laid out the geographic mix argument: TSMC's Taiwan capacity running at roughly a 95% rate versus something nearer 70% elsewhere, meaning what shows up as a ~25% surface-level margin conceals actual profit that is, in his words, "more than double." That's the standard rebuttal to any contraction thesis — that headline numbers systematically undersell the profitability of the advanced-node fleet, so even a modest reported decline would flatter the underlying economics.

Sitting between the two is the valuation observation from 2026-07-05: surprise that TSMC's market value had surpassed Samsung, with the pointed aside that "Samsung does a lot of things" — implicitly a note that TSMC gets its premium as a pure-play foundry while Samsung's breadth dilutes the comparison. Read together, the file sketches a debate that tightened between mid-June and mid-July 2026: one camp arguing the margin peak is in, another arguing reported margins understate reality, and a third mulling what the Samsung crossover means for the multiple. Nobody in this sample actually committed to bullish or bearish — which tells you the honest position here is watchful, with the margin trajectory as the tiebreaker.

ticker/^N225.text:
There isn't a real bull-versus-bear fight on the Nikkei 225 in this corpus — every call on file comes from a single unnamed, Cantonese-language commentator, and the whole set nets out to four neutrals, zero bulls, zero bears. What makes the page worth reading is that this one voice is running the entire debate internally. On July 5, 2026 they noted the index "has risen, from 39,000 to 70,000," and the day before flagged Japan as *the* market to watch as it broke its all-time peak in the 69,000–70,000 zone (July 4 call). A level near 70,000 is roughly double where the Nikkei traded through most of its modern history, so this is no shrug-your-shoulders rally — yet the speaker pointedly refuses to call it bullish; the July remarks describe the move, they don't chase it.

The bear case here exists only as a conditional, and interestingly it came *first*. On June 18 the speaker revived the August 2024 script — the yen carry-trade unwind that produced the Nikkei's worst single-day point drop since the 1987 crash — warning that the same thing "will blow up once more" if it repeats. On June 30 they sketched the exit: leave "quickly," because the down day could run "at least 15 percent." (What trips the fuse — the transcript's garbled "once nine times" — is unspecified, so treat the trigger as unknown.) Note the arc: crash scenario flagged in mid-June, then the index broke records anyway in early July, and the speaker shifted to watch-mode rather than doubling down on the short side. Both postures are framed as scenarios, not verdicts — which is exactly why the tally reads neutral.

The honest caveat is that coverage is thin. One voice, unnamed in our source, four data points across three weeks, no institutional bulls or bears on record, no earnest price targets. The "debate" around the Nikkei here is really a single watch-list entry: a market extended enough to demand monitoring, momentum-rich enough that nobody dares fade it, and 2024-scarred enough that the speaker keeps one hand on the fire exit.

weekly/2026-06-07.text:
It was a thin week — two items, two names, and only one piece of real substance — so this digest will be short and should be read as such. What little discourse existed leaned heavily toward rates and bonds, which dominated the week's extracted views, with macro-and-indices close behind and credit and oil-energy as secondary threads. The centerpiece was Jeff Snider's June 13 video for Eurodollar University, [Europe Just Made A Historic Policy Mistake](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bBMP-s5PzKo), in which [Jeff Snider](../People/jeff-snider.md) takes aim at the European Central Bank for raising interest rates on Thursday even as the eurozone economy is already contracting — his "historic policy mistake" framing doing most of the rhetorical work.

Snider's actual market stance underneath the critique is bullish bonds: Treasury yields collapsed again, and his view has the Fed and ECB following the market by cutting policy rates aggressively ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bBMP-s5PzKo)). That sits in visible tension with the ECB hike he spent the video criticizing — the digest gives us both the stance and the summary without fully reconciling them, though the natural reading is that he expects the hike to be overwhelmed by market-forced cuts. The more actionable open question he flags is the Fed's: whether it sees through the oil shock or gets pulled into "the same mistake" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bBMP-s5PzKo)). That is the week's sharpest fault line in miniature — a central bank tightening into weakness, a bond market pricing the opposite, and the Fed choosing sides.

As for the other two questions this essay is meant to answer: there are no genuinely differing viewpoints to line up, because no second analyst took the other side of Snider's ECB call this week — the debate is entirely one-sided in the record. And nobody changed their mind; with no prior stances on file for the period, there is no pivot to report. The only other item, AM Invest's Patreon post sharing a Zoom login link for a workshop titled 「攻守轉換全攻略」 ([link](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/gong-shou-zhuan-160950208)), is pure administrative housekeeping with no market views attached. The week's takeaway, such as it is: Snider's blast at the ECB and his bond-bullish read, and a Fed decision on the oil shock still hanging.

weekly/2026-06-14.text:
Oil owned the week — 24 WTI calls, more than any other ticker — and the argument ran straight through the Iran ceasefire. David Woo, long crude since the war's early days, put the bull case starkly: if the strait is still shut by the end of July, "oil price is going to be $150" ([David Woo](../People/david-woo.md), [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=760Bpzc1cYM)). Eurodollar University took the other side, walking listeners down curve mechanics to "how you get to $50 a barrel" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DTh7cPI8z3E)) — and by Wednesday Jeff Snider was narrating oil *and* rates plunging, telling viewers to watch for the front of the WTI curve flipping into contango ([Jeff Snider](../People/jeff-snider.md), [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IpZ_HYxaU_8)). Joseph Wang's weekly confirmed spot Brent had "absolutely plummeted" ([Joseph Wang](../People/joseph-wang.md), [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fI3fVnAqi80)), while Patrick Ceresna noted equities "rallied on the deescalation with the S&P 500 climbing over 2% to 7420" ([Patrick Ceresna](../People/patrick-ceresna.md)). Then the new Fed chair's first FOMC landed hawkish: rates held at 3.5–3.75% ([Simplify](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQd7TRakAnw)), a signal of hikes later this year that knocked US stocks down about 1% ([Dr Ng Ming Tak](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7Ms1r4rmC9M)), and Wang — whose debrief was billed as exactly that, "hawkish" — saw equities, bonds and gold sell off together and read it as pointing to "a sustained and meaningful decline in risk assets" ([FOMC debrief](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Njd_JuRuEcI)). Jim Bianco expects the Fed to raise at least once, probably in October ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ljPRDXx_g-8)); 何啟聰 flagged that chair Warsh himself conceded inflation runs far above the 2% target ([column](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4435475/AI%E7%A1%AC%E4%BB%B6%E6%BC%B2%E5%83%B9%E9%80%BC%E8%81%AF%E5%84%B2%E5%B1%80%E5%85%A5%E6%AD%BB%E8%A7%92)).

The sharpest lines were drawn on metals, duration and the SpaceX IPO. Inside a single CPM Group update, Jeffrey Kushin was reminding listeners they called buy at $1,211 in 2014 — "a few years early" — and expecting silver to consolidate between $60 and $90 before higher prices in the year's final months, while Jeffrey Christian warned a spike below $60 in silver is a "very high" probability over the next two and a half months and floated gold targets of 3,800 or 3,500 on a break ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1jdQOS8Lu8)); Christian doubled down on the $60 silver risk by Thursday ([update](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z1btQrMgRwo)), and Gary Wagner flatly declared "sustained technical chart damage… definitely in a correction" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tMzlpYpNi_w)). On yields, Komal Sri-Kumar argued that if inflation isn't controlled by year-end, "expect the 10-year and 30-year to move up as well" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FHtb-uCMgLU)); Ceresna countered that yields near 4.70 look like "a key high," even if not yet a confirmed downtrend ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqHNNzR9WNc)). SpaceX split the room just as cleanly: JD on Macro Dirt could see the "middle finger chart formation, goes parabolic" ([Macro Dirt](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-mvJ6poUk4)), Wang warned the lockups unlock in coming months and "the people sell" ([debrief](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Njd_JuRuEcI)), and 徐家健 framed the ~19.2% first-day pop against Krugman's "Human Ponzi Scheme" charge and a price-to-sales near 100x ([article](https://www.master-insight.com/article/48758)). George Noble drew the equity line — "absolutely no way that I would go outright long the S&P 500 right now" — in a Gammon conversation that still hedged with a token $10,000 SPY long and a homebuilder short ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QxR6yvf8ueU)).

The week's whiplash shows up best in the flips. Erik Townsend and Brent Johnson both turned from oil bulls to bears inside 24 hours as the deal took hold: Townsend, who had said "someday we're going to get a real peace deal and when we do, oil is going to sell off and sell off hard," got exactly that, with WTI testing the 200-day near 73.50 ([MacroVoices transcript](https://www.macrovoices.com/podcast-transcripts/1536-brent-johnson-there-s-no-turning-back), [Erik Townsend](../People/erik-townsend.md), [Brent Johnson](../People/brent-johnson.md)). Johnson's other reversals were stranger — to dollar-bullish on the grounds that "99% of all outstanding stable coins in the world today are US dollar stable," and to calling national defense "probably going to be the biggest investment opportunity any of us have ever seen" ([transcript](https://www.macrovoices.com/podcast-transcripts/1536-brent-johnson-there-s-no-turning-back)). In Hong Kong, 高天佑 flipped within 48 hours: Tuesday's piece championed the "Hefei model" of state-guided capital (ChangXin earning RMB33 billion in a single quarter as one of four HBM producers) ([column](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4431990/%E5%8C%97%E9%83%BD%E5%8F%AF%E5%80%9F%E9%91%91%E3%80%8C%E5%90%88%E8%82%A5%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F%E3%80%8D), [高天佑](../People/person-010.md)); Thursday's had mainland e-commerce's 618 invasion crushing small local retailers, with knock-on pressure on jobs, rents and property values ([column](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4434076/618%E6%94%BB%E6%94%BB%E6%B8%AF+%E6%9C%AC%E5%9C%B0%E9%9B%B6%E5%94%AE%E9%9B%A3%E6%8D%B1)). Snider, too, swung from bullish to bearish on rates and the dollar in two days ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ocd1ZMBGcRw)) — less conviction than headline-chasing.

Beneath the macro noise ran a strikingly one-sided AI-skeptic current. David Woo argued "token maxing" and component inflation are manufacturing an illusion of accelerating profits ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=760Bpzc1cYM)); Jim Chanos said Meta's AI strategy "makes no sense to me whatsoever… definitely consider me a bear," even while conceding outright shorting semis "might not be a risk worth taking" ([Jim Chanos](../People/jim-chanos.md), [panel](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlIsoPhQePs)); Patrick Boyle asked how to lose a global AI monopoly in one afternoon, pointing to Anthropic's export-control shutdown of foreign users ([Patrick Boyle](../People/patrick-boyle.md), [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0RxMj0L0-fY)); and 雷鼎鳴 tallied four and a half years of US equity gains as the work of eight tech giants plus inflation ([article](https://www.master-insight.com/article/48855)). 何啟聰 tied it back to the Fed: AI hardware inflation, not productivity, is what corners rates ([column](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4435475/AI%E7%A1%AC%E4%BB%B6%E6%BC%B2%E5%83%B9%E9%80%BC%E8%81%AF%E5%84%B2%E5%B1%80%E5%85%A5%E6%AD%BB%E8%A7%92)). Add Snider's China gloom — a record plunge in household borrowing, "China's credit machine is lost" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d7cNjW_mcEM), [Hang Seng follow-up](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3j8NhL0FTo4)) — and the bear case is getting crowded, which is exactly why Meredith Whitney's dissent lands: "I don't see a recession in the next couple of quarters," with growth possibly accelerating into year-end ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibrkjqo7eZA)). The honest shape of this week: oil and gold are truly two-sided fights, the AI bears are louder than they've been all cycle, and nearly everyone repositioned faster than they explained.

weekly/2026-06-21.text:
Gold and Bitcoin topped the call ledger this week — 23 and 25 calls respectively — but the metal earned its billing by actually moving: Jeffrey Christian of CPM Group had gold "testing $4,100" with a break pointing "toward $3,800," and by Friday his firm was describing "a very clear downward trend since we reached that record peak around $5,500 at the end of January" ([CPM Group](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O-RRUlGQb6o), [CPM Group](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YWeAUtiILYM)). The backdrop did the rest: US AI leaders fell more than 10% on Tuesday, South Korea dropped 9.99%, and Hong Kong hit a one-year low ( [高天佑](../People/person-010.md) ), before a "spectacular" Micron beat triggered what Lyn Alden called a relief rally still "carried by a very narrow group of momentum names" ( [MacroVoices](https://www.macrovoices.com/podcast-transcripts/1538-lyn-alden-is-the-war-really-over-and-what-s-next-for-markets) ). Add SpaceX sliding to $173 in its listing week ( [何啟聰](../People/person-001.md) ), Keir Starmer's resignation — "It is the economy, stupid," per [Jeff Snider](../People/jeff-snider.md) ( [Eurodollar University](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wL63-KdtuEE) ) — and Apollo Debt Solutions fielding repurchase requests equal to 16.8% of its shares ( [Snider](../People/jeff-snider.md) ), and the bears had a surplus of raw material.

The sharpest line ran through the AI trade itself. [Ed Zitron](../People/ed-zitron.md), on [Jack Farley](../People/jack-farley.md)'s network, brought receipts — $34 billion of OpenAI spending in 2025 with losses up nearly 8x — put the pop at "2027's the safe bet," and gave Nvidia "two, three more earnings calls" to keep guidance miraculous ( [Monetary Matters Network](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xFd8X7TI7Sc) ). [Mike Alfred](../People/mike-alfred.md) told [Ash Bennington](../People/ash-bennington.md) the opposite: AI is a land, power and compute trade, he's holding his Iron position, and he's running "a straight long Bitcoin position" as his only public one ( [Real Vision](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-p3DhlY2TEk) ). [Matthew Tuttle](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IhP8-hw8OZM) leaned bull — AI's potential is "immense," it's a race with China, and "memory, photonics, all of that" ramps — while [高天佑](../People/person-010.md) staked the thoughtful middle: the narrative is neither falsified nor proven and needs "再驗證" before a next leg ( [HKEJ](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4438934/AI%E6%95%8D%E4%BA%8B%E4%BA%9F%E9%9C%80%E3%80%8C%E5%86%8D%E9%A9%97%E8%AD%89%E3%80%8D) ). Michael Nicoletos added the market-structure sting: with roughly half of equity flows passive, the same index holds stocks up 300% and down 80% ( [Maggie Lake Talking Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eiYWo4uTosE) ).

The macro splits were just as clean. On the dollar, Chris Vermeulen — of "24% Collapse Incoming" fame — argued "the stock market will fall if the dollar rallies" ( [David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0f1pMEpQ61U) ), [Todd Horwitz](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=76T7U8Q1Kmo) and Brent Johnson ("there's nothing the rest of the world can do to make the dollar... fall") joined the bull camp ( [Rebel Capitalist](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmNZLvOBu8M) ), while [George Noble](../People/george-noble.md) offered "pair of twos no opinion on the dollar — I actually think it goes lower" and Macro Dirt co-host JD called it "a false breakout... I'm very bearish" ( [The Macro Dirt Podcast](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4) ). On the S&P, Horwitz sees "a great shot that we see 4,500 on this next up leg" against Vermeulen's 24% haircut. Oil split between a buyer on dips ("I'm a buyer down here of oil as well"), Noble's bet that the next $10–15 in crude is higher, and a bear expecting "the mid-50s before this move is all done" — with Doomberg notably refusing the crisis framing ("the LNG market is actually pretty well-behaved") while still warning of an inflation "bulge" ( [David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FNj9Ux9iNwo) ). SpaceX produced the week's widest gap: JD's "if there was any stock that had a chance of going to a 10 trillion market cap" versus Zitron's "trundling down" and 何啟聰's warning that the premium belongs to Musk alone — though even Noble, buying puts "big time," concedes "it may go to 300 before it goes to 50."

Flips were unusually easy to spot. 高天佑 went from bullish on China and Hong Kong equities to bearish inside twenty-four hours as the crash unfolded ( [HKEJ](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/finnews/article/4438934/AI%E6%95%8D%E4%BA%8B%E4%BA%9F%E9%9C%80%E3%80%8C%E5%86%8D%E9%A9%97%E8%AD%89%E3%80%8D) ). George Noble reversed on bonds and the dollar in five days — from bearish on June 18 to "I'm putting it all in bonds" on June 23 — and JD flipped the dollar from bullish to "very bearish" in the same stretch ( [Macro Dirt](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDrOV4i0EU4) ). Jeff, the recurring Eurodollar University guest, turned bullish on both oil and Chinese equities between June 14 and June 21 ( [Eurodollar University](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c2LzapdRuT4) ). And aminvest didn't flip so much as hedge: roughly 80% bull versus 20% bear on US stocks, exposure cut to about half, with call options staged "如果我見到美股重新出現上升動力" ( [AM Invest](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/cang-wei-wu-da-161877458), [AM Invest](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-161958989) ).

Underneath the ticker talk, two anxieties kept surfacing. Private credit: Snider spent the week on it — Blue Owl "keep hitting new lows," MFIC at "85 cents on the dollar relative to net asset value," Apollo's fund "now cash flow negative" with redemptions partly blocked and Q3 requests projected "even higher" ( [Eurodollar University](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SibAV9HRe1I), [Eurodollar University](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=biyCX7UYAfQ) ). Fed leadership: michaelwgreen's "Rinse, Warsh, Repeat" ( [yesigiveafig](https://www.yesigiveafig.com/p/rinse-warsh-repeat) ), Dr Ng's teardown of the viral Trump–Musk–Warsh "debt meltdown" rumor ( [Dr Ng Ming Tak, Victor](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dYng6Mw9b-8) ), and Joseph Wang hearing from "very connected people" that a Fed chair hire is coming ( [Forward Guidance-adjacent Markets Weekly](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzRGWHUuJRI) ). The yen's break of 160 got two readings — George Gammon's MOF/BOJ intervention watch versus Peter Schiff's "it's a yen weakness story. It's not a dollar strength story" ( [George Gammon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kGK6CyiNj3g), [David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IIBguZNDuzs) ) — while Dr Ng walked through China halving its Treasury stack to $650 billion, an 18-year low, rotating into gold nobody "can freeze" ( [Dr Ng Ming Tak, Victor](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9OqIYmCLPb4) ). Hong Kong's own house views split as ever: 湯文亮 arguing record rents and prices still ~30% below peak mean the rally is nowhere near done ( [master-insight](https://www.master-insight.com/article/48919) ), against aminvest's "熊市二期" call and Dr Ng's Singapore-ization thesis. Tellingly thin spot: the junior-mining circuit, uniformly noncommittal — Kingfisher's own guest conceded the space "is highly likely to lose you money. Failure is the norm" ( [Resource Talks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BgR0bNaPWlE) ).

weekly/2026-06-28.text:
The loudest argument this week was about the AI trade, and for once the bears set the tempo. Meta's latest unilateral move — 何啟聰's word for it was 任性, "wilful" — shook markets and was promptly read as a bearish signal for the entire chip complex, "basically a sign that the day of reckoning" has arrived, in David Woo's telling ([Meta「任性」震動市場](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4447682/Meta%E3%80%8C%E4%BB%BB%E6%80%A7%E3%80%8D%E9%9C%87%E5%8B%95%E5%B8%82%E5%A0%B4), [David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QjuThPhidXY)). Forward Guidance declared "The AI Trade Is Finally Cracking" ([Weekly Roundup](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=18-zFIyoJAo)), Eurodollar University went further and said private credit "just burst the $25 trillion AI bubble" ([YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ktLyXGRHNCk)), and even 何啟聰 flagged memory-chip fat margins as a hidden vulnerability rather than a triumph ([HKEJ](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4442430/%E5%85%A7%E5%AD%98%E8%A8%98%E6%86%B6%E9%AB%94%E9%AB%98%E6%AF%9B%E5%88%A9%E5%8F%8D%E6%88%90%E9%9A%B1%E6%86%82)). The bull case didn't go quiet, though: Erik pushed "The Reverse Crash" — S&P 500 straight to 10,000 by 2027, hyperscalers "not backing off… actually accelerating the bet," even as he conceded semis are "crowding out every other sector" and worried aloud about Meta glasses flopping ([Monetary Matters](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fcuaGmxTFZk)). Real Vision's panel split the difference — Ram still sees a bull market, Jeff insists earnings drive everything, and someone noted the extra $20–25 billion from Anthropic and Google renting Colossus capacity ([Real Vision](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3LVb6esEFOk)) — while Liaquat Ahamed supplied the historian's warning: data centers at roughly 2% of GDP, competitive herd behavior producing "poor returns for everyone," and "a series of mini booms and busts" in the AI boom ([Ahamed](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=czdGQG9HvGM)).

Gold was the week's most-trafficked ticker — 18 calls on GC=F — and the metals crowd talked like a bottom was being mapped, not a top. Jeff, the analyst who called the drop, noted gold has broken below $4,100 repeatedly but expects consolidation "over the next few two months, then rise in the final part of this year," and said flatly he is "most bullish on gold and silver" ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Nz7zxxJBNfo)). CPM Group countered with a rates framework — gold rises when real T-bill returns are zero, goes neutral at 2% — and flagged platinum at $1,211 risking a slide back into its $900–1,200 range, plus 78 million ounces of silver dumped by ETF investors ([CPM Group](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-6Zt6_Rj4EQ)). On the mining side, Ryan tied the metals complex to an inevitable "major debt crisis" reckoning while admitting Equinox Gold is down since the Orla deal and "we are price takers" ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NBToObvXTmI)); Mithril was modeling $3,500–3,600 gold while its interviewer reminded everyone that "failure is the norm" in exploration ([Resource Talks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WIZH1VMJSYA)) — and Surge Copper's $4.6 billion BC capex question kept SURG.V, with ten calls, the busiest small-cap of the week ([Resource Talks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvML35iIl2k)).

Hong Kong and China was the other dense cluster, and Dr Ng Ming Tak, Victor basically was the cluster: capital flight from Hong Kong getting harder ([淺見回顧](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IXQkE20FFa8)), Beijing re-raising 公私合營 with a 25-year retroactive look at outflows and his call that the HSI "will reflect these measures — already down ten" ([YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QDPaFmGE2ug)), the HSBC "vanished" NT$200,000 deposit as evidence a big bank is "losing the people's trust" ([YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UoPfdIK-NpE)), the HKMA's sudden disclosure of dollar assets in the Exchange Fund, and $430 billion of reserves against a trillion in planned issuance ([YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xNv8gt0ojIM)). He capped it with a defense of 22,500 on the HSI — the HKEX reforms are "tool-level" convenience, not a savior, but if US stocks hold, "at least in Q3" Hong Kong won't crack ([YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZbDIpbS3gjo)) — and a recap of the IMF's claim that the yuan's "rise" masks a 16% real devaluation ([YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0yAFQSCUJEU)). The sharpest local clash: 施永青's forecast of 20% property gains within a year and 85% by 2031, which Victor rebutted point by point ([施永青](https://www.master-insight.com/article/49024), [反駁影片](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EsLONcdNitc)), while 徐家健 used JD.com's Hong Kong "迫爆" opening — HK$35 billion-plus deployed, half-price promos — to argue this is structural creative destruction, not retail apocalypse ([Master Insight](https://www.master-insight.com/article/48974)).

The cleanest opposing lines formed around oil. The bulls had EJ Antoni arguing "we're basically replacing a negative supply shock with a positive demand shock," with chip and laptop price hikes already in the PPI ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0zIks7TeCWI)), and the MacroVoices camp expecting "additional upward pressure on prices for a while until those reserves get refilled" even as Rory Johnston asked whether the Hormuz crisis is "really over" ([MacroVoices #539](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V8hpqXTS6Q4)). The bears — Eurodollar University prominent — see the energy shock fading and pump prices back at pre-war levels "for a very long time" ([YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=21KrmQp4FWQ)).
