Equities drew a three-way split: George Gammon put 67% odds on a ≥20% S&P decline and a GFC-rival recession if it lands in 2026, yet refused a directional bet and traded the STRC/MSTR divergence instead ([Gammon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8QB9yHWVumQ)); Joseph Wang said we "could actually see new all-time highs" in the S&P before anything bad, while Nasdaq's failure to make new highs "could be the beginning of" something uglier ([Wang](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P9oxwMfNItU)); David Woo wants another 20% of downside priced and, on gold, blames higher real yields ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QjuThPhidXY)). On rates, Sam Burns sees no reason for the Fed to cut ([Burns](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2mVsHCgJcVc)) — the Macro Dirt crowd insists rates are "far too high" for an equity-funded market ([Macro Dirt](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0JS8MCvpqoE)).

As for genuine conversions, the record is thin — nearly everything in this week's 256 views is tagged neutral, which is itself the story of a hedge-everything stretch. The closest thing to a pivot is Jeff, the gold-crash caller, now selling a two-month consolidation followed by a year-end rally ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Nz7zxxJBNfo)), and AM Invest's explicitly conditional flip: no bottom call at pre-market strength, but a decisive NQ break of resistance turns them bullish mid-term, while failure risks an MNQ slide toward 28,300 ([AM Invest](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-162393012)). Even the analyst famous for calling the Bitcoin top spent his airtime looking for new equity highs by end-2027 ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dK393rKN-a4)) — less a conversion than the week's pattern: everyone holding triggers, nobody pulling them.

weekly/2026-07-05.text:
By raw count this was gold's week — seven separate calls on GC=F across 94 items and 107 extractable predictions — and the split was unusually clean. Adrian Day closed the week telling David Lin that as central banks reduce their dollar exposure, gold is the beneficiary, calling for "a meaningful revaluation in the gold price… over the next few years," with a falling dollar against other fiat as "a huge tailwind" ([Adrian Day on David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=irw_Z6o1r44)). CPM Group published twice and pulled the other way both times, first on "the real reason investors are selling" ([CPM Group, Jul 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VwM4Z2yXxD0)) and then a Friday alert that prices are "under pressure" ([CPM Group, Jul 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8b3o8gWKdeQ)). Lobo Tiggre straddled, keeping his bullish base case while conceding it's "possible that January of this year was another one of those peaks" ([Lobo Tiggre on David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4rPvgifBkwg)), and Dan Wilton's segment staged the fight outright as "50% Crash Or Violent Rally?" ([Dan Wilton on David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3er9kLfhyLY)). Oil (five calls on CL=F) had the same two-sided texture: Eurodollar University read the crude tape as "the worst possible scenario" ([Eurodollar University, Jul 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bwBj2SgdolY)) and China's demand as the biggest macro signal right now ([Eurodollar University, Jul 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tST_j1gvIYU)), while Adam Parker on MacroVoices #540 treated price as a positioning machine — $6–10 of upside from spec normalization alone, $15–20 if momentum piles in, and $10-plus of room for Brent shorts ([MacroVoices #540, Adam Parker](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nIFH7B6OQzs)). The sharpest oil clash was about transmission: a David Lin guest warned of "severe recession" once prices spike on critical reserves ([David Lin, Jul 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r3eu01cXsVE)); Day countered that past oil-spike recessions hit a net-importer America, which no longer imports what it needs ([Adrian Day](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=irw_Z6o1r44)).

The number-two battleground was memory, and it produced the week's most direct call-versus-call: The Macro Dirt Podcast called Micron's bounce "a dead cat bounce" ([Macro Dirt, Jul 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8IA0EW7aGYA)) the same week AM Invest's desk notes insisted "DRAM 不會是一跌不起的股份" and that the Nasdaq could yet rise ([AM Invest, Jul 10](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-163435342)). 何啟聰's HKEJ reporting explains why both camps watch the same tape — the leveraged memory trade is crowded, with Hong Kong and US Hynix-leverage products carrying similar risk ([何啟聰, HKEJ](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4454123/%E5%85%A7%E5%AD%98%E6%93%81%E6%93%A0%E4%BA%A4%E6%98%93+%E6%A7%93%E6%A1%BF%E5%A5%97%E6%88%A5%E5%90%84%E6%9C%89%E7%9B%A4%E7%AE%97)). Dr Ng Ming Tak had already gone bearish on SK Hynix after its ~14.6% plunge around July 2, even while noting Taiwan's index has doubled from 20,000 to 46,000 — his framing question was whether selling US stocks to buy Korean/Taiwanese AI is opportunity or a bigger trap ([Dr Ng, Jul 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r88X-YkTmcY)). Parker's episode title, "Beyond the AI Bubble," was its own stance ([MacroVoices](https://www.macrovoices.com/1540-macrovoices-540-adam-parker-beyond-the-ai-bubble-diversifying-portfolios-in-an-earnings-driven-market)), and Bitcoin drew the bleakest thought experiment of the week: quantum "Q day" compressed from "decades away" to perhaps two-and-a-half to five years, IBM's ~2030 roadmap cited as the marker, with the twist that a reversed public key means total, irreversible loss ([David Lin, Jul 8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWOFw-CUrQA)).

The deeper argument was about the dollar, and the camps genuinely opposed. The debasement side: Matthew Piepenburg ("your currency has nowhere to go but to be debased," roughly a trillion in new liquidity coming) ([Piepenburg on David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nLzZM5YW5SA)), The Jay Martin Show's "hidden machine keeping the dollar alive is breaking" — pointedly "not a story about the dollar crashing tomorrow" ([The Jay Martin Show](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V3uGNl3qreE)) — and Day again. Against them, Dr Ng's Hong Kong vantage: brokers tightening foreign-currency collateral, no dollar *liquidity* problem but a high dollar *cost*, and US indices at record highs precisely because the world is scrambling for dollars ([Dr Ng, Jul 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ku5Wyn-WpcI)). The recession chorus ran loud — Harry Dent's 90%-collapse-since-1929 call ([David Lin, Jul 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3oRNtmTE0gA)), Rick Rule's credit-collapse fear ([David Lin, Jul 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1_GGrQyesfc)), a breakdown of HSBC's banking warning arguing widening spreads can overwhelm "months or even years of extra yield" in mark-to-market losses ([Eurodollar University, Jul 8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aOYRaNIz-NY)), and a consumer double-header reading Walmart's price cuts as shoppers being "out of money" ([Eurodollar University, Jul 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMG9-0SZIXU)) and Pepsi's warning as "disinflationary signals outside the direct energy shock" with an unhealthy labor market ([Eurodollar University, Jul 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVKgqxFCXmw)). Figuring Out Money added chart work where prior ratio extremes preceded 10% S&P 500 corrections, with the JPM collar's upper bound near 8,000 in view ([Figuring Out Money](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvdwBimyqy4)). The sober counterweight was Joseph Wang's plumbing take: QE will be hard to repeat, the balance sheet trends smaller, and the dot plot may not survive to next year ([Joseph Wang](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cpxOs7TnBZ0)) — while the yen ran its own mini-theater of a July 2 surge Dr Ng read as intervention-adjacent ([Dr Ng, Jul 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vlfT3MqQSwo)), a macro CIO expecting BOJ hikes ([Monetary Matters Network](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2hJOcV53Nng)), and Eurodollar University declaring war on the carry trade ([Eurodollar University, Jul 11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q0f2BYzrkic)). Note the symmetry of contrarianism on inflation: Juliette Declercq says the consensus is "completely wrong" ([Maggie Lake Talking Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=20SxYVwZDLE)) and Maleeha Bengali says the market is "misreading inflation, oil, and the Fed" ([Real Vision](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YsR_uqKU-5s)) — two claims that everyone else is wrong, which is itself the tell of an unclear regime.

Hong Kong property was the running local story, with Dr Ng as chief skeptic: against record-luxury-transaction headlines he countered that monthly volumes around 6,000 haven't recovered, that he can't see a significant rebound in the next few years, and that prices won't necessarily crash precisely because everyone is waiting ([Dr Ng, Jul 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d4f7RQmX4ew)); he flagged shop rents down roughly 80%, from HK$1M to HK$100–200K ([Dr Ng, Jul 8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XFvEBVUS4_A)), while 施永青 read the same softness from falling primary-market transactions ([施永青, Master Insight](https://www.master-insight.com/article/49150)). Geopolitics framed the China thread: the EU's 45.3% tariff and Germany's exposure ([Dr Ng, Jul 11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aukiciXgDcQ)), a new US–Mexico–Canada arrangement said to shake Chinese supply chains ([Dr Ng, Jul 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UoIDOYpRETU)), and two America-at-250 hegemony-decline essays from 雷鼎鳴 ([Master Insight](https://www.master-insight.com/article/49136)) and 陸振球 ([Master Insight](https://www.master-insight.com/article/49168)). Prediction markets even became content about themselves: Dr Ng speculated over Polymarket odds ([Dr Ng, Jul 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ihEnGkFbPQU)) the same week 李聲揚 warned in HKEJ that such markets tempt people to manipulate "reality" itself ([李聲揚, HKEJ](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4454127/%E9%A0%90%E6%B8%AC%E5%B8%82%E5%A0%B4%E8%AA%98%E4%BA%BA%E6%93%8D%E6%8E%A7%E3%80%8C%E7%8F%BE%E5%AF%A6%E3%80%8D)). And Macro Dirt left the most falsifiable claim on the table: SpaceX "is going to trade the IPO price in two weeks" ([Macro Dirt](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8IA0EW7aGYA)) — echoed by Dr Ng's take that Xiaohongshu's IPO ambitions, snarled by a real-name complaint, prove it's "better to burst now than after listing" ([Dr Ng, Jul 11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RT3wjLMIE_8)).

On who actually changed their mind, the honest answer is that this week's record shows hedging, not reversals. Tiggre's concession that January may have been a peak — while keeping the bullish base case — is the closest thing to a live revision ([Lobo Tiggre](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4rPvgifBkwg)). CPM Group's sequencing deteriorated across the week, from explaining investor selling to a Friday pressure alert ([Jul 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VwM4Z2yXxD0), [Jul 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8b3o8gWKdeQ)), and a Resource Talks guest tied the tape to "a pretty significant decrease in gold sentiment" ([Resource Talks, Jul 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i0k8oYkeNhY)). AM Invest drifted from a Tuesday primer on judging a bear market ([AM Invest, Jul 8](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/you-peng-you-wen-163209080)) to "納指有機會再升" by Friday ([AM Invest, Jul 10](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-163435342)) — a tone shift, not a documented flip. If coverage is thin anywhere, it's here: no clean before-and-after stance change appears in this week's items, and saying otherwise would manufacture a verdict the data doesn't show.

weekly/2026-07-12.text:
Gold owned this week — gold futures drew 28 calls, more than double crude's 13, and the metal itself supplied the drama: gold testing $4,000 while silver slid below $58, with the miners taking real damage (GDX down 4%, GDXJ down 5%, SILJ down 4.5%) ([Resource Talks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YElviHEcLw0), [CPM Group](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o-FOwKtBoTA)). The debate split unusually cleanly. CPM Group's Friday line was that gold and silver had "just hit CPM's targets" and further declines may be next ([CPM Group](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=npwugboj_Pw)); Gareth Soloway allowed a flush toward $3,500 even while keeping "a lot of positivity into year end" ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxFD9ufn8wg)). Against them, The Jay Martin Show framed July 24 as "the day China reveals gold's real price," expecting a paper-physical gap like silver's last January and central banks preferring bullion to Treasuries ([The Jay Martin Show](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hHNDgjan15c)), while Collin Kettell held juniors as "the trade of a lifetime" on a long-term bull ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K7KJIVyp2SA)). Gary Wagner stood in between — a bottom forming just above $4,080, but he won't call a base until gold takes out $4,300, the 23.6% retracement ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6OJe2rdK9M)). Cutting across both camps, Real Vision's macro desk argued the metals decoupling trade "won't work" while the dollar stays strong, even as their own data "screams" inflation down and a softer dollar ([Real Vision](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G8WqFYZW08s)); Dr Ng Ming Tak added the collateral damage — gold and Korean stocks had both tumbled into bear-market territory within weeks ([Dr Ng Ming Tak, Victor](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5Yxr454gQHA)).

Oil was the week's second pillar, and the puzzle was why the war premium was so small. Ng's Sunday rundown had crude pinned under $100 through a 106-day war — paused, remarkably, for the World Cup — with the real risk sitting in war-risk insurance premia and a five-to-seven-year fix, measured against 1973's quadrupling from $3 to nearly $12 ([Dr Ng Ming Tak, Victor](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ynk0MppJxoo)); after the overnight blockade of Iran's ports he was back asking when oil breaks $126 again ([Dr Ng Ming Tak, Victor](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6mMtuFf011g)). Doomberg told Maggie Lake that "everybody got the oil spike wrong": the tightness is a "very temporary shortage of refined products," NGL supply is exploding, and Russia's rail closures are a separate matter ([Maggie Lake Talking Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0PEQQJ1FZTY)). Anas Alhajji pointed at Bab el-Mandeb as the chokepoint nobody is watching — and, in the same breath, at coffee positioning possibly graduating from short-covering rally to durable bull ([MacroVoices](https://www.macrovoices.com/1541-macrovoices-541-dr-anas-alhajji-bab-el-mandeb-the-next-oil-chokepoint-nobody-s-watching)).

The equity argument centered on whether the AI trade broke. George Gammon declared the bubble "officially popped," with the base case that the giants become part of government — "too big to fail before they actually fail" ([George Gammon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=paLy21TVecw)); Forward Guidance called the result a historic rotation ([Forward Guidance](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BW9n619JbQI)); a guest on David Lin's show put the Mag 7 top "behind us" and doubted data centers get built at Wall Street's pace — while conceding the economy may do fine in the second half ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=alCUSrfQYw4)). The counterweight: semiconductors are "gushing cash" even as NVDA's pricing power slides from extremely high to merely very high ([The Monetary Matters Network](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1PiHrb6mmo4)), and 龔成 noted the Magnificent 7 lagging the chip stocks this year while still ranking Apple the steadiest hold of the big three ([龔成](https://businessfocus.io/article/359590/龔成專欄-美股七雄-蘋果)). Levels told the stakes: Soloway's S&P bull case lives only above 7,300 ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxFD9ufn8wg)), Figuring Out Money's Nasdaq optimism "fades dramatically" under 29,250 on the NQ ([Figuring Out Money](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WG7FxB71PV4)), and 何啟聰 captured the regime in one line — HK stocks bounce on "not that bad" news while US stocks fall on "not that good" ([何啟聰](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4459314/%E6%B8%AF%E8%82%A1%E3%80%8C%E7%84%A1%E5%92%81%E5%B7%AE%E3%80%8D%E5%8D%B3%E5%BD%88+%E7%BE%8E%E8%82%A1%E3%80%8C%E7%84%A1%E5%92%81%E5%A5%BD%E3%80%8D%E5%8D%B3%E8%B7%8C)).

The sharpest macro disagreement was the direction of rates. Eurodollar University ran "CPI SHOCKS the Markets as Interest Rates PLUNGE" ([Eurodollar University](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dLPgpg9WHRg)) and Danielle DiMartino Booth asked whether the Fed's next move crushes markets ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XUj1myVJU4k)); Frank Cappelleri managed to be an equity bear and a rates bull at once — "I'm a bear. I'm bearish," and "I do think rates are going lower" ([The Macro Dirt Podcast](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=emHaEtcrAuY)). Against the disinflation read, David Lin hosted the "greatest financial bubble in history" case with a guest still insisting "we inevitably retest 5%" on yields ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qNPA6-0AmYw)), while Ng split the difference with a 40% chance of renewed hikes — reading Li Ka-shing and Buffett as signaling at least two more, with a stronger dollar pressing the yuan ([Dr Ng Ming Tak, Victor](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4R-iFL8VEOs)). That anxiety ran through the Hong Kong thread: the first takeover of a mainland private bank, Wuhan Zhongbang ([Dr Ng Ming Tak, Victor](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1HZKO42eDHs)), Li Ka-shing cashing out while the public assumes all is fine ([Dr Ng Ming Tak, Victor](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ByoMKzI5MfU)), 施永青's warning that banning capital outflows is no long-term cure ([施永青](https://www.master-insight.com/article/49238)), and Ng's Hang Seng map of a third quarter carrying "four storms" with key support near 22,000 ([Dr Ng Ming Tak, Victor](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-9Gy58Swoq4)).

As for actual conversions — the record shows none this week, and that's worth saying plainly. The closest thing to a shift is CPM Group, which moved within days from calling the drop a "one-month aberration" that reverses next month, with a midterm-election surge thesis attached, to "targets hit, further declines may be next" — a consistent bearish progression rather than a flip ([CPM Group](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o-FOwKtBoTA), [CPM Group](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=npwugboj_Pw)). Wagner's stance is deliberate non-commitment until $4,300 breaks ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6OJe2rdK9M)), and AM Invest absorbed DRAM option assignment at the $65 and $60 strikes while admitting "我也不敢肯定" on further downside, betting forced liquidation tends to precede bigger rebounds ([AM Invest](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-164086007)). The week's most honest verdict on conviction may have been Patrick Boyle's Friday title: how to be right and lose everything ([Patrick Boyle](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nJtL9MBVj48)).

weekly/2026-07-19.text:
The week's center of gravity was unambiguous: the S&P 500 drew 16 calls, more than double anything else, and nearly all of it was one argument — whether the tech-led slide is a crash or just a correction. The bear evidence kept piling up: Figuring Out Money flagged DRAM down 40% from its highs and Korea's EWY in bear-market territory, while noting 20–30% corrections are "very very common" in semis ([You've Seen This Before...](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OOLz2iSE-iY)). David Lin's channel ran a full conveyor belt of gloom — a guest billed as warning the biggest bubble in history is unwinding "17x worse" than 2000, with Oracle among the names he touched ([Biggest Bubble In History…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_XC8leI9eCY)), Clem Chambers on tech "blowing up" ([Why Tech Stocks Are Blowing Up Now](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=12GGEIB4Tco)), and Eurodollar University framing Google's own warning about the AI boom ([Google Issues a Dire Warning…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3JjkvLAvS9w)). Gold took 10 calls and crude 7, the latter fed by Goehring & Rozencwajg's commodity outlook in the wake of the US-Iran war ([Commodity Outlook…](https://blog.gorozen.com/blog/commodity-outlook-in-the-wake-of-the-us-iran-war)), a Resource Talks guest relaying crude "headed to 120" chatter ([1M Ounces of Gold in Idaho…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gXgvIhQTUI0)), and Eurodollar University's odd couple of a rising yield curve and sticky oil ([The Oil Market and Yield Curve Just Did Something Really Strange](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Rl_wTYKfiyg)).

The sharpest fault line, though, was *where* the next crisis lives — a genuine five-way split. The Monetary Matters Network argued it's not banks but insurance and private credit, citing a $10 trillion insurance balance sheet running 150% of the Fed's, while liking FSK at a 50% discount ([The Next Financial Crisis Isn't In Banks…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5qkNpMxD9kw)); Eurodollar University declared the private credit crisis "just reached Amazon" ([BREAKING…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lSLkb3BB_0M)) and by Saturday was asking whether Asian Financial Crisis 2.0 had begun, with the rupee falling sharply and India's dollar demand repeatedly exceeding private supply ([Is This the Beginning of an Asian Financial Crisis 2.0?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C4gNWY4bHYQ)). Russell Clark planted his flag elsewhere entirely — the crisis isn't in AI, it's in Treasuries ([The Next Financial Crisis Isn't In AI…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wS4MV0FbVm8)) — while Michael Howell told Real View… Real Vision that policymakers can delay market stress but not avoid it, calling GFC 2 a serious long-term risk ([Why Global Liquidity May Be Turning Against Markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HHeRDiWWprk)), and George Gammon added a "$10 trillion derivatives timebomb" for good measure ([WARNING…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YbIKPH-rK8w)). The counters mattered: Joseph Wang was breezy — "there's never going to be an implosion of the bond market… controlled by the government," and the S&P "could just be a correction, maybe down to the 200-day moving average around 7,000" ([Markets Weekly July 25, 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9MGlq_4xxjE)). Closer to home, Dr Ng Ming Tak devoted an entire segment to debunking the viral claim that banks borrowing from the HKMA signals a financial tsunami, urging viewers to watch five real warning signs instead ([小心被誤導…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kFVTy5Hg39Y)).

Gold produced its own civil war among people who nominally agree it goes higher. Mike Allen pronounced "Gold's Crash Is Over" with a new floor ([Gold's Crash Is Over](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AfX_ZBF53HQ)); Shane Williams called the same market a "brutal shakeout" while hunting the next bullish pivot ([Gold's Brutal Shakeout…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DB-0gMxwmzw)); and CPM Group stayed deliberately boring, noting silver's test of $55 and some 19.3 million ounces of August COMEX open interest that could support prices "during the next week or two" ([Gold Price WARNING…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u9jx89f0P3I)). The target ladder stretched absurdly — Joe Cavatoni at $5,000 ([…Breakout Starts](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MIRTnky8Hkg)), Steve Hanke at $6,000 ("going to take longer… but we will hit it") alongside a yes on further yen lows ([…Steve Hanke Answers](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X_D5weq9KrY)), Willem Middelkoop at $14,000 gold and $500 silver ([…'Big Reset' Is Coming](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fqY4zMtBS74)). Todd Horwitz offered the twist: he wouldn't be surprised if rates were hiked in September and gold rallied off it ([Markets Repeating 2008](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3lcf3jksM-4)). Dr Ng supplied the week's best ground-level irony — 老舖黃金 down 67% and a thousand billion in market cap gone, even as the PBoC bought gold for a 20th straight month ([大鑊❗️老舖黃金暴跌67%…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6iaBj14yT1Y)).

On AI and memory, the divides were just as clean. Steve Hou argued efficiency is repricing compute — memory is "ultimately a commodity," and he'd be "very very shocked" if memory makers' gross margins were still this high in two years ([AI Efficiency Is Repricing The Compute Market](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CJE3YWA4LLk)) — which is roughly Russell Clark's bubble thesis stated as fundamentals: generic DRAM and NAND now "priced like Nvidia chips," though Clark was openly skeptical of headlines claiming Microsoft, Meta, Google and Amazon would cut AI capex by 50% ([Russell Clark, above](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wS4MV0FbVm8)). AM Invest split the difference on DRAM itself —未必跌到那麼低, and any rebound could be sharp ([美股市況短評 (20260720)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-164345791)) — before declaring Micron the strongest stock, out of its downtrend channel ([美股市況短評 (20260724)](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-164723944)). The passive money quietly voted too: 綠角's VT breakdown shows Taiwan jumping from the #10 to #3 country weighting and Micron displacing JPMorgan in the top ten ([Vanguard Total World Stock ETF分析](https://greenhornfinancefootnote.blogspot.com/2026/07/vanguard-total-world-stock-etfvt2026.html)). In Hong Kong, Dr Ng called 25166 a fake breakout with roughly $300 billion of unlock pressure concentrated late July to mid-September ([恒指一開市扯升200點後狂瀉800點](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YRWS-k3V1Co)), and kept insisting the real direction — for markets and the CE succession alike — waits for September ([美中貿易戰暫停火…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AUvvBgTbZxY)); 何啟聰 added the political overlay, with a reported US ban on Chinese large models putting not-cheaply-valued 智譜 and MinMax at risk even as Google fell on its own capex news ([中美全面AI爭霸](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4464337/%E4%B8%AD%E7%BE%8E%E5%85%A8%E9%9D%A2AI%E7%88%AD%E9%9C%B8)).

On actual mind-changes, the record is thin, and it's worth saying so plainly — almost everything extracted this week is tagged neutral, which tells you the posture was hedging, not conviction. The closest thing to a live shift is Figuring Out Money, which moved from diagnostic calm early in the week ("very positive on the year" on Korea, corrections are normal) to, by Wednesday, "I'm not really that confident about being bullish… I need price action to prove it" ([Nothing Is As Calm As It Seems…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qoim_txtgWM)) — a tone change, not a documented flip. The week's most honest stance belonged to Horwitz, who simply refused to move: still looking for a 40–60% haircut, "I'm not changing my views… there's more coming" ([Markets Repeating 2008](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3lcf3jksM-4)). In a week of $5,000-to-$14,000 gold targets and five competing crisis locations, stubbornness was at least consistent.

weekly/2026-07-26.text:
The Federal Reserve owned this week. Ten of the digest's 129 extracted calls landed on the 10-year yield (^TNX), second only to the S&P 500's eleven, and the interview circuit circled the July FOMC and Kevin Warsh's second meeting almost obsessively. The most concrete read came from Joseph Wang's [July 2026 FOMC debrief](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l5IGlZ8TXZk): the long bond's yield "explode[d] higher during the press conference" as the market grew concerned, even while the front end and belly rallied on the Fed's refusal to hike. Around that anchor sat a remarkably skeptical chorus — Komal Sri-Kumar on [Fed-triggered "carnage"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2jxIHKDzMw0), Eurodollar University on a [shocking Fed statement](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lb7AFr5adWw), Kathryn Rooney Vera on the ["Mum's The Word" second Warsh meeting](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fMNSCF1bW0w), Danielle DiMartino Booth ["Nobody's Happy, Cracks Are Showing"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GNIFA-Mm7fI), Jim Bianco [asking whether the Fed or the market solves inflation](https://www.macrovoices.com/1543-macrovoices-543-jim-bianco-who-solves-inflation-the-fed-or-the-market), Forward Guidance on [Warsh's long-end gamble](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PW2tgckfEtA), and Chris Whalen on [Warsh's credibility problem](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BgRvK6Ug-SA) — with Dr Ng Ming Tak adding the political layer of the US president [loudly demanding rate cuts](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=APg1De0Fe-s). When that many independent voices converge on "the Fed has a long-end problem," that's the week's story.

The second live wire was AI credit. Eurodollar University's [alert on AI credit spreads blowing out "just like 2008"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KgZ2j6yI16A) came with evidence rather than vibes: a blue-chip data-center deal priced at a 7.53% yield — among the highest for that financing type — Amazon paper drawing noticeably unenthusiastic demand, and Google telling investors spending will "rise significantly again in 2027." Its companion piece argued [private credit defaults are exploding into public markets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8XK1DP46RWk), AM Invest wrote up the [AI arms race](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/ai-ju-qi-jun-bei-165157899) and separately suggested it was [time to watch SQQQ again](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/shi-shi-hou-zai-165282941). The counterweight came at the week's open from the Monetary Matters Network, arguing the [next crisis is unlikely to start in private markets because fundamentals are solid](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wM0_rexOj_w). Behind both sits the consumer: Eurodollar University heard the ["safest" companies warning the consumer is breaking](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I475w6xb8LI) — another layoff wave coming, rates down "quite a bit," oil substantially lower — while Joanne Hsu discussed [worst-ever consumer sentiment](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g_FUXW-09Yg).

The sharpest split was deflation versus debasement. A [David Lin guest](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_wm2gO04z_I) laid out the full deflation trade — gold to $3,000, oil to $40, the S&P down 10–20%, and Bitcoin where he'll "still make the call that I don't think Bitcoin's going to bottom till around $10,000." Lined up against him: Doug Casey, for whom the dollar is [being "inflated out of existence"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ca9zCylJcEA) and war in that region "a permanent feature," with an "excellent chance" the Fed is forced into yield curve control; Luke Gromen titling flatly that [YCC is the only way to stop a global bond crisis](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lS67XZP81Tc); and Tarek Saab calling for ["gold's going to 10,000"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z__R2asKZVk) with silver at 200 — with John Butler's oil-bullish take in the same [David Lin slot](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SjxmpuoQvVc) a week earlier in spirit. CPM Group split the difference twice in four days — [breakout or breakdown before August](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y44xymVXMOg), then an [August drop before the next rally](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EajzJMTVieM) — and Dr Ng cautioned retail that paper gold is a ["賭具" whose biggest risk is counterparty, not price](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5TlZuLlikYo). On equities, Real Vision's Caleb Franzen conversation argued the [bull market still has room to run](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hzD3kSL_haE), buying dips even in Bitcoin, while Figuring Out Money admitted [wanting the market to "bleed a little bit more"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6_4qbQS8XXM) before titling its August 1 video ["Nobody Knows Which Way To Feel"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ft2ftremg_4), with the monthly SPX implied move priced at 720 down / 774 up.

On mind-changers: honestly thin. Every call in this extraction arrived tagged neutral with no person-level stance history, so no verifiable reversals can be claimed. The closest is Peter Grandich [selling all his stocks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=20QLicjAfbo) and rotating elsewhere — a de-risking pivot by any reading, but the digest offers no prior-week baseline to certify it as a flip. The rest was drift, not conversion. Meanwhile the periphery produced the rawest event: Dr Ng covering [Korea's one-day 11% crash](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iqTyfm2BIzo) and leveraged ETFs becoming "automatic selling machines," echoed by 李聲揚's column on [Korean retail investors and a government caught flat-footed](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4469701/%E5%8D%97%E9%9F%93%E6%95%A3%E6%88%B6%E8%BC%B8%E6%89%93%E8%B4%8F%E8%A6%81+%E6%94%BF%E5%BA%9C%E9%80%B2%E9%80%80%E5%A4%B1%E6%93%9A), plus his two-parter on [the yen breaking a 40-year low](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q_CWAqllGas). The shape of the debate is telling: aside from the Monetary Matters bull case on private markets, almost nobody argued "all clear" — the argument is over sequencing, whether the bond market or AI credit breaks first, and whether the deflation trade or the debasement trade pays.

weekly/2026-08-02.text:
Volume-wise this was an index-and-metal week — the S&P 500 drew 22 calls and gold 18, with bitcoin a distant third at 10, out of 229 predictions and 113 market views across 73 items — but the narrative spine was Japan. The yen-carry complex ran through the feed from Sunday to Saturday: Eurodollar University opened the week asking whether the U.S. is secretly bailing out the yen ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kw_Zy_mpbyg)), David Lin's desk hosted both a "U.S. Bails Out Japan" segment with David Nicoski ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=irq5IUDIB3Q)) and Michael Gayed warning that Japan's entire market is insolvent ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W4X3h-BvyuU)), and the week closed with Chris Whalen suggesting the yen — at roughly a 50-year low — should simply be allowed to fall until it finds its level ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zchpmTKOouI)) and Joseph Wang's Markets Weekly ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aMg4pQg1hlI)). Gold supplied the price action, breaking above $4,300 on Friday coverage built around Gary Wagner, presented as the trader who called the bottom ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Et2zvu5og-I)).

Everyone agreed the yen was the problem; the week's cleanest fault line was over who was driving it. The intervention school reads recent stability as manufactured: Dr Ng Ming Tak's account of the Japanese finance minister baiting the big crocodile aboard and gradually grinding down its strength before a carry-trade unwind can detonate ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=peHwWFtH77s)), plus the "secret bailout" framing at Eurodollar University. The fundamentals school is blunter: Steve Hanke says the yen keeps falling because fundamentals point down, even as he calls the run in 30-year JGB yields overdone and expects them lower ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sIFVn-StiBk)); Wang agrees the "fundamentals of a weaker yen are just too strong" while arguing the coming hikes will have to come at "a more aggressive pace" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aMg4pQg1hlI)). The unwind segment supplied the stakes: Japan revised its debt forecast up to 187.6% of GDP, and a substantially weaker yen drags the region's currencies with it ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gdSCfWZp1oQ)).

That suspicion of official market management wasn't confined to Tokyo. Forward Guidance spent its roundup arguing Washington is suppressing volatility to keep the AI boom alive — Treasury "taking control of volatility," intervention starting preemptively with the S&P off just 2.5%, state-directed capitalism, and the worst seasonal month ahead ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L_g9MNO2tvE)), with Cem Karsan on Real Vision discussing the government's new plan for markets along similar lines ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5KrgIjDDYYg)). Notably, despite the loudest headlines being apocalyptic — Todd Horwitz warning of a "major meltdown" as rates exploded ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=95se0_3Wun0)), Jay Martin rebuilding 2008's dominoes out of AI ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zgbzdk-eqJ0)) — the numeric targets skewed bullish: Ed Yardeni is shooting for 8,250 on the S&P by year-end and 10,000 by decade-end ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aaaDQUPB4KY)); AM Invest found valuations not yet extreme enough and no event driver for a cyclical bear ([link](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/pou-xi-xiong-shi-165656202)) while calling the medium-term path higher with positions back near highs ([link](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-165738141)); and Julien Bittel and Raoul Pal argued liquidity keeps extending the business cycle unless oil breaks back above $120–130 ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dEDMg2M5Mio)). The negative payrolls print fed the bears — Eurodollar University called it a fragile labor market, not a resilient one, and noted the return of the rate-cut agenda ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZrygAEYWTqc)) — while even the Fed's direction is contested: cuts per Eurodollar University versus Whalen's idea of a quarter-point hike just to "show that we're in the game" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zchpmTKOouI)), with UWM's 49% crash as the mortgage-credit canary ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ha8BacVMsEg)).

Gold produced the week's strangest split. Marc Faber declared the first phase of "the greatest investment mania" pierced, called the fiscal situation "actually hopeless," and simultaneously argued gold should already be at $100,000, repricing only in a crisis where people and governments can't pay ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kvTo7xzwqlk)) — while Chris Vermeulen, himself expecting a 20% surge before a "global financial reset," wants 20–40% haircuts in gold and silver at that reset, with semis falling 50–85% ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7bqs3hKc-fk)). The technicians split the difference: Patrick Karim sees gold bottoming but far from its 36-month moving average, needing to build a base, with copper yet to have its move ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Bim10l6khY)). The AI-credit debate ran parallel: the Monetary Matters Network called the AI trade "dead money" but macro "pretty risk-on" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q4eRWt2Zxx8)), then relocated the beneficiaries to power stocks rather than semis, noting the memory complex down 40–50% in a month and open weights as bullish for the ecosystem but not frontier labs ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cUO79k97pJ8)); Patrick Boyle flagged the Big Tech debt Wall Street is ignoring ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NufJ7g63KSY)); and hevangel documented Thoma Bravo's ~$5 billion Pluralsight equity being wiped out, with CLO trouble only if software distress turns systemic ([link](https://hevangel.substack.com/p/private-equity-software-roll-ups)).

On mind-changing, the record is thin — most items don't state prior stances, so clean U-turns are hard to verify. The clearest documented shift is Figuring Out Money: constructive on August 6 with the S&P above the gamma flip line and bitcoin possibly popping higher, then by August 8 running "It's Time To Lock In," expecting a sell signal within the week and reading MSTR's tight $100-to-$90 range as bearish context ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OxRxUBqEdMI), [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Meo_bPlCseI)). The Monetary Matters arc — from "dead money" AI to power-stock beneficiaries — reads as a relocation of exposure, not a reversal. Otherwise bitcoin, the third-most-called ticker, drew mostly hedges: Forward Guidance called it a middle ground with no good entry either direction ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L_g9MNO2tvE)). A week of strong convictions, in short, but very few people actually moving.

weekly/2026-08-09.text:
Gold wasn't just the most-discussed asset this week — with 42 calls it out-drew the S&P 500's 26 by half again — and the discourse around it split cleanly into breakout euphoria and exhaustion suspicion. Chris Vermeulen managed to hold both positions at once, warning that the move looks like "short covering" and "FOMO buying" that "could easily sell" while simultaneously allowing that gold can rally to about $4,500 an ounce [VRIC Media](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jvVzlUayDlc). The bulls were more committed: Frank Giustra and Ian Harris declared the supercycle "not coming, it's here" [David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ua2V6X1ZqdE), one David Lin panel had the debasement trade "exploding" with a $9,000 gold target [David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7JoEdBLw_JM), Jim Rickards built his $10K case on Iran-war uncertainty — the straits still closed, US midterms two months out — calling it "one more thing that favors gold" [The Julia La Roche Show](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_9uX8_jha68), and Mark Newton told Jimmy Connor he sees "a very strong 2027 for gold and silver" [Jimmy Connor](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bkL0lcYOTMA). The macro backdrop feeding all this: headline CPI cooled to 3.4% with core at 2.5%, a 2021-era low, per AM Invest, who framed the real question as when hikes start and how big they'll be [AM Invest](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-ji-xu-kan-166536089).

Rates and bonds were the week's largest view theme, and the Fed — now under Warsh — got it from every direction. Daniel Lacalle argued the Fed is simply wrong about rates [Real Vision](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U2WwLW-m-Qc); Christopher Whalen went further, saying the Fed "has lost control," that the dollar is "unusually strong" given the fiscal situation, and that inflation has always been America's mechanism for avoiding repaying its debt [VRIC Media](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k802efbalbg) — before returning later in the week to call private credit's first big unwind, with insurance next [The Julia La Roche Show](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=400m6gYSRCE). Darius Dale's take was the Fed is trapped: deficits argue for tightening, but "on net they're essentially saying the Fed should remain on hold," long credit and stocks, not bonds [Forward Guidance](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vvMTOKRR0SE). On Warsh himself, Dave Collum cast him as Volcker 2.0 sent through the "valley of death" [VRIC Media](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ku8l-I6IU1A), while Mark Thornton called the appointment a "hit job" on gold and thinks Warsh "may prove less hawkish than expected" [VRIC Media](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=raWvZvwCtJs). Meanwhile Milton Berg, after "the worst panic in 4 years," was VERY bullish on stocks and fine with 10- and 30-year yields climbing toward 6-8% as normal fluctuation [The Monetary Matters Network](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Idj7jAOtE50), and the bond market itself got a strange 30-year auction [Eurodollar University](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hkyS0rLy1Uo) plus Patrick Boyle's warning that Japanese selling pushing yields higher would flow straight into American mortgage rates [Patrick Boyle](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yh18YXKMk3g).

The sharpest divergences were in AI and the yen. On AI, Collum's layered-bubble thesis — "an AI bubble on top of a real estate bubble on top of a general equity bubble" that will "break down VERY quickly" [VRIC Media](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ku8l-I6IU1A) — and Norway's wealth fund preparing for an AI crash, on the logic that "passive confidence is not a risk management strategy" [Eurodollar University](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=votJ0sjvFmI), ran straight into Raoul Pal and Blue Macellari's counter: Anthropic is "the largest, fastest scaling of revenues in any company in human history," with intelligence-output efficiency doubling every five months [Raoul Pal The Journey Man](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q2TAHZIBpdE). Thomas Hayes took the middle path — not wipeout but rotation, into Disney and even Diageo, because "people are drinking less, they're drinking better" [David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8kFLx1lEzU0); George Gammon, watching BlackRock and Nvidia together, just found it "dangerous" [George Gammon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gb5hBqdmnUI). The yen debate was nearly unanimous in its pessimism: after joint US-Japan intervention moved the pair from 161 to ~156 before drifting back above 158 [何啟聰](https://www1.hkej.com/dailynews/investment/article/4479275/%E7%95%99%E7%B5%A6%E4%B8%8B%E4%B8%80%E4%BB%A3+%E8%B2%B7%E7%BE%8E%E5%82%B5%E9%82%84%E6%98%AFSpaceX+%3F), Eurodollar University observed that short sellers "retreated, but that didn't change anything, which is why the yen went right back down," with a 160 breach forcing three obvious choices and a rushed BOJ hike risking JGB destabilization [Eurodollar University](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QNDwry7_6C4); Boyle's verdict — intervention "buys you a few days, a week maybe" — and Jay Martin tied it to the S&P's worst day in two years off "one small tap in Tokyo" [The Jay Martin Show](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_i-MswQoweE).

On stance changes, the evidence is subtler than outright flips but real: the veteran trader on David Lin's show said "Now I'm getting back into gold," an implicit admission he'd been out during the run [David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kmOsTT2grwk), and Figuring Out Money flagged he'll "probably get back into my crypto position" on strength [Figuring Out Money](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UFACPcXvCqc) — a notably brave re-entry given Michael Howell, the week's most ubiquitous voice across three appearances, put crypto "under a cloud" as liquidity turns and positioned structurally dollar-bull and defensively on financial assets [MacroVoices](https://www.macrovoices.com/1545-macrovoices-545-michael-howell-warsh-vs-the-markets), [The Julia La Roche Show](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FPB4Z1KhE3s), though even Howell split himself: structurally bullish gold, tactically near a correction inflection [Macro Voices](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c06eQWQljXo). The metals camp's own internal fight — Rick Rule arguing copper has "WAY more potential than gold," that there isn't "enough euphoria in the gold stocks yet," and that near-term rising rates are "hard on the precious metals" [VRIC Media](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mfhDfeJuY6Y), against Ian Harris's smart-money-copper-and-Colombia thesis [VRIC Media](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5ql9wm7AQs8) — rounded out a week where, honestly, almost nobody planted a flag: 281 views tagged and most hedged, the discourse less about calling the top than about positioning for whichever way the turn comes.

weekly/2026-08-16.text:
With 395 predictions and 397 market views logged from 47 voices, the week's center of gravity was unmistakable: rates and bonds (55 views), specifically the Treasury's bond buyback and whether it amounts to yield-curve control in all but name. Eurodollar University set the skeptical tone on August 19, calling the program "a pitiful $2 billion, two and a half billion when you include the tips" and wondering how the yield curve gets controlled "with just a couple billion extra buybacks" — a day after flagging the 30-year's surge, which MacroVoices' desk pegged near 5.30% before the reversal. By August 20 David Lin was hosting panels on why the Treasury had doubled the buybacks, and Joseph Wang's Sunday verdict was that the intervention "definitely buys time" but is "ultimately temporary," noting there's "no limit to this — he could just really buy it all if he really wanted to." Luke Gromen framed the trap most crisply: 10-year yields "have to go way higher," yet Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (transcribed as "Besson") won't let them clear roughly 4.7–4.8% — so either the dollar weakens a lot or yields get forced down, and "all roads lead to gold." Chris Whalen asked the darker question — when is the next Treasury-market crisis, and how much paper must the Fed absorb — while michaelwgreen supplied the structural backstory across three posts: Japan's exit shrinks the automatic bid for Treasuries, the marginal buyer sets the price, and the bond sleeve of American retirement saving has become "a private-sector successor to QE, minus the discretion" ([Anchors Aweigh, My Boys](https://www.yesigiveafig.com/p/anchors-aweigh-my-boys)).

The currency side of the same trade drew heavy fire too — the yen racked up 13 calls, the dollar index 10. Weston Nakamura argued dollar-yen "would have already hit 200 if not for these kind of yen intervention caps," and that over the long term you'll "see dollar yen 200," adding that Japan's broken inflationary mindset is itself "unprecedented." Whalen agreed the yen "is going to continue to weaken," and characterized the dollar as sought after as "a means of exchange, not a store of value." [Darius Dale](../People/darius-dale.md) threaded the middle: the move "has neutralized the prior bull market" in the dollar, but "does that make me an outright bear? Probably not" ([MacroVoices #546](https://www.macrovoices.com/1546-macrovoices-546-darius-dale-darius-dale-for-potus-2028)), while [Peter Boockvar](../People/peter-boockvar.md) stayed with the dollar "ultimately" ending lower ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UrCuK2K8mAU)). George Gammon was the designated deflator of the genre, putting reserve-currency loss "at the very least 25 years and probably a lot longer." Gold, meanwhile, was the release valve everyone kept citing — Dale watching for "legitimate progress back to those April highs near 4,800," Gromen's "all roads," and a 14-call week on GC=F.

The ^GSPC split was the sharpest of the week, with 26 calls. The bull case had echelons: Erik of YWR told Maggie Lake that the $400 EPS he expected for 2028 "is happening in 2027," and "put a 25 times on it and that's S&P 10,000 — one way or the other, we're going to 10,000," because government, companies and banks are all spending ([For The Record](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wV4dksg_XjE)). [Chris Vermeulen](../People/chris-vermeulen.md) called the "next leg higher started" after support held ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=81UzjvXn2no)), the MacroVoices desk gave Nvidia solid odds of a beat-and-raise, and Dale argued "the bond market's already beat you to the task forces... stocks will beat you to the task force." Against that, Harry Dent offered the maximal bear case — "the biggest reversal in history... bigger than '29 to '32," a good time to be "as conservative as you can be," with tech to be bought again only "when they're down the most in history" ([Julia La Roche](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TInyOyKDOgI)). The credit complicates the equity story: [Robin Wigglesworth](../People/robin-wigglesworth.md) sees $1.5 trillion of hidden debt behind the AI boom, public BDCs going to "30 cents or 40 cents of net asset value" in a crisis, and "a bad default cycle" that's "started already" ([Monetary Matters](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kZXjQZWUHH0)); Patrick Boyle cited Fitch's record July private-credit default rate, one large fund with 7% of its portfolio distressed, and the pattern that manias fade "around the fifth year — we're currently in year three" ([Patrick Boyle](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wTiYaWFP59Q)); and Eurodollar University flagged Nvidia's own collateral clauses as the gray-swan X-factor ([Eurodollar University](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O450x8yyZ-k)). On the panel consensus, [Gareth Soloway](../People/gareth-soloway.md) put the pivot cleanly: 5% on the 10-year is the number — below it, the game of chicken continues ([David Lin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SWsGPoxqcR0)).

Beneath the macro noise, the speculative tail was busy. CoTec (CTH.V, 13 calls) got a full Rule Investment Media pitch — pellet-quality results "in the next few days," pig iron at "roughly 300 to 350" cost, and an admission no raise happens at the $2.5B pre-tax valuation, only "a significant discount" ([Rule Investment Media](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)). Silvercorp (SVM, 11 calls) called its China "safety shutdown... annoying" with no hard date for GC, while noting the register has flipped to roughly 60/40 institutional with quant funds circling ([Resource Talks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ialp-FjJiRI)); Justin Huhn had NXE with hyperscalers and BHP "sniffing around" ([VRIC Media](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eDPDUFOi6Uw)). The disagreements ledger also flagged long Treasuries as a trade — one camp noting TLT rose 40% in the 2008 crash and could "literally double" in a serious downturn, the other treating a break toward 80 as a sell trigger — and a purely conditional housing-index debate hinging on whether the long end gets taken down.

On mind-changing, the week was thin, and it's worth saying plainly: nearly every extracted view was tagged neutral, and nobody issued a full reversal. The closest thing was Dale's dollar recalibration, retiring his prior bull-market read without going bear. Vermeulen's arc ran within a single interview — waiting for the post-August 21 window before fully committing to the new leg higher. And AM Invest documented a genuine intraweek adjustment: trimming positions on August 18 ("減倉了，沒有大礙"), conceding the earlier conservative option strikes reflected a view that US stocks "有機會下跌一點," then by August 21 writing that a recovery "有機會再創新高" ([Aug 18](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/jian-cang-liao-167026322); [Aug 21](https://www.patreon.com/aminvest/posts/mei-gu-shi-kuang-167280931)). Otherwise this was a week of conviction expressed almost entirely in conditionals — if the buyback fails, if 5% breaks, if the 21st confirms.

weekly/2026-08-23.text:
Gold owned the week. Out of 86 items and 46 voices, GC=F drew 46 calls — comfortably the most-discussed instrument, ahead of Bitcoin (28) and GoGold (26) — and the target ladder kept ratcheting higher. Nomi Prins made the case for $6,000 gold on a physical market "very close to a deficit," citing a Morgan Stanley estimate of a 600,000-ton copper deficit this year while admitting she "wouldn't necessarily buy copper" even expecting higher prices (). Don Durrett floated $8,000 gold and $200 silver, favoring producers over early-stage explorers at this phase of the bull market (), Ted Oakley called gold still cheap at $4,600 (), Darius Dale is watching for a return to the April highs near $4,800 (), and CPM Group pinned the metal in a $3,800–4,300 band (). The miners rode the same tide: GoGold management pitched the Los Ricos North permits as a "more than doubling" catalyst in a "tremendous bull market" (), and Agnico's $57 million investment in the RDS.V Quebec project gave the juniors their headline (). The other center of gravity was fiscal — Treasury's $1 trillion buyback/warchest — which Danny Moses framed as outright crisis ("$2 trillion deficit, debt over 40 trillion. We need to keep interest costs low and we'll do anything") (), Todd Horwitz gamed the cross-asset fallout (), and Dr Ng asked plainly whether the long-bond buyback is QE in disguise (). Rates-and-bonds was the biggest view theme at 51 entries.

The sharpest fault line ran between the "it's already breaking" camp and the "the market says otherwise" camp. Michael Oliver's trigger is a bond and financial-sector crisis that sends gold soaring (). Against that, Eurodollar University audited the Ray Dalio debt warning and found markets unbothered — TIPS and inflation swaps "not signaling an uncontrolled monetary response," term-premium estimates contained, and "if any of that changes, we will know about it" (). The Macro Dirt podcast built an entire episode on the calm: hiking angers Trump, cutting steepens the curve, but for now bond volatility sits "in the gutter" (), which Forward Guidance echoed alongside oil vol near its year-to-date lows (). Daniel Lacalle split the difference — Trump won't annihilate the system and a BRICS currency is "going to the past," though every fiat currency is "worsening relative to gold" (). Inside that, a genuine hawk-dove collision: Real Vision flagged three same-direction dissents for a rate hike at the last FOMC and a policymaker's "I stand ready to raise rates" as a possible fourth (), while Eurodollar University's consumer-side reading — employment down over 900,000, full-time jobs falling — concluded the long end faces "the exact opposite" of an inflation shock (). Collin Martin split the baby: the dire scenario is a risk, but "not in the here and now," with political pressure on the Fed very real ().

The AI-bubble argument ran on parallel tracks. Dr Ng mined the dot-com analogy — Cisco, the world's priciest company in 1999, fell 90% and only reclaimed that high last year; Amazon fell just as hard before 40x-ing — while conceding in the same video that big-tech earnings and cash flows remain strong (). 胡孟青 tallied the excess: HTX research says diffusion is early but capex and valuations are ahead, the five giants' 2026 AI capex is pegged near US$75.5 billion (up ~80% year-on-year), Goldman sees ~US$5.3 trillion of big-tech capex through 2030, and BofAML has called it a "super bubble" (). Warren Pies expects software to take the first pain in the IPO cycle and likes "energy as diversifier" (), Macro Dirt shrugged that Nvidia earnings would be a "non-event" (), and Forward Guidance doubted Anthropic's moat is durable (). Bitcoin split the same way: Jason Yanowitz rode the debasement trade toward $200,000, with Reuters tying the move to a softer dollar (), and Todd Horwitz saw another $10,000 before a pullback (), but Ben Cowen warned of "at least one more scare in Q4" and noted a true alt season would require a parabolic Bitcoin (). On tariffs, Matt Gertken argued the 50% move only unites Canadians behind Mark Carney, who won't touch critical minerals or fuel (), while The Plain Bagel documented the deal falling apart, with Canada delaying retaliation to September 8 amid sluggish GDP ().

Mind-changes were thin — worth saying outright. The clearest update came from CPM Group, whose standing view had gold range-bound through August and who now warn of "another wave of investor buying," their 51-year veteran calling current volumes the biggest he has ever seen (). Jeff Christian is a trim, not a flip: still bullish but taking profits off to reposition, on inflation staying above 3% and possibly pushing 4–5% (). Cowen spent part of his slot re-litigating the "four-year cycle is dead" argument the market already disproved (). AM Invest showed patience rather than reversal — Alibaba's earnings improved but sell pressure remains heavy, so buy back only on a resumed uptrend or a panic drop (), and by Thursday they noted positions nearing record highs and advised against attacking too early (). Beyond that, the record skews heavily neutral and hedged: the "Big Short" guest on David Lin's show offered "literally no idea" on both Bitcoin and gold (), and the Resource Talks crew repeated its mantra — "nobody out there has any special predicting abilities" — across multiple mining interviews ().

The shape of the debate, then, is a broad consensus that something in the fiscal-rates complex eventually breaks, set against positioning and volatility signals saying nothing is breaking yet — which is why gold targets ratchet while bond vol sits in the gutter. The skeptics' counterweight came largely from the Hong Kong side: in a recap on the $40-trillion debt question, Dr Ng argued the US won't collapse within a decade and the dollar won't fall from 99 toward 85 under Trump (); he read Hong Kong's rising deposits despite emigration as the city remaining a "savings pool" () and saw the renminbi's fastest appreciation leg done, settling into 6.6–6.98 (). 施永青 made the boldest structural call of the week — that the mainland should halt land sales entirely, since cheap auctions drag down home prices and household balance sheets alike (). A week that talked constantly about breakage while, in positioning terms, betting on none.

study/cpm-group/topic/fed-policy-interes.text:
The spine of this archive is a single recycled thesis: that gold's relationship to interest rates is the "most complicated and important" one, laid out in January 2021 ([Interest Rates: Gold's Most Complicated and Important Rel…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y39eAhDCdI4)), hardened into [Why Interest Rates Won't Hurt Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RiRYdTEmEpw) that August, and generalized by October 5, 2021 into [Gold and Silver Are Adjusting To A New Monetary Policy Regime](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0obgfA3eB0Q). From there the cadence turns industrial: six titles in the ten weeks between October 5 and December 14, 2021 ([one](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0obgfA3eB0Q), [two](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5o9BHtiXJ_M), [three](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AbmjEzDxiGY), [four](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ScFb681FrjA), [five](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LqwpX2Qgck4), [six](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L_igFqCmfZI)), then two four days apart in January 2022 as markets digested Fed minutes ([Jan 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4zoD4yd1V_4), [Jan 11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3iijoftbjEk)), then three in three weeks in June 2022 ([Jun 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tbpqSM5puYU), [Jun 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L-R8CIE_qME), [Jun 24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=10zL22_Y39s)). These are event-triggered re-runs — each Fed meeting or inflation print resets the numbers, never the frame. Thirteen of the listed titles fall in 2022 alone.

Three arguments carry the reuse. The low-base claim: on March 7, 2022, with inflation at 7% and talk of 14%, "now it's from zero percent to two percent" ([The Rise Of Gold: Betting Against the Fed](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pHw0NWad6U0)); by July 29, 2022 it is "from 0 to 2.5 in the fed funds rate," yet still below pre-2006 levels. The Fed-versus-market thread is the most durable: named in a [June 3, 2022 title](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tbpqSM5puYU), formalized November 11, 2022 with the CME FedWatch path (hikes to roughly 4.75% by March, a 2023 plateau, cuts from November 2023), and sharpened on March 14, 2023, when CPM stuck with 25bp hikes in March and May while post-SVB markets flipped to easing. It returns May 16, 2023 — "The Disconnect between how the Federal Reserve says they will raise interest rates, and the market perception…" — and runs through 2024: January 5, only 2–3 cuts (~75bp) against market hopes of six; August 13, with core PPI at 3.3% ex food and energy, "there's been so much enthusiasm and expectation that the Fed will definitely cut interest rates in September…". Meanwhile the inflation-gold explainer recycles on [Oct 15, 2021](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5o9BHtiXJ_M), [Aug 19, 2022](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kYkxdMHkAG0), and [Feb 14, 2023's "It's Not So Simple"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aiGDIKClJT8); [How Interest Rates May Affect Gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=im271XZWR18) in May 2022 is the same video family as January and August 2021.

The declared turning points are datable because the author flags them. On December 7, 2021 — between the [Dec 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LqwpX2Qgck4) and [Dec 14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L_igFqCmfZI) videos on gold's odd softness amid rising inflation and oil — the Fed "announced that given stronger and more persistent inflation than perhaps some of them thought unexpected" an earlier bond-purchase exit, yet "since the feds started talking about tapering uh 10-year bond yields have actually come down." On March 7, 2022: "we need to withdraw monetary accommodation we need to buy fewer bonds in our portfolio." On July 29, 2022, two changes at once: "inflation rates are still very high but the rate of increase is declining," and "we've probably seen the bulk of the increases in interest rates now already." September 23, 2022 widens the lens — "there are recessionary conditions present in Europe and in the United States and Japan and the UK" — and November 11, 2022 completes the arc: "there are signs of peaking inflation there are signs that we are potentially moving toward peaking interest rates." The 2024 entries are an echo of that peak call: "the decline will be slower than it has been over the last 18 months," with "slightly higher inflation numbers coming in in Germany the EU and the UK over the past month."

Genuinely new material is scarcer and easy to date. War enters between February 22 and March 7, 2022 ([Part 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jk5ZPSXui3Y), [invasion](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pHw0NWad6U0), [war-and-rates](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nZrR3D_TfDc)); SVB resets market expectations in March 2023; the [gold-standard/FedNow piece](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y6LEB_R7gA0) of August 4, 2023 is a one-off structural detour; May 17, 2024 adds cross-asset breadth (record US stocks, ~45bp off 10-year corporate yields, a COMEX copper squeeze). One entry carries the only non-recurring flag in the deep-read record: November 4, 2025, where "the Fed signaled that it was growing increasingly concerned about economic weakness" after Jackson Hole, and the gold rally "came off very sharply two weeks ago and it's been treading water this week, waiting for a direction."

As for the shape of the reuse: it tracks the drama. Sparse before 2021 — a lone dollar title from June 2016, the fourth in some earlier series ([How Strong is the US Dollar 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QSBDIUoKWV0)), a pair in 2020 ([All Roads Lead To Gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNkMV4Je9Fk), [Gold and the Dollar Can Rise Together](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EdlOqZEF_xA)) — then weekly-to-biweekly through the tightening shock, quarterly in 2023 ([Feb](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aiGDIKClJT8), [Apr](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oH_UVuotrnE), [Aug](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y6LEB_R7gA0), [Sep](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9u03GgrWg1A)), semiannual through 2024, then a fifteen-month silence before November 2025. Note the thin patch honestly: the listed title run stops at [September 5, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9u03GgrWg1A) while deep reads continue to late 2025, so title-level cadence after 2023 can't be audited here. The through-line is striking: for nearly three years every entry assumed markets were too dovish relative to the Fed — until the dovish turn finally came from the Fed itself, leaving the franchise's core argument, like the gold price it tracks, "waiting for a direction."

person/aiden.text:
Aiden is one of the thinnest files in this corpus — no listed role, no firm affiliation, and no track record of directional calls on either side of the ledger. What the record does capture, dated August 18, 2026, is a single neutral-toned contribution to a discussion of a new copper-gold discovery in Australia, where he reaches back to market history for context: a crash in the copper markets at the end of the 1990s that he recalls as producing "the lowest copper price since the Great Depression" ([New Copper-Gold Discovery in Australia, But Is There Enough…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lXeJq-yjICU)). The transcript fragment is conversational and garbled in places, but the substance is clear — he was supplying historical frame, not a verdict.

That lone entry shapes the honest portrait: the stance mix reads zero bullish, zero bearish, one neutral, and that is not a hedge but simply all there is. Aiden, as logged, is a context-setter rather than a caller — the kind of voice who anchors a debate about whether a copper-gold find matters by reminding listeners where copper has been before. It would be premature to call that a style or a philosophy off one quote, and this page does not pretend otherwise. If future digests surface actual positions, they should be added and this framing revised; for now, the fair summary is one historical aside on copper and nothing directional on record.

person/bp-silver-executive.text:
This is a profile that can only be drawn in pencil. The subject is an executive at BP Silver, a silver mining and exploration company working in Bolivia, who appears in the source record exactly once: an interview or podcast appearance dated August 19, 2026, framed around a high-grade silver discovery in Bolivia ([High-Grade Silver Discovery in Bolivia, But Is There Enough…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fxlw0GyW6d8)). No name, no title, no career history survives in the material — just the role and the company — so everything below rests on a single conversation.

What the executive argues for is a two-track Bolivian story. The main project — rendered as "Consunia" or "Cassuno" in the transcript, with the obvious caveat that these are likely transcription artifacts rather than verified property names — is awaiting an award or concession decision, and the executive's argument is notable for what it doesn't depend on: even if the award landed today, they say, the work program there would stand "clearly just based on drill results" ([High-Grade Silver Discovery in Bolivia, But Is There Enough…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fxlw0GyW6d8)). In other words, the case for the flagship is geology-first, with the administrative timeline treated as separable from the technical one. The second project — tagged in the material as TTD, with "Tyrion" and "Terry" appearing as alternate renderings — sits lower on the sequence: drilling there "would be later, probably next year" ([High-Grade Silver Discovery in Bolivia, But Is There Enough…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fxlw0GyW6d8)).

The concrete commitments, such as they are, are calendar-based rather than price-based. As of that August 2026 appearance, the stated aim is to be actively working the second property "as we get into 2027" ([High-Grade Silver Discovery in Bolivia, But Is There Enough…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fxlw0GyW6d8)) — a 12-to-18-month operational runway that investors can actually check the company against, which is more than most explorers offer in passing podcast remarks. On the metal itself, there is no call to score. The only silver-price commentary on record is a throwaway — "obviously a healthy silver price helps as well" ([High-Grade Silver Discovery in Bolivia, But Is There Enough…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fxlw0GyW6d8)) — which acknowledges a tailwind without predicting one.

As for how the views have moved: they haven't, or at least the record can't show it. All four coded stances from this person are neutral, all from the same date, all from the same conversation. That's not hedging so much as an artifact of thin coverage — one snapshot of a company insider talking about their own properties, where measured neutrality is the natural register. Anyone picking up this page hoping for a documented evolution of views, a bold metal call, or even a name to attach to the argument will need to wait for a second source.

person/bernardo-azevedo.text:
Bernardo Azevedo is an investor and commentator working the natural-resources beat, with a focus on junior mining and precious-metals exploration companies. His footprint in this corpus is a single appearance: a Resource Talks interview logged 24 August 2026, on the episode "[Very High-Grade Rare Earths, But Can They Get the Funding? …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iSYYQqlo7qI)", where per the corpus summary he walked through the outlook for Breaker Resources (ASX: BRE), an ASX-listed gold developer — the usual development gauntlet of scoping, prefeasibility and feasibility studies plus permitting, and the possibility that further exploration success re-rates the stock over a 12–24 month horizon.

The substance of his commentary sits in scale, metallurgy and product streams rather than ratings. person/eurodollar-university-guest-jeff.text:
Jeff Snider is an American macro analyst whose reputation rests on one stubborn thesis: the global economy doesn't run on the money central banks print — it runs on the offshore dollar-funding network known as the eurodollar system, and when that system tightens, you get structural dollar shortages, deflationary pressure and low growth no matter how much the Fed "prints." He leads macro research at Alhambra Investments and founded Eurodollar University, the research and education platform behind the podcasts and video analysis where he works through household-survey labor data, full-time versus part-time employment, Treasury yields, private credit, oil and bitcoin. The posture is deliberately contrarian to the mainstream "money-printing means inflation" narrative, and his track record in this corpus reflects it: 5 bullish, 6 bearish and 17 neutral tags — far more signal-interpreter than directional tipster.

His sharpest dated call came on June 14, 2026, in [Now That Iran Is Done, The Real Oil Crisis Begins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DTh7cPI8z3E). Against the reflex that a supply shock must be inflationary, he argued the opposite: "Energy shocks are not inflationary. They end up destroying demand, especially for an economy that's weak to begin with... They don't end in inflation." His evidence was physical, not financial — "Chinese imports of petroleum absolutely crashed... physical crude imports were down by 3% in March, 20% in April, and 29% in May." He mapped a path rather than shouting a price: the front of the curve would "come down and then bounce," traders would rediscover that "the fundamental value is what we saw in December, not" April's spike, and that's "how you get to $50 a barrel" — while conceding prices weren't snapping straight back down, with "how long they take" the open question.

A week later, on June 21, came [Swiss Bond Market Just Gave A Dire Warning to the World](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c2LzapdRuT4), where he flagged that "Swiss bond rates are almost back at zero all over again. The critical two-year instrument yielding just a couple of basis points," and that "Chinese rates are similarly ultra and that curve is bull steepening." The stance tracker duly flips both his oil and Chinese-equities views from bearish to bullish on that date — though the supporting quote is about bonds, not barrels, and it arrives under a "dire warning" headline. That tension is worth flagging rather than smoothing over: whatever the tags encode, in Snider's framework the bond market is the tell, and collapsing short-end yields across two major markets are a deflationary signal he treats as dependable — bullish in the sense of conviction about what bonds are saying, not optimism about growth.

By June 27, in [Bitcoin And BlackRock Just Did Something VERY Strange](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=biyCX7UYAfQ), his attention had shifted to late-cycle plumbing. He dismissed a causal link between bitcoin and BlackRock's moves — "it's not Bitcoin leading to BlackRock or BlackRock leading to Bitcoin. It's these common late cycle stage behaviors that are acting on both" — and zeroed in on private-credit stress: "Apollo's fund is now cash flow negative. They have more redemption requests. They blocked off the redemption requests," while stock investors treat BlackRock as "one of the biggest examples of a private credit manager" and head for the exits. He also pushed back on the "strong and resilient" US economy narrative and offered the Hang Seng as his gauge — rising, "a pretty dependable" reflationary signal; falling, the opposite.

One honest caveat: every citation here comes from a two-week window in June 2026 — three episodes. Within it, the most durable positions are the June 14 demand-destruction oil argument and the June 21 short-end yield warning; the rest is his eurodollar framework applied to headlines. The corpus is simply too thin to chart a longer evolution of his views — a limitation of the record, not of the analyst.

person/julian-treger.text:
Julian Treger is a natural resources financier and mining company executive, best captured in this corpus as the voice of CoTec Holdings — theTSX-V-listed resources holding vehicle (CTH.V, with a related CTE.V entry) whose fortunes he was laying out in detail on the "Pitch Rick Ep #2" interview of August 19, 2026. He speaks in the register of an operator-promoter rather than an outside commentator: capital structures, hub-by-hub financing schedules, and spin-off mechanics, not directional market calls.

What he argues for, in that single appearance, is a value-unlock thesis built in stages. He described Mag Iron raising capital at a $550 million internal valuation via a rights issue, with CoTec holding 17% of it, and Hypermag being taken to market for funding on a hub-by-hub basis, with the first hub valued at "several hundred" million ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)). The endgame he sketched is an IPO raising ideally $200 million of equity, spinning off the bulk of CoTec's stake to CoTec shareholders ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)), backed by roughly $100–120 million of project finance debt being negotiated with two commercial banks and XM ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)). On the operating side, he put the concentrator reformat and plant restart at $350 million — $200 million debt, $150 million equity — with domestic pig iron production costs of roughly $300–350 against a $500–550 pig iron price ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)), and flagged an 18-month runway before revenues start at the end of the following year or the beginning of 2028 ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)).

Notably, he tempers his own story. He pointed to the gap between a $2 million figure and roughly $100 million of NPV before beneficiation as an indication of the value he thinks is being missed ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)), yet conceded outright that any raise won't come near the $2.5 billion pre-tax valuation — "a significant discount to that" ([Pitch Rick Ep #2 - CoTec Holdings Corp.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i25DJxYcDGw)). That mix of pitch and candor is the most distinctive thing the record shows about him.

On the question of how his views have moved: the digest simply doesn't show movement. Everything traces to the same August 2026 interview, all fifteen stance datapoints are neutral, and there are no bullish or bearish calls on record — his "strongest calls" are capital plans and timelines rather than ratings. Coverage this thin means any portrait of Treger as a market forecaster would be manufactured; what the corpus supports is a picture of a financier mid-pitch, walking through a multi-year funding and spin-off roadmap for CoTec's iron assets.

person/macro-voices-guest-eric.text:
