One River built its name on two fronts simultaneously: a set of macro hedge funds run in the discretionary global-macro tradition, and an unusually early institutional allocation to bitcoin at a time when most allocators still treated crypto as untouchable. The vehicle that made him a household name among macro readers, though, is the weekly investor commentary that went out under his name — widely read, widely forwarded, and the reason his voice travels well beyond One River's client base.

Thematically, Peters operates at the junction of liquidity, inflation, monetary policy, and bitcoin, and his media footprint reflects it: he has appeared on Macro Voices at least three times as an interview guest, alongside regular turns on Real Vision and Bloomberg's Odd Lots. The intellectually interesting thing about his positioning in the debate is that he argues for bitcoin from inside the institutional macro establishment rather than against it — a Caxton-trained macro manager making the case that digital assets belong in serious portfolios, which carried more weight with pension CIOs than crypto-native advocacy ever did. That bridging role, more than any single trade, is what the record here emphasizes.

person/mark-skousen.text:
Mark Skousen is one of the more recognizable voices of the Austrian school — a longtime economics writer and author (best known for *The Making of Modern Economics*), the editor of the *Forecasts & Strategies* investment letter since 1980, and the founder of the annual FreedomFest gathering. Within this corpus, though, his footprint is narrow: everything on file comes from a single dated appearance, a YouTube discussion titled [The Market’s $40T Question: Can Treasury Keep Yields Under …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SWsGPoxqcR0) from August 22, 2026.

That one appearance is nonetheless flavorful. Skousen's signature line from it is a piece of market fatalism with teeth: the stock market will "never commit suicide, but it can be murdered" — his argument being that markets don't kill themselves, bad fiscal policy does. He grounds that in the numbers, noting the United States is "approaching $40 trillion on our national debt" and framing the whole discussion around whether the Treasury can keep yields contained under that weight ([The Market’s $40T Question: Can Treasury Keep Yields Under …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SWsGPoxqcR0)).

His most concrete positioning in the same session — and the closest thing to a call in the record — is a haven ranking. "There's no place to hide except to go to gold or go to the Bitcoin," he said, before answering his own question: "But probably gold," because central banks are buying the metal "hand over fist" ([The Market’s $40T Question: Can Treasury Keep Yields Under …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SWsGPoxqcR0)). Worth flagging: the corpus tags all four of his topic stances as neutral, but the actual language contains a clear preference ordering — gold over crypto, driven by official-sector demand. The neutral label understates what he actually said.

As for movement over time: the timelines simply don't show any. Every dated entry in the file sits on August 22, 2026, drawn from the same source, so there is no before-and-after to narrate. What we have is a single snapshot — a debt-hawk who thinks markets get murdered by fiscal profligacy and would rather own gold than Bitcoin while central banks stack it. A fuller portrait of how his views have evolved (or hardened) will have to wait for more coverage.

person/mike-green.text:
Mike Green is a portfolio manager and market strategist whose name has become shorthand for one argument: the rise of passive index investing is quietly rewiring how markets price, volatility behaves, and capital gets allocated. After a career in macro-oriented hedge funds, he served as Chief Strategist at Simplify Asset Management and later took the same title at Logica Capital Advisers, and he has become a fixture on macro and investing podcasts — the kind of guest summoned whenever the debate turns to market structure rather than next quarter's earnings.

His signature claim is mechanical rather than mystical: retirement money is being funneled into indices on autopilot, and that flow — indifferent to fundamentals — reshapes valuation and volatility in ways most investors haven't priced in. He put a number on it in the Quarterly Market & Strategy Update from July 2026, estimating that "somewhere in the neighborhood of 95 cents of every retirement dollar in the United States flowing through a 401k program is going into passive indice[s]" ([Quarterly Market & Strategy Update - July 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RVKdhYU4nVU)). Around that core thesis, his discussion ranges across equity market dynamics, retirement-fund flows, demographics, monetary and fiscal policy, and even the implications of Japanese policy — a reminder that he treats passive flows as one strand in a larger structural story rather than a standalone bear case.

On direction, the record here is deliberately thin. His single dated stance on the S&P 500 is neutral, logged with that same July 2026 update, and the stance mix shows zero bullish and zero bearish calls alongside it — so there is no timeline of conviction shifts to chart, and it would be dishonest to manufacture one. That neutrality is arguably the tell: Green's framework is about plumbing, not prophecy. A man who argues that 95 cents of every retirement dollar moves on schedule rather than on judgment is describing a slow structural force, not issuing a market call — and in this corpus, at least, he has largely resisted turning his structural critique into a directional bet.

person/mohamed-cisse.text:
Mohamed Cisse is a mining and exploration executive with a West Africa focus, though the corpus captures him in exactly one setting: an August 12, 2026 video interview pointedly titled [3M Ounces of Gold in DR Congo, But is it Really Economic? |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j_t-RAAdzA8). His specific role at the company tagged under AGC.CN isn't recorded here, and that gap matters — this is a one-source portrait built from a single dated appearance, so treat it as a snapshot, not a track record.

What the snapshot shows is a development-stage pragmatist. Speaking about the roughly three-million-ounce Congolese gold deposit, Cisse laid out a stepwise plan: expand the resource "very quickly because we see a lot of quick wins to increase the resource" [3M Ounces of Gold in DR Congo, But is it Really Economic? |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j_t-RAAdzA8), then get the project "to a reasonable size" before starting the PE process [3M Ounces of Gold in DR Congo, But is it Really Economic? |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j_t-RAAdzA8). His supporting argument was efficiency of discovery: the deposit's profile had been established "with only 20,000 m of drilling," which he characterized as historical work — "This was historical drilling" [3M Ounces of Gold in DR Congo, But is it Really Economic? |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j_t-RAAdzA8). person/daniel-lacalle.text:
Daniel Lacalle is a Spanish economist and fund manager — best known publicly as chief economist at Madrid-based Tressis and as a fixture of financial media making the free-market case against central-bank overreach and deficit spending. Within this corpus, however, the record on him is strikingly narrow: all sixteen coded stances come from a single conversation, MacroVoices episode #547, "The Future of Reserve Currencies," dated August 27, 2026, and every one of them lands on neutral — zero bullish, zero bearish calls logged. That makes this less a portrait of a famously pointed commentator than a snapshot of one argument, mirrored across two video uploads of the same show.

The argument itself is the dollar's reserve status, and Lacalle's position is conditional rather than maximalist: "if the US government really reigns on its massive imbalances, the US dollar will continue to be the world fiat reserve currency" ([MacroVoices #547 Daniel Lacalle: The Future of Reserve Curr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KwlbirZxPQc)). He sketches a policy path in which Washington "bans central bank digital currencies and forces a sort of new paradigm" centered on the dollar ([MacroVoices #547 Daniel Lacalle: The Future of Reserve Curr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J0R7IlQ5L_c)), and reads the US government as eyeing "the opportunity created by stable coins and by cryptocurrencies in order to cement the position" of the dollar ([MacroVoices #547 Daniel Lacalle: The Future of Reserve Curr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KwlbirZxPQc)). Crypto as a rival reserve gets dismissed on arithmetic — bitcoin and crypto market caps are "exceedingly small compared to the market cap of fiat currencies" ([MacroVoices #547 Daniel Lacalle: The Future of Reserve Curr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J0R7IlQ5L_c)) — while he notes central banks are concluding it is better to strengthen their own currencies "through decen…" ([MacroVoices #547 Daniel Lacalle: The Future of Reserve Curr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KwlbirZxPQc)), with the excerpt cutting off mid-word.

The undercurrent is harder-edged than the "neutral" tags suggest. He observes that the euro has lost second place among central-bank reserve assets "in favor of gold" ([MacroVoices #547 Daniel Lacalle: The Future of Reserve Curr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KwlbirZxPQc)), and that talk of one currency being stronger than another reflects no good policy anywhere — "all of them are worsening relative to gold" ([MacroVoices #547 Daniel Lacalle: The Future of Reserve Curr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KwlbirZxPQc)). He also lumps the United States in with the euro area, Japan, the UK and China as governments that "have surpassed the economic, the fiscal…" ([MacroVoices #547 Daniel Lacalle: The Future of Reserve Curr…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J0R7IlQ5L_c)) — the quote truncates, but the grouping is the point: nobody is exempt from his ledger.

As for how his views have moved over time, the timeline simply can't say — one date, one episode, no directional calls to chart. Anyone wanting his evolution on rates, gold or energy will need far more source material than this. What the record does capture is his method: measure every fiat currency against gold and against fiscal arithmetic, and treat dollar primacy as a policy outcome to be defended rather than a fact of nature. The flat neutral coding undersells that structure — dollar-constructive if and only if Washington repairs its balance sheet is the shape of the argument these excerpts actually show.

person/gary-wagner.text:
Gary Wagner is a veteran precious-metals technician — long known in gold circles for Fibonacci-based chart work and his gold-focused market commentary — but within this corpus he appears exactly once: an appearance on 2026-06-17 framed around the provocative question of whether gold is about to repeat its 2012-style 50% collapse ([Is Gold About To Crash 50%? 2012 Repeat Pattern Explained |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tMzlpYpNi_w)). That thin coverage matters: with a single dated appearance and a stance mix of zero bullish, one bearish and eight neutral, the timelines show a snapshot rather than an evolution, so any verdict on how his views have moved over time simply isn't available from this data.

What the snapshot does show is a technician who entertains the bears' crash scenario and then talks it down with arithmetic. On gold (GC=F), he framed the 2012 repeat as a stretch, noting that a 50% washout would take the metal "from call it 5,500 down to just below 3,000," and instead offered a floor thesis: "around $4,000 will be a floor in gold," based on the prior week's low ([Is Gold About To Crash 50%? 2012 Repeat Pattern Explained |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tMzlpYpNi_w)). Even that is hedged — "if this area holds, and that's a big if" — with the payoff being a "much more shallow correction" than gold's historical drawdowns ([Is Gold About To Crash 50%? 2012 Repeat Pattern Explained |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tMzlpYpNi_w)). The load-bearing part of his argument is central-bank demand: he cites a survey showing central banks believed to accumulate "vast amounts" of gold over the next year, calls them the biggest purchasers of the metal this year, and reads their fiat-to-hard-asset conversion as a sign that official reserve managers are losing faith in fiat currency itself ([Is Gold About To Crash 50%? 2012 Repeat Pattern Explained |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tMzlpYpNi_w)). In other words, his floor isn't just a chart level — it's anchored to a structural buyer.

His one unambiguous directional call in the corpus is bearish, and it isn't gold — it's crude oil (CL=F): "I would look for it if it's not there already to go back to around 80 and 80 being a benchmark" ([Is Gold About To Crash 50%? 2012 Repeat Pattern Explained |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tMzlpYpNi_w)). That oil view plugs directly into his inflation read, which he put at 4.2% from May's CPI but characterized as roughly 60% energy- and crude-driven ([Is Gold About To Crash 50%? 2012 Repeat Pattern Explained |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tMzlpYpNi_w)). On the geopolitical driver behind energy, he was similarly non-committal, observing that markets had set aside the Iran war on the back of a peace agreement — "we'll see if it holds" ([Is Gold About To Crash 50%? 2012 Repeat Pattern Explained |…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tMzlpYpNi_w)).

The shape of his positioning, then, is defensive-neutral with a bearish tilt on oil: he takes the most bearish gold framing of the moment seriously enough to engage it, but his conclusion — central banks as the marginal buyer making the correction shallower — leans constructive under a heavily conditional surface. Whether that posture holds when gold actually tests his $4,000 floor, or whether his oil call to ~$80 proves the one dated call worth grading, is something this corpus can't yet answer; it's a one-day portrait, not a track record.

person/joe-argenta-silver-ceo-first-name.text:
Joe — identified in the source transcript by first name only, though Argenta Silver's chief executive is Joaquin "Joe" Mariasch — runs Argenta Silver Corp., a silver exploration company built around a single asset: the high-grade El Quevar silver project in Salta Province, Argentina, picked up from Golden Arrow Resources. His one recorded appearance in this corpus is a Resource Talks interview dated June 25, 2026, and the episode title itself frames the debate he had to answer: 45 million ounces of silver in Argentina, but can the concentrate actually be sold? ([45M Ounces of Silver in Argentina, But Can the Concentrate …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dc1_pJVDXXg))

His pitch on that appearance split neatly in two. On the company side, he put the treasury at roughly C$3 million on the books — a thin war chest by exploration-sector standards, which he presumably presented as adequate for the work at hand ([45M Ounces of Silver in Argentina, But Can the Concentrate …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dc1_pJVDXXg)). On the asset side, he leaned on El Quevar's historical metallurgy: concentrate grades of 11,000–13,000 g/t silver, potential recoveries above 90%, and — the crucial selling point — no sale penalties attached to the concentrate ([45M Ounces of Silver in Argentina, But Can the Concentrate …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dc1_pJVDXXg)). The counterweight he himself raised is the crux of that title question: China's environmental laws prohibit any concentrate running 0.5% arsenic or higher, a threshold any El Quevar offtake story has to clear ([45M Ounces of Silver in Argentina, But Can the Concentrate …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dc1_pJVDXXg)).

As for how his views have moved over time: there is no trajectory to chart. The corpus logs exactly two stances, both neutral, both from the same June 25, 2026 appearance — one the arsenic rule above, the other a piece of market context in which he dated the discussion's backdrop to before the silver squeeze, "silver still at 20 large or early $30 per ounce" ([45M Ounces of Silver in Argentina, But Can the Concentrate …](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dc1_pJVDXXg)). That is the profile of an operator walking through his project's specifics, not a market caller — no bullish or bearish positions on record here, and coverage limited to a single interview. Read it as a first-pass portrait, not a track record.

person/john-wang.text:
John Wang enters this corpus as a voice rather than a caller. The record on him is a single appearance: a June 25, 2026 YouTube discussion grandly titled "The $90 Trillion Market You Don't Know About Can Change Inv…" — the kind of title that usually means tokenization or stablecoins, and in his case it does. His role and affiliation aren't specified in the material on file, and his stance tally is telling: zero bullish, zero bearish, four neutral. Across everything captured, he is analyzing structure, not issuing ratings — which makes him harder to score than the average pundit, and arguably more interesting for it ([The $90 Trillion Market You Don't Know About Can Change Inv…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kb-voDc27hY)).

The substance of his argument, as of that June appearance, runs on two tracks. The first is an infrastructure thesis: with stablecoins and AI in the picture, he sees "the rails of the future for the internet" as "programmable determinist[ic]" systems — a claim that treats crypto rails less as a trade and more as plumbing that will eventually be unavoidable ([The $90 Trillion Market You Don't Know About Can Change Inv…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kb-voDc27hY)). The second is a liquidity caveat that cuts against the enthusiasm: "there are definitely also macro factors that are affecting the liquidity of the whole industry," and in his framing, "AI has been a huge liquidity suck" ([The $90 Trillion Market You Don't Know About Can Change Inv…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kb-voDc27hY)). There's a mild but real tension in holding both views at once, and he seems aware of it — on crypto specifically he argues "the fundamentals are there," pointing to the most pro-crypto administration and the deepest institutional development the sector has ever had, while still declining to translate that into a directional call ([The $90 Trillion Market You Don't Know About Can Change Inv…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kb-voDc27hY)). Structurally bullish, tactically agnostic is the fairest read of the shape.

On movement over time: there is none to trace. Every recorded stance lands on the same date, from the same source, so any narrative about how his views have shifted would be fabrication. What the corpus does show is a commentator whose value lies in framing — the internet's future rails, the liquidity cost of the AI buildout — rather than in stock-level conviction. That makes this page a stub by necessity, and the honest verdict is that Wang's file needs more appearances before anyone can call him a forecaster at all.

person/komal-sri-kumar-referred-to-in-tr.text:
Komal Sri-Kumar — referred to simply as "Sree" on air — is a macroeconomist and global strategist who runs his own shop, Sri-Kumar Global Strategies, after a long tenure as TCW's chief global strategist. His research on interest rates, inflation, and global asset allocation is aimed at institutional clients, and he is a regular presence on CNBC and Bloomberg, where his calls on Treasury yields and Fed policy get picked up widely in the financial press. The record in this corpus rests on a single appearance: a June 18, 2026 interview on David Lin's show, framed around the signals coming from a new Fed chair ([New Fed Chair Drops Bombshell Signals, 'No Escape' From Co…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FHtb-uCMgLU)).

The through-line of that appearance is distinctly hawkish, and notably pre-dated the geopolitical catalyst — he stresses he had been arguing in his writings, and on Lin's show, "even before the Iran war" that the Fed should be raising rates ([New Fed Chair Drops Bombshell Signals, 'No Escape' From Co…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FHtb-uCMgLU)). His framing is unsentimental: "If you have maintained a very easy monetary policy for a long period of time, you have to pay the price for it. There is no free lunch" ([New Fed Chair Drops Bombshell Signals, 'No Escape' From Co…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FHtb-uCMgLU)). The payoff he sketches is stagflation — inflation still elevated even as higher rates bite — with the warning signs arriving "during calendar year 2027" ([New Fed Chair Drops Bombshell Signals, 'No Escape' From Co…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FHtb-uCMgLU)). He casts the whole scenario as a trap for Kevin Warsh's Fed: "All the interest rates turn out to be higher, and that is the risk for Kevin Warsh and for this economy" ([New Fed Chair Drops Bombshell Signals, 'No Escape' From Co…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FHtb-uCMgLU)). The priority ordering matters to him — curb inflation first, because without that nothing else can be controlled ([New Fed Chair Drops Bombshell Signals, 'No Escape' From Co…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FHtb-uCMgLU)).

His strongest directional call, and the only clearly bullish stances in the record, sit on the long end of the Treasury curve: "if inflation is not controlled before the end of the year, expect the 10-year and 30-year to move up as well" ([New Fed Chair Drops Bombshell Signals, 'No Escape' From Co…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FHtb-uCMgLU)). Around that core he is more hedged. He doubts the recent slide in oil prices is sustainable ([New Fed Chair Drops Bombshell Signals, 'No Escape' From Co…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FHtb-uCMgLU)), suggests that higher cap rates could offer "some amount of protection" for entrants into real estate ([New Fed Chair Drops Bombshell Signals, 'No Escape' From Co…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FHtb-uCMgLU)), and reaches back to October 2007 — the S&P 500's record high just three months before recession began that December — as a reminder that markets can look peachy at the exact peak ([New Fed Chair Drops Bombshell Signals, 'No Escape' From Co…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FHtb-uCMgLU)).

A word on what this record does and doesn't show. Of his nineteen documented stances, seventeen are neutral, two bullish, and zero bearish — the profile of an analyst whose convictions are concentrated in one big macro thesis (higher rates for longer, inflation unresolved) rather than scattered across asset calls. And because everything here dates to that single June 2026 conversation, there is no timeline to trace any evolution in his views; whether his rate-hawk posture held up, or shifted as the Warsh Fed's choices played out, is a question this corpus simply can't answer yet.

person/lyn-alden.text:
Lyn Alden is an American investment strategist and the founder of Lyn Alden Investment Strategy, an independent research service she launched in 2016 after a first career in aviation — she holds a BS in engineering and an MS in engineering and technology management from Oklahoma State University. She is best known for data-driven macro analysis spanning monetary policy, fiscal policy, currency markets, and long-term portfolio construction, and has become one of the more prominent voices bridging monetary history and Bitcoin. Her 2023 book, *Broken Money: Why Our Financial System Is Failing Us and How We Can Make It Better*, states the thesis plainly, and she carries it through frequent podcast appearances on Treasury markets, the dollar, and emerging market currencies. The engineering background is not incidental to her style: the work is frameworks and long-run datasets first, market calls a distant second — which shapes what her tracked record actually looks like.

That record, at least as captured here, is a study in deliberate non-direction. On MacroVoices #538 (June 25, 2026), in an episode framed around whether "the war" was really over, she declined to take a side on almost everything she touched. On the dollar, she said that "for the foreseeable future, at least any sort of time horizon I'm monitoring, I think the dollar trades in this choppy band" — a range view, not a break-down call ([Lyn Alden: Is The War Really Over and What's Next For Marke…](https://www.macrovoices.com/podcast-transcripts/1538-lyn-alden-is-the-war-really-over-and-what-s-next-for-markets)). On crude, she judged that "if the strait stays open," the prevailing price was "a near term rational place for oil to be" ([Lyn Alden: Is The War Really Over and What's Next For Marke…](https://www.macrovoices.com/podcast-transcripts/1538-lyn-alden-is-the-war-really-over-and-what-s-next-for-markets)). Her preferred lens in the same conversation was the dollar against the Chinese yuan and emerging market currencies, which she watches "often more than" the usual gauges ([Lyn Alden: Is The War Really Over and What's Next For Marke…](https://www.macrovoices.com/podcast-transcripts/1538-lyn-alden-is-the-war-really-over-and-what-s-next-for-markets)).

The one place she revealed prior positioning was energy: her view "going into" the war was that she "wanted to be long energy companies," before the group ran up ([MacroVoices #538 Lyn Alden: Is The War Really Over and What…](https://www.macrovoices.com/1537-macrovoices-538-lyn-alden-is-the-war-really-over-and-what-s-next-for-markets)). She also spent part of the interview characterizing others' policy leanings rather than her own — describing one official as historically "on the hawkish side… on the balance sheet, but also on interest rates" ([MacroVoices #538 Lyn Alden: Is The War Really Over and What…](https://www.macrovoices.com/1537-macrovoices-538-lyn-alden-is-the-war-really-over-and-what-s-next-for-markets)). It is worth being honest about the coverage here: all six tracked stances in this corpus are neutral, and every one of them dates to that single June 2026 appearance. There is no visible drift or reversal in this record — no "turned bearish by X" arc to write, because the digest contains none. That flatness is arguably the point: Alden's influence runs through her monetary and fiscal regime analysis and her long-horizon framing rather than through timed calls, and anyone reading her for a directional verdict is probably reading the wrong analyst.

person/matt-gertken-bca-research.text:
Matt Gertken is Chief Geopolitical Strategist at BCA Research, the independent investment research firm headquartered in Montreal, where he leads the firm's Geopolitical Strategy service. The job, as BCA frames it, is to take political and policy developments — elections, conflicts, sanctions, US-China relations, energy security — and translate them into implications for global markets, which is a more demanding brief than the usual punditry: the work has to end in a tradable view, not just a commentary. Gertken joined BCA in 2015 and is a regular presence in financial media when geopolitical risk is the story.

The recorded track record in this corpus is thin, and it's worth saying so plainly: two logged stances, both neutral, both dated August 27, 2026, and both from the same appearance on the video ["50% Tariff Attack: Canada, U.S. Brace For 'Massive Pain'"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=edwp5mhmgcs). There is no view migration to chart here — no early call that flipped by a later date. But the two comments together do show the method. On the tariff escalation against Canada, his read is that the aggression is fundamentally domestic politics: "he's just trying to fire up his base with nationalism so that they turn out for the election" — a calculated mobilization play rather than a durable policy commitment ([50% Tariff Attack: Canada, U.S. Brace For 'Massive Pain'](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=edwp5mhmgcs)).

The companion comment supplies the counterweight, and it's the more market-relevant of the two. However loud the escalation rhetoric gets, the expectation is restraint where it actually bites: "He doesn't want to touch critical minerals or fuel. You know, oil is one of the biggest imports from Canada. He doesn't want to dabble with that" ([50% Tariff Attack: Canada, U.S. Brace For 'Massive Pain'](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=edwp5mhmgcs)). Read together, the pair sketches the classic geopolitical-strategist distinction — nationalism as electoral theater, hard economic dependencies as the real constraint — which is the analytical lens his role exists to provide. With only two neutral data points, there is no bullish or bearish record here to grade him on; the portrait rests on the framework, not a scored call.

person/matt-gertken-transcribed-as-matt-.text:
Matt Gertken (whose name shows up in transcripts as "Matt Girkin") is the Chief Geopolitical Strategist at BCA Research, an independent investment research firm, where his job is translating geopolitics — US foreign policy, great-power competition with China and Russia, elections, global conflict risk — into terms that matter for global markets. He came up as an analyst at Stratfor, the geopolitical intelligence shop, which tells you the lineage: scenario-crafting and risk framing rather than ticker-level calls. He appears regularly in financial media, including David Lin's show, to do exactly that.

His one appearance captured in this corpus, on August 27, 2026, is a good specimen of the style. The episode was framed around escalation — ["50% Tariff Attack: Canada, U.S. Brace For 'Massive Pain'"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=edwp5mhmgcs) — but Gertken's actual read was cooler than the title: tariffs are "at least a mild drag" on the US economy, one that "somewhat offsets other things that are stimulating." He framed the tariff regime as a new "annualized multi-hundred-billion-dollar tax" spread across American consumers and businesses, and he grounded the discussion in the structural plumbing of dollar hegemony — the US runs large trade deficits, and the surplus countries recycle those dollars into US assets ([50% Tariff Attack: Canada, U.S. Brace For 'Massive Pain'](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=edwp5mhmgcs)). The gap between the headline's "massive pain" and his "mild drag" is the whole persona: de-dramatizing geopolitics for an investor audience.

It's worth being plain about what the record here shows: a single appearance, three stances, all neutral, zero directional calls, and therefore no observable movement in his views over time. That isn't evasion so much as the job description — Gertken's contribution is analytical scaffolding (who bears the tax, how deficits get financed) rather than bull-or-bear verdicts. A proper portrait of his convictions will need more appearances than this one.

person/shashank-chiranewala.text:
Shashank Chiranewala shows up in this corpus as a single-appearance interview guest on The Monetary Matters Network, featured in the June 24, 2026 episode "The Secret to Investing Like Substack & FinTwit's Top Researchers." That framing tells you the territory he was brought on to discuss: the gap between the advice retail investors actually get — often from finfluencers and Substack writers — and what those same voices do or believe when pressed. His own recorded position from that conversation sits firmly in the neutral column, twice over, and both statements point at the same target: the reflexive default of index-only investing.

His argument isn't a bearish call on equities or a market-timing thesis. It's a critique of the canonical advice itself. "I don't think it's ideal for everyone to just have all of their money in the S&P 500, even though that's become somewhat canonical," he said on the show — a direct push at the Bogle-era orthodoxy that the total-market index fund is the answer for everybody ([The Secret to Investing Like Substack & FinTwit's Top Resea…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IHFVBrwt54s)). His second recorded quote explains why the orthodoxy fails: investors "start out confident and say index investing or something like that. But then we find out... that doesn't really do justice to my needs" ([The Secret to Investing Like Substack & FinTwit's Top Resea…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IHFVBrwt54s)). In other words, the friction isn't in the strategy's returns — it's that a one-size default ignores individual circumstances, which is where his episode title's promise presumably kicks in.

That's the entire record here, and it's worth being plain about the limits: one appearance, no dated calls, no positions on specific sectors or assets, and no timeline along which to trace a change of mind. Both quotes come from the same conversation, so there's no evidence yet of his views moving in either direction. What the record does show is a guest whose contribution is skepticism about consensus rather than a contrarian forecast — a "the default isn't for everyone" stance rather than a "sell everything" one. Until he returns to the network or another source fills in his track record, this page can grade the shape of his argument but not the quality of his calls.

person/interviewee.text:
This page has an honest problem: the corpus files its subject under the placeholder label "interviewee," and that label is accurate to what's on record — a single conversation, hosted by David Lin and dated June 25, 2026, under the title [The $90 Trillion Market You Don’t Know About Can Change Inv…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kb-voDc27hY). The record credits them as a solo author/host with just that one appearance, so everything below is a snapshot of one interview, not a body of work. What the episode does contain is mostly market-structure explanation rather than direction: the "$90 trillion" of the title sits alongside their most distinctive material, which is about prediction markets and crypto derivatives.

Their through-line is a preference for instruments with defined outcomes. Prediction markets, they argued, "give you those guardrails of… when this is going to end, all the strike prices that you can buy in at" — the appeal being a known endpoint rather than an open-ended bet ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kb-voDc27hY)). On crypto plumbing, they were emphatic that perpetuals are "the biggest instrument… trading instrument in crypto actually," and walked through the mechanics plainly: instead of buying Bitcoin directly, "you're trading… the price of it" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kb-voDc27hY)). The closest thing to a market call in the episode is downbeat: "not only is Bitcoin down, the entire crypto market" is "going through a winter right now," and on the long-awaited altcoin rotation they hedged mid-sentence — people have been waiting for altcoin spring, "I don't kno…" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kb-voDc27hY)). On rates, they stayed comparative rather than predictive, noting they've seen offerings run "10x more expensive from a cost perspective" elsewhere ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kb-voDc27hY)).

As for movement over time: there is none on record. All six coded stances are neutral and every one is stamped with the same date, so any trajectory would be invented. Worth flagging, too, that the tagging is loose — the "AI & Semiconductors" bucket quotes the exact same crypto-winter passage, which looks like a mis-tag rather than a genuine second theme. Until a second appearance is logged, the fair portrait is an explainer of prediction markets and perpetuals with a weary, neutral read on crypto — not a forecaster with a gradeable track record.

ticker/0017.HK.text:
There is no real bull-bear fight on record for 0017.HK (New World Development) in this corpus — and that absence is the most telling thing about it. The consensus tag reads neutral/watch with zero bullish and zero bearish calls attached; the only two entries are unattributed Cantonese commentary, roughly a month apart, and neither commits to a price target or a rating. Whoever tracks this name here is circling the balance sheet without anyone willing to plant a flag.

The timeline, such as it is: on 18 June 2026 an unidentified speaker remarked — in a tone closer to a shrug than a warning — that New World is "so broke these days" that creditors might as well go easy on it (a loose rendering of "新世界而家咁窮咁咪放過你一馬咯"). It was logged explicitly as commentary on the company's weak finances, not a call. Four weeks later, on 16 July 2026, a second unnamed voice took the same theme a step darker, arguing that prevailing conditions "increase repayment pressure" on New World and other heavily indebted borrowers alike. Both entries are classified neutral, but the direction of drift across the month is unmistakable: from wry acknowledgment of a weak balance sheet toward treating the debt load as an active, tightening squeeze.

As for the shape of the debate — there isn't one, strictly speaking. No one in this digest argues the bull side: no refinancing-success narrative, no asset-sale optimism, no contrarian value case is on record. The nearest thing to disagreement is one of tone, not substance — the June comment treats the company's distress as background fact hardly worth getting exercised about, while the July remark frames it as mounting pressure with real consequences for servicing the debt. Nobody changed their mind, because nobody staked out a position in the first place. That consistency is worth noting: two separate speakers, a month apart, landed on the same premise without either being moved to call the stock.

A fair caveat: coverage here is thin, the speakers are unidentified, and the quotes are conversational fragments rather than research output — so this page reflects commentary drift, not an analyst consensus in any meaningful sense. Until someone in the corpus actually takes a side on 0017.HK, neutral/watch is less a verdict than a placeholder.

ticker/CGNT.text:
The honest summary of the CGNT debate is that, as of the record here, there barely is one. The consensus sits at neutral/watch with zero bullish and zero bearish calls — two neutral stances and nothing else. The only substantive commentary on file comes from a single speaker on June 18, 2026, whom the transcript leaves unattributed, though the first-person framing ("we've got two drills running," "we see that as the number one quickest way of creating value") reads like company management rather than outside analysis. That absence matters: with no analyst or investor stances on record, nobody has changed their mind, because there's been nobody on the other side to change it.

What management laid out on that June call is effectively the bull case by default, and it's a catalyst-path argument. The speaker pointed to Colombian elections on the calendar, two drill rigs running, and a push toward a preliminary economic assessment (PEA) that will wrap economics around an updated resource — with the PEA explicitly framed as "the number one quickest way of creating value." Implicit in that is a sequencing story: drill results feed a resource update, the resource update feeds PEA economics, and each step is meant to be a value-printing milestone rather than a distant promise. For a neutral-to-constructive watcher, that's the case worth tracking — a dated, concrete sequence beats vague exploration talk.

The bear-shaped counterpoints aren't in the record either; they have to be inferred from what management said and didn't say. A PEA is early-stage, low-confidence economics — it's the first look at a project's numbers, not a de-risked feasibility study, and "quickest way to create value" is also what issuers say when they need the market to stay patient through the wait. The Colombia elections cut both ways: management flagged them as context, but an election is political overhang as much as backdrop, and the commentary offers nothing on how policy risk gets priced. Notably, the quotes stop short of timelines, tonnage, or grade — the specifics that would let anyone take a real position.

So the timeline of calls, such as it is, contains one entry: June 18, 2026, management's catalyst-heavy progress update, and a consensus that remains firmly on the fence. The neutral/watch label is defensible precisely because the debate hasn't been written yet — the PEA and the resource update are the events that will finally give bulls something to champion and bears something to attack. Until then, the coverage here is thin enough that silence, not disagreement, is the dominant position.

ticker/PLTR.text:
The honest starting point for any PLTR debate page built on this corpus is that there isn't much of a debate yet. The consensus sits at neutral/watch with zero bullish and zero bearish calls logged, and both entries trace back to a single, unidentified speaker. So what we're really charting is one voice's evolution over six weeks — useful, but thin, and it should be flagged as such rather than dressed up as a bull-bear standoff.

The timeline does show a genuine swing, though. On June 26, 2026, the speaker was recounting the downside: "look what happened to Palantir. Palantir got down to 106, okay? Before coming back" — a reference to the drawdown to $106 and the recovery off it. Notably, that entry is marked as an observation, not a call; the speaker is describing pain that already happened, not predicting more of it. By August 8, 2026, the tone had flipped toward temptation: "This thing looks like it could run and the next big target around number could be $200 for all we know." Whether that counts as changing their mind is a judgment call — it's less a reversal than a drift from narrating the scar tissue to entertaining the upside as the stock recovered.

The hedging in both quotes is the most telling detail. The August line is loaded with qualifiers — "could run," "could be," "for all we know" — which is why it landed as neutral rather than bullish despite gesturing at a $200 target. A target floated with that much escape hatch isn't a call; it's speculation offered with plausible deniability. Similarly, the June remark earns no bearish credit because it's retrospective. What the corpus lacks is the other half of the argument: no named bull staking a price target with conviction, no named bear laying out a valuation case against one. Until someone in this corpus actually commits, the PLTR debate is one anonymous analyst moving from rattled to curious — which is a sentiment indicator, not a debate.

person/collin-martin.text:
Collin Martin is a Managing Director and Fixed Income Strategist at the Schwab Center for Financial Research, where — as a CFA charterholder — he covers the bond complex end to end: U.S. Treasuries, investment-grade and high-yield corporate debt, and municipals, with regular commentary on rate trends, credit conditions, and government and corporate issuance. He's a frequent guest on financial media and podcasts, and in this corpus he appears exactly once: on David Lin's show, in an episode framed around a Fed-driven market sell-off and the question of whether rate hikes are coming back ([Fed Sparks Market Bloodbath: Rate Hikes Coming Back? | Coll…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CcecLrxrhF0)).

What's notable about that appearance is how firmly Martin resists the panic the framing invites. He lays out the bear case on fiscal grounds plainly enough — total debt around $40 trillion, debt-to-GDP above 100%, and "very, very large deficits" in non-recessionary periods — and he worries that too much market intervention, whether via the Treasury General Account or by changing the size of coupon issuance, can backfire ([Fed Sparks Market Bloodbath: Rate Hikes Coming Back? | Coll…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CcecLrxrhF0)). But he also pushes back on the doom narrative from the macro side: the economy is resilient, corporations are posting record earnings, and the labor market is stable ([Fed Sparks Market Bloodbath: Rate Hikes Coming Back? | Coll…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CcecLrxrhF0)). His sharpest analytical point is about transmission: higher long-end yields are "a negative for businesses" because it boosts borrowing costs — and not everyone borrows at the short end ([Fed Sparks Market Bloodbath: Rate Hikes Coming Back? | Coll…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CcecLrxrhF0)).

His strongest calls are range calls rather than directional bets, which is itself telling. He expects the 10-year Treasury to hold in a 4.25% to 4.75% band, and he tracks the 30-year around the 5.2–5.3% area, noting it touched 5.3% before settling roughly 10 basis points lower ([Fed Sparks Market Bloodbath: Rate Hikes Coming Back? | Coll…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CcecLrxrhF0)). The closest thing to an outright stance in the record is on credit, where he says Schwab has held "a more favorable view" on investment grade and high yield "for a few months now" and that it hasn't changed — a relative preference, not a bull call ([Fed Sparks Market Bloodbath: Rate Hikes Coming Back? | Coll…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CcecLrxrhF0)).

As for how his views have moved: the corpus can't really say. Every datapoint comes from the same August 28, 2026 appearance, and all eight recorded stances are neutral. The only evidence of evolution is internal to that conversation — his credit preference dates to roughly mid-2026 by his own account. That's thin coverage, and readers should treat the portrait as a snapshot of one measured house-strategist performance: precise about ranges, alert to fiscal risk, and conspicuously unwilling to call a breakout in either direction.
