person/author.text:
綠角 is one of the best-known voices in Taiwanese personal finance: a blogger, author, and investing educator who has spent his career pushing a simple and, in the local context, genuinely contrarian argument — that ordinary investors are best served by low-cost, passive index investing rather than stock-picking or fund-chasing. His writing, centered on his long-running 綠角財經筆記 blog and a string of books, leans hard into the evidence on fund fees, survivorship, and the poor odds of beating the market, and he has been a persistent critic of the high-fee active fund culture that dominates Taiwan's retail investing scene. Beyond writing, he teaches — most visibly through his 綠角金融咖啡館 lecture format — making him less a market commentator than a philosophy-of-investing educator.

His core stance has been notably stable rather than theatrical: pro-index, anti-cost, skeptical of anyone selling the promise of outperformance. There is no record in this corpus of him swinging bullish or bearish on any asset, sector, or macro theme — the digest logs zero directional calls across the board, and no topic timelines at all.

That is the honest limit of what can be written here. The material available contains no dated positions, no calls, and no documented shifts in view, so any narrative of how his opinions have moved over time simply cannot be constructed from this corpus. What can be said is the shape of the person: a steady, single-minded advocate whose influence rests on consistency and education rather than market calls — the opposite, in an interesting way, of the tip-driven commentary that fills much of the surrounding financial media.

ticker/ATX.V.text:
On ATX.V, the honest starting point is that there isn't much of a debate yet. The tracker shows six observers, all in neutral/watch mode, zero bulls, zero bears — and the entire recorded record consists of a single company interview dated June 15, 2026 (the speaker is unnamed in our transcript data, though the first-person framing — "we right now we have 150 million in cash" — reads as management). That means the bull case, such as it is, currently exists only in management's own telling, and the six watchers are effectively declining to underwrite it.

What that telling contains is a funding story and a catalyst calendar. The company sits on roughly $150 million in cash with the stock trading around $3, and management flagged warrant-driven financing optionality: "at $4 we could bring in another $140 million." On timing, the near-term hook is vague — "there'll be news on that in the next… three to five months" — while the substance is stacked out further: a couple of holes hoped for on the Nueva Horizonte ground, and "the outcome of the resource, likely in the fall of 27." Drilling more broadly is a 2027 story, contingent on geophysics and geochemistry results that, as of mid-June 2026, were not yet in hand.

The shape of the debate, then, is an asymmetry of specificity. The bull reading — implicit in management's framing rather than argued by any outside voice — is a well-funded junior that doesn't need the market's money and has a dated path to a resource estimate. The bear reading is embedded in the same sentences: the cash claim and the $140 million warrant scenario are one and the same coin at two prices, meaning the funding upside is also a dilution scenario above the current quote; and the nearest "catalyst" is an unspecified news promise inside five months, with everything verifiable pushed to late 2027. Six neutrals and no convictions is a defensible posture — the record simply doesn't yet contain enough sourced argument for anyone to take a side, and we won't manufacture one where the data doesn't show it.

ticker/EVRYF.text:
For a tin-exposed small cap, EVRYF's file is strikingly empty of combat: the running tally shows zero bullish calls, zero bearish ones, and just two neutral "watch" stances. There is no recorded bull case and no recorded bear case — nobody on record arguing the royalty stream justifies the price, and nobody calling the valuation stretched. The only substance on the page dates from a single day, June 16, 2026, and comes from a speaker the record leaves unnamed. The first-person phrasing — "We're about a $120 million market cap" — has the texture of transcribed management remarks rather than third-party analysis, but the attribution gap matters: unattributed guidance can't carry an analyst's conviction behind it, however specific it is.

And it is specific. The speaker committed to revenues between 5 and 7 million this year, growing to over 10 million next year, against that roughly $120 million market cap. The second thread is a royalty expected to pay "between 4 and 5 million per year at current tin prices" — a figure that makes the tin-price assumption explicit rather than incidental. Strip tin strength out of the picture and that $4–5 million annual royalty yield is the first number that moves, which is why the commodity exposure isn't a footnote here; it's the load-bearing part of the story.

So the honest answer to "what's the debate?" is that there isn't one yet, and it's worth saying plainly: this is a thin record. The fault lines are at least visible in the numbers themselves — a ~$120 million market cap set against $5–7 million of near-term revenue, with a doubling promised for next year — and that gap between price and present revenue is exactly where a bull (growth plus a durable royalty stream justify it) and a bear (rich for a tin-price-contingent royalty) would plant their flags. Until someone actually takes a side, the two neutral stances are the whole story: a holding pattern, not a fight.

ticker/WREXF.text:
There isn't much of a debate here yet — and that's the honest starting point. Across seven tracked voices, the consensus on WREXF is uniformly neutral/watch: zero bullish calls, zero bearish calls. What the record actually contains is a single monologue from an August 28, 2026 call by an unidentified speaker — almost certainly management, given the "we" framing — laying out the bull case for the Gravel Creek project while nobody on record pushes back.

That bull case, as presented, rests on three legs. First, permitted runway: the speaker emphasized "we still have four years of drilling we can do at Gravel Creek under our exploration plan with the Forest Service" (2026-08-28 call). Second, scale and character: roughly "a million ounces gold equivalent," which the speaker was careful to frame as gold and silver rather than a polymetallic story (2026-08-28 call). Third, demonstrated growth — the 2023 and 2024 drill programs at Gravel Creek "added a quarter million ounce[s]" (the quote trails off, so the resulting total and the math behind the million-ounce figure are not in the record) — plus a hint of third-party validation: the speaker claimed concentrate buyers "like Glen Core and Ora" (the transcript's phonetics — presumably Glencore among them) looked at the concentrate and called it "very high" quality (2026-08-28 call).

The bear side of this debate is, for now, an absence rather than an argument. Nothing in the record shows an analyst challenging the resource estimate, the economics, or the long runway of exploration still ahead of any development decision — and even the concentrate-quality claim is management paraphrasing unnamed counterparties, not a directly attributable endorsement. It's also worth noting what the framing itself concedes: four years of drilling is an option on information, not a path to production, and a million-ounce gold-equivalent resource is a starting inventory, not a mine. As for mind-changes — there are none to report. No upgrades, no downgrades, no one turning bullish or bearish; everyone sits at neutral/watch, which says less about conviction than it does about how thin the coverage on this name currently is.

study/cpm-group/topic/investment-demand-.text:
The spine of this topic is CPM Group's recurring trade-signal video, which in 2020 lands on a one-to-three-week rhythm — May 19, June 8, June 12, July 6, July 14, then roughly monthly after that ([May 19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ef8-E4UMeW4), [June 8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KzmKuzuz2DQ), [June 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jbWsOJYnrtg), [July 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zTueacq7_r8), [July 14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qjkFnDZ2YME)). What's genuinely new in each installment is almost always just updated levels: on May 19, 2020 Christian raised a short-term target of 1765 for May 29 with follow-ons at 1775 and a test of $1,800, then conceded gold "blew right past 1760 got up to 1776 and then came off it," announcing he was "looking at a new target on a short-term basis" — last week's forecast superseded, framework untouched. On that same cadence the recommendation wheel spins: "Why It Is Time To Stand Aside" on July 27 ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=efUpv9lqFe8)), "All Roads Lead To Gold" three weeks later ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNkMV4Je9Fk)), "No One Should Be Short On Gold" ten days after that ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fRzghWogdJg)), a "short term SELL recommendation" in January 2021 ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JFZi4kXULCI)), then "STAND ASIDE recommendation for Gold; BUY for Silver" in March ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q8N1yQ5R8c0)) — a full long-to-flat-to-short-to-flat cycle in eight months.

What never changes is the core allocation thesis. On August 21, 2020 the deep-read flags two entries as "nothing" new, just the standing case: "we have written extensively and studied extensively the value and benefits of having gold as part of your wealth" ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNkMV4Je9Fk)). Nearly three years later, on June 30, 2023, the same line reappears, again flagged "nothing": "CPM group has always advised that… you should always have some physical metal as that long-term insurance." The hedging series recycles verbatim across months — on February 1, 2022 Christian says "as i said last month when i started talking about hedging and hedging with uh for investors options are like dynamite," repeating January's warning word for word. And the purest repackaging: August 26, 2022's history of investor net-selling ("from 1990 until 2005 2006 you had about 16 years of consistent net sales") is restated on November 18, 2022 with three separate "nothing" flags, the old position now "packaged as a five-page market alert issued 17 Nov 2022 off the FTX collapse." New hook, same argument.

Genuinely new information arrives as event triggers, not thesis revisions. November 20, 2020 brings investment demand "more than double what it was last year," the contested election, the January Senate runoff, and a real shift in CPM's own activity: "we're actually talking to various companies about that right now" on producer hedging. February 2022 adds named option structures — an October 2022 1750 put at $58.30, a 1650 put funded by a 1900–2000 call spread for $3.60 net — alongside a stance flip: "today we issued new trade recommendations on gold and silver saying stay long because we do think that the prices have further to…," ending a stretch where "we've had a lot of stand asides." Then April 2022's tout pricing ($31–33 asked, $29 accessed), January 2023's disclosure that he "may be one of the largest silver stackers in the world," July 2024's spike ("it spiked higher on uh Thursday to about $2,425") and the intraday flip — "so now we have issued a new Ultra shortterm gold trade recommendation uh saying go long" — November 2024's handoff ("those risks and uncertainties disappeared with the election… a whole new set of risks and uncertainties have appeared"), April 2025's mea culpa ("I had said $1,200 to 3500. I had meant to say $2,600 to 3500"), January 2026's broadening of momentum flows into copper and aluminum ("This is not a silver event. This is a global event"), and February 2026's January ETF holdings data with Lunar New Year demand holding up.

The tell is what "changed" means in Christian's mouth: a trade, a price, or a news hook — never the thesis. The only regime-level change he declares is regulatory and about crypto, not metals: "central banks have taken a hands-off approach toward cryptocurrencies for most of the period since 2009. That's starting to change…", alongside governments gaining "the ability to come in and reverse transfers." The nearest thing to a metals-demand revision is February 2022's re-anchoring — "investors have backed away from their fear of recession," inflation down seven months, demand falling from 40m oz in 2020 to 26–27m oz in 2021. On cadence: the documented reuse is roughly monthly, with the deep-reads themselves flagging "nothing" new at least eight times — and since the deep-reads cover only about two dozen of the 161 archive items, with long unexamined stretches (February to November 2021; August 2023 to July 2024), the true recycling rate is almost certainly higher than the record shows.

study/cpm-group/topic/debunking-precious.text:
This is Jeffrey Christian and CPM Group's five-year one-front war — 92 items running from [Gold: Myth vs Reality](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtuyP7NiPsg) on July 17, 2020 through late 2025 — and the recycling starts almost immediately. The January 2021 WallStreetBets silver squeeze turns a modest fact-checking sideline into a production line: [Silver, Gamestop, and WallStreet Bets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N54_h29SeUY) on January 29, [conspiracy and manipulation rebuttals](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9rVxB_tvGuM) on February 5, a [Silver Fact and Fantasy webinar](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OrzpZKm-oGc) on March 4, buying guidance on April 23, and [The Company You Keep – An Open Letter to Silver Investors](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7K3yzsxzlaI) on April 27 — posted twice, same day, the first hint that this archive recycles itself literally, not just thematically. The bluntest tell of all: [Conspiracy Theories Are A Distraction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lM-Wl8tCaJg), posted May 5, 2021, is a 2008 artifact dusted off because the arguments it rebuts never died.

What repeats is the entire slate, on a roughly annual loop. Manipulation claims get [Who's Been Fooling Whom](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nnX-4J3WOlk) on August 17, 2021 (also double-posted). The silver fact-vs-fantasy format gets a literal sequel, [Silver Facts and Fantasies II](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w00fMT8MVHg) on June 17, 2022 — the existence of a sequel is the tell. Inflation-versus-gold runs [October 15, 2021](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5o9BHtiXJ_M) and [February 11, 2022](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WVfJrXAS2sU); hyperbole warnings arrive via [Fatal Market Hyperbole](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sOZzfktO8ko) on May 6, 2022 (doubled); fear-mongering via [Ending Irrational Fears](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5HnOqjjws00) on August 5, 2022 (also doubled); inventory mythology via [Low Silver Inventories Do Not Cause High Silver Prices](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=71QcOEr8EaE) on November 4, 2022, with [3 Debunked Myths](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p1r-5R4CpXU) as the year-end summary. The cadence: a dense April–August 2021 cluster, a steadier 2022 drumbeat against the same claims, same-day duplicates scattered throughout, and [Overcome Misinformation and Fear](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dwkmQyCIdyQ) on December 7, 2021 as the thesis statement of the whole project.

The moments Christian says something HAS changed are mostly about data or audience, not the myths themselves. In the August 2020 deep-read, updated real-vs-nominal gold charts since 1700 and 1968 prompt him to note "the gold price has probably passed that 800 on a real basis has definitely passed 1680 or 1640" — gold topping its 2011–2012 real peak. December 21, 2021 is his optimistic entry: "the dollar and other currencies were not recalled there wasn't a great reset," and, better, "some investors have actually begun gone to learn to tune those folks out," now shopping for fair prices. November 18, 2022 pivots to FTX with fresh statistics — crypto scam losses up sixty-fold from 2018 to 2021, over $3 billion stolen in the first nine months of 2022, down 65% versus 2021, bitcoin off its November 2021 peak — new evidence, same sermon. Then comes the most honest entry in the corpus: January 10, 2023, with new material logged as "nothing." And on January 9, 2024 he delivers the counter-declaration, Hannah Arendt's *Lying in Politics* in hand: "we have thought misinformation dishonesty misrepresentation in the markets really since the late 1970s," and, of an earlier episode, "that was 1998 2001 we're in 2024 and as Billy Holiday would say it still is true." That is the one moment he explicitly says nothing has changed in a quarter-century.

Genuinely new information enters only via news hooks, and he flags each one as a fresh wave of an old problem. February 28, 2024: "we have another round of bad information flooding the silver market" — silver-in-missiles claims, solar demand, dollar-collapse price spikes, "Little Mikey Maloney was was was talking about silver going to $5,000" — with a callback to the WallStreetSilver crowd that polluted the discourse back in 2021. The same session surfaces something genuinely new: an anonymous company that has sat on known-wrong central bank gold and refining data since 1990, which "has looked into correcting it but... unwilling to actually say you know what we have been wrong." April 9, 2024 brings gold promoters "making a big deal out of this statement" by Powell on 60 Minutes. March 11, 2025 deploys record COMEX gold inventories — surpassing the 2020–21 record of roughly 39.3 million ounces — against viral "inventories falling" claims, and spots a truly new vector: "and then there's the AI." By September 30, 2025 he is still pledging a Friday video on the same trio — central banks and gold, silver fabrication demand, auto demand — which tells you the queue of myths never empties. The shape of it: annual waves (2021's squeeze, late 2022's FTX, 2024's Powell and solar hype, 2025's COMEX data and AI), with the myths frozen in place and only the wrappers changing.

study/cpm-group/topic/market-structure-m.text:
The Jeffrey Christian / CPM Group archive on silver market structure runs from September 11, 2020 — an ETF-holdings video that opens the whole thread [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X7l3Jq4O5uw](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X7l3Jq4O5uw) — into 2026, and it is unusually candid about its own recycling: several entries are flagged outright as "nothing — restatement of CPM's standing multi-year structural theme," and one, from July 30, 2021, records simply "nothing." The genuinely new material arrives in bursts. The first burst is late 2020: by November 20 Christian is walking through December-to-February roll arithmetic (~44M oz of December open interest, roughly 22M rolled, 22M left), and reporting live change — "about half of that has rolled into the February contract," the August-spike support has vanished ("that price support disappeared and the price came down $217"), and "we've seen investors selling some of their gold ETFs over the last few days."

The WallStreetBets squeeze then forces the densest cluster in the corpus — January 29, February 3 (twice), February 5 — and crystallizes the argument Christian will repeat for the next five years [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N54_h29SeUY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N54_h29SeUY), [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=stQWKxqKfZc](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=stQWKxqKfZc). February 12 contains both modes at once: one entry a pure restatement, another genuinely new — the mechanism by which pandemic-era investor selling backed metal onto dealer balance sheets ("you've seen record levels of inventories in new york in london") and banks "selling that some of that metal because they wanted to reduce their exposure and buying etf shares." Hard new data follows on April 9, when fresh LBMA figures show London silver stocks "now at a record 1.25 billion ounces," surpassing the Q1 2020 peak [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tn8tkU67WHE](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tn8tkU67WHE). June 2 brings the US Mint episode and one of his rare explicit redefinitions: "so today they issued a clarification... it's not that there's a shortage of silver it's a shortage of blanks" [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gVEVhwK4UOc](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gVEVhwK4UOc) — alongside Comex registered stocks back to September 2020 levels, "most of the withdrawals have been by financial institutions," and "that arbitrage opportunity is gone." By December 21 he delivers a year-end verdict: "silver prices didn't rise to 100 or triple digits or anything else there was no squeeze on comex," even as COMEX inventories sat at or near record levels.

2022 contributes two durable rhetorical tools. On April 19, with 333M oz of May open interest against 335M oz of COMEX inventory (249M eligible, 86M registered), he reaches for the 2011 case study and declares "2022 is not 2011. it's a radically different situation" — "it's the stuff of myths" — with no replay of the 2011 spike expected. On July 15 he refreshes his decades-old short-position dataset to the present and widens it to copper, gold, platinum and palladium, with a telling aside about the driver: "we've done this data for decades uh and we updated it recently simply because people were talking about it" [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O76GMFE5gMY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O76GMFE5gMY). The deep-read record then thins through 2023 — though the archive titles show the same machinery grinding ("Manipulating Silver Investors: The JP Morgan Verdict, Spoofing" that August, "Low Silver Inventories Do Not Cause High Silver Prices" in November, "Silver Deficits Don't Exist And Other Silver Myths" in August 2023) — before resuming as numbers-only updates: the July 2024 drawdown (registered stocks from 70.6M oz to 29M as July-contract open interest collapsed from 733M oz, delivered metal that "stayed in the depositories so far") and a November 2024 open-interest price read.

The 2025–26 stretch exposes the recycling mechanism with the label on. May 27, 2025 is flagged for naming "The reduction in liquidity and major market making capacity in the silver market" and "The increased availability of inaccurate and misleading information, statistics, and commentary" — but that liquidity point is itself a four-year-old restatement of what he said in February 2021, when closing bullion desks "reduced the liquidity in these markets both in terms of depth and breadth." The genuinely new entries are easier to count: September 30, 2025 debunks the "6% silver lease rate" chatter ("people were talking about a 6% lease rate but they weren't saying who that lease rate was to or what the maturity rate was") and adds near-record bullion-bank profits as an incentive argument against suppression; November 14 brings October London flows ("London unallocated silver inventories have risen sharply" — 53.8M oz added from New York and Shanghai imports, 19.9M oz of ETF metal liquidated); January 6, 2026 updates COMEX to "about 449 million ounces registered and eligible," down from 530M in September, while stressing "the deliveries, deliveries are in line with what they have been over the last many years" and stocks remain roughly four times pre-2017 levels; February 20 adds Shanghai futures data, with volume surging while "the open interest actually hasn't increased and if anything it's actually trended down."

The cadence, then, is a dense crisis cluster (January–February 2021), then monthly-to-quarterly data-refresh videos in which the argument never changes and only the numerators do, punctuated by new arguments maybe once or twice a year: the bank-inventory mechanism (February 2021), the 2011 case study (April 2022), the widened short dataset (July 2022), lease rates and bank profits (September 2025), Shanghai (February 2026). Tellingly, virtually every moment Christian says something "has changed" refers to market data — a price, an inventory level, a roll, a flow — never to his thesis. The one true novelty arrives at the end, on August 28, 2026, when he describes a phenomenon the digest marks as entirely his first: "some investors selling smaller physical quantities are being offered discounted prices to spot" even as prices rise. After six years of arguing that the physical market behaves normally and only the narrative around it is distorted, the first crack he records is in the physical market itself.

study/cpm-group/topic/economy-recession-.text:
The template barely moves across six years. Nearly every episode couples a macro headline to the metals — [Global GDP Trends; Gold and Silver Buy Signals](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_Qta2pUGmTc) (October 22, 2021), [Inverted Yield Curve, Recession, and What It Means For Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-LVZJXDP3Wc) (April 1, 2022), [How Inflation, Interest Rates and Recession May Affect Gold and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=10zL22_Y39s) (June 24, 2022) — and the recession stays permanently "coming": flagged via the yield curve in April 2022, declared outright in [A Recession Is Coming - This Is Why](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dvWvJK5b8Kw) on October 28, 2022 — a title the archive lists three times that day — and still hypothetical as [The Next Recession?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QyOCdpZkhtU) by March 14, 2023. Even metaphors recycle verbatim: investors [Hold Their Breath](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xAqv33uwyUg) on May 3, 2022, and markets do the same thirteen months later on [May 23, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XhH4vjG29Ao). The titling runs hotter than the stance — by the author's own later account, the internal call was 2024–25 all along, not the imminent event the October 2022 title implies.

Genuinely new material enters in narrow injections. The record itself starts sparse — a lone [oil-market explainer](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6FepdXXoaNs) from August 13, 2015, then nothing until [Economics 101 vs Commodities Super Cycle](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bp4IOm8hPks) in February 2021 — and the deep-reads flag only three episodes as non-recurring. May 19, 2020 rode reopening optimism into "stronger prices in equities oil and most commodities"; November 9, 2021 was a supply-chain-and-chips explainer "to clear up observer confusion." November 20, 2020 delivers the sharpest declared change, quoted at the moment it landed: "this morning you had the treasury say that it wanted $455 billion do back from the FED," alongside vaccine-timeline skepticism and the warning that "we're moving toward shutdowns in those two major economic engines of the world." Other novelties arrive as bolt-on specials — [European Natural Gas](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OrJeb7JfHxY) (October 18, 2022), [The Energy Transition Will Be Delayed](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AOiIWRI6FJ4) (May 26, 2023) — or as the July 15, 2022 brief [update](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O76GMFE5gMY) the notes say was made "only because audience members asked."

The cadence is data-reactive to the point of whiplash: [Economic Trends Likely To Push Gold and Silver Higher](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ICt3JcGEvkg) on November 16, 2021 becomes [Gold and Silver Plunge As New Economic Realities Set In](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WmMk8JglQo8) seven days later. The declared changes cluster where prints forced them. On June 30, 2023, the author quotes his own record — "we thought we've been saying for some time that we thought a recession might come in 2024 2025. so far we've been right" — while conceding "the economy has been stronger than a lot of mainstream economists including those at the Federal Reserve Bank have been thinking," pinned to that week's Fed review of ~23 big banks and ~2 percent Q1 GDP. Then comes purest recycling: May 31, 2024 logs "nothing" new, restating that "growth remains healthy and inflation rates are slowly declining." November 22, 2024 turns the call into an all-weather fork — a "deeper recession than has been expected" arriving sooner, or policy that "could protract the current expansion." July 8, 2025 adds a new villain: "the big beautiful bill, a budget bill is going to blow up the deficit," "adding anywhere from three to five trillion dollars to an already bloated deficit spending over the next five to 10 years," with the chief of staff's 3-percent growth claim waved off as Reagan-style voodoo economics.

The 2026 episodes run the same machine on fresh data: February 20 — "The GDP for the fourth quarter was lower than had been expected," PCE "remains high or just below 3%"; August 28 — "that 1.5% is down from 2.1%," "a sharp decrease in the consumer spending," job creation "declining really since 2023 2022 and it's gotten down to very low levels." At that point the standing call is finally being serviced by the data rather than waiting on it. Roughly three-quarters of the sampled episodes are flagged recurring; new facts arrive at annual or event-driven intervals; and between injections the framework simply restates itself — growth, inflation, sentiment, gold, silver — with the author meanwhile policing "charlatans" and "The Truth About the Economy" ([June 2, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GG2yfKiZPzc)) while his own archive triple-lists identical titles. The record is honest about uncertainty; it is just honest about the same uncertainty, repeatedly.

study/cpm-group/topic/geopolitics-politi.text:
Elections are the metronome of this file. The 2016 vote gets a single entry — posted twice on the same day in June of that year ([The US Election 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1GMvuyc5gVQ)) — but by 2020 the template has become a serial: a pre-election gold-and-silver read on October 9 ([CPM Group - Gold and Silver heading into the US Elections](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=375ocZPpiqI)), an aftermath-framing piece on October 23 ([CPM Group - Gold, Silver, The Election and its Aftermath](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yCcUJABE6F8)), a "how high can gold go" follow-up on November 6 ([CPM Group - How High Can Gold Go After the US Election?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nlSXt8Fkww0)), and a December detour into the 1933 gold lessons ([CPM Group - Politics and Gold, The Lessons of 1933](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PVznAwB10mQ)). The counterintuitive payoff lands January 8, 2021: gold *fell* as DC burned ([Gold Fell As DC Burned](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gN-aOb4Iqag)). Between cycles, the political-risk frame hardens rather than resets — in December 2021 he declares "we have a very significant constitutional crisis in the united states" and warns "the next inauguration is setting itself up to be... really scary." The genuinely new material there is thin; what's new is the escalation, not the argument.

The densest recycling engine, though, is Russia-and-gold. It ignites February 18, 2022 with [The Finance of War: Russia, Gold, and Silver](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZdP2OsZ8eIo) (duplicated that day), runs through [The Rise Of Gold](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jk5ZPSXui3Y), the invasion-reaction piece of February 25 (also duplicated: [War: Gold and Silver React As Russia Invades Ukraine](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cu5lREgEB5Q)), then near-weekly through spring — [March 8's rally-as-Russia-looks-for-buyers](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=20QsWnUrRD0), [March 18's why-prices-aren't-reacting piece](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=77RCqH8YI64), [April 4 on Russian gold and the ruble](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7q88UbXPoC0) — until June's "[Has Russia Just Sold Its Gold?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4LQa4a0hNgM)". The one injection of genuinely new analysis in that window comes March 11: the war as a supply shock layered onto already-tight fundamentals, where he notes "we're coming out of a period of depressed prices with the economic lockdown" ([Commodities After Russia](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JutgSZHugvQ)). After that the thread goes evergreen — reprised as [Russia's Gold — Why Now?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=slXsrJgOrw0) in March 2023, [as Russia faces unrest](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jOMCS0SJHW4) that June, and again in January 2025, when the new twist is that "Russia's Central Bank has been using its gold reserves to support the war effort" and household scrap-selling is masking the aggregate data. The recycling even reaches the archive layer itself: the November 1, 2022 "[Big Political Issues](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iK5iW6FRyng)" video appears three times on one day.

The October 4, 2024 entry is a microcosm of the whole file's method. It carries genuinely new event coverage (Iran's direct missile attack on Israel), a new analytical claim — "oil is a less useful political tool now than it used to be," with "the Russian invasion of Ukraine [having] further reduced the usefulness of oil as a political weapon" — plus a recycled riff on discourse decay ("I first noticed in 2000 that people didn't want to talk about politics to each other"), and one tracked thread that logs literally *nothing* new. A pure rerun. The election template then reruns on schedule: by July 2024 both major-party candidates are deemed bad and election risk is "one of the major factors driving... prices sharply higher in the next five months," before the November 22 post-election read admits the pre-election hedge — "it was too early to really say." From there the cadence accelerates into something near-monthly: March 2025 forces entirely new evidence onto the stage (the digest flags "everything" as new — first-ever use of the 2018 tariff history); April brings the realignment scenario upgraded by a magazine cover — "maybe it wasn't all that outrageous to think..." — then May's volatility spike, and November's twist that "the reopening of the government has brought with it a number of uncertainties economically," uncertainty arriving *after* resolution rather than before.

The loop closes in classic self-citing fashion: January 6, 2026 recycles the 2025 political-risk forecast as evidence for itself — "that has in fact been the case over the course of 2025" — before February 20 delivers the file's newest event, that "the Supreme Court ruled that the Trump tariffs were invalid, unconstitutional." The cadence pattern is clear: bursts every election and war, weekly recurrence within each burst, and between bursts the Russia-gold and oil-as-weapon threads (the latter dating back to an August 2015 oil primer, [What You Need To Know About The Oil Market](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6FepdXXoaNs), with a 2020 price-war truce update) keep the topic warm. The stray outlier — a June 2023 Independence Day segment on Samuel Adams — apart, the format is commentary-as-rerun: a stable analytical frame, a fresh news hook, and a running self-audit of which predictions landed.

study/cpm-group/topic/metals-supply-inve.text:
The spine of this archive is a spring ritual: CPM Group's silver yearbook and forecast cycle, running [April 2019](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-jGHFUKTio), [April 2020](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tc3mkX101uc), the [May 2022 forecast](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YbpwAZcr6Pw), and the [May 2023 outlook](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UQYhSIcpCq4) — and, per the deep reads, the same ritual was already recurring in April 2015. Everything between launches restates one standing thesis: aboveground silver stocks are enormous, inventories are ample, and scarcity doesn't drive price. That argument is repriced, never revised — "Ample Supplies If You Know How To Look" in [May 2022](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jDwWMa22XcQ), "Inventories Not A Problem" by [June 2022](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h0v-RpGUQTY), "Low Silver Inventories Do Not Cause High Silver Prices" in [November](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=71QcOEr8EaE), "Plenty Of Available Metal" in [December](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CdXwDvPhsaI), then "How Much Silver Is Really Available" in [September 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IPMS5mYzvXE) followed four days later by "Record Prices and Availability" [again](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZtaqCjAx4E4). The reuse is even mechanical: the same URLs appear twice in the archive for identical dates — jewelry demand twice on [December 3, 2021](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wnvy8UElMW4), "Silver Fundamentals" twice on [November 8, 2022](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x8fZurPafMY), "Who Owns Hundreds Of Millions Of Ounces" twice on [January 17, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wEfAOXG0gcY).

The genuinely new data is thin and datable. The spring 2021 yearbook prep is one such moment: "we're in the process of producing our silver yearbook for this year and we're in the process of updating that data," culminating in a newly quantified fungible stock — "about 3.5 to 4.6 billion of that is in bullion and coin form." The same session recycles provenance lore as a credential: "when we walked away from the silver institute in 1994 after we created the world silver survey." That's new number, old story.

The only stretch where the underlying data visibly moves is late 2021, in the [November 9 inventory discussion](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7FnCTOBpyhA), which adds Shanghai alongside London and New York. Even here the "changes" are levels, not thesis: "they've come off a little bit in october uh but they're still at record highs," and COMEX registered gold at "not only record highs but record highs by a multiple of what they were in the past," while "you've seen a little bit of a reduction in the inventories in london over the last couple months." Ample inventory becomes record inventory without the argument budging — which is either flexibility or unfalsifiability, depending on your read.

January 2023 shows what "changed" mostly means in this corpus: the calendar. "we're seeing gold and silver prices strong in the first week of so of 2023," "Lunar New Year this year is I believe January 22nd," and "silver has come back off a bit and it's around 23 70s" — price ticks and holiday timing, dressed as updates. Tellingly, the deep read of May 19, 2023 — days after the [annual outlook](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UQYhSIcpCq4) — records new information as literally "nothing." Peak recycling season, right on the yearbook cadence.

The few real argumentative additions cluster late: China's reserves and mine supply enter on [January 27, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BNUrHI4gHNY), solar demand as a depletion question arrives [March 17, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F673kCAYyZo), and by [October 31, 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z9L6KgzSEqQ) the framing has stretched to "Manipulation, Allocations, and Militarization." By the May 2025 refresh, the identical ample-supply template has acquired an opponent — it now exists explicitly to rebut deficit claims with "refreshed" London and COMEX figures. The cadence, then: annual spring spine, near-continual restatement in between, duplicated uploads, and a thesis that has not flipped once since at least 2015 — only its calendar, its inventory levels, and its adversaries change.

study/cpm-group/topic/cpm-group-research.text:
The spine of this archive is a machine built to repeat itself. CPM Group's public record runs on an annual yearbook cycle — gold in early spring, silver in late spring, platinum group metals by mid-year — and the organization is unusually candid that repetition is the point. At the April 1, 2015 Gold Yearbook launch, Jeffrey Christian noted "we've hosted this for several years" and that CPM has "change[d] the format over the years to modify and meet the needs of our clients" ([2015 launch panel](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c48O8Oq1920)). The genuinely new material that day was delivery, not analysis: live streaming via Bloomberg LiveGo with archive access promised afterward. The 2017 and 2019 gold launches ([2017](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hO7redj87Uw), [2019](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QgF10YLHwM0)) repeat the ritual, with 2019 adding the silver ([April 23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-jGHFUKTio)) and PGM ([July 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lMwjUDAUAR8)) editions into a full three-metal rotation. Notably, 2016 and 2018 are simply absent from the archive — the cadence looks continuous in the narration but the record itself is patchy before 2020.

The 2020 pandemic year compressed and accelerated everything. The gold, silver, and PGM yearbooks all launched as webinars within three months ([March 24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OWNX0_Q6H80), [April 28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tc3mkX101uc), [June 30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dYlXqaZ6hds)), with the PGM event flagged weeks in advance: "our next event will be a webinar launching our platinum group metals to your book that will be June 30th." From there the output cadence shifts from annual to near-monthly, and the recycling becomes explicit. A June 2023 video reuses the same chart with the admission that "this is a chart that we use we publish this then we update it every month in our precious metals advisory," while declaring "continuing the theme that I've had in the last few videos probabilities are very important." Even the metadata recycles: the August 18, 2020 "Introduction To CPM Group" appears twice in the archive on the same day, as do the 2021 gold preview, the 2021 silver launch, and the March 2022 investing-approach video.

Genuinely new information enters in bursts tied to market stress. The first is the 2021 silver squeeze: a March 3 video defending CPM's record on manipulation research ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bxcPKsYf25o)), a March 4 "Silver Fact and Fantasy" webinar ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OrzpZKm-oGc)), and a May 26 open forum ([link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O1-rPAF-usQ)) — the start of a counter-offensive franchise that returns as sequels in 2022 ([June 17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w00fMT8MVHg)), January 2023 (["Let Silver Facts Dispel Your Silver Theories"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zuiJqCBlKC8)), and March 2023 ([the 2023 edition](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-IUr4LYXzxk)). Within that same year comes the archive's rarest kind of moment: on July 30, 2021, Christian publicly corrected "a misstatement uh that i made 10 years ago in a debate in 2011." That is real change, self-declared, a decade in arrears. May 2022 brought another explicit reversal, this time editorial: "we tend to assume people are more interested in gold and silver than platinum and planium," he conceded, "that's probably a bad assumption because we have a lot of commercial clients and contacts around the world who tell us that they…" — the video's gold-and-silver bias was changing because the audience had.

The fall of 2023 is the flattest stretch in the deep-read record — three separate entries flagged "nothing" new, including two on the same day (September 29) — before the cadence resets with the November announcement of a December 6 client Q&A forum. Then January 9, 2024 is the densest new-information day in the file. Christian frames a fresh slate: "it's going to be important as we discuss some of the things that we need to discuss this year." He discloses previously unrecorded history — "we actually were talking with the Chinese government the Chinese gold Association and other groups several years ago" about a global refining census, which died because "on a global basis there wasn't insufficient interest in doing this" — and reaches back to gold trading below $300 from "1998 into 2002" when miners were "borrowing money in order to stay afloat." February 2024 adds more archaeology: the annual online seminar, launched when PDAC was cancelled — "we were interrupted in 2021," then "pdac resumed its conferences we said well we'll go back to the silver reception" — drew 450-plus registrants and 140-plus questions, with the Silver Institute joining as sponsor; Christian also recaps taking over J. Aron's research department in 1980 and the lineage through Handy & Harmon, which ended its report "after CPM group hit spun off the report," and Consolidated Goldfields, broken up after a takeover by "someone named Hansen in London."

The verdict on cadence: roughly two-thirds of this archive is scheduled repetition — annual yearbooks, monthly advisories, sequenced myth-busting — and the deep-read confirms it, with the author openly refreshing the same chart and themes. What's new tends to arrive either defensively (the manipulation rebuttals of 2021–2023) or as archival disclosure (the 2011 correction, the failed China census), and once new, it too gets recycled into the rotation. By August 23, 2024, the loop closes on itself: "I'm going to continue with uh program I started on Tuesday."

study/cpm-group/topic/platinum-battery-m.text:
CPM Group's platinum-and-battery-metals coverage runs off a calendar more than a news feed. A PGM yearbook or mid-year market update lands every early summer — July 9, 2019 ([CPM PGM Yearbook 2019 Release Event](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lMwjUDAUAR8)), June 30, 2020 ([CPM Group's 2020 Platinum Group Metals PGM Market Update and Yearbook…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dYlXqaZ6hds)), July 13, 2021 ([CPM Group's 2021 Platinum Group Metals Market Update](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ehnP-WKg6N4)), July 27, 2022 ([CPM Group's 2022 Platinum Group Metals Market Outlook](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AkmHW6aHP8E)), the July 25, 2023 virtual seminar ([The 2023 Platinum Group Metals Virtual Seminar](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7JxQ7KY-HM4)), and July 17, 2024 ([2024 Platinum Group Metals Market Outlook](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=STXWslwykhg)) — bracketed by a January 2022 price forecast ([2022 Platinum Group Metals Price Forecast - Jeffrey Christian](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HJUEmBg027g)) and fall outlooks in October 2021 ([CPM Outlook for Gold, Copper, Energy Metals, and Electric Vehicles](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cQSUlmpzA8E)) and October 2022 ([Market Alert: The Energy Transition and Platinum Group Metals](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sZb5sH7W1sw)). The literal reuse is baked into the record itself: nine entries in the listing are same-day duplicate uploads. If nothing shocks the tape, you get a summer update, a winter forecast, and a fall alert, with the substance largely carried forward.

Genuinely new information arrives in bursts, and the first real one is March 11, 2022 ([Commodities After Russia: Long-term Outlooks for Gold, Silver, Nickel…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JutgSZHugvQ)): nickel spiking to roughly $100,000 per metric ton, the London Metal Exchange suspending nickel trading, and the line that "nickel has entered the [rarefied] club of being a precious metal." Alongside the shock came a new structural argument — stainless steel demand not just recovering but "rising much more sharply," plus investment demand "predicated on the idea that the world was going to move very quickly toward electric vehicles." That EV-investment-demand frame is the piece that gets recycled hardest; two years later it resurfaces attached to platinum and palladium.

The author does flag his own turning points, and one of the cleanest is May 31, 2022 — a video absent from the archive listing provided — where the prior bearish platinum call is declared realized ("our expectation had been that platinum prices would come down… to about where they are now") and a fresh bullish recovery call is opened on palladium at the lows. Then comes the purest specimen of the format: the April 7, 2023 manganese update ([High Purity Manganese Market Update - March 2023](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VlPlnNPC7Hk)), framed as a ~9-month follow-up to the June 23, 2022 introduction ([Introduction to High Purity Manganese](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rbB9fZoHojI)). In the same video the author says "a lot of things have changed since we last spoke" and, almost in the next breath, "a lot of things has not changed and the overall picture is still very much the same." The genuinely new material is narrow but real: "battery chemistries continue to evolve and a new subspecies appear all the time," with NMC 451 and NMC 90/5/5 cited as arrivals, and HLM entering the vocabulary via Umicore's February 2023 industrialization push. Everything else — including a fresh UK consultancy infographic omitting manganese — is a new prop for the same standing complaint.

The titles alone show the standing argument drifting: the energy transition goes from demand tailwind in October 2021 and 2022 to an explicit headwind with [The Energy Transition Will Be Delayed](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AOiIWRI6FJ4) on May 26, 2023, while platinum-as-bargain is a refrain — [Platinum Vs Palladium: Analysis, Projections, and Opportunities](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g1RIFSJl9dk) in May 2023, then [A Platinum Opportunity: Analysis and Forecast](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ft7aOru4DLE) that September. The clearest "this has changed" moment, though, comes after the documented record thins post-July 2024. On September 30, 2025: "platinum has spiked up over 1,600 for the first time since... probably 2013," a spike underway "since June" that "is continuing," judged overbought and partly credited to lower South African production. By November 14, 2025 the framing cools: "As with gold and silver, they're consolidating, they're bouncing around trying to figure out what exactly the state of the econom[y]…" And on January 6, 2026 the change is quantitative — "palladium prices more than double" during 2025, alongside record platinum — with the rallies attributed to investment demand rather than fundamentals. So the cadence reads: calendrical reuse punctuated by shock-driven novelty (March 2022), terminology churn (April 2023), and, at last, a price-regime break in late 2025 that the format was built to annotate.

study/cpm-group/topic/us-dollar-federal-.text:
The recycling spine of this corpus is a single, stubborn thesis: the dollar is not collapsing, and the people saying otherwise are selling something. It is there at the origin — a June 9, 2016 video, "How Strong is the US Dollar 4," uploaded twice the same day ([1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QSBDIUoKWV0)) — and it resurfaces intact on July 30, 2021, when Jeffrey Christian of CPM Group frames the collapse story as pure marketing: "people are trying to drive investors into gold by telling them that the dollar is collapsing and the financial system is crumbling" ([Which Falls First - Gold, Silver, or the Dollars?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kBbCcNzS9mE)). That session is logged as containing "nothing" new — pure reprise. The duplication is a cadence signature: five titles appear twice on their own upload dates ("Nostalgia For A Gold Standard That Never Was" on August 27, 2021 ([gTCGEdqDwWk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gTCGEdqDwWk)), "What The Rising Dollar Means For Gold" on October 7, 2022 ([TBXzM5GSB_w](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TBXzM5GSB_w)), "Vladimir Putin's Golden Pipedream" on July 11, 2023 ([m2gPR0OSap8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m2gPR0OSap8)), and the China/Japan commentary on November 28, 2023 ([KD0RCTD9zDI](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KD0RCTD9zDI))), so the archive inflates without new substance.

The 2020–2021 run is the dense stretch. The 2020 titles themselves state the co-rise thesis — "Gold Will Stay Strong and The Dollar Will Too" ([mClCYeoAw6s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mClCYeoAw6s)), "Gold and the Dollar Can Rise Together" ([EdlOqZEF_xA](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EdlOqZEF_xA)) — and by June–July 2021 the output is near-monthly: central bank practices and US debt ([fimg7ZB8wGA](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fimg7ZB8wGA)), "Tired Gold and Silver Bulls and Treasury Truths" ([KMfFk1wajtQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KMfFk1wajtQ)), the debt ceiling ([cWcWZxI5WEY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cWcWZxI5WEY)). A second recycling loop runs alongside: gold-standard debunking, from "Nostalgia For A Gold Standard That Never Was" to the constitutional argument ([NDU7yndPMC0](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NDU7yndPMC0)) to, two years later, "Why The Gold Standard Is A Terrible Idea And Fednow Is The Future" ([Y6LEB_R7gA0](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y6LEB_R7gA0)). Genuinely new material enters sparingly — most notably on December 21, 2021, when the 1909 Tsarist five-ruble gold-backed note appears as fresh evidence that gold backing does not make a currency safe. Meanwhile the dollar's actual strength keeps intruding on the doom narrative: Turkey fleeing the lira *into* dollars ([9jlXuHXmc7E](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9jlXuHXmc7E)), gold, silver and equities all falling as the dollar rises ([qQsH2ZNj6CM](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qQsH2ZNj6CM)).

October 7, 2022 is the corpus's biggest single injection of new numbers and new arguments. Updated data: the dollar "has been rising — it's actually been rising since 2011," up 31% over that span and more than 10% in the prior eighteen to twenty months, with central banks now "selling dollars, buying their own currencies" ([TBXzM5GSB_w](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TBXzM5GSB_w)). Two genuinely new arguments arrive the same day: that a 1985-style Plaza Accord is impossible because "you can't make an argument that the US government wants to see a weaker dollar" — government preferences have flipped since 1985 — and the historical arc from Nixon closing the gold window through the dirty float to the doctrine that central banks "cannot reverse trends but we can accelerate trends that exist." By January 10, 2023 the declared change is merely a retraced chart: "it's gotten all the way back to where it was say about four months ago" — elevated still.

The 2023 debt-ceiling episode is the one moment market expectations themselves change: "it's become clearer, I think, across financial markets that the US government is unlikely to default," gold and silver "come off sharply," and "now that it looks like that silly little issue is going to be resolved" the risk premium drains — though Christian adds a new credibility twist: "there has been damage done to the credibility of the US Treasury just by virtue of the stupidity of the impasse" ([rc4ygr_fBe0](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rc4ygr_fBe0)). The BRICS loop opens with "Putin's Golden Pipedream" ([m2gPR0OSap8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m2gPR0OSap8)) and updates on August 18, 2023 — "Putin isn't even going to attend; he's afraid that he might be arrested for war crimes if he shows up" — while conceding "a continuation in an acceleration of decades-long pattern of trying to use currencies other than the US dollar," with roughly 90% of trade still dollar-settled. April 9, 2024 is the densest data drop: Powell's February 4 "60 Minutes" warning ("they are unsustainable") set against Greenspan's identical 1987 warning — "the debt and deficits were unsustainable in 1987 at a fraction of what they are now: $1.3 trillion deficit, $34 trillion debt" — Congress having "basically haven't done anything"; the 2010–12 "Five Easy Pieces" report upgraded to "Seven Easy Pieces" in late 2023; and record offshore Treasury holdings of $8 trillion, up 10.5%, with "investors shifting their assets… into treasuries" — the standing rebuttal to de-dollarization. August 2024 refines the framing: gold has "lost that unit of account value" and no longer settles trade, but "is still a store of value, it's a reserve asset."

From 2025 the cadence thins to quarterly updates bolted onto the same spine. January 21, 2025: the dollar rising "contrary to de-dollarization narratives," with central banks "using their dollars to help stimulate their domestic economies" from the 58–60% of FX reserves they hold. April 22, 2025: "it was off 6% from the end of 2024, three and a half months ago," yet "the March average was the highest dollar exchange rate since 2002… so yes, the dollar has fallen, but it is still very high" — plus a rare self-audit, "it's not the correlation from 1868 to 2024. It's a correlation from 1968 to 2024." July 8, 2025 recycles the BRICS summit with only a new agenda and odds assessment; August 19, 2025 delivers the corpus's one wholly new topic — a viewer question answered with the conclusion that no definitive debt threshold exists — along with updated figures: debt growth "accelerated again after the financial crisis in 2007 to 2011 and… accelerated even further since 2020, 2021," with debt-to-GDP "at the highest level it's been at really since 1947." The August 28, 2026 session is flagged as containing nothing new at all: "the Congress has almost abrogated all of its responsibilities here" amid "out-of-control deficit spending and behavior on the part of the administration and the Congress" — lines that could have aired in 2024. That is the shape of the reuse: the thesis never turns; what changes, by his own account, is the data — dollar levels, debt totals — and the crisis du jour hung on it.
